subject: MA MPJE original 4-choice legal verification ledger
disclaimers: Each entry contains an original question and four as-authored answer rationales. PENDING items have NOT been independently checked even if their author citations exist.
SOURCE_CORROBORATED reflects an AI cross-check against official published law/policy, not independent qualified legal-professional approval.
WITH_CAVEAT and HOLD are not fully released; full normative USP text remains inaccessible where stated. No original question files or learning history are modified.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist earned a PharmD in 2022 and has practiced as a licensed pharmacist for four years. The pharmacist holds an unrestricted Massachusetts license, maintains the required liability insurance, and wishes to enter a FIRST CDTM agreement in November 2026. The Board has not determined that any education or residency is equivalent to five years of experience. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.option_text: The pharmacist qualifies because a PharmD automatically replaces the experience requirement.
options.original_rationale: The PharmD exception in 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) applies only when the pharmacist entered a CDTM agreement on or before June 30, 2017.

options.option_text: The pharmacist qualifies once the supervising physician signs the agreement.
options.original_rationale: Physician agreement and other CDTM conditions cannot replace the pharmacist's separate statutory qualification.

options.option_text: The pharmacist does not yet qualify absent five years of licensed experience or a recognized exception.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) requires five years of licensed experience unless a precisely defined historic PharmD or Board-recognized equivalent qualification applies.

options.option_text: The pharmacist can qualify immediately by completing five additional CDTM CE hours.
options.original_rationale: Five additional relevant contact hours are an annual requirement during an agreement, not a substitute for the five-year qualification.

questions.question_stem: A certified Massachusetts pharmacy technician holds current Board-accepted certification. A pharmacist on duty approves the delegated task. Which activities may this technician legally perform? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Receive a new or omitted prescription detail from a prescriber without exercising professional judgment, when otherwise permitted by law.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) allows certified technicians, with pharmacist approval and identification, to receive permitted new or omitted prescription information not requiring professional judgment.

options.option_text: Personally counsel a patient about a serious drug interaction after pharmacist review.
options.original_rationale: A technician cannot counsel or resolve a clinical conflict under 247 CMR 8.04(4)(e), regardless of prior pharmacist review.

options.option_text: Transfer a Schedule VI prescription between pharmacies with pharmacist approval and under transfer rules.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) expressly authorizes this limited prescription-transfer function for certified pharmacy technicians.

options.option_text: Perform final dispensing validation after the prescription passes an automated barcode check.
options.original_rationale: Final dispensing process validation remains a pharmacist function under 247 CMR 9.04(1); automation does not delegate it to a technician.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts patient picks up a chronic-medication refill and a newly prescribed inhaler. The patient declines counseling for the refill but accepts it for the inhaler. A pharmacist, pharmacy intern, and suitably trained pharmacy technician are on duty. Which workflow BEST complies with Massachusetts law?

options.option_text: The technician offers counseling for both drugs and personally counsels on the inhaler; the pharmacist validates.
options.original_rationale: A technician may relay the offer but may not provide the clinical counseling under 247 CMR 9.18(3).

options.option_text: The technician offers counseling for both drugs; the intern counsels on the inhaler; the pharmacist completes final validation.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.18 permits a trained designee to offer counseling to each recipient and a pharmacist or pharmacy intern to counsel; 247 CMR 9.04(1) reserves final dispensing validation to the pharmacist.

options.option_text: The technician offers counseling only for the inhaler; the intern counsels; the pharmacist validates.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.18(1) requires offering counseling to each person receiving prescription medication, not just new prescriptions.

options.option_text: The technician offers counseling for both; the intern counsels and completes the final dispensing validation.
options.original_rationale: An intern may counsel, but final dispensing validation must be completed by the licensed pharmacist.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts facility prepares a sterile injectable antineoplastic drug designated hazardous under applicable NIOSH criteria. The drug requires manipulation and is subject to USP <800>. Which statements correctly describe sterile hazardous-drug compounding? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: USP <800> containment engineering controls and CSTD provisions

options.option_text: A sterile hazardous-drug preparation must be made in an externally vented containment primary engineering control providing ISO Class 5 or better air quality.
options.original_rationale: USP <800> requires an externally vented C-PEC with ISO Class 5 or better air quality for sterile hazardous drug manipulation.

options.option_text: The containment secondary engineering control must maintain negative pressure compared with adjacent areas, including outside active compounding periods.
options.original_rationale: USP <800> requires continuous negative pressure for the appropriate containment secondary engineering control.

options.option_text: Outdoor exhaust from the containment secondary engineering control must in every case pass through an additional HEPA filter.
options.original_rationale: Externally vented secondary room exhaust is required, but universal additional HEPA filtration of that outdoor exhaust is not the categorical USP <800> rule.

options.option_text: A closed-system drug-transfer device must be used during every hazardous-drug compounding procedure.
options.original_rationale: USP <800> recommends a CSTD for hazardous-drug compounding rather than mandating it for every compounding procedure; administration standards differ.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts patient comes to pick up a valid Schedule II prescription but lacks government-issued identification. The pharmacist reasonably believes that refusing to dispense would cause serious hardship. No other identifier exemption applies. Which action is permitted if all other dispensing conditions are satisfied?

options.option_text: Dispense only after the prescriber orally confirms identity and authorizes pickup.
options.original_rationale: Prescriber confirmation does not, by itself, substitute for the documented hardship pathway in 247 CMR 9.04(14).

options.option_text: Document the serious-hardship reason and have the customer print a name and address and sign the reverse of the prescription or a prescription log.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.04(14)(c) allows this alternative identification procedure if the serious-hardship criteria and documentation requirements are met.

options.option_text: Dispense using the existing patient history without a hardship notation or signed log.
options.original_rationale: An established pharmacy relationship alone does not replace the state customer-identifier requirement.

options.option_text: Refuse all Schedule II pickups without government identification, regardless of hardship.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.04(14)(c) expressly recognizes a properly documented serious-hardship exception.

questions.question_stem: A Rhode Island physician issues a valid methylphenidate Schedule II prescription for 60 tablets on November 4, 2026. The patient presents it to a Massachusetts pharmacy on November 8, requests a 20-tablet initial partial fill, and receives 20 tablets. On November 27, the patient requests the remaining 40 tablets from that SAME pharmacy. The initial patient-requested partial fill was documented, and all other requirements are met. What is the MOST accurate answer?

options.option_text: A new prescription is mandatory because completion must occur within 72 hours.
options.original_rationale: The 72-hour stock-shortage rule is different from the patient-requested partial-fill rules.

options.option_text: The remaining 40 tablets may be dispensed because the initial and subsequent fills meet their respective deadlines.
options.original_rationale: 105 CMR 721.055 requires initial presentation of an out-of-state Schedule II prescription within five calendar days and completion at the same pharmacy no later than 30 days after issuance, consistent with federal requirements.

options.option_text: An out-of-state Schedule II prescription can never be partially filled in Massachusetts.
options.original_rationale: 105 CMR 721.055 specifically provides for patient-requested partial fills of qualifying out-of-state Schedule II prescriptions.

options.option_text: The prescriber must issue a new prescription merely because the patient requested a partial fill.
options.original_rationale: When properly documented and completed within the legal window, a patient-requested partial fill does not automatically require a new prescription.

questions.question_stem: A patient asks a Massachusetts pharmacy to transfer several NEVER-FILLED prescriptions to another licensed Massachusetts pharmacy for INITIAL dispensing. Systems and pharmacist-to-pharmacist procedures otherwise comply with law. Which transfers are permitted? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Board Policy 2023-10; 21 CFR 1306.08

options.option_text: A never-filled original electronic Schedule II prescription, transferred electronically once at the patient's request.
options.original_rationale: Board Policy 2023-10 and 21 CFR 1306.08 allow the one-time electronic transfer of an unfilled original EPCS for initial dispensing.

options.option_text: A never-filled paper Schedule IV prescription scanned and sent as though it were a valid original electronic controlled-substance prescription.
options.original_rationale: Scanning a paper prescription into a computer does not transform it into EPCS; federal controlled paper originals are not transferable for initial filling under this provision.

options.option_text: A never-filled oral Schedule VI prescription transferred under Massachusetts pharmacy transfer rules.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2023-10 permits initial-dispensing transfer of unfilled oral, paper, fax, and electronic Schedule VI prescriptions under state rules.

options.option_text: An original electronic Schedule III prescription transferred to a second receiving pharmacy after it already underwent its one initial-dispensing transfer.
options.original_rationale: The EPCS initial-dispensing transfer permitted by 21 CFR 1306.08 is one-time, not unlimited.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a qualifying emergency oral prescription for a Schedule II medication and satisfies verification, documentation, quantity, and other legal requirements. The prescriber proposes sending the follow-up prescription within seven BUSINESS days. What is MOST appropriate?

options.option_text: Accept seven business days because Massachusetts rules displace the federal timetable.
options.original_rationale: A longer state deadline cannot override the stricter federal seven-day deadline in 21 CFR 1306.11(d).

options.option_text: Explain that federal law requires the compliant follow-up within seven CALENDAR days and requires emergency-order documentation.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(d) uses seven days, not business days; Massachusetts' separately worded timeframe does not eliminate the federal requirement.

options.option_text: Require the follow-up in 72 hours because every emergency oral Schedule II order is a partial fill.
options.original_rationale: The 72-hour shortage partial-fill rule is not the emergency oral prescription follow-up deadline.

options.option_text: Accept the plan without any follow-up because the pharmacist verified the prescriber.
options.original_rationale: Verification does not dispense with the required follow-up or the DEA notification required if follow-up is not received.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses the wrong strength. The patient has the medication but calls BEFORE taking any dose, and the pharmacist confirms the error. The patient is uninjured. Under the state's continuous quality improvement rules, which statements are true? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 15.03(1)–(2), QRE patient notification and initial 24-hour record (official MA Board version dated Dec. 6, 2024); 247 CMR 15.02(1) CQI scope

options.option_text: The pharmacist must promptly notify the patient and provide correction directions and instructions to reduce negative impact.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 15.03(1) requires prompt appropriate patient notification, correction instructions, and harm-minimization guidance.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must initially document the quality-related event within 24 hours of learning of it.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 15.03(2)(a) requires initial QRE documentation within 24 hours of discovery or notification.

options.option_text: There is no QRE because the patient did not swallow the medication.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect dispensing received by the patient is a QRE even without ingestion or resulting injury.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must notify the prescriber in EVERY case, irrespective of professional judgment.
options.original_rationale: The regulation requires prescriber notification when indicated in the pharmacist's professional judgment; it is not unconditional.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives four otherwise valid new prescriptions, each requesting a 90-day supply. Assume no other patient, federal, or payer restriction bars the full quantity. Which prescription MAY be filled as one 90-day dispensing under Massachusetts law?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §23(d); Board Policy 2024-05

options.option_text: Methylphenidate, Schedule II, for ADHD.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.94C §23(d) and Policy 2024-05 permit a 90-day supply of non-opioid Schedule II–III drugs, including stimulants, when otherwise lawful.

options.option_text: Hydrocodone/acetaminophen, Schedule II, for chronic pain.
options.original_rationale: This opioid analgesic is outside the stated 90-day exceptions; the general 30-day Schedule II–III limit applies.

options.option_text: Acetaminophen/codeine, Schedule III, for postoperative pain.
options.original_rationale: The Schedule III opioid is not a non-opioid or OUD-treatment exception; the 30-day limit applies.

options.option_text: Buprenorphine transdermal analgesic patches, Schedule III, for chronic pain rather than opioid use disorder.
options.original_rationale: Buprenorphine products used for OUD have a special exception, but this analgesic use is not the OUD-treatment exception.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist seeks renewal in December 2026. The pharmacist does not compound or immunize and has no CE waiver. In 2025, the pharmacist earns 22 contact hours: 18 home-study/mediated hours (including two law hours) and four live hours. In 2026, the pharmacist earns 24 hours: ten home study and 14 live (including two law hours). Every activity is approved; no more than eight hours are earned on any one day. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.option_text: The pharmacist qualifies because 46 earned hours exceed the biennial 40-hour requirement.
options.original_rationale: The 40-hour total does not override the minimum 20 allowable hours in EACH calendar year and the 15-home-study-hour annual cap.

options.option_text: The pharmacist qualifies because the extra 2026 hours can compensate for a 2025 deficit.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 4.03(5) does not allow CE hours to be carried between calendar years.

options.option_text: The pharmacist does not qualify because only 19 allowable CE hours count in 2025.
options.original_rationale: Only 15 of 18 home-study hours count toward 2025's minimum, plus four live hours, for 19; the 2026 surplus does not cure this.

options.option_text: The pharmacist does not qualify because no more than 20 hours may be earned per year.
options.original_rationale: Twenty hours is an annual MINIMUM, not a ceiling; the problem is the annual home-study limit.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy and a nonresident mail-order pharmacy dispense controlled substances to Massachusetts patients. No reporting waiver applies. Which statements correctly distinguish MassPAT pharmacy reporting duties from prescriber query duties? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: The Massachusetts pharmacy generally reports outpatient Schedule IV alprazolam dispensing by the end of the next business day.
options.original_rationale: 105 CMR 700.012 and the DPH pharmacy reporting instructions require covered Schedule II–V dispensing reports within the applicable 24-hour or next-business-day deadline.

options.option_text: The nonresident pharmacy reports a Schedule IV tramadol prescription mailed to a person in Massachusetts.
options.original_rationale: The reporting obligation extends to out-of-state pharmacies delivering covered prescriptions to Massachusetts residents.

options.option_text: Morphine given to a hospitalized inpatient under an inpatient medication order must be reported as a retail outpatient fill.
options.original_rationale: 105 CMR 700.012 excludes controlled substances dispensed pursuant to inpatient hospital medication orders from this pharmacy reporting requirement.

options.option_text: A pharmacist still reports a covered outpatient dispensing even if the prescriber qualified for a hospice exemption from mandatory MassPAT lookup.
options.original_rationale: An exemption from a prescriber's obligation to query MassPAT does not by itself exempt the dispensing pharmacy from submitting data.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy compounds patient-specific nonsterile preparations under USP <795>: X is a NONPRESERVED aqueous oral suspension (water activity 0.95); Y is a nonaqueous oral liquid (water activity 0.45). There is no applicable USP–NF monograph or preparation-specific stability data, and no shorter BUD factor. Which pair matches the DEFAULT maximum beyond-use dates?
questions.author_citation: USP <795>, Section 10, Table 4
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: MA Board Retail Inspection Template item 90; nonpreserved aqueous 14d refrigerated, nonaqueous oral liquid 90d room/refrigerated
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Direct Board inspection rule summary supports each tested BUD; current full USP <795> normative table not independently authenticated.

options.option_text: X: 14 days at controlled room temperature; Y: 90 days at room temperature or refrigerated.
options.original_rationale: X must be refrigerated under the default BUD; room temperature is not its default 14-day storage condition.
options.independent_option_analysis: Nonpreserved aqueous default 14d is refrigerated, not ambient.

options.option_text: X: 35 days refrigerated; Y: 90 days at room temperature or refrigerated.
options.original_rationale: Thirty-five days is the preserved aqueous category, not nonpreserved aqueous.
options.independent_option_analysis: 35d is preserved aqueous category, not nonpreserved suspension.

options.option_text: X: 14 days refrigerated; Y: 180 days at room temperature or refrigerated.
options.original_rationale: The 180-day default applies to OTHER nonaqueous dosage forms, not nonaqueous oral liquids.
options.independent_option_analysis: 180d applies other nonaqueous forms, not oral liquids.

options.option_text: X: 14 days refrigerated; Y: 90 days at room temperature or refrigerated.
options.original_rationale: USP <795> Table 4 gives 14 days refrigerated for nonpreserved aqueous preparations and 90 days at controlled room temperature or refrigerated for nonaqueous oral liquids.
options.independent_option_analysis: 14d refrigerated and 90d nonaqueous oral liquid match MA Board inspectable BUD table.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy vaccinates a 55-year-old against herpes zoster under an otherwise valid standing order. A qualified pharmacist is on duty; the patient is eligible and has no contraindication. Under the Massachusetts vaccine workflow and federal VIS requirements, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Board Policy 2023-02 (revised 2025); 42 USC 300aa-26

options.option_text: A properly qualified pharmacist may select, counsel about, and administer the vaccine under a valid applicable standing order.
options.original_rationale: MA vaccine administration authority and Board Policy 2023-02 permit a properly qualified pharmacist to vaccinate an eligible patient under the applicable standing order.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must review the Massachusetts Immunization Information System (MIIS) before giving this non-influenza, non-COVID-19 vaccine.
options.original_rationale: Board Policy 2023-02 requires checking MIIS before vaccines other than influenza and COVID-19, including recombinant zoster vaccine.

options.option_text: A pharmacy technician trainee may independently administer the vaccine after completing a short training course.
options.original_rationale: A trainee has no independent vaccination authority merely from training; pharmacist and technician authority and supervision have separate legal limits.

options.option_text: The appropriate Vaccine Information Statement may be furnished after the injection if the patient already signed a consent form.
options.original_rationale: The Vaccine Information Statement must be provided before vaccination; consent does not replace the VIS delivery rule.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy performs its biennial controlled-substance inventory and has: (1) an opened Schedule II oxycodone bottle with 42 tablets; (2) an opened 2,000-tablet Schedule III container holding about 1,250 tablets; (3) an opened 1,000-tablet Schedule IV container holding about 400 tablets; and (4) ten expired Schedule II tablets secured and awaiting reverse distribution. The pharmacy maintains a Schedule II perpetual inventory. Which method is MOST accurate?

options.option_text: Exactly count Schedule II and IV, estimate Schedule III, and remove expired Schedule II from perpetual records.
options.original_rationale: Federal law requires an exact count for an opened container of more than 1,000 Schedule III tablets; expired Schedule II stock remains inventoried.

options.option_text: Exactly count Schedule II and the 2,000-tablet Schedule III container; estimate the Schedule IV container; retain expired Schedule II in inventory and reconciliation.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6) requires exact Schedule II counts and exact counts for opened Schedule III–V containers exceeding 1,000 tablets/capsules; 247 CMR 9.21 requires the expired Schedule II stock to stay in perpetual inventory and reconciliation.

options.option_text: Estimate all opened bottles based on electronic data and add expired Schedule II only when the reverse distributor receives them.
options.original_rationale: Electronic records do not remove the federal exact-count rules, and the expired product remains controlled stock until transferred or destroyed.

options.option_text: Exactly count every opened bottle but exclude expired Schedule II from perpetual reconciliation.
options.original_rationale: Exact counting above minimum is allowed, but 247 CMR 9.21(10) includes expired and pending-destruction Schedule II stock in inventory duties.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy has only one pharmacist. During a scheduled 25-minute meal break, the pharmacist remains on the premises but outside the prescription area. Before leaving, the pharmacist has prepared, visually checked and performed prospective DUR on a NEW prescription for a patient. The pharmacy has compliant break policies and preserves drug security. Which pickup procedure is MOST consistent with 247 CMR 9.19(17)?

options.option_text: The patient may pick it up during the break without additional records because the pharmacist checked it.
options.original_rationale: The special new-prescription exception requires a log, including the patient's phone number, and post-break follow-up counseling as appropriate.

options.option_text: The patient cannot pick up any new prescription until the pharmacist physically returns to the prescription area.
options.original_rationale: A narrowly specified exception permits release of a previously prepared, visibly checked, DUR-reviewed new prescription during a compliant temporary absence.

options.option_text: The new prescription may be released with a transaction log including the patient's phone number; the pharmacist must call afterward within a reasonable time about pertinent counseling.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.19(17)(b) specifies the log and pharmacist follow-up for a new prescription already prepared, visibly checked and DUR-reviewed.

options.option_text: A technician may complete final validation during the break because the pharmacist remains in the building.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.04(1) requires pharmacist final validation. A temporary break does not transfer this responsibility to technicians.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts resident community pharmacy plans a permanent closure on December 20, 2026. Assume no Board waiver. Under 247 CMR 6.13, which actions are required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Notify the Board in writing by certified mail at least 14 days before the planned closure with the required information.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.13(1) requires the resident pharmacy's advance certified-mail Board notice with closure details and other specified items.

options.option_text: Attempt to notify patients whose prescriptions were filled in the prior 90 days at least 14 days before closure, using an approved method.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.13(4) establishes this 90-day lookback and advance-notice rule and also requires conspicuous posted notice.

options.option_text: Destroy all patient prescription files at the moment the pharmacy stops dispensing to prevent privacy violations.
options.original_rationale: Patient files must be handled or transferred in accordance with closure and record-retention laws, not summarily destroyed.

options.option_text: Submit the original pharmacy license and controlled-substance registration plus the required disposition attestation to the Board within 14 days after closure.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.13(6) requires those submissions after closure for a resident pharmacy, with controlled-substance disposition compliance.

questions.question_stem: On a Monday, a Massachusetts DEA-registered resident community pharmacy confirms an actual theft of a bottle of Schedule II oxycodone and becomes aware of it that morning. No holidays or special exemptions apply. Which reporting plan BEST meets federal and Massachusetts reporting rules?

options.option_text: Notify the DEA after the pharmacy's next full inventory and submit the Massachusetts report at the next license renewal.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1301.76(b) requires prompt DEA written notice within one business day of discovery; Massachusetts has its own shorter reporting window than renewal.

options.option_text: Provide written notice to the local DEA Diversion Field Office within one business day, complete DEA Form 106 as required, and submit the Massachusetts RLCS and applicable Form 106 to the Board within seven calendar days.
options.original_rationale: DEA requires written notification within one business day and subsequent Form 106. Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-01 requires its loss report and Form 106 if applicable within seven calendar days for confirmed thefts.

options.option_text: Report only to the Massachusetts Board within seven calendar days because state reporting satisfies DEA notice.
options.original_rationale: State Board reporting does not replace separate federal DEA notification and Form 106 duties.

options.option_text: Submit DEA Form 106 immediately but omit Massachusetts reporting if all missing tablets are later recovered.
options.original_rationale: Confirmed theft is reportable under Massachusetts Policy 2026-01 regardless of quantity; later recovery does not erase the original federal theft reporting duty.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy evaluates prescriptions for a brand product for which a less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable product is listed, along with a different FDA-authorized generic. No patient-specific exception or safety issue applies. Which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: If the prescriber has not indicated 'no substitution,' the pharmacist is generally required to dispense the less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable listed product.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.112 §12D, 105 CMR 720 and the DPH interchange policy generally mandate the lower-cost eligible interchangeable drug unless the prescriber prohibits substitution.

options.option_text: A clear 'no substitution' direction by the prescriber may always be disregarded whenever a generic is less expensive.
options.original_rationale: A valid prescriber prohibition prevents mandated interchange; lower price alone cannot override a lawful no-substitution instruction.

options.option_text: For a product newly listed as interchangeable, a prescriber can prevent midstream interchange by issuing a new prescription indicating 'no substitution.'
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts midstream interchange policy specifies a new properly marked no-substitution prescription as the mechanism to prevent the switch.

options.option_text: An FDA-authorized generic may be interchanged with the brand when there is no 'no substitution' direction, even if the authorized generic does not have a separate Orange Book therapeutic-equivalence listing.
options.original_rationale: DPH Circular DCP 22-01-112 explains that an authorized generic is the same approved product marketed without the brand name and may be interchanged when the prescriber does not prohibit substitution.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts practitioner plans a 10-day outpatient oxycodone prescription for a 17-year-old after acute surgery. The practitioner determines in professional medical judgment that more than seven days is required for the acute condition, documents that condition and why a non-opiate alternative is inappropriate, and discusses opiate risks and necessity with the minor's parent. All other prescription and dispensing rules are satisfied. Which statement is MOST accurate under M.G.L. c.94C §19D?

options.option_text: The prescription is prohibited because no minor may receive more than a seven-day opiate supply.
options.original_rationale: Section 19D(b) permits documented medical-necessity exceptions for adult or minor patients when its conditions are met.

options.option_text: It is permitted only if the minor has cancer or is receiving palliative care.
options.original_rationale: Section 19D(b) also includes an acute medical condition and chronic pain management when the required professional judgment and documentation are satisfied.

options.option_text: It may be issued under the documented medical-necessity exception, despite the standard seven-day limit for minors.
options.original_rationale: Section 19D(a) establishes the ordinary minor limit, while subsection (b) expressly permits exceptions for acute medical needs with required documentation and consideration of non-opiate alternatives.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may extend any original seven-day opiate prescription to ten days after the parent signs consent.
options.original_rationale: The statute's prescribing exception depends on the practitioner's medical judgment and documentation; it does not give the pharmacist general authority to extend the prescription based only on parental consent.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered practitioner in a Massachusetts emergency department is not registered as an opioid treatment program (OTP). A patient with opioid use disorder needs short-term withdrawal treatment while the department arranges referral to an OTP. Assume Massachusetts and other applicable laws permit the contemplated on-site dispensing, and no separate prescription authorization is being used. Under the federal exception in 21 CFR 1306.07(b), which action is MOST appropriate?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1306.07(b) (amended effective Aug. 8, 2023)

options.option_text: Write an outpatient prescription for a three-day supply of methadone and send it to a community pharmacy for the patient to pick up.
options.original_rationale: The special emergency provision in 21 CFR 1306.07(b) permits the practitioner to dispense, but not prescribe, a narcotic drug while referral arrangements are made. A community pharmacy prescription is not authorized by this exception.

options.option_text: Directly dispense no more than a three-day supply of the narcotic medication at one time while arranging referral; do not renew or extend this emergency course.
options.original_rationale: The amended 21 CFR 1306.07(b) permits a non-OTP practitioner to dispense, but not prescribe, up to a three-day supply at one time while arranging referral; the emergency treatment cannot be renewed or extended.

options.option_text: Directly dispense a seven-day supply whenever the nearest OTP cannot offer an appointment within three days.
options.original_rationale: An unavailable appointment does not expand the special federal three-day maximum. Other independent treatment authorities are outside the stated emergency exception.

options.option_text: Dispense only one day's medication at a time for up to three consecutive days, because a three-day supply may never be given at once.
options.original_rationale: This describes the older pre-August-2023 federal limitation. The revised regulation allows up to three days' supply to be dispensed at one time, subject to the other requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives otherwise valid, prescriber-transmitted facsimile prescriptions for Schedule II medications. Assume an applicable Massachusetts exception permits paper/fax transmission, all necessary federal prescription elements are present, and no oral emergency authorization is involved. In which cases may the fax itself serve as the original prescription under 21 CFR 1306.11? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: A fax for morphine oral solution for a patient enrolled in a state-licensed hospice program; the prescription notes that the patient is a hospice patient.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(g) permits a facsimile to serve as the original for a Schedule II narcotic prescribed to a qualifying hospice patient when the required hospice notation is included.

options.option_text: A fax for oxycodone tablets for a homebound patient with a terminal diagnosis who is not enrolled in hospice, does not reside in an LTCF, and will not receive an infusion.
options.original_rationale: A terminal diagnosis alone does not meet the special hospice-fax condition. Nor does this ordinary oral prescription meet the LTCF or compounded infusion exception, so the original signed paper prescription is generally required.

options.option_text: A fax for methylphenidate tablets for a resident of a qualifying long-term care facility (LTCF).
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(f) allows a facsimile to serve as the original for a Schedule II prescription for an LTCF resident; unlike the hospice exception, the provision is not limited to narcotics.

options.option_text: A fax for a Schedule II narcotic to be compounded specifically for direct administration to the patient by intrathecal infusion.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(e) allows the fax as the original when a Schedule II narcotic is to be compounded for direct administration by a qualifying parenteral, including intraspinal, infusion.

questions.question_stem: A patient brings two sealed prescription packages back to the same Massachusetts pharmacy. Package X contains the wrong strength, which the pharmacy confirms it dispensed in error. Package Y was correctly dispensed, is not suspected to be defective or contaminated, and the patient simply no longer wants it. Neither medication has been taken, and the packages appear unopened. Which response BEST complies with 247 CMR 9.01?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.01(5),(7): error/defective returns vs previously dispensed inventory

options.option_text: Accept both packages and return them to saleable inventory after the pharmacist confirms the seals are intact.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.01(5) and (7) do not permit re-dispensing or returning error-related or suspected defective/contaminated patient returns to saleable stock merely because they are sealed.
options.independent_option_analysis: Redispensing error returns is prohibited regardless of seal.

options.option_text: Refuse both returns unless the patient proves an actual injury from taking the wrongly dispensed medication.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.01(7) requires the pharmacy to accept a medication it dispensed in error; proof of ingestion or injury is not a condition.
options.independent_option_analysis: Wrong strength dispensed in error must be accepted; no injury condition.

options.option_text: Accept both packages because all previously dispensed medication must be taken back, then dispose of only Package X.
options.original_rationale: The rule requires acceptance of medication dispensed in error or suspected defective/contaminated; it does not require accepting a properly dispensed, nondefective medication merely because it is unwanted.
options.independent_option_analysis: No obligation to accept properly dispensed, nondefective product; acceptance is not blanket.

options.option_text: Accept Package X, quarantine it and properly dispose of it; the pharmacy is not required by this provision to accept Package Y.
options.original_rationale: Under 247 CMR 9.01(7), wrongly dispensed medication must be accepted and cannot return to inventory. Properly dispensed medication that was not defective at dispensing need not be accepted.
options.independent_option_analysis: Error return accepted, quarantined and disposed; other return need not be accepted.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered Massachusetts retail pharmacy wishes to transfer controlled-substance stock to a second DEA-registered retail pharmacy for that pharmacy's general dispensing to patients (not a patient-specific prescription transfer). Assume every other Massachusetts and federal condition is satisfied. Under 21 CFR 1307.11, which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: If the annual volume of qualifying distributions is exactly 5% of the total controlled-substance dosage units distributed and dispensed in the same calendar year, the distributing pharmacy may use the exemption from separate distributor registration if all other conditions are met.
options.original_rationale: The 5% ceiling in 21 CFR 1307.11(a)(1)(iv) is inclusive: qualifying distributions must not exceed 5% of the total dosage units distributed and dispensed during that calendar year.

options.option_text: A Schedule II transfer under this exemption needs only matching electronic inventory entries at both pharmacies; DEA Form 222 or an appropriate electronic order is unnecessary.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1307.11(a)(1)(iii) and Part 1305 still require the controlled-substance order form or compliant electronic ordering method when Schedule II stock is distributed.

options.option_text: The receiving pharmacy must be registered to dispense the controlled substance, and the distribution and receipt must be properly documented by both parties.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1307.11(a)(1)(i)–(ii) requires the receiving practitioner to be registered to dispense and both the distributing and receiving parties to maintain transaction records.

options.option_text: The 5% limit is measured by the wholesale dollar value of the stock transferred, rather than the number of controlled-substance dosage units.
options.original_rationale: The regulation uses dosage units, not purchase cost, prescription revenue, number of packages, or wholesale dollar value.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives requests to compound a preparation with the same active ingredient, similar strength, and route as an FDA-approved product that remains commercially available and is not on the FDA drug shortages list. Assume the pharmacy otherwise meets applicable 503A, Massachusetts, and USP requirements. Which request BEST supports lawful patient-specific compounding of an essentially similar preparation?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.112 §39D(a); MA Board Policy 2020-02; FD&C Act §503A(b)(1)(D)

options.option_text: A prescriber requests the compounded preparation solely because it would cost the patient 30% less than the commercially available product.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.112 §39D and Massachusetts Board Policy 2020-02 expressly reject price difference alone as the significant medical difference needed to justify compounding a copy.

options.option_text: A pharmacist documents an individual patient's reported preference for a dye-free version, but the prescriber makes no patient-specific determination of a medically significant difference.
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts requirement calls for documented medical need as determined by the prescribing practitioner. The pharmacist's unilateral preference documentation does not substitute for that prescriber determination.

options.option_text: A prescriber provides a patient-specific prescription and documents that a dye in the approved product causes this patient's allergic reaction and that removal creates a significant clinical difference.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.112 §39D and Board Policy 2020-02 recognize a patient-specific, prescriber-documented medical need such as removal of a dye as a potential significant difference; all other compounding safeguards still apply.

options.option_text: The pharmacy routinely prepares copies for future walk-in patients because its local wholesaler is temporarily out of stock, even though the approved product remains commercially available.
options.original_rationale: Local inventory inconvenience alone does not authorize routine compounding of essentially identical products. Patient-specific conditions and the federal 503A restriction against routinely compounding copies still apply.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy is not providing vaccination services. One pharmacist supervises four Massachusetts-licensed support personnel who are actively filling prescriptions. A fifth licensed technician is on the premises but performs only inventory receiving and does not participate in prescription preparation or filling. No waiver or dedicated-trainer arrangement applies. Under Board Policy 2026-02, which four-person filling team satisfies the ordinary 1:4 supervisory ratio?
questions.author_citation: MA Board Policy 2026-02 §§I(A), I(C), II; 247 CMR 8.01(16)

options.option_text: One certified pharmacy technician and three noncertified pharmacy technicians.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2026-02 does not allow a four-person filling team with only one certified technician and no intern. At 1:4, the permitted compositions include two certified technicians, two interns, or a certified technician together with an intern.

options.option_text: Two certified pharmacy technicians and two noncertified pharmacy technicians.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2026-02, Section I(A)(1)(b), permits 1:4 when at least two active support personnel are licensed certified pharmacy technicians. The fifth employee doing only inventory receiving need not be included in the filling ratio under Section I(C).

options.option_text: One licensed pharmacy intern and three noncertified pharmacy technicians.
options.original_rationale: A single pharmacy intern permits only the ordinary 1:3 composition unless another qualifying person is present. Four active support personnel need an additional certified technician or a second intern.

options.option_text: Four licensed pharmacy interns performing prescription-filling duties under the same pharmacist.
options.original_rationale: Four interns filling prescriptions are not permitted under the ordinary intern-supervision provisions. The exceptional four-intern supervisory arrangements in Policy 2026-02 do not authorize four interns to fill prescriptions in a nonvaccinating community pharmacy.

questions.question_stem: In November 2026, a Massachusetts-licensed community pharmacist plans to independently prescribe an FDA-approved oral HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medication for an eligible adult. The pharmacist holds an NPI, completed an appropriately accredited 2.5-hour course addressing HIV risk assessment, symptoms, and prevention modalities (not only pharmacology), and will follow the applicable statewide PrEP guidance, counseling, documentation, and referral requirements. The prescription and dispensing will occur at the SAME pharmacy. The pharmacist does not hold a separate Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration (MCSR). Which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19F; DCP Circular 26-08-125, General Prescribing Requirements and HIV Prevention

options.option_text: The pharmacist must first obtain a physician-signed collaborative drug therapy management agreement, even though the 2026 state pharmacist-prescribing guidance is followed.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.94C §19F independently authorizes qualifying pharmacists to prescribe covered HIV-prevention medications under statewide guidance. A separate CDTM agreement is not required simply to invoke this authority.

options.option_text: The pharmacist cannot prescribe because a personal MCSR is mandatory for every prescription issued by a pharmacist, even when it is dispensed at the same pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Massachusetts Circular DCP 26-08-125 expressly states that a pharmacist need not obtain a personal MCSR when both the prescribing and dispensing occur at one pharmacy location, provided all other applicable conditions are met.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may omit the NPI and document the encounter only if the pharmacy transfers the resulting prescription to a different pharmacy for dispensing.
options.original_rationale: DCP 26-08-125 requires the pharmacist to obtain an NPI and document prescribing and dispensing activities. Dispensing elsewhere would also fall outside the circular's specifically described same-location MCSR exemption.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may prescribe and dispense oral PrEP under §19F without a separate personal MCSR in this same-location situation, provided all other applicable requirements are met.
options.original_rationale: DCP 26-08-125 permits pharmacist prescribing of covered HIV-prevention medications under statewide guidance and qualifying training. It requires an NPI and expressly waives a separate pharmacist MCSR when prescribing and dispensing both occur at a single pharmacy location.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy receives ordinary substance-use-disorder treatment records from a federally assisted 42 CFR Part 2 program pursuant to the patient's valid, written single consent for future treatment, payment, and health care operations (TPO). The pharmacy is also asked to obtain a separately maintained set of the treating counselor's SUD counseling notes, but the patient has NOT given any separate consent for those notes. No other disclosure exception or state-specific restriction applies. Under the Part 2 rule with a February 16, 2026 compliance date, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 42 CFR Part 2 (2024 final rule; compliance Feb. 16, 2026); HHS Part 2 Final Rule Fact Sheet, Patient Consent and SUD Counseling Notes

options.option_text: The single TPO consent automatically authorizes the pharmacy to obtain the separately maintained SUD counseling notes on the same terms as the ordinary treatment record.
options.original_rationale: The 2024 Part 2 rule expressly creates special protection for separately maintained SUD counseling notes; a broad TPO consent does not replace the separate patient consent required for those notes.

options.option_text: For the ordinary Part 2 treatment records received under the valid TPO consent, the HIPAA-covered pharmacy may make later disclosures as HIPAA permits, subject to Part 2's additional prohibition on using records in proceedings against the patient.
options.original_rationale: HHS's 2024 Part 2 final rule allows HIPAA-covered entities receiving Part 2 records under a single TPO consent to redisclose according to HIPAA, except for the more protective restriction on legal proceedings against the patient.

options.option_text: Once the pharmacy has the ordinary records under a TPO consent, a general subpoena alone makes their use in criminal proceedings against that patient permissible.
options.original_rationale: Part 2's special protection against using SUD records against the patient remains in force. A general subpoena alone is not equivalent to the specific patient consent or Part 2-compliant court-order process required for such proceedings.

options.option_text: The pharmacy generally needs separate consent for the separately maintained SUD counseling notes; the ordinary TPO consent does not cover that special note category.
options.original_rationale: The revised 42 CFR Part 2 rule treats separately maintained SUD counseling notes analogously to psychotherapy notes and requires specific patient consent, rather than relying on a broad TPO consent.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts patient with limited hand dexterity specifically requests a conventional (non-child-resistant) container for ONE newly prescribed oral medication subject to the federal Poison Prevention Packaging Act (PPPA). The pharmacist documents that request and dispenses the medication accordingly. Two weeks later, the patient presents a DIFFERENT new prescription for another PPPA-covered oral medication. No blanket packaging request was made, the prescriber has not requested conventional packaging for the second prescription, and the patient makes no new packaging request. What is the BEST legally supported dispensing approach?
questions.author_citation: Poison Prevention Packaging Act §4(b); 16 CFR 1701.1; CPSC Poison Prevention Packaging Guide (Jan. 2023), p. 12

options.option_text: The first prescription may use conventional packaging at the patient's request, but the second generally needs child-resistant packaging absent a new specific request, a valid blanket request, or a prescriber direction.
options.original_rationale: CPSC's PPPA guidance permits a patient-specific packaging request while explaining that a request for one prescription does not extend to an unrelated future prescription. Without a separate exemption or request, the second prescription uses compliant packaging.

options.option_text: The first conventional container was impermissible because only a prescriber, not a patient, can authorize dispensing without child-resistant packaging.
options.original_rationale: The PPPA permits a consumer or the prescribing practitioner to specifically request conventional packaging for a covered prescription; a patient request is legally sufficient for the first prescription.

options.option_text: Use conventional packaging for the second prescription because the first documented request permanently waives child-resistant packaging for all future prescriptions.
options.original_rationale: CPSC expressly distinguishes a specific request for one prescription from a request covering all medications. The first request does not automatically become a blanket waiver for other prescriptions.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may independently choose conventional packaging for the second prescription based on the patient's known dexterity limitations, without a new patient or prescriber request.
options.original_rationale: The patient's difficulty opening packaging can inform counseling but does not independently authorize the pharmacist to waive special packaging. The choice must come from the patient or prescriber unless another specific exemption applies.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy is a dispenser subject to the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA). It finds a questionable product identifier on a prescription drug package that it holds in inventory and determines the package is a SUSPECT product. The pharmacy begins an investigation with its trading partners. Later, evidence establishes that it is an ILLEGITIMATE product. Assume no applicable waiver, exemption, or enforcement-discretion relief. Which statements accurately describe the dispenser's federal DSCSA obligations? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: FD&C Act §582(d)(4)(A)–(B) (21 U.S.C. §360eee-1); FDA DSCSA Verification Systems Guidance (Dec. 2023)

options.option_text: At the point the package is determined to be suspect, it must be quarantined apart from product intended for distribution while the pharmacy promptly investigates.
options.original_rationale: FD&C Act §582(d)(4)(A) requires the dispenser to quarantine a suspect product and promptly investigate its legitimacy; it cannot simply continue dispensing it while verifying the identifier.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must notify FDA and all immediate trading partners within 24 hours of the initial SUSPECT classification, even before it determines the product is illegitimate.
options.original_rationale: The federal 24-hour illegitimate-product notification requirement for dispensers is triggered by the determination of illegitimacy, not merely by the initial classification of a product as suspect.

options.option_text: After determining that the product is illegitimate, the pharmacy must notify FDA and appropriate immediate trading partners within 24 hours of that determination.
options.original_rationale: Under §582(d)(4)(B)(ii), the dispenser must notify FDA and immediate trading partners that it has reason to believe may have received the illegitimate product within 24 hours after determining illegitimacy.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must retain records of the suspect-product investigation for at least six years after the investigation is concluded.
options.original_rationale: FD&C Act §582(d)(4)(A)(iv) requires dispensers to retain suspect-product investigation records for at least six years after the conclusion of the investigation, regardless of the outcome.

questions.question_stem: Two first-time Massachusetts pharmacist-licensure applicants submit internship records in November 2026. Applicant X graduated from an ACPE-accredited PharmD program in 2026 and has Board-acceptable verification of 1,500 hours acquired through experiential pharmacy education, but no additional paid internship. Applicant Y graduated from an ACPE-accredited program in 2011 and can verify only 1,000 school rotation hours; Y has no other Board-approved internship hours. Assume all other licensure requirements can be met. Which interpretation of the Massachusetts internship requirement is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.01(1)(a)–(b); MA Board, Intern Hours Requirement for Pharmacist Licensure (2012 graduate transition)

options.option_text: Both applicants satisfy the requirement because an ACPE pharmacy degree always replaces separate internship-hour documentation regardless of graduation year.
options.original_rationale: The Board's 2012-and-later ACPE graduate policy is not automatically retroactive to the 2011 graduate. Applicant Y has only 1,000 verified hours, with no additional approved internship hours.

options.option_text: Applicant X must obtain 500 additional hours outside the PharmD curriculum because every applicant must separately complete the 1,000-plus-500 internship pathway.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.01(1)(b) provides a separate route for 1,500 qualifying hours from ACPE experiential pharmacy education. The 1,000-plus-500 route is not a mandatory extra requirement for X.

options.option_text: Applicant Y qualifies through the pre-2012 graduation policy, but Applicant X must complete 500 hours after graduation.
options.original_rationale: The Board's guidance for graduates through 2011 describes 1,000 school rotation hours plus 500 additional verified hours. It does not impose an extra post-graduation 500-hour requirement on a 2026 ACPE graduate.

options.option_text: Applicant X satisfies the internship-hour requirement through qualifying ACPE experiential education; Applicant Y needs additional Board-acceptable internship hours.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.01(1)(b) recognizes 1,500 hours of ACPE experiential pharmacy education. The Board's guidance treats 2012-and-later ACPE graduates as satisfying the intern-hour requirement, but the 2011 applicant with only 1,000 documented school rotation hours has not fulfilled the historic additional-hour requirement.

questions.question_stem: In November 2026 a Massachusetts community pharmacist receives a valid first prescription for clozapine. The pharmacy is not enrolled in the former Clozapine REMS, and the patient's absolute neutrophil count (ANC) has not been entered into a REMS portal. The pharmacist has assessed the prescription and the prescriber will arrange ANC monitoring according to current labeling. No other dispensing concern exists. Which conclusion BEST reflects FDA requirements in effect on this date?
questions.author_citation: FDA Drug Safety Communication, Aug. 27, 2025: Clozapine REMS eliminated effective June 13, 2025; 247 CMR 9.01(21)

options.option_text: Dispensing must wait until both the patient and pharmacy reenroll in the Clozapine REMS and the ANC is uploaded to the REMS portal.
options.original_rationale: FDA eliminated the Clozapine REMS effective June 13, 2025. Enrollment and REMS ANC submission are no longer federal prerequisites to clozapine dispensing.

options.option_text: The prescription may be dispensed without former REMS enrollment or REMS ANC verification, while the drug's neutropenia warnings and clinical ANC monitoring guidance remain important.
options.original_rationale: FDA formally removed the Clozapine REMS effective June 13, 2025. Pharmacies no longer verify eligibility through the REMS, but the boxed neutropenia warning and recommendations for prescriber ANC monitoring remain in the labeling.

options.option_text: The removal of the Clozapine REMS also removed the boxed warning and the clinical need for ANC monitoring during treatment.
options.original_rationale: FDA retained the warning about severe neutropenia and expressly advises prescribers to continue ANC monitoring as outlined in labeling; removing an administrative REMS does not remove the safety risk.

options.option_text: The REMS exemption is limited to patients who have already taken clozapine for six months; new-start prescriptions still require mandatory pharmacy certification.
options.original_rationale: The FDA removal applies to clozapine prescriptions generally, including new starts; it is not a conditional six-month grandfathering or stabilization exemption.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy and its business associate discover a reportable breach of UNSECURED protected health information affecting EXACTLY 500 Massachusetts residents. The parties confirm the breach is reportable after risk assessment, have valid contact information for affected people, and have no applicable law-enforcement delay. Consider only the FEDERAL HIPAA Breach Notification Rule; any separate Massachusetts notification obligations must be addressed independently. Which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.404, 164.406 (>500 state residents), 164.408 (≥500 individuals), 164.410; HHS HIPAA Breach Notification Rule

options.option_text: The covered pharmacy must notify affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after the breach is discovered under HIPAA.
options.original_rationale: 45 CFR 164.404 requires individual notification without unreasonable delay and not later than 60 calendar days after discovery. The exact 500-person count does not eliminate individual notice.

options.option_text: The covered pharmacy must notify the HHS Secretary for this breach on the timetable for 500 or more individuals, rather than waiting for the annual report for smaller breaches.
options.original_rationale: 45 CFR 164.408(b) applies to breaches involving 500 or more people, including exactly 500. The Secretary is notified contemporaneously with individual notice, subject to the rule's timing requirements.

options.option_text: Because exactly 500 Massachusetts residents were affected, the pharmacy must also provide federal media notice to prominent Massachusetts outlets.
options.original_rationale: 45 CFR 164.406 requires media notice when a breach involves MORE THAN 500 residents of a state or jurisdiction. Exactly 500 triggers HHS reporting at the larger-breach threshold but not the federal media-notification requirement.

options.option_text: The business associate must notify the covered pharmacy without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after the business associate's discovery of the breach.
options.original_rationale: 45 CFR 164.410 requires a business associate to notify the covered entity without unreasonable delay and not later than 60 calendar days after discovery. The covered entity remains responsible for ensuring required individual notifications occur.

questions.question_stem: A patient has a valid, previously filled Schedule IV prescription with authorized refills remaining. Two Massachusetts pharmacies (X and Y) do NOT share a real-time online database. Another pair (R and S) electronically share the same real-time online prescription database. The patient requests refill transfers, all pharmacies are properly registered, and no separate restrictions apply. Under current federal requirements and Massachusetts pharmacy law, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: A refill transfer between X and Y is generally limited to one transfer and must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists under the federal controlled-substance transfer procedure.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25(a) provides a one-time rule for Schedule III–V refill transfers between pharmacies lacking a shared real-time online database. Subsection (b)(1) requires direct pharmacist-to-pharmacist communication.

options.option_text: A Massachusetts certified pharmacy technician may independently communicate the Schedule IV refill transfer with on-duty pharmacist approval because technician transfer authority extends to every Schedule II–VI prescription.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) allows a certified technician with pharmacist approval to transfer Schedule VI prescriptions. It does not extend to Schedule IV transfers; federal 21 CFR 1306.25(b)(1) requires two licensed pharmacists.

options.option_text: R and S may use the shared real-time online database exception for additional Schedule IV refill transfers, but only within the refills legally available and authorized by the prescriber.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25(a) permits multiple transfers when pharmacies electronically share a real-time online database, only up to the maximum authorized refills and applicable law; the other documentation requirements remain.

options.option_text: The original and transferred Schedule IV prescription records must be retained for at least two years measured from the date of the last refill.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25(c) requires both original and transferred prescription records be kept two years from the last refill; that clock is not simply two years after the original issue date.

questions.question_stem: At 8:15 a.m., appropriately trained personnel begin preparing a patient-specific immediate-use compounded sterile preparation (CSP) in a hospital patient-care area. They use TWO vials of the same sterile drug, ONE vial of Sterile Water for Injection, and ONE bag of sterile normal saline: four physical containers, but three different sterile products. Aseptic technique, compatibility, preparation-specific conditions, and all other USP <797> immediate-use requirements are satisfied. A different clinician, not witnessed by the preparer, will begin administration at 12:05 p.m. The CSP bears the required immediate-use label. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: USP <797> §1.3 Immediate-Use CSPs; USP official <797> FAQs (Dec. 11, 2023), items 22, 25, 40

options.option_text: The CSP must be discarded because immediate-use preparations are limited to three physical vials or bags, regardless of whether they contain the same sterile product.
options.original_rationale: USP <797> limits immediate-use preparation to three DIFFERENT sterile products, not three total containers. Two vials of an identical sterile drug count as one different product.

options.option_text: The CSP must be discarded because administration must start within one hour of the end of compounding, even when all other immediate-use requirements are satisfied.
options.original_rationale: The revised USP <797> immediate-use standard permits administration to begin within four hours following the START of preparation, not a universal one-hour period following completion.

options.option_text: The CSP can qualify for immediate-use administration because it contains only three different sterile products, administration begins within four hours of the start, and the required label is present.
options.original_rationale: USP <797> Section 1.3 and USP's official FAQs permit multiple containers of the same sterile product as long as there are no more than three different sterile products. From 8:15 a.m. to 12:05 p.m. is 3 hours 50 minutes, within the four-hour start-of-preparation limit. When the preparer does not administer or witness administration, the immediate-use label is required.

options.option_text: The CSP may be administered as late as 12:35 p.m. because the four-hour period begins when preparation is finished rather than when it starts.
options.original_rationale: The four-hour immediate-use clock starts when preparation BEGINS (8:15 a.m. in this case); administration at 12:35 p.m. would exceed that time limit regardless of the completion time.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist has all required CDTM qualifications and a current MCSR. A supervising physician and pharmacist have signed a collaborative practice agreement with written diabetes-management prescribing protocols. A 52-year-old patient has a patient-specific written referral identifying diabetes, has provided written informed consent, and is already receiving metformin (Massachusetts Schedule VI) prescribed by that physician. The pharmacist proposes to modify the metformin dose under the protocol. No urgent circumstances or other legal restrictions apply. Which plan is FULLY consistent with 247 CMR 16.03 and 16.04?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)–(e), 16.04(1)–(2): community CDTM patient referral, limited prescribing, and physician notification

options.option_text: Modify metformin under the protocol, document the change in the patient's medical record, and forward a copy of the modification to the supervising physician within 72 hours.
options.original_rationale: The appropriate therapy and medical-record documentation are not enough: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)2 requires a copy of a modification to be provided to the supervising physician within 24 hours of issuance unless more urgent notification is needed.

options.option_text: Modify metformin under the protocol and send the physician a copy within 24 hours, but record the action only in a pharmacy dispensing worksheet rather than the patient's medical record.
options.original_rationale: The 24-hour notification is appropriate, but 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)2 and 16.04(2)(e) also require the action to be noted in the patient's medical record; a dispensing worksheet alone does not satisfy that duty.

options.option_text: Modify metformin under the protocol, note the action in the patient's medical record, and send the supervising physician a copy of the modification within 24 hours.
options.original_rationale: The patient-specific referral, written consent, covered diagnosis, authorized Schedule VI therapy, permanent medical-record documentation, and 24-hour transmission of the medication modification satisfy the stated community-CDTM requirements.

options.option_text: Instead of modifying metformin, use the same CDTM agreement to increase the patient's Schedule IV clonazepam dose after the supervising physician verbally approves and receives written notice within 24 hours.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)3 prohibits a community-pharmacy CDTM pharmacist from prescribing Schedule II through V controlled substances even if the physician approves and receives prompt notice.

questions.question_stem: At a Massachusetts community pharmacy, a properly qualified pharmacist administers an indicated recombinant zoster vaccine to a 55-year-old patient under a valid standing order. All screening and pre-administration VIS requirements are met. At the visit, the patient completes a Massachusetts Immunization Information System (MIIS) data-sharing objection form and gives it directly to the pharmacist. The pharmacy has MIIS GUI access and no regulatory waiver. Which response MOST accurately satisfies Massachusetts requirements?
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 222.100(A) and 222.105(A)–(B): immunization reporting and MIIS data-sharing objections

options.option_text: Do not report this dose to MIIS because the patient's written data-sharing objection exempts the pharmacy from submitting the immunization record.
options.original_rationale: 105 CMR 222.100 requires reporting of new immunizations within 72 hours. An objection to MIIS data sharing limits access among MIIS users; it does not cancel the provider's reporting duty.

options.option_text: Report the immunization to MIIS within 72 hours; forward the objection form to DPH within 24 hours of receipt and change the patient's MIIS data-sharing status in the GUI.
options.original_rationale: 105 CMR 222.100(A) requires reporting within 72 hours. Section 222.105(B)(2) separately requires a provider receiving the objection form to send it to DPH within 24 hours and update the recipient's data-sharing status in the MIIS GUI.

options.option_text: Report the immunization within 72 hours and retain the objection in the pharmacy's records, but leave the patient's MIIS data-sharing setting unchanged until DPH contacts the pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: The provider must not merely retain the objection: 105 CMR 222.105(B)(2) requires the form to be returned to DPH within 24 hours and the sharing status to be changed in the GUI.

options.option_text: Forward the patient's objection form to DPH within 72 hours, then report the vaccination only if the patient subsequently withdraws the objection.
options.original_rationale: The form must be forwarded within 24 hours of receipt, not 72 hours. The dose must still be reported within 72 hours even when data sharing has been restricted.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy fills a NEW oral antibiotic suspension and sends it to a patient who elected delivery to their home. The pharmacy provides the patient with a toll-free number enabling direct contact with its pharmacist; the patient is reached, is offered pharmacist counseling, and expressly declines. A pharmacy technician prepares the package, and the pharmacist has not yet performed the prospective drug utilization review (DUR). Assume no inpatient exception or other special waiver applies. Which actions or conclusions are consistent with Massachusetts law? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §21A; 247 CMR 9.17 and 9.18(9); 130 CMR 406.446: mail-delivery counseling, DUR, refusal and measuring devices

options.option_text: For a patient electing delivery away from the pharmacy, access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist may satisfy the statutory counseling-access requirement.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.94C, §21A allows counseling-access obligations for delivery outside a pharmacy to be met by giving the recipient access to a toll-free telephone service for communication with the pharmacist.

options.option_text: The technician's completion of a computerized interaction screen substitutes for the pharmacist's prospective DUR, allowing this new prescription to be released without pharmacist review.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.94C, §21A and 247 CMR 9.17 place the prospective drug review responsibility on a pharmacist before a new prescription is dispensed or delivered. A technician's computerized screening alone does not replace it.

options.option_text: The pharmacy should record the patient's refusal of counseling in the appropriate patient record or signature log, even though the offer was made.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.94C, §21A requires reasonable efforts to document patient information, including any failure to accept a counseling offer; 130 CMR 406.446 likewise specifies documenting patient refusals for MassHealth prescriptions.

options.option_text: The pharmacist or pharmacy must dispense or recommend an appropriate measuring device for the liquid antibiotic suspension.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.18(9) requires a pharmacy and pharmacist to dispense or recommend a proper measuring device with liquid medications, independent of the patient's decision to decline counseling.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses prescribed gabapentin (Massachusetts Schedule VI), a Schedule IV tramadol prescription, and naloxone to eligible Massachusetts residents. A separate patient receives gabapentin from a federal Veterans Affairs (VA) pharmacy. The community pharmacy is reviewing its MassPAT data obligations and what prescribers will see on patient PMP profiles. Assume no waivers apply to the community pharmacy. Which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1),(5),(8); DPH Pharmacy Reporting and Data Submission: Gabapentin, VA dispensings, and naloxone

options.option_text: Prescribed gabapentin dispensed at the Massachusetts community pharmacy must be reported to the PMP, even though it remains a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug.
options.original_rationale: Massachusetts DPH designates gabapentin an additional drug for PMP reporting under 105 CMR 700.012. Schedule VI classification does not remove the community pharmacy's reporting obligation.

options.option_text: The VA pharmacy's gabapentin dispensing may not appear in MassPAT because federal VA reporting is limited by statute to federally controlled Schedule II–V prescriptions.
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts DPH reporting guidance explains that VA pharmacies are limited by federal statute to reporting Schedule II–V dispensings, so their Schedule VI gabapentin transactions will not appear on a patient's PMP report.

options.option_text: An out-of-state mail pharmacy delivering prescribed gabapentin to a Massachusetts resident is exempt from Massachusetts PMP reporting solely because gabapentin is not federally scheduled.
options.original_rationale: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) extends reporting to covered out-of-state pharmacies delivering controlled substances or designated additional drugs to people in Massachusetts. Gabapentin's federal unscheduled status alone is not an exemption.

options.option_text: DPH permits naloxone dispensing information to be included in daily PMP submissions for data collection; that naloxone information does not appear on the patient's PMP profile, and patient ID collection is not required for those dispensings.
options.original_rationale: Massachusetts DPH describes daily PMP submission as its preferred naloxone-reporting method under M.G.L. c.94C §19B, clarifies that naloxone entries are data-collection-only and not visible on patient profiles, and does not require patient ID for naloxone submissions.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered Massachusetts retail pharmacy executed a valid PAPER DEA Form 222 on September 1, 2026, ordering ten commercial containers of a Schedule II medication. The supplier shipped four containers on September 12. It can ship the other six 45 days after the form was executed, directly to the registered location printed on the order. The pharmacy maintains a copy of its order and is able to document the actual quantity and receipt date for each shipment. No military procurement or other exception applies. Which statement BEST describes the lawful procedure under 21 CFR 1305.13?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1305.13(a)–(e): DEA Form 222 partial shipments, location, purchaser records and 60-day limit

options.option_text: The supplier may supply the remaining six containers through additional shipments within 60 days of the form date, and the purchaser must record the containers furnished and the receipt dates on its retained copy.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1305.13(b) permits partial shipments completing the balance within 60 days after the Form 222 date. Subsection (e) requires the purchaser to record the number of containers received and receipt dates on its retained copy.

options.option_text: The first partial shipment automatically closes the paper DEA Form 222, so an entirely new form is required for the remaining six containers even within 60 days.
options.original_rationale: A supplier may supply the unfilled balance of a Form 222 in later partial shipments during the 60-day validity period. A new form is not inherently necessary merely because the first shipment was partial.
