options.option_text: The 60-day validity clock starts with the first shipment on September 12 rather than the execution date, so the supplier can ship the balance for 60 days after that shipment.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1305.13(b) measures the 60-day limit from the date of the DEA Form 222 as executed by the purchaser, not from the first shipment or the supplier's acknowledgment.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may redirect the remaining containers to a different branch with its own DEA registration without changing the paper DEA Form 222 because both locations belong to the same owner.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1305.13(c) generally requires the supplier to ship to the purchaser and location printed on the Form 222. Common ownership and separate DEA registration do not independently authorize delivery to another location.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy technician trainee is 19 years old and has worked 1,505 cumulative hours as a trainee over ten months. The person has neither obtained a pharmacy technician license nor received a Board extension, and no other exception to the trainee employment limit applies. A pharmacist offers to supervise the trainee for another month and asks the trainee to accept new verbal prescriptions from prescribers during that period. Which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.03(4)(b)–(c), 8.03(5): trainee scope and 1,500-hour/one-year limit

options.option_text: The trainee can continue filling prescriptions until one full year has elapsed but must refer telephone prescriptions to the pharmacist.
options.original_rationale: The employment limit in 247 CMR 8.03(5) is 1,500 hours OR one year, whichever occurs first, absent a stated exception. Already exceeding 1,500 hours disqualifies continued trainee work despite having fewer than 12 months of experience.

options.option_text: The trainee may continue working if a certified pharmacy technician directly supervises the filling work and a pharmacist later validates each prescription.
options.original_rationale: The regulation requires direct supervision by a pharmacist and does not permit additional trainee employment beyond the statutory hour limit through certified-technician supervision or a final pharmacist check. Taking prescriptions by telephone is also prohibited for trainees.

options.option_text: The trainee cannot continue working as a trainee under these facts, and receiving prescriptions by telephone is prohibited for trainees even before reaching the employment limit.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.03(5) bars trainee employment after 1,500 hours or one year, whichever is shorter, absent an exception; none applies. Separately, 247 CMR 8.03(4)(c) prohibits a trainee from taking prescriptions over the telephone.

options.option_text: The trainee may restart a new 1,500-hour limit on January 1 because the trainee-hour maximum is measured separately for each calendar year.
options.original_rationale: The regulatory 1,500-hour trainee period is cumulative employment, not an annual allowance that resets each January. The pharmacist cannot create an exception by changing the calendar year.

questions.question_stem: In November 2026, a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist with the appropriate contraceptive-prescribing training and an NPI evaluates a clinically eligible adult requesting a first oral hormonal contraceptive. The pharmacist uses the required self-screening risk assessment, provides counseling, and will meet all documentation and dispensing requirements. No previous contraception prescription, CDTM agreement, or primary-care visit is documented. Under M.G.L. c.94C §19F and current DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19F(a)–(c); DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 (Aug. 25, 2026), Hormonal Contraceptives

options.option_text: The pharmacist may prescribe an eligible FDA-approved self-administered oral hormonal contraceptive without proof that a primary care practitioner previously prescribed contraception for this patient.
options.original_rationale: The amended §19F(a) authorizes pharmacist-initiated oral hormonal contraceptive prescribing regardless of the patient's previous prescription history, provided applicable screening, training and clinical safeguards are met.

options.option_text: A patient-specific collaborative drug therapy management agreement or authorization from a physician is a mandatory prerequisite for an initial pharmacist-issued oral contraceptive prescription.
options.original_rationale: The independent pharmacist-prescribing authority in M.G.L. c.94C §19F does not require a CDTM agreement or a patient-specific physician prescription when the pharmacist follows its specific requirements.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must not require the patient to make a scheduled pharmacist appointment solely to obtain the authorized oral contraceptive prescription and dispensing.
options.original_rationale: The 2026 DPH circular states that a scheduled pharmacist appointment shall not be required for oral hormonal contraceptive or patch prescribing/dispensing under §19F.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may issue a valid oral hormonal contraceptive prescription for up to a 12-month supply when the required self-screening, training, counseling and other requirements are satisfied.
options.original_rationale: Circular DCP 26-08-125 permits a prescription for up to, but not more than, a 12-month supply, subject to manufacturer labeling and clinical eligibility.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts resident asks a community pharmacist for a naloxone rescue kit to keep available for a coworker at risk of overdose. The resident has no individual naloxone prescription and wants to use the resident's own prescription insurance. The pharmacy participates in the Massachusetts statewide naloxone standing order; no coverage exclusion or other dispensing restriction is present. Which workflow is MOST consistent with Massachusetts law and Board Policy 2024-01?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19B(b)–(e); MA Board Policy 2024-01 Naloxone Dispensing, §§I(B), I(D)–(G)

options.option_text: Decline to dispense until the coworker is present and presents an individual naloxone prescription, because insurance billing must be under the intended recipient's name.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.94C §19B and the statewide standing order permit a person to obtain naloxone to administer to someone else. An individual prescription or the intended recipient's presence is not necessary under that pathway.

options.option_text: Provide naloxone only as a retail OTC purchase; the statewide standing order cannot be used when the purchaser intends to help another individual.
options.original_rationale: The statewide standing order expressly supports dispensing to a person purchasing naloxone for another individual, including handling the transaction as a prescription for insurance billing.

options.option_text: Dispense under the standing order but bill the coworker's prescription insurance even though the purchaser is the resident, because the coworker will ultimately use the medication.
options.original_rationale: For insurance billing and cost sharing, §19B(e) directs the pharmacy to treat the purchaser as the prescription recipient regardless of who ultimately uses the antagonist. Billing the coworker solely because of intended use would disregard this distinction.

options.option_text: Dispense under the statewide standing order, make a reasonable effort to identify and bill the purchaser's insurance, and provide naloxone counseling and the required opioid-antagonist information material.
options.original_rationale: M.G.L. c.94C §19B permits third-party naloxone purchase and calls for reasonable purchaser-insurance identification/claim submission unless the purchaser elects to pay out of pocket. Board Policy 2024-01 also requires counseling and an opioid-antagonist information pamphlet.

questions.question_stem: A self-certified Massachusetts community pharmacy sells scheduled listed pseudoephedrine products in person, not by mail order or mobile vendor. A purchaser who presents valid government-issued photo identification has already bought 2.70 grams of pseudoephedrine BASE on the current calendar day and 8.30 grams during the relevant rolling 30-day period (including today's earlier purchases). All proposed quantities below are stated in pseudoephedrine BASE equivalents; there is no other applicable restriction or exemption. Which proposed transaction is legally permissible under the federal CMEA rules?
questions.author_citation: 21 U.S.C. §§830(d)–(e), 844(a); 21 CFR 1314.20, 1314.25: retail pseudoephedrine base limits and sales records

options.option_text: Sell an additional 0.90 grams with a signed log entry, because the calendar-day amount becomes exactly 3.60 grams.
options.original_rationale: The single-day quantity would be within the 3.6-gram daily limit, but the 30-day total would become 9.20 grams, above the separate 9-gram purchaser limit in 21 U.S.C. §844(a). Both limits must be satisfied.
options.independent_option_analysis: 0.9g would yield 9.2g in 30d despite daily 3.6g.

options.option_text: Sell an additional 0.60 grams with compliant photo-ID verification and logbook documentation, because the daily and rolling 30-day totals remain below their respective limits.
options.original_rationale: The resulting quantities are 3.30 grams today (2.70 + 0.60), below 3.60 grams, and 8.90 grams in 30 days (8.30 + 0.60), below 9.00 grams. The seller must also comply with the behind-the-counter and logbook requirements.
options.independent_option_analysis: 0.6g yields 3.3g today and 8.9g 30d, both lawful if identification/logbook satisfied.

options.option_text: Sell an additional 0.75 grams in two separate transactions at different registers, each with its own log entry, because no single transaction exceeds the daily limit.
options.original_rationale: Splitting does not evade the aggregate purchase limit. The 30-day total would be 9.05 grams, above 9.00 grams, even though the same-day total would be 3.45 grams.
options.independent_option_analysis: Splitting 0.75g into registers does not avoid 9.05g 30d maximum.

options.option_text: Sell an additional 0.60 grams without a photo ID or logbook signature because a quantity below the 3.60-gram daily ceiling is exempt from the identification requirement.
options.original_rationale: The low quantity does not create a general photo-ID and logbook exception; normal CMEA retail identification and recordkeeping apply to this sale.
options.independent_option_analysis: Under-limits sales are not a blanket exemption from retail ID/logbook requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts institutional pharmacy handles a NIOSH Table 1 ANTINEOPLASTIC hazardous drug that must be crushed or otherwise manipulated for compounding. A portion of the same hazardous antineoplastic inventory requires refrigeration. The facility is reviewing compliant hazardous-drug storage under USP <800>; assume no other exemption applies. Which requirements or conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: USP <800> §5.2 Storage; USP <800> FAQs (Jan. 21, 2026), questions 25, 26 and 28; NIOSH 2024 HD list classification

options.option_text: The Table 1 antineoplastic stock requiring manipulation must be stored separately from nonhazardous inventory in an externally ventilated negative-pressure room with at least 12 air changes per hour.
options.original_rationale: USP <800> storage requirements, summarized in USP's January 2026 FAQs, apply to NIOSH Table 1 antineoplastic drugs requiring manipulation beyond counting/repackaging final dosage forms. Such stock requires separation and externally vented negative-pressure storage with at least 12 ACPH.

options.option_text: All sterile and nonsterile hazardous drugs must always be stored in separate rooms, regardless of their other storage or compounding conditions.
options.original_rationale: USP <800> permits storage of sterile and nonsterile hazardous drugs together, although hazardous inventory for nonsterile compounding should not be stored inside the sterile compounding area to avoid unnecessary traffic.

options.option_text: Refrigerated NIOSH Table 1 antineoplastic drugs must be kept in a dedicated hazardous-drug refrigerator located in a negative-pressure area with at least 12 air changes per hour.
options.original_rationale: USP <800> requires refrigerated Table 1 antineoplastic hazardous drugs to be kept in a dedicated refrigerator in an appropriate negative-pressure storage or containment area with at least 12 ACPH.

options.option_text: Negative pressure may be shut off overnight when the hazardous-drug storage room is unoccupied, provided the ventilation is restored before handling resumes.
options.original_rationale: USP <800> requires the negative-pressure condition of the hazardous-drug storage room to be maintained at all times; reducing or turning it off during nonuse is not permitted.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacist allowed a Massachusetts registration to expire on December 31, 2022, but has continuously practiced under an unrestricted New Hampshire license. In November 2026, the pharmacist wants to resume work in a Massachusetts community pharmacy. Neither license has been suspended or revoked, and no military-service extension or waiver applies. The pharmacist can document the required continuing education and pay the outstanding fees. Which statement BEST describes the Massachusetts reactivation requirements?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 4.02(3)-(5), pharmacy practice not authorized after license expiration; Massachusetts Board Policy 2020-01 (adopted Feb. 6, 2020, revised May 14, 2021) reactivation after expiration more than one renewal cycle; Board approval of petition first, MPJE pass before license reactivation

options.option_text: The pharmacist must complete the reactivation process, pass the MPJE, and satisfy the Board's other conditions before resuming Massachusetts practice.
options.original_rationale: Under 247 CMR 4.02(5), an otherwise nondisciplinary registration that has expired for more than two years requires passing the MPJE and meeting Board conditions before renewal. The current Massachusetts Pharmacist Licensing page describes reactivation application approval followed by MPJE eligibility. Active practice in another state does not itself reactivate the Massachusetts registration.

options.option_text: Payment of the overdue fees and proof of current CE restore authority to practice as soon as a complete application is submitted.
options.original_rationale: Submitting the application and paying fees do not establish an active Massachusetts registration. The greater-than-two-year lapse invokes the additional requirements of 247 CMR 4.02(5). Practicing while the registration remains expired is unlicensed practice under 4.02(3).

options.option_text: Continuous practice under the New Hampshire license eliminates the MPJE requirement, although the pharmacist must still submit CE and fees.
options.original_rationale: The greater-than-two-year expiration rule does not contain an automatic MPJE exemption for a pharmacist who has practiced in another jurisdiction. Other-state license verification is part of the reactivation process, not a substitute for the required examination.

options.option_text: Every pharmacist whose registration has expired for more than two years must automatically retake both the NAPLEX and the MPJE.
options.original_rationale: Section 4.02(5) expressly requires the MPJE and other Board-determined conditions; it does not automatically mandate the NAPLEX for every nondisciplinary expiration. The stem does not describe a suspended or revoked license, and Board-specific conditions should not be converted into a universal NAPLEX requirement.

questions.question_stem: A patient diagnosed with chlamydia brings two separate, otherwise valid prescriptions from an authorized Massachusetts practitioner: one for the patient's own treatment and a signed paper prescription for an unexamined sex partner. The second prescription uses 'EPT' instead of the partner's name and address. The partner's identity is unavailable. The pharmacist has no clinical reason to withhold the appropriately prescribed Schedule VI therapy. Which dispensing approach is BEST supported by Massachusetts requirements?
questions.author_citation: MA Board/DCP Policy 2020-08, sections I-II; 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) and 721.070(A)(7); 105 CMR 700.003 EPT provision

options.option_text: Request a replacement electronic prescription identifying the partner by name and address before dispensing the partner's treatment.
options.original_rationale: The EPT framework expressly permits 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the partner's name and address. An otherwise lawful paper EPT prescription is also covered by the ePrescribing exception in 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7); a replacement is not necessary solely for these features.

options.option_text: Fill both prescriptions under the diagnosed patient's profile and place the patient's name on both labels because that patient is collecting the drugs.
options.original_rationale: The partner's treatment requires its own prescription and appropriate EPT profile and label. The collecting patient's identity should not be substituted as the treated recipient merely because the patient presents both prescriptions.

options.option_text: Process the partner's separate prescription using an EPT patient profile and an EPT label rather than substituting the diagnosed patient's identity.
options.original_rationale: Board/Drug Control Program Policy 2020-08 permits a separate EPT prescription for chlamydia with 'EPT' replacing the partner's name and address and directs creation of the corresponding EPT patient profile and prescription label. The absence of a direct examination is intrinsic to authorized EPT, not an automatic reason for refusal.

options.option_text: Require confirmation that the practitioner examined the partner before dispensing, even though the prescription is expressly designated EPT.
options.original_rationale: The Massachusetts EPT policy concerns treatment of the sex partner of a person diagnosed with chlamydia without examining or testing that partner. Requiring a prior examination in every such case would defeat this specifically authorized pathway. Clinical concerns must still be addressed when present.

questions.question_stem: An adult submits a valid request directly to a HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy for an electronic PDF copy of the adult's own prescription and billing records. The records belong to the designated record set and are held electronically by the pharmacy's business associate. A PDF is readily producible. Identity has been verified, but the patient owes an unrelated unpaid prescription bill. No permitted ground for denying access or special confidentiality restriction applies. Considering the federal HIPAA access rule, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.524(b)(2), (c)(2)(ii), (c)(4); HHS individual-access FAQs on unpaid bills, fees and business-associate records

options.option_text: The pharmacy may withhold the records until the patient pays the outstanding prescription bill, even if any lawful copying charge has been paid.
options.original_rationale: HHS expressly states that unpaid charges for health care services are not a basis for denying an individual's access to their own PHI. Any permissible copying fee is a separate matter and does not turn the unrelated prescription debt into a lawful access condition.

options.option_text: Any fee charged for the copy must be reasonable and cost-based; permitted copying labor may be included, but search and retrieval costs may not.
options.original_rationale: 45 CFR 164.524(c)(4) limits an individual's copy fee to specified costs, including copying labor and applicable supplies or postage. HHS clarifies that searching for and retrieving the records are not chargeable components of this individual-access fee. This request is for the patient's own copy, not a third-party records request.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must provide the electronic PDF requested rather than insist on paper solely for administrative convenience.
options.original_rationale: Under 45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(ii), electronically maintained PHI must be provided in the requested electronic form and format when readily producible. The stem establishes that PDF is readily producible, so convenience alone does not justify substituting paper.

options.option_text: Because the business associate holds the records off-site, the pharmacy automatically has 60 days to respond without sending an extension notice.
options.original_rationale: The ordinary outer limit is 30 calendar days from receipt of the request, including when records are held by a business associate. Only one extension of up to 30 additional days is available when needed, with written reasons and a completion date provided within the initial period. Off-site storage does not automatically grant 60 days.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives an otherwise valid in-state electronic Schedule II prescription for 60 tablets. At 4:00 p.m. Friday, it dispenses its only 10 tablets and records a partial fill solely because of insufficient stock. The patient is not terminally ill or an LTCF resident. Neither the patient nor prescriber has requested a partial fill under the separate request-based pathway. The remaining stock arrives at 5:00 p.m. Monday; no clock change occurred over the weekend. What is the MOST appropriate action under the stock-shortage partial-fill provision?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1306.13(a), contrasted with 1306.13(b)-(c) and 105 CMR 721.055

options.option_text: Dispense the remaining 50 tablets under the original prescription because fewer than 30 days have elapsed since it was issued.
options.original_rationale: The separate 30-day request-based pathway is not the documented basis for this partial fill. Under 21 CFR 1306.13(a), the stock-shortage balance must be supplied within 72 hours of the first partial filling; the stem expressly excludes the other pathways.

options.option_text: Start a new 72-hour completion period when the shipment arrives and dispense the balance within that new period.
options.original_rationale: The shortage deadline runs from the first partial dispensing, not from replenishment or the date the pharmacist learns that stock is available. New inventory does not restart the clock.

options.option_text: Dispense the balance because Saturday and Sunday are excluded when calculating the 72-hour completion period.
options.original_rationale: The regulation specifies 72 hours, not 72 business hours. Friday at 4:00 p.m. to Monday at 5:00 p.m. is 73 elapsed hours when no clock change occurs, so the shortage-completion period has ended.

options.option_text: Do not dispense the remaining balance under the original shortage partial fill; notify the prescriber, and obtain a new prescription before supplying any further quantity.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(a) requires prescriber notification when the balance is not or cannot be filled within 72 hours and states that no further quantity may be supplied beyond that period without a new prescription. The state request-based rule in 105 CMR 721.055 is a distinct route, not an automatic extension of this shortage fill.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has modified its DEA registration to become an authorized collector and meets applicable state and environmental requirements. Its patient drug-collection receptacle is at the pharmacy's registered premises, not at an LTCF. The inner liner needs replacement. Separately, the pharmacy has expired Schedule II stock that has never been dispensed to a patient. Which procedures comply with the federal disposal rules? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Place the expired pharmacy stock into the patient collection receptacle after documenting a deduction from the pharmacy's inventory.
options.original_rationale: A patient collection receptacle is not a disposal route for the registrant's own controlled-substance inventory. The pharmacy must use an authorized registrant-disposal method under 21 CFR 1317.05(a), such as transfer to a reverse distributor; an inventory entry does not convert the stock into an ultimate-user return.

options.option_text: Have the inner liner installed and removed by, or under the supervision of, at least two collector employees, and have two employees seal it immediately upon removal.
options.original_rationale: For this on-site retail receptacle, 21 CFR 1317.75(g) requires at least two collector employees for installation/removal or their supervision. Section 1317.60(c) additionally requires two employees to seal the liner immediately after removal. The separate LTCF staffing rules are not the scenario presented.

options.option_text: Reopen the sealed liner with two pharmacist witnesses to count the controlled substances before sending it for destruction.
options.original_rationale: Two witnesses do not create an exception to the prohibition. Under 21 CFR 1317.60(c), a sealed liner must not be opened, x-rayed, analyzed or otherwise penetrated. Section 1317.75(c) also prohibits counting, sorting or inventorying individual contents after deposit.

options.option_text: Arrange a lawful transfer of the pharmacy's expired stock to a registered reverse distributor separately from the ultimate-user collection process.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(2) authorizes disposal of practitioner inventory through delivery to a reverse distributor by the permitted pickup/carrier arrangements. Applicable controlled-substance transfer records and state requirements still apply; this is distinct from accepting patients' medications into a collection receptacle.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy's Manager of Record (MOR) is unexpectedly hospitalized. The pharmacy learns that the MOR is likely to be unavailable for 45 days, cannot participate in the controlled-substance inventory, and has not resigned or been terminated. A Massachusetts-registered staff pharmacist is available to help. The absence ultimately lasts 105 days. Under 247 CMR 9.23(5), which response MOST completely satisfies the requirements?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.23(5)(b)–(d); MA Board Information for Managers of Record (unplanned absence guidance)

options.option_text: Appoint a Board-registered Interim Manager within five days of the unplanned absence; have another registered pharmacist perform the required controlled-substance inventory because the MOR is unavailable; submit an application to change the MOR when the absence reaches 100 days.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 9.23(5)(b) requires an Interim Manager within five days of an unplanned absence likely to last at least 30 days. Section 9.23(5)(c) allows another registered pharmacist to perform the controlled-substance inventory if the MOR is unexpectedly unavailable. Section 9.23(5)(d) requires a change-of-MOR application if the absence reaches 100 days.

options.option_text: Appoint an Interim Manager within 14 calendar days; have another registered pharmacist complete the required inventory; submit a change-of-MOR application when the absence reaches 100 days.
options.original_rationale: The inventory and 100-day elements are appropriate, but the deadline for appointing an Interim Manager for this unplanned absence is five days, not 14. The separate notification period for a resignation or change of MOR is not the interim-appointment deadline.

options.option_text: Appoint an Interim Manager within five days and file a change-of-MOR application after 100 days, but postpone the controlled-substance inventory until the hospitalized MOR can sign it.
options.original_rationale: An unexpected absence does not waive the inventory requirement. The regulation specifically provides that another registered pharmacist shall perform the controlled-substance inventory if the MOR is unexpectedly unavailable.

options.option_text: Appoint an Interim Manager within five days and have another registered pharmacist perform the inventory; a change-of-MOR application is unnecessary after 100 days as long as the Interim Manager remains licensed.
options.original_rationale: An Interim Manager's continuing licensure does not erase the separate 100-day threshold in 247 CMR 9.23(5)(d). An application for a change of MOR is required when the original MOR has been away for 100 days or more.

questions.question_stem: A specially certified Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives an otherwise valid prescription for mifepristone for medication abortion from a certified prescriber. The required Patient Agreement Form has been completed, the pharmacy has verified prescriber certification, and no clinical or other state-law restriction is present. The pharmacy's tracked shipping service estimates the medication will reach the patient MORE THAN FOUR CALENDAR DAYS after the pharmacy received the prescription. Under the FDA Mifepristone REMS, which action is MOST appropriate?
questions.author_citation: FDA Mifepristone REMS Pharmacy Agreement requirements; FDA 2023 REMS modification review, pharmacy certification §2(a)(iv)(b)–(c)

options.option_text: Ship without additional contact because using a tracked carrier automatically waives the REMS delivery timeframe.
options.original_rationale: Tracking is a separate pharmacy-certification safeguard. When delivery will take more than four calendar days after receipt of the prescription, the REMS also requires confirmation with the certified prescriber that dispensing remains appropriate and documentation of the decision.

options.option_text: Require in-person pickup, because a certified retail pharmacy may not dispense mifepristone through a shipping service.
options.original_rationale: The current Mifepristone REMS permits dispensing by specially certified retail pharmacies and does not impose a categorical in-person dispensing rule. The pharmacy must follow tracking and other REMS safeguards.

options.option_text: Reject the prescription permanently and require a new prescription even if the certified prescriber determines that delayed delivery would still be appropriate.
options.original_rationale: The REMS provides a mechanism for delayed delivery: contact and confirm the certified prescriber's clinical determination and document it. It does not universally require a newly issued prescription merely because shipping exceeds four calendar days.

options.option_text: Contact the certified prescriber, confirm that dispensing remains appropriate despite delivery taking more than four calendar days, document the prescriber's decision, and use a compliant tracked service if dispensing proceeds.
options.original_rationale: The FDA-approved pharmacy-certification requirements specifically direct a certified pharmacy to confirm with the prescriber the appropriateness of dispensing when delivery exceeds four calendar days after receipt of the prescription, and to document that decision. Tracked shipping and all other REMS safeguards still apply.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses a routine Schedule VI medication. The patient pays its entire charge out of pocket and explicitly asks the pharmacy NOT to disclose information solely about that prescription to the patient's health plan for PAYMENT or HEALTH CARE OPERATIONS. No law independently requires such a disclosure. A second, unrelated prescription is only partially paid for by the patient; the health plan pays the rest, and the pharmacy has not voluntarily agreed to a restriction for it. Later, another treating clinician requests relevant prescription history for treatment. Assume no other federal or Massachusetts confidentiality rule applies. Which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.522(a)(1)(vi) (fully paid health-plan restriction); 45 CFR 164.506 (TPO); 45 CFR 164.502(b)(2)(i) (treatment exemption)

options.option_text: The pharmacy must honor the requested health-plan restriction for the fully self-paid prescription, as long as the contemplated disclosure is for payment or health care operations and is not required by law.
options.original_rationale: 45 CFR 164.522(a)(1)(vi) requires a covered health care provider to agree to an individual's requested restriction on disclosures to a health plan for payment or health care operations if the individual paid in full for the item or service and disclosure is not otherwise required by law.

options.option_text: HIPAA automatically obligates the pharmacy to extend the identical restriction to the second prescription even though the health plan paid part of its cost.
options.original_rationale: The mandatory exception turns on full payment of the specific item or service by the individual or someone other than the health plan. The pharmacy may voluntarily agree to other restrictions, but it is not automatically required to extend this one to a different, partly plan-paid prescription.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may disclose relevant prescription history to another clinician for the patient's treatment without a separate HIPAA authorization, when otherwise permitted; the stated restriction concerning health-plan payment or operations does not itself prohibit that treatment disclosure.
options.original_rationale: The mandatory self-pay restriction concerns specified disclosures to a health plan for payment or health care operations, not all permitted treatment disclosures to another treating provider. HIPAA generally permits provider-to-provider treatment disclosures without a separate patient authorization, subject to other applicable law and any separately agreed restriction.

options.option_text: For disclosure of the fully paid prescription to a treating clinician, HIPAA always requires a minimum-necessary determination and an individual authorization before any information may be released.
options.original_rationale: Disclosures to, or requests by, a health care provider for treatment are exempt from HIPAA's minimum-necessary requirement under 45 CFR 164.502(b)(2)(i). HIPAA does not ordinarily require a signed authorization for permissible disclosures for treatment.

questions.question_stem: On May 1, 2026, a Massachusetts prescriber issues an otherwise valid Schedule IV prescription for 90 tablets with ZERO authorized refills. The patient requests and receives 30 tablets on May 3 and another 30 tablets on June 3 as documented PARTIAL FILLS of the same 90-tablet prescription. On November 14, 2026, the patient asks for the last 30 tablets. Assume no change in prescriber authorization, no other restriction, and all relevant pharmacy documentation was made for the earlier installments. Under the federal Schedule III–V partial-filling rule, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1306.23(a)–(c) (Schedule III–V partial fills); 21 CFR 1306.22(a) (Schedule III–IV refills); DEA Pharmacist's Manual, partial dispensing

options.option_text: The June partial dispensing was automatically unlawful because the prescription authorized zero refills, even though the total dispensed had not reached 90 tablets.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.23 permits a Schedule III–V prescription to be partially filled and requires each partial to be recorded in the same manner as a refill. A partial fill of the original prescribed total is not automatically a new authorized refill merely because the documentation resembles refill records.

options.option_text: Each partial filling must be documented in the same manner as a refilling, and the combined quantity from all portions cannot exceed the prescribed 90 tablets.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.23(a) requires refill-style records for each partial filling; subsection (b) prohibits the sum of all partial quantities from exceeding the amount prescribed.

options.option_text: The final 30 tablets cannot be supplied on November 14 under the May 1 prescription, because no Schedule III–V partial dispensing is allowed more than six months after the original issue date.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.23(c) bars partial dispensing after six months from the date the prescription was issued. November 14 is well beyond six months from May 1, even though some of the original prescribed quantity remains.

options.option_text: A pharmacist cannot reset the six-month clock by documenting the June 3 installment as a refill; the six months are measured from the original prescription issue date.
options.original_rationale: The six-month maximum in 21 CFR 1306.23(c) runs from the date the practitioner issued the original prescription, not the date of the most recent partial dispensing or pharmacy record entry.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed originating retail pharmacy uses a properly licensed and DEA-registered central-fill pharmacy. The shared-service records, patient notice and opt-out mechanism, relevant DEA requirements, and all other conditions are satisfied. Three different prescriptions are to be centrally filled: Schedule II oxycodone, Massachusetts Schedule VI gabapentin (reportable to MassPAT), and Massachusetts Schedule VI lisinopril (not reportable to MassPAT). Under the Board's Shared Pharmacy Services Policy 2021-02, as revised February 6, 2025, which delivery plan is MOST appropriate?
questions.author_citation: MA Board Policy 2021-02, revised Feb. 6, 2025, §§III(k)–(l), IV(b)(i)–(v), Shared Pharmacy Service Models

options.option_text: Have the central-fill pharmacy send gabapentin and lisinopril directly to the patient while sending oxycodone to the originating pharmacy, because only federally scheduled drugs need to be routed through the originating pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: The central-fill policy specifically excludes Schedule VI products requiring MassPAT reporting, such as gabapentin, from the Schedule VI direct-to-patient shipment exception. Gabapentin's federal nonscheduled status alone does not make direct shipment from central fill permissible.

options.option_text: Send centrally filled oxycodone and gabapentin to the originating pharmacy for final dispensing; the non-PMP-reportable lisinopril may instead be shipped directly to the patient by central fill when all other requirements are met.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2021-02 IV(b)(iii) requires centrally filled Schedule II–V drugs to be delivered to the originating pharmacy. Section IV(b)(iv) permits direct patient shipment of Schedule VI drugs except those requiring PMP reporting, such as gabapentin. Lisinopril is a Schedule VI example not subject to PMP reporting.

options.option_text: Route every Schedule VI prescription through the originating pharmacy, because the Board categorically prohibits all direct-to-patient shipment from central-fill pharmacies regardless of PMP reporting.
options.original_rationale: The Board's revised policy expressly allows certain non-PMP-reportable Schedule VI prescriptions to be delivered or shipped directly from central fill to the patient. Therefore this blanket description is incorrect.

options.option_text: Send oxycodone and lisinopril directly to the patient while routing gabapentin through the originating pharmacy, because the central-fill pharmacy's DEA registration replaces the originating pharmacy's final-dispensing duty for Schedule II medications.
options.original_rationale: Even when the central-fill pharmacy is properly DEA registered, the Board policy expressly directs centrally filled Schedule II–V controlled substances to the pharmacy where the prescription originated for final dispensing, not directly to the patient.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist preceptor is comparing staffing plans for an institutional pharmacy's dispensing area and a separate, exclusively immunization-focused outreach clinic. Unless otherwise stated, every pharmacy intern holds an active Massachusetts intern license, is properly qualified for the proposed activities, and will be directly supervised; there is no separate Board waiver. Under 247 CMR 8.01 and Board Policy 2026-02, which arrangement is permissible?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.01(3)–(4),(16); Board Policy 2026-02, Section II(A)–(E) (adopted Sept. 3, 2026)

options.option_text: One pharmacist directly supervises three licensed pharmacy interns concurrently filling and dispensing prescriptions in the institutional pharmacy, because the Board permits four interns whenever a pharmacist stays on the premises.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.01(16) ordinarily limits a pharmacist preceptor to directly supervising two pharmacy interns at a time. Policy 2026-02 allows up to four only under specifically limited conditions, including an exclusive immunization clinic, not three interns concurrently filling prescriptions.

options.option_text: One pharmacist preceptor directly supervises four appropriately licensed and qualified pharmacy interns exclusively conducting an immunization clinic, with all applicable immunization requirements satisfied.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2026-02, Section II(B), expressly permits a preceptor to directly supervise up to four pharmacy interns at one time when exclusively conducting immunization clinics. Their active Massachusetts intern licenses, appropriate qualifications, and continuing direct supervision remain necessary.

options.option_text: An unlicensed PharmD student may begin a hospital internship under close preceptor supervision as long as the student does not handle Schedule II medications before obtaining a Massachusetts intern license.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2026-02, Section II(E), requires pharmacy students, including foreign pharmacy students, to be licensed as Massachusetts pharmacy interns before starting an internship in any practice setting, including hospitals. Avoiding Schedule II products does not replace intern licensure.

options.option_text: A licensed intern who works 14 hours in one day during an emergency may receive all 14 hours as Massachusetts pharmacy internship credit when the pharmacist documents the emergency.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 8.01(4) limits pharmacy internship credit to no more than 12 hours per day. An exception permitting extended work in certain circumstances does not change the independent 12-hour daily internship-credit limit.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist receives a buprenorphine/naloxone sublingual prescription for opioid use disorder from a Massachusetts-authorized practitioner with a current DEA registration that includes Schedule III authority. The pharmacist confirms a legitimate medical purpose, proper prescription elements, and compliance with all applicable state requirements. The practitioner treats more than 275 patients with OUD, has no former DATA/X-waiver number, and has satisfied the applicable federal training or alternative-qualification attestation at DEA registration renewal. Which conclusion is MOST accurate in November 2026?
questions.author_citation: Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 §§1262–1263; 21 U.S.C. §823(l); 21 CFR 1306.04(a); DEA Buprenorphine (MOUD) Q&A (Nov. 28, 2023)

options.option_text: The pharmacist must reject the prescription until the practitioner obtains a new X-waiver identifier, because the repeal applies only to patients who began treatment before 2023.
options.original_rationale: The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 eliminated the federal DATA-waiver requirement effective December 29, 2022, for authorized practitioners. This change is not limited to patients already receiving treatment, and an X-waiver number is no longer a prescription requirement.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may dispense only after confirming that the practitioner treats no more than 275 OUD patients, because the former federal patient-cap system is still enforced for office-based treatment.
options.original_rationale: The former federal DATA-waiver patient caps were removed along with the waiver requirement. The pharmacist must still evaluate an otherwise valid controlled-substance prescription and applicable state law, but the old numerical patient cap is not a federal reason to reject this prescription.

options.option_text: Before dispensing any buprenorphine prescription, federal law requires the pharmacist to obtain and retain the prescriber's eight-hour MATE Act course certificate for that individual patient.
options.original_rationale: The MATE Act training, credentialing, or education attestation is a condition associated with the qualified practitioner's first applicable DEA registration or renewal, not a requirement that the dispensing pharmacy collect a training certificate for each prescription. Recognized alternative qualification pathways also exist.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may dispense after the usual Schedule III validity and corresponding-responsibility checks; no X-waiver number or former federal patient cap is required, and MATE Act attestation is handled through the practitioner’s DEA registration process.
options.original_rationale: DEA and SAMHSA confirm that the DATA/X-waiver identifier and associated federal patient caps were eliminated. The qualified practitioner must maintain ordinary Schedule III prescribing authority, comply with applicable registration/training obligations, and issue prescriptions for a legitimate medical purpose. The pharmacist retains normal corresponding responsibility.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-authorized practitioner cannot use ePrescribing because of a temporary electrical failure. The practitioner telephones an otherwise valid Schedule IV lorazepam prescription to a community pharmacist. The pharmacist verifies the order, its legitimate medical purpose, and the prescriber's identity and records the oral prescription. No effort to circumvent ePrescribing and no other exception is involved. Which conclusions are supported by Massachusetts and federal law? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §20(a)-(c); 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2),(B),(C); 21 CFR 1306.21; DPH DCP 19-12-108 (statute/regulation follow-up day-count discrepancy noted; not resolved)
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: M.G.L. c.94C §20(c) vs 105 CMR 721.070(B) clock discrepancy (2 calendar days for eRx vs 7 business days in rules under eRx exception)
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: HOLD until authoritative interpretation reconciles statute and regulation/DPH circular; key A,C,D not proven incorrect, but do not teach a single deadline.

options.option_text: The temporary electrical failure can qualify as an ePrescribing exception; the pharmacist may accept an otherwise lawful oral Schedule IV prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) expressly permits an oral or written prescription during temporary technological or electrical failure. Federal 21 CFR 1306.21 generally allows lawful Schedule IV oral orders when ordinary authenticity and prescription requirements are satisfied.
options.independent_option_analysis: Failure exception and lawful oral Schedule IV are textually supported.

options.option_text: Because federal law permits oral Schedule IV prescriptions, Massachusetts never requires the prescriber to send a follow-up prescription documenting the oral order.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §20(c) imposes a subsequent prescription duty for oral Schedule II–V prescriptions, and 105 CMR 721.070(B) implements follow-up for oral prescriptions issued under ePrescribing exceptions. No universal absence of follow-up can be inferred from federal Schedule IV rules.
options.independent_option_analysis: No-follow-up claim is clearly wrong, but exact applicable deadline remains conflicted.

options.option_text: A separate written or electronic follow-up documenting the earlier oral order is required under Massachusetts law, and the dispensing pharmacy must associate the follow-up with its written record of the oral prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The follow-up and pharmacy record-attachment duties are supported by M.G.L. c.94C §20(c) and 105 CMR 721.070(B). The statute describes a two-day electronic default or seven-calendar-day written exception, whereas the DPH implementing rule uses seven BUSINESS days for an ePrescribing exception. Because these differ, this question deliberately does not assert one universal deadline; practitioners should comply with applicable requirements and obtain agency clarification when necessary.
options.independent_option_analysis: Follow-up record attachment text supported, clock unresolved.

options.option_text: The pharmacist is not required to independently verify that the prescriber qualifies for an ePrescribing exception when the oral prescription is otherwise valid, but must still establish authenticity and legal dispensing requirements.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 105 CMR 721.070(C) specifically relieves the pharmacist from verifying the qualifying ePrescribing exception. That narrow exception does not excuse pharmacist verification of an oral prescription's lawful source or medical legitimacy.
options.independent_option_analysis: Pharmacist not obliged to verify exception if otherwise valid; authenticity checks remain.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts walk-in retail pharmacist evaluates FOUR unrelated prescriptions written by practitioners who are not registered in Massachusetts but are properly licensed, authorized, and DEA-registered in the states where they reside or practice. Assume every prescription otherwise satisfies federal and Massachusetts requirements, no special M.G.L. c.94C §18A exception applies, and the pharmacy is not acting as a mail-order pharmacy. Under M.G.L. c.94C §18, which prescription may the pharmacist legally fill?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §18(c),(d½): out-of-state Schedule III–VI prescriptions and Schedule II narcotic limitations

options.option_text: A Rhode Island prescriber's Schedule IV temazepam prescription issued 24 days ago, after the pharmacist independently verifies the prescription with the prescriber and confirms its validity.
options.original_rationale: Under M.G.L. c.94C §18(c), a Massachusetts retail pharmacist may fill an otherwise valid out-of-state Schedule III–VI prescription issued within the preceding 30 days. For Schedule III–V drugs, the pharmacist must verify the prescription by telephone or other means. This 24-day-old, verified Schedule IV prescription satisfies those stated conditions.

options.option_text: A Connecticut prescriber's Schedule IV zolpidem prescription issued 33 days ago, after the pharmacist directly verifies the prescription and confirms it was valid when issued.
options.original_rationale: Verification does not extend M.G.L. c.94C §18(c)'s requirement that an out-of-state Schedule III–VI prescription be issued within the preceding 30 days. At 33 days, it is outside that authorization.

options.option_text: A New Hampshire prescriber's Schedule III prescription issued 10 days ago when the pharmacist cannot obtain prescriber verification despite documented, reasonable good-faith efforts.
options.original_rationale: Section 18(c) specifically prohibits filling out-of-state Schedule III–V prescriptions when the required prescriber verification cannot be obtained. Documented good-faith attempts protect the pharmacist's refusal; they do not substitute for successful verification.

options.option_text: A Florida prescriber's Schedule II narcotic oxycodone prescription issued two days ago and successfully verified, even though the prescriber is not licensed or registered in Maine or a state contiguous with Massachusetts.
options.original_rationale: Section 18(d½) generally restricts out-of-state Schedule II narcotic prescriptions filled for Massachusetts patients to authorized practitioners in Maine or a state contiguous with Massachusetts, subject to specified exceptions excluded by the question. Florida does not qualify merely because the prescription is recent and verified.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy without a complex nonsterile-compounding specialty license has appropriate facilities and staff for routine nonhazardous Schedule VI dispensing. For Patient A, staff reconstitute a commercially manufactured antibiotic powder exactly according to its FDA-approved labeling. For Patient B, staff add a flavoring agent to a conventional oral suspension at the patient's request, confirming suitable stability and concentration and recording the change. For Patient C, staff use a premeasured compounding kit to prepare a patient-specific nonsterile drug. No hazardous ingredients, complex technique, or additional restriction applies. Under Massachusetts Board Policy 2023-07 (revised February 6, 2025), which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2023-07 §§II(B),III(B)–(E),V(B),VI(A)–(C) (revised Feb. 6, 2025)

options.option_text: Adding flavor to the conventionally manufactured suspension is treated the same as manufacturer-directed reconstitution; neither activity counts as nonsterile compounding, so no compounding record or special label statement is needed for Patient B.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2023-07, Section III(B), excludes simple manufacturer-directed reconstitution from the compounding definition, but Section III(C) explicitly classifies flavoring a conventionally manufactured nonsterile drug as compounding. Compounding records and the appropriate nonsterile-compounded and flavoring label statements remain necessary.

options.option_text: Reconstituting the antibiotic exactly in accordance with the manufacturer's labeling does not itself constitute nonsterile compounding; the Board recommends a reconstitution log for such manufactured products.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2023-07, Section III(B), excludes straightforward, manufacturer-directed reconstitution from the nonsterile-compounding definition. Section VI(A) recommends a reconstitution log or similar documentation for commercially available products; this recommendation is not equivalent to saying that this activity is a separately compounded preparation.

options.option_text: For a Schedule VI preparation, a patient or the patient's agent may request flavoring without a new prescriber order when appropriate; the pharmacy must comply with compounding documentation and add the applicable nonsterile-compounded and flavored labeling.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2023-07, Section II(B), permits patient- or agent-requested flavoring of Schedule VI medications, with prescription updates under Board Policy 2018-01. Sections III(C), V(B), and VI(B)–(C) require stability attention, a compounding record, and appropriate compounded-preparation and flavoring label statements.

options.option_text: A premeasured kit does not escape the nonsterile-compounding rules merely because its ingredients were measured beforehand; applicable USP requirements and a compounding record still apply.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2023-07, Section III(E), states that premeasured compounding kits remain compounding and must meet relevant USP standards. Section VI(C) permits appropriate compounding record and master formulation information to be captured on a retrievable log sheet, rather than waiving it.

questions.question_stem: A qualified Massachusetts community pharmacist and supervising physician signed a compliant collaborative drug therapy management (CDTM) agreement on November 1, 2024. The pharmacist maintains the required professional qualifications, annual CDTM continuing education, and written patient referrals and consent. As of November 15, 2026, neither professional has reviewed or renewed the agreement, and they are considering ending the collaborative service. No replacement agreement has been executed. Which statements accurately describe the obligations under 247 CMR 16.04? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 16.04(4)–(6): biennial renewal, termination, written patient notice, and original-versus-copy records

options.option_text: The pharmacist may continue initiating and modifying therapy under the original agreement indefinitely because both professionals remain licensed and no written termination has been issued.
options.original_rationale: Maintaining individual qualifications does not extend an unrenewed agreement indefinitely. Section 16.04(4) requires the pharmacist and supervising physician to review and renew the agreement at least every two years; an expired agreement is not a current basis to exercise CDTM authority.

options.option_text: The authorized pharmacist and supervising physician must review and renew their collaborative practice agreement at least every two years; the original referral and consent do not replace this renewal duty.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 16.04(4) imposes biennial review and renewal on the agreement itself. A valid prior patient referral, consent, and current licensure are separate prerequisites and cannot automatically extend the expired agreement.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must keep the originals of the agreement, the patient referral, and consent exclusively at the pharmacy, while the supervising physician may retain copies instead.
options.original_rationale: This reverses 247 CMR 16.04(6): the pharmacist maintains readily retrievable copies at the primary practice site, while the supervising physician retains the originals of the current agreement, referral, and consent in the patient's medical record.

options.option_text: Before nonrenewal or termination, the pharmacist and supervising physician must arrange uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy and inform the patient in writing of the termination and how therapy will continue.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 16.04(5) requires an uninterrupted-care arrangement before termination or nonrenewal and written patient notification describing the termination and procedures for continuation of drug therapy; simply ending the agreement without transition planning is insufficient.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy plans to administer an indicated routine influenza vaccine to an eligible FIVE-year-old under a valid standing order. The supervising pharmacist is properly immunization-trained, has current CPR certification, will assess and counsel the patient, and will select the vaccine. All otherwise applicable documentation, VIS, storage, consent, and reporting rules are satisfied. Which proposed vaccinator is permitted by Board/DPH Policy 2023-02, revised September 4, 2025?
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board/DPH Policy 2023-02, revised Sept. 4, 2025, §§I–III; 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6)

options.option_text: A licensed pharmacy technician trainee with 650 hours of trainee employment, the required immunization coursework, current CPR certification, and direct pharmacist supervision.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2023-02 explicitly prohibits pharmacy technician trainees (PTTs) from administering vaccines, regardless of training, experience, direct supervision, or the age of the patient.

options.option_text: A Massachusetts-licensed but non-nationally-certified pharmacy technician with 400 hours worked after receiving the technician license, an ACPE-accredited six-hour training program, two documented hours of on-the-job training, and current CPR certification.
options.original_rationale: A pharmacy technician must be nationally certified OR have at least 500 hours worked after obtaining the technician license. This technician is not nationally certified and has only 400 qualifying post-license hours, so completing the other training does not cure the shortfall.

options.option_text: A Massachusetts-licensed but non-nationally-certified pharmacy technician with 600 hours worked after licensure, the ACPE-accredited six-hour course including at least two hours of live hands-on training, two additional documented on-the-job training hours, current CPR, and the directly supervising pharmacist's approval.
options.original_rationale: Under Policy 2023-02 Section III(D), a licensed technician may qualify through national certification OR at least 500 post-license hours. The additional six-hour ACPE course (including two live hands-on hours), two documented on-the-job hours, CPR, pharmacist approval and direct supervision satisfy the described qualifications; the pharmacist, not the technician, performs assessment, counseling and vaccine selection.

options.option_text: A fully trained licensed pharmacist may administer the indicated routine influenza vaccine to a FOUR-year-old under this pharmacy policy whenever the child's parent gives informed consent.
options.original_rationale: Policy 2023-02 Section II and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(6) establish a five-years-and-older age limit for pharmacy vaccine administration under this authority. Parental consent does not itself waive that minimum.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts REMS-certified pharmacy receives a first-treatment isotretinoin prescription for a patient who can become pregnant. The prescriber is certified, the patient has completed both required pre-treatment pregnancy tests in medical settings, the latest negative test specimen was collected five days ago, and the iPLEDGE system currently confirms the patient is authorized for dispensing. The otherwise valid prescription specifies a 90-day supply with two authorized refills. Assume no other state-law or clinical concern. Which action BEST complies with the iPLEDGE REMS?
questions.author_citation: FDA iPLEDGE REMS revised requirements IMPLEMENTED Nov. 15, 2026; FDA iPLEDGE REMS official update and Q&A, first-course pregnancy tests in medical setting, seven-day window, 30-day dispensing and no refills; FDA current isotretinoin label §5.2

options.option_text: Ask the prescriber to issue or correct the order to a compliant prescription with no refills and no more than a 30-day supply; dispense only with REMS authorization, the Medication Guide, and within the patient's valid seven-day prescription window.
options.original_rationale: FDA-approved isotretinoin labeling requires certified-pharmacy authorization for each dispensing, a maximum 30-day supply, a Medication Guide and no refills. A patient who can become pregnant must obtain the medication within the seven-day prescription window tied to the pregnancy-test specimen collection. A corrected compliant order addresses the inappropriate 90-day quantity and refills.

options.option_text: Dispense the first 30 days from the 90-day prescription and keep both authorized refills available for the next two months, provided the pharmacist rechecks iPLEDGE at each refill.
options.original_rationale: The iPLEDGE requirements explicitly prohibit dispensing refills. A subsequent treatment cycle needs its own appropriately authorized prescription; splitting a 90-day prescription into repeated refills does not make the order compliant.

options.option_text: Dispense the full 90-day supply immediately because the two negative pretreatment tests and a current REMS authorization cover the entire initial treatment course.
options.original_rationale: Even with documented pretreatment testing and a positive authorization-to-dispense result, the maximum supply per dispensing is 30 days. A REMS authorization does not override that per-fill limit or allow the two refills.

options.option_text: Hold the prescription until at least 30 days after the most recent pregnancy-test collection because the REMS prohibits dispensing within the first week after a negative test.
options.original_rationale: For a patient who can become pregnant, the REMS provides a seven-day dispensing window linked to pregnancy-test collection, not a mandatory 30-day waiting period after the latest negative test. Waiting would risk missing the valid window; the pharmacy should obtain a corrected, compliant prescription and proceed if authorization remains valid.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives an otherwise valid WRITTEN Schedule II prescription for 30 morphine tablets for a documented resident of a long-term care facility (LTCF). The prescription was issued October 1, 2026. The pharmacist made properly documented unit-dose partial dispensings on October 3 and October 20; the remaining authorized balance has not been dispensed and treatment has not been discontinued. On November 4, the LTCF asks for another partial dispensing under the ORIGINAL prescription. There is no stock shortage, patient-requested partial-fill pathway, or other special exception. Under federal law AND Massachusetts law, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1306.13(c)–(d) LTCF/terminal-illness partial fills; M.G.L. c.94C §23(a) 30-day Massachusetts Schedule II expiration

options.option_text: The federal LTCF provision permits Schedule II prescriptions to be dispensed in partial quantities, including individual dosage units, if the pharmacist notes LTCF status and meets the applicable recordkeeping requirements.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) permits unit-dose partial fillings for LTCF patients and requires the prescription to be designated 'LTCF patient.' It is a separate mechanism from the 72-hour shortage or patient-requested 30-day partial-fill pathways.

options.option_text: The November 4 installment is permitted because federal law allows LTCF Schedule II prescriptions to remain valid up to 60 days and therefore overrides Massachusetts' 30-day expiration rule.
options.original_rationale: The federal 60-day period is a maximum permission, not preemption of a more restrictive state law. Massachusetts M.G.L. c.94C §23(a) invalidates written or electronic Schedule II prescriptions 30 days after issuance. November 4 is beyond 30 days after October 1; the original prescription cannot be used for that installment.

options.option_text: For each authorized partial dispensing, the pharmacist must record the date, quantity dispensed, remaining authorized quantity, and dispenser identity; the sum of the installments may not exceed the prescribed amount.
options.original_rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) requires a readily retrievable partial-fill record with date, quantity, remaining quantity and pharmacist identification; all partial quantities together must stay at or below the original total prescribed.

options.option_text: Despite the federal LTCF provision's maximum 60-day validity, Massachusetts' 30-day expiration rule prevents a further partial dispensing on November 4 under this October 1 written prescription.
options.original_rationale: Massachusetts M.G.L. c.94C §23(a) imposes a 30-day expiration on written or electronic Schedule II prescriptions. A federal regulation allowing up to 60 days for LTCF partial filling does not eliminate the stricter Massachusetts expiration; a new lawful prescription is needed for further dispensing after it becomes invalid.

questions.question_stem: An operating Massachusetts retail pharmacy is being purchased by a different parent company, and the pharmacy's federal employer identification number (FEIN) will change. The location, pharmacy name, and Massachusetts-licensed Manager of Record will remain unchanged. The parties plan to transfer ownership in six weeks and can prepare the controlled-substance inventory, an official bill of sale, and all other required records. No waiver applies. Which approach BEST meets 247 CMR 6.11 and the Board's July 2026 Pharmacy Application Checklist?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 6.11(1)–(3); Massachusetts Board Pharmacy Application Checklist (revised July 15, 2026), Ownership Changes

options.option_text: Continue dispensing under the current pharmacy license after the sale because retaining the pharmacy address and Manager of Record means the Board regards the change only as an administrative update.
options.original_rationale: The Board's July 2026 checklist treats changes to direct or parent-company ownership or to the FEIN as ownership changes requiring closure of the current pharmacy license and a new application. The same location, name, and MOR do not make the old license transferable to the new owner.

options.option_text: Have the outgoing licensee notify the Board at least 14 days before the proposed transfer and address the required closure and controlled-substance transfer steps; the incoming owner must apply for a new pharmacy license at least 14 days in advance, with approval before operating under the new ownership.
options.original_rationale: 247 CMR 6.11 requires advance notification by the outgoing licensee and a new application by the proposed new licensee at least 14 days before ownership transfer, supported by controlled-substance transfer/inventory documentation and bill of sale. The Board's July 2026 checklist clarifies that the old license closes and recommends filing at least 45 days early for review, but 45 days is not the minimum mandated by §6.11.

options.option_text: Submit an application for a change of Manager of Record at least 45 days before the sale; a new pharmacy license is unnecessary because the pharmacy name and dispensing staff will stay the same.
options.original_rationale: Changing the manager is not the same as transferring the pharmacy license to a new owner. The question states that the MOR remains unchanged; ownership/FEIN changes instead trigger the new-license process under §6.11 and the Board checklist.

options.option_text: Transfer ownership first and have the buyer apply for a new pharmacy license within 14 calendar days afterward, while continuing to use the seller's license during application processing.
options.original_rationale: Section 6.11 calls for the proposed new licensee's application at least 14 days BEFORE ownership transfer, not after. The incoming owner does not gain authority to operate under the seller's former license merely because an application is pending.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy is preparing valid Schedule II prescriptions. The on-duty pharmacist directly supervises a licensed pharmacy technician and a licensed certified pharmacy technician, has approved permitted Schedule II handling under written pharmacy policies, and will personally complete final dispensing validation. The pharmacy has immediate-release oxycodone tablets and a hydrocodone-only extended-release product that is NOT abuse-deterrent. Which staff assignment is permissible?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.02(6)(d); 247 CMR 8.05(1)–(3) (technician Schedule II handling and product-specific exclusion)

options.option_text: Assign the licensed, noncertified pharmacy technician to COUNT the oxycodone tablets, because a technician may assist with transporting Schedule II stock.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 247 CMR 8.05(2), a licensed pharmacy technician may assist in TRANSPORTING Schedule II controlled substances under supervision and approved written procedures; that permission does not extend to handling or counting the stock. Counting is not merely transport.

options.option_text: Assign the licensed certified pharmacy technician to COUNT the oxycodone tablets under the pharmacist's supervision and documented approval.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 8.05(2)(b) permits a licensed certified pharmacy technician to assist in transporting AND HANDLING Schedule II controlled substances under pharmacist supervision when the pharmacist has approved the role as reflected in the pharmacy's written policies. The pharmacist remains accountable and performs final validation.

options.option_text: Assign the licensed certified pharmacy technician to COUNT the non-abuse-deterrent hydrocodone-only extended-release product because certification removes all Schedule II handling exclusions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.05(3) specifically prohibits certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians, and technician trainees from handling hydrocodone-only extended-release medication that is not abuse-deterrent. Certification does not override that product-specific exception.

options.option_text: Assign the licensed pharmacy technician to perform the FINAL patient dispensing validation of the oxycodone after the computer's barcode verification.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.02(6)(d) prohibits pharmacy technicians from performing final dispensing-process validation. Computer checks or later pharmacist review do not transfer that professional task to a technician.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy has confirmed several quality-related events (QREs). The pharmacist has already addressed immediate patient needs and made each required initial event report on time. A corporate quality team offers centralized electronic storage of QRE records, while the pharmacy's Manager of Record revises the local continuous quality improvement (CQI) program. Under 247 CMR 15.02–15.04, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must keep a written description of its CQI program ON THE PREMISES and make that description readily available to pharmacy personnel.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 15.04(1) requires the written CQI program description to be maintained on the pharmacy premises and readily available to pharmacy personnel. This differs from the location allowed for individual QRE records.

options.option_text: QRE records may be maintained off-site if they are kept in an orderly manner, filed by date, and retained for at least TWO YEARS from the QRE REPORT date.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 15.04(2)–(4) sets a minimum two-year period from the date of the QRE report, requires orderly date filing, and expressly permits off-site storage. The on-premises program DESCRIPTION requirement does not require every event record to be on-site.

options.option_text: Once all personnel finish onboarding, annual CQI education may be discontinued if no QRE caused documented patient injury that year.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f) requires ongoing CQI education for pharmacy personnel at least annually. The duty does not depend on whether any patient was harmed or how many events occurred.

options.option_text: The CQI process must analyze system and workflow contributors and inform pharmacy personnel about policy or process changes resulting from CQI recommendations.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 15.02(1)(d)–(e) requires cause analysis and improvements; 247 CMR 15.03(3)(a)–(b) requires consideration of systemic factors and communicating resulting changes to personnel.

questions.question_stem: A federally assisted Massachusetts substance-use-disorder treatment program with an on-site pharmacy is subject to 42 CFR Part 2. The local public-health authority requests data to plan overdose-prevention services. The program can provide either (1) patient records fully de-identified under the HIPAA standard, with no reasonable basis to identify a patient, or (2) a named list linking patients to SUD diagnoses and prescriptions. No affected patient has consented; no Part 2 court order or other disclosure exception applies. Under the Part 2 rules applicable in November 2026, which approach is permissible?
questions.author_citation: 42 CFR 2.54(a)–(b); 45 CFR 164.514(b); HHS 2024 Part 2 Final Rule (compliance February 16, 2026)

options.option_text: Release both datasets, because HIPAA's public-health disclosure permission automatically overrides the stricter Part 2 protections.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. HIPAA's general public-health disclosure permissions do not automatically authorize a Part 2 program to release identifiable Part 2 records. Part 2's specific limits still apply.

options.option_text: Release the named list only if the recipient promises confidentiality; the de-identified dataset still requires each patient's consent.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The public-health authority's confidentiality promise is not itself Part 2 consent or another lawful exception. Conversely, 42 CFR 2.54 expressly permits qualifying de-identified disclosure without patient consent.

options.option_text: Release the properly de-identified records to the public-health authority without patient consent, but do not release the named list solely under the Part 2 public-health exception.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 42 CFR 2.54 permits disclosure to a defined public-health authority WITHOUT consent only where record content meets 45 CFR 164.514(b)'s de-identification standard and there is no reasonable basis to identify any patient. Identifiable SUD records require some other valid authorization or exception, none of which is present here.

options.option_text: Withhold both datasets, because Part 2 always requires written patient consent even when information is properly de-identified for a public-health authority.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. This ignores the express exception in 42 CFR 2.54, added by the 2024 rule with required compliance as of February 16, 2026, for records de-identified to the HIPAA standard.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts RETAIL pharmacy dispenses four separate, otherwise lawful prescriptions. All required prescription labeling, counseling, and clinical checks have been completed. Under M.G.L. c.94C §21, for which dispensings is the pharmacy REQUIRED to give the consumer pamphlet addressing narcotic risks and non-opioid pain-treatment alternatives? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY. Assume no exception other than those stated.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §21, third paragraph (Schedule II/III consumer pamphlet and palliative-care, LTCF, OUD exceptions)

options.option_text: Schedule II oxycodone for routine postoperative pain in a community-dwelling adult who is not receiving outpatient palliative care.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 21 requires the pamphlet when a retail pharmacy dispenses a Schedule II or III narcotic or controlled substance, absent a listed exception. Routine outpatient postoperative pain does not qualify for the palliative-care, LTCF, or SUD-treatment exceptions.

options.option_text: Schedule II oxycodone prescribed to a patient who is a resident of a long-term care facility.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect as a REQUIRED-pamphlet choice. Section 21 expressly says pharmacists are not required to distribute the pamphlet when the patient resides in a long-term care facility. Optional provision is different from a legal requirement.

options.option_text: Schedule III transdermal buprenorphine prescribed for CHRONIC PAIN, not for opioid use disorder or opioid dependence, to a community-dwelling adult.
