options.original_rationale: Correct. The Schedule III controlled-substance pamphlet rule applies and the special exception for medication prescribed to treat SUD or opioid dependence does NOT apply when buprenorphine is prescribed for chronic pain. Drug name alone does not establish the exception.

options.option_text: Schedule III buprenorphine/naloxone prescribed specifically for treatment of opioid use disorder to a community-dwelling adult.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect as a REQUIRED-pamphlet choice. M.G.L. c.94C §21 expressly removes the distribution requirement when the controlled substance is prescribed for treatment of SUD or opioid dependence. The indication, not simply the Schedule, determines this exception.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives a valid prescription for a biological medication identified by its BRAND name. The prescriber has not given a patient-specific written 'no substitution' instruction. The proposed alternative is FDA-designated INTERCHANGEABLE with the prescribed reference biologic, and the pharmacist judges substitution appropriate. The pharmacy cannot enter a note in the prescriber's interoperable EHR, but it maintains a patient record accessible to the prescriber upon request. Which procedure BEST complies with M.G.L. c.112 §12EE?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.112 §12EE(b)–(f) (interchangeable biologics, prescriber/patient notices, minimum retention)

options.option_text: Substitution is mandatory whenever the interchangeable biologic costs less, and no patient or prescriber notice is necessary if the original prescription remains in the file.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 12EE(b) says a pharmacist MAY substitute an interchangeable biologic, not that every eligible substitution is mandatory. Sections 12EE(d)–(f) also impose notification and recordkeeping duties after substitution.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must obtain a new, individually signed prescriber authorization before every substitution because the pharmacy cannot enter data directly into the prescriber's interoperable EHR.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. When no patient-specific written prohibition applies, §12EE(b) permits substitution; §12EE(d) provides alternative prescriber notification methods when the pharmacy cannot annotate an interoperable EHR. Prior affirmative authorization is not universally required by this section.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may substitute and give only a verbal notice to the patient, provided that the pharmacy destroys the interchange record after the next refill is completed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 12EE(e) requires WRITTEN patient notification, and §12EE(f) requires a substitution record retained for at least one year from the last entry in the profile record. Verbal notice alone and early destruction do not meet those obligations.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may substitute, notify the prescriber within a reasonable time through the accessible pharmacy-record route, notify the patient in writing, and retain the substitution record for at least one year from the last profile entry.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under §12EE(b)–(f), FDA interchangeability and absence of a patient-specific written no-substitution instruction permit the switch. Where an interoperable-EHR notation is not possible, a pharmacy-record notation accessible by the prescriber on request is a permitted notice method; the patient receives written notice, and records are retained at least one year from the last profile entry.

questions.question_stem: Two pharmacists who graduated from ACPE-accredited PharmD programs in 2019 receive their FIRST Massachusetts pharmacist licenses by license transfer in 2026. Pharmacist X is licensed on September 30; Pharmacist Y is licensed on October 1. Neither performs immunization, compounding, or CDTM duties, and neither qualifies for another waiver. Both are reviewing their 2026 continuing education obligations before the December 2026 renewal. Under Massachusetts Board Policy 2021-04, as revised September 4, 2025, which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 4.03(4),(5),(8); Massachusetts Board Policy 2021-04 §II (revised Sept. 4, 2025)

options.option_text: Both pharmacists have until April 30, 2027 to complete their 2026 CE because their first Massachusetts licenses were issued in the final four months of 2026.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Board Policy 2021-04, §II sets a specific cutoff of ON OR AFTER OCTOBER 1 for initial licensure through exam or transfer. September 30 does not satisfy that cutoff, even though it is late in the calendar year.

options.option_text: Neither pharmacist qualifies for a grace period because 247 CMR 4.03 imposes the standard annual CE requirement regardless of the date of first Massachusetts licensure.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Although 247 CMR 4.03 sets the general annual CE requirement, Board Policy 2021-04, §II specifically grants qualifying late-year examination and transfer licensees a grace period through April 30 of the following year.

options.option_text: Only Pharmacist Y qualifies for a grace period through April 30, 2027 to obtain the required 2026 CE; it is not a permanent exemption and does not eliminate the separate 2027 CE requirement.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Board Policy 2021-04, §II covers licenses obtained by examination or transfer on or after October 1. Y qualifies on October 1; X does not on September 30. Both graduated in 2019, so the separate graduation-year exception in 247 CMR 4.03(8) does not apply. Annual CE obligations remain separate.

options.option_text: Pharmacist Y is exempt from all 2026 CE because receiving a license on October 1 is equivalent to graduating from an accredited pharmacy school in that calendar year.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The graduation-year CE exemption in 247 CMR 4.03(8) depends on the actual year of graduation, here 2019. A late-year license TRANSFER creates a deadline extension under Board policy, not a graduation-year exemption.

questions.question_stem: At a Massachusetts retail pharmacy, a patient being treated for laboratory-confirmed chlamydia presents a separate, otherwise valid prescription for the patient's unexamined partner. The partner prescription properly identifies the recipient as 'EPT' rather than by name. The pharmacy cannot obtain the prescribed medication in time to dispense it. Later, another patient asks the pharmacist to process a similar EPT prescription for a partner exposed ONLY to gonorrhea, relying solely on Massachusetts Board/DCP Policy 2020-08. No other independent prescribing or dispensing authorization has been established. Which response BEST follows that policy?
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board/Drug Control Program Joint Policy 2020-08 §§I–II (Expedited Partner Therapy Prescriptions; May 25, 2023)

options.option_text: Keep the unfilled chlamydia EPT prescription without referring the patient elsewhere, because stock shortages relieve pharmacists of all EPT-related responsibilities.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Joint Board/DCP Policy 2020-08, §II requires a pharmacist who is unable or unwilling to fill a qualifying EPT prescription to REFER the patient to an alternate pharmacy. A stock-out is not an exception to that obligation.

options.option_text: Process the gonorrhea-only EPT request under Policy 2020-08 because every sexually transmitted infection is covered whenever a partner cannot attend an appointment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Policy 2020-08 expressly applies ONLY to chlamydia treatment. Its specific authority cannot be extended to gonorrhea merely because it is another STI; a separate applicable authority would have to be established.

options.option_text: Require the chlamydia partner to undergo an examination and provide a legal name before giving a referral, because EPT prescriptions without a name are invalid.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section I of Policy 2020-08 explicitly allows a separate chlamydia EPT prescription to substitute 'EPT', 'E.P.T.' or 'Expedited Partner Therapy' for the partner's name and address without an exam.

options.option_text: Refer the patient with the unfilled CHLAMYDIA EPT prescription to another pharmacy, while recognizing that Policy 2020-08 alone does not authorize a GONORRHEA-only EPT prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under Board/DCP Policy 2020-08, §II(2), an unable or unwilling pharmacist must refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy. The policy states that it applies only to chlamydia; the gonorrhea request requires its own independent legal basis rather than an assumed extension.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts retail pharmacy examines four separate possible privacy incidents. Consider ONLY the federal HIPAA Breach Notification Rule; there is no applicable law-enforcement delay, and no exception beyond the facts stated should be assumed. Which conclusions are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.402; HHS HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, Definitions and Guidance to Render PHI Unusable, Unreadable, or Indecipherable

options.option_text: A hard drive containing ePHI encrypted in accordance with HHS guidance is stolen, but the separate decryption key is not compromised; theft of that drive alone does not trigger federal breach notification.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 45 CFR 164.402 defines unsecured PHI, and HHS encryption guidance recognizes qualifying encrypted ePHI with uncompromised decryption keys as secured. The federal breach-notification obligation does not arise solely because such secured data were stolen.

options.option_text: An unencrypted USB drive with identifiable prescription records is stolen; no one can prove the thief opened the files, so the pharmacy can automatically close the incident without risk assessment or notification.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An impermissible disclosure or acquisition of unsecured PHI is presumed a breach unless an exception applies or a documented assessment shows low probability of compromise. Lack of proof of actual viewing is relevant but is not automatically conclusive.

options.option_text: For an impermissible disclosure of unsecured PHI, a documented four-factor assessment supporting a low probability of compromise can rebut the presumption of breach and make federal notification unnecessary.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 45 CFR 164.402, the assessment considers the nature and extent of PHI, the recipient, actual acquisition/viewing, and mitigation. A supportable low-probability finding may mean notification is not required; without it, the breach presumption applies.

options.option_text: If an appropriately encrypted laptop and its accessible decryption key are stolen together, the original encryption always guarantees the HIPAA notification safe harbor without further analysis.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under HHS guidance, a confidential key or decryption process enabling access must not have been breached. When the key is stolen with the device, encryption does not automatically establish the safe harbor; further assessment is needed.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist evaluates FOUR separate, otherwise authorized NEW prescriptions before initial dispensing. Assume any added identifier is verified, the authorized overall quantity remains unchanged, all modifications are documented, and there are no separate clinical safety concerns. Under Massachusetts Board/DCP Policy 2018-01, revised January 11, 2024, which actions are permitted as stated? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: MA Board/DCP Policy 2018-01 §§II(E), III(A)(i)(d), III(C)(iii)(a), IV (revised Jan. 11, 2024)

options.option_text: After consulting the prescriber by telephone, change the 'earliest date to be filled' on a Schedule II prescription instead of requiring a new prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Policy 2018-01, §II(E) lists a Schedule II EARLIEST FILL DATE among elements that may never be changed or added. Prescriber consultation does not cure the restriction; a new prescription is required.

options.option_text: Verify and add a missing prescriber's DEA registration number to a Schedule II prescription WITHOUT contacting the prescriber, recording the modification.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2018-01, §III(A)(i)(d) permits adding the DEA number without consultation. Section IV requires recording the date, the change and the pharmacist, while the prescription must remain otherwise valid.

options.option_text: Convert a PMP-reportable Massachusetts Schedule VI gabapentin prescription from a 30-day supply with 11 refills to a 90-day supply with three refills WITHOUT consulting the prescriber because it is Schedule VI.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Policy 2018-01, §III(C)(iii)(a) only permits independent days'-supply conversion for Schedule VI drugs NOT subject to PMP reporting. Gabapentin is a Massachusetts PMP additional drug, so the premise does not meet the exception.

options.option_text: For a non-PMP-reportable Schedule VI amlodipine prescription, use professional judgment to convert a 30-day supply with 11 refills into a 90-day supply with three refills WITHOUT prescriber consultation, preserving the overall amount and documenting the change.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2018-01, §III(C)(iii) explicitly recognizes this conversion for non-PMP-reportable Schedule VI drugs where professionally appropriate. Section IV requires documentation. The case rules out separate clinical concerns.

questions.question_stem: A corporate entity owns THREE Massachusetts retail pharmacies. As of November 27, 2026, across the ENTIRE company it has 16 full-time licensed pharmacists, nine full-time qualified pharmacy technicians, and 20 full-time cashiers who are not pharmacists or pharmacy technicians. On December 1, 2026, one location identifies a SUSPECT prescription-drug package while management is implementing FDA's August 6, 2026 DSCSA exemption. No other waiver or exemption applies. Which interpretation is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: FDA DSCSA Exemptions for Small Business Dispensers (Aug. 6, 2026), FD&C Act §§582(a)(3), 582(d)(4), 582(g)(1), effective Nov. 27, 2026–Nov. 27, 2027

options.option_text: The company qualifies for the specified small-dispenser exemptions until November 27, 2027 because it has 25 qualifying full-time pharmacists/technicians across the corporation; suspect-product quarantine, investigation and other non-exempt DSCSA requirements remain.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FDA's August 6, 2026 notice counts full-time LICENSED PHARMACISTS and QUALIFIED PHARMACY TECHNICIANS across the corporate entity as of November 27, 2026. Sixteen plus nine equals 25; cashiers do not count under this exemption definition. The specified enhanced tracing and product-identifier verification exemptions do not waive other section 582 obligations.

options.option_text: The company is ineligible because FDA counts all 45 full-time employees, including cashiers, toward the 25-person exemption threshold.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA's August 2026 notice expressly limits the qualifying employee count to licensed pharmacists and qualified pharmacy technicians across the owning company. Non-pharmacy cashiers are excluded from that count.

options.option_text: The company qualifies, but the pharmacies must obtain individual FDA approval of a special exemption application before using their existing transaction-information methods.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The FDA's August 2026 notice announces a class-wide exemption; small dispensers and their trading partners utilizing it do NOT have to submit extra information to FDA or await individual approval.

options.option_text: Each store is counted separately regardless of corporate ownership, and the exemption suspends all suspect-product investigation and quarantine obligations for stores under the threshold.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The notice uses corporate-entity-wide counting, not store-by-store headcounts. It also retains non-exempt section 582 requirements; suspect-product quarantine and investigation obligations are not automatically erased.

questions.question_stem: An ACPE-accredited PharmD graduate begins a PGY1 residency in a Massachusetts hospital. The resident has passed the NAPLEX and holds a current Massachusetts pharmacy intern license, but the Board has NOT issued a Massachusetts pharmacist license. A licensed pharmacist preceptor is on the premises, directly supervises the resident, and can complete final dispensing validation. A licensed pharmacy technician also needs supervision. Assume staffing ratios and all other duties are otherwise compliant. Which arrangement is permitted?

options.option_text: Allow the resident to serve as the only pharmacist on duty during a staff pharmacist's absence because passing the NAPLEX and entering an accredited residency temporarily confer pharmacist authority.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.01(8) requires a Massachusetts residency graduate to hold either a Massachusetts pharmacist license or a Massachusetts intern license with pharmacist supervision. NAPLEX success and residency status alone do not provide pharmacist licensure or permit the resident to replace the pharmacist on duty.

options.option_text: Allow the resident to work under direct supervision as a licensed pharmacy intern and supervise the technician in that supervised role, while the licensed pharmacist retains responsibility for final dispensing validation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 8.01(8) and (10), an approved PharmD graduate may work as a licensed pharmacy intern during residency until pharmacist licensure. Section 8.01(15) allows an intern acting under direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor to supervise technicians. Section 9.04(1) reserves final dispensing validation to a licensed pharmacist.

options.option_text: Have the resident independently perform the final validation of prescriptions because a pharmacist's on-site availability automatically converts an intern's validation into licensed pharmacist validation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The resident remains an intern until licensed as a pharmacist. Although the intern may perform supervised functions, 247 CMR 9.04(1) makes a licensed pharmacist responsible for final dispensing-process validation. On-site supervision does not change the resident's license category.

options.option_text: Require the resident to stop all pharmacy-intern activities immediately upon graduation, even though the Massachusetts intern license remains active, until the pharmacist license is issued.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.01(10) expressly allows graduates of an approved pharmacy school to continue acting as pharmacy interns until licensed as pharmacists, and 8.01(8) specifically addresses the supervised intern pathway during Massachusetts residencies.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy administers routinely recommended, FDA-licensed, NON-COVID, NON-MPOX adult vaccines under appropriate standing orders. Later, the pharmacy learns of four separate events: (1) an event identified in the manufacturer's labeling as a contraindication to later doses; (2) an event in the VAERS Table of Reportable Events Following Vaccination occurring within the specified interval for the vaccine; (3) transient injection-site soreness that is neither in the table nor a labeled contraindication; and (4) a vaccine-administration error with no adverse event. Consider the general federal National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act (NCVIA)/VAERS rules, with no additional vaccine-program reporting condition. Which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 42 U.S.C. §300aa-25(b); VAERS Healthcare Provider Guidance and FAQs; Massachusetts DPH Vaccine Administration and Clinical Guidance (reporting recommendations)

options.option_text: The event the manufacturer lists as a contraindication to subsequent doses must be reported to VAERS by the healthcare provider.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The NCVIA and VAERS healthcare-provider guidance require a provider to report an adverse event listed by the vaccine manufacturer as a contraindication to further doses. This duty is not erased merely because the clinician has not proved vaccine causation.

options.option_text: Transient injection-site soreness that is neither in the applicable reportable-events table nor a labeled contraindication must automatically be reported under the NCVIA's mandatory provider categories.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Ordinary mild soreness that does not meet a Table of Reportable Events criterion or a manufacturer-listed contraindication is not automatically mandatory under those two federal NCVIA reporting categories. VAERS can accept voluntary reports, and clinically significant events are encouraged for reporting.

options.option_text: A VAERS-table event occurring within its specified postvaccination time interval is federally reportable even when a causal relationship has not been conclusively established.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The NCVIA/VAERS provider reporting requirement uses the listed event and specified interval, not a requirement to prove causation. VAERS is a safety-monitoring system rather than a determination that a vaccine caused each event.

options.option_text: The administration error with no associated adverse event may be reported to VAERS and is encouraged, but an error alone does not automatically meet the two general NCVIA mandatory adverse-event categories under the stated assumptions.
options.original_rationale: Correct. VAERS explicitly accepts vaccination-error reports and encourages reporting errors. For the ordinary licensed vaccines and facts stated, the two general NCVIA mandatory categories concern specified adverse events and labeled contraindications, not every error by itself; particular programs or emergency authorizations may impose additional duties.

questions.question_stem: An unconscious patient arrives at a Massachusetts emergency department following a suspected overdose. The treating emergency physician contacts a federally assisted substance-use-disorder (SUD) treatment program subject to 42 CFR Part 2 to learn the patient's most recent medication dose before providing emergency treatment. No patient consent is on file, and prior written consent cannot be obtained while the patient is unconscious. The physician reasonably needs this information now to prevent a dangerous dosing error. No other disclosure authority is asserted. Which response BEST complies with 42 CFR 2.51?
questions.author_citation: 42 CFR 2.51(a)(1), (c) (medical emergency disclosures and immediate documentation; 2024 rule text, confirmed applicable in November 2026)

options.option_text: Withhold all identifying SUD treatment information until the patient can sign a consent, because Part 2 has no exception for medical emergencies.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 2.51(a)(1) permits disclosure to medical personnel to the extent necessary for a bona fide medical emergency when prior written consent cannot be obtained. It does not categorically require waiting for the patient to regain consciousness.

options.option_text: Provide the patient's entire SUD treatment file to the emergency department's administrative and billing staff because HIPAA treatment/payment/operations permissions automatically override Part 2.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The specific 42 CFR 2.51 emergency exception permits necessary disclosure to medical personnel. It does not authorize release of an entire record to administrative staff merely because the emergency department may otherwise be a HIPAA-covered entity.

options.option_text: Provide the necessary dosing details to the treating physician, but document only that an emergency occurred when the program next performs its routine quarterly privacy audit.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Although limited disclosure to treating medical personnel can be permissible, 42 CFR 2.51(c) requires WRITTEN documentation immediately following disclosure, including recipient and facility affiliation, person disclosing, date/time, and nature of the emergency. A delayed generic audit entry is insufficient.

options.option_text: Disclose only the medication information necessary to the treating emergency physician now, then immediately document the recipient and affiliation, person making disclosure, date/time, and nature of the emergency in the patient's record.
options.original_rationale: Correct. A bona fide emergency where prior written consent cannot be obtained meets 42 CFR 2.51(a)(1). The information may be disclosed only to medical personnel and only to the necessary extent. Section 2.51(c) requires specified written documentation in the patient's record immediately after disclosure.

questions.question_stem: On November 16, 2026, a Massachusetts community pharmacist reviews FOUR independent prescriptions for substances correctly classified as Schedule V in Massachusetts. Each prescription was otherwise properly issued by an authorized practitioner, has a legitimate medical purpose, has appropriately recorded prior dispensings, and satisfies all other dispensing and identification requirements. No new authorization or exception is available. Under 247 CMR 9.04(13), which request MAY be dispensed under the ORIGINAL prescription?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.04(10), (13) (Schedule V fill/refill expiry and limit); comparison: federal 21 CFR 1306.22–1306.23

options.option_text: A prescription issued May 20, 2026, first dispensed May 21, with FOUR subsequent refills already dispensed and FIVE refills originally authorized; the patient requests the FIFTH refill today.
options.original_rationale: Correct. November 16 is within six months of the May 20 issuance date, and the requested dispensing is refill number five (following the original fill and four earlier refills). 247 CMR 9.04(13) permits up to five Schedule V refills within the six-month validity period, assuming all other requirements are met.

options.option_text: A prescription issued June 20, 2026, initially dispensed June 21, with FIVE refills already dispensed; the prescriber wrote '7 refills' and the patient requests a SIXTH refill today.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Even though the date is within six months, 247 CMR 9.04(13) expressly prohibits refilling a Schedule V prescription more than five times. An original prescription authorizing additional refills cannot override the Massachusetts limit.

options.option_text: A prescription issued May 1, 2026, initially dispensed May 3, with only TWO refills used; the patient requests the THIRD refill today.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The November 16 request is more than six months after the May 1 issuance date. Under 247 CMR 9.04(13), unused authorized refills do not extend the Schedule V prescription's six-month expiration window.

options.option_text: A prescription issued May 1, 2026, which has NEVER been filled and still has all its authorized refills available; the patient asks for the INITIAL fill today.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.04(13) prohibits BOTH an initial fill and a refill more than six months after Schedule V prescription issuance. Having zero earlier fills does not rescue an expired original.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy maintains electronic Schedule II perpetual inventory records. Some expired Schedule II tablets remain physically secured on the pharmacy premises pending lawful reverse distribution. Its most recent physical reconciliation was TEN DAYS ago. Today the Manager of Record (MOR) is temporarily absent, a designated licensed pharmacist is present, and a licensed certified pharmacy technician and an unlicensed cashier are available. The pharmacy already performs the federal biennial inventory separately. Under 247 CMR 9.21(8) and (10), which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.21(8)(a)–(f), 9.21(10); 21 CFR 1304.11(c) (separate federal biennial inventory)

options.option_text: Because the pharmacy completes a federal biennial inventory, electronic Schedule II perpetual records need no separate physical reconciliation until the next federal biennial inventory.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal biennial inventories do not displace Massachusetts' separate 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) rule requiring a physical reconciliation of EACH Schedule II perpetual inventory at least once every ten days.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must perform an accurate physical count and reconcile each Schedule II perpetual record at least every ten days, including Schedule II stock that is expired, quarantined or awaiting reverse distribution.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.21(8)(c) requires reconciliation at least once every ten days using a physical count. Section 9.21(10) explicitly extends the security and inventory provisions to expired, quarantined and pending-reverse-distribution controlled stock; it is not excluded merely because it is unsaleable.

options.option_text: The certified technician may make routine entries in the Schedule II perpetual ledger, but a discrepancy adjustment is reserved for the MOR or, during the MOR's absence, a pharmacist designee who reports the adjustment to the MOR.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(f) allows a certified technician to make ledger entries, while (8)(d) restricts discrepancy-based inventory adjustments to the MOR or a pharmacist designee when the MOR is absent, with reporting to the MOR. Ordinary data entry is not the same as discrepancy adjustment.

options.option_text: The unlicensed cashier may not enter data into or adjust the Schedule II perpetual inventory, even if a licensed pharmacist intends to review the entry afterward.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(e) expressly prohibits an unlicensed individual from making ANY entry into, or adjustment of, the Schedule II perpetual inventory. A future pharmacist review does not create an exception.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy employs a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy technician who is not nationally certified and a separately licensed certified pharmacy technician. The on-duty pharmacist has approved appropriate delegated work and will perform final dispensing validation. A prescriber's authorized agent agrees to add three refills to an existing Schedule VI lisinopril prescription with NO change in drug, strength, directions, or other prescription information. In a separate call, the agent proposes a dose increase on another patient's lisinopril prescription but describes it as 'just a refill.' Assume the communication method is otherwise legally permitted and all prescriptions are legitimate. Which division of responsibility BEST complies with 247 CMR 8.02 and 8.04?

options.option_text: The noncertified licensed technician may request an unchanged refill authorization but cannot receive it; only a certified technician may accept even an unchanged refill.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.02(6)(c) permits a licensed pharmacy technician, with the on-duty pharmacist's approval, to request AND accept authorizations for refills when no prescription information changes. National certification is not a prerequisite for this limited unchanged-refill activity.

options.option_text: Either licensed technician may accept the dose increase as a refill authorization if the prescriber's agent agrees and the pharmacist validates the dispensed product afterward.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Changing the prescribed dose is therapy modification, not an unchanged refill. 247 CMR 8.02(6)(d) and 8.04(4)(e) prohibit pharmacy technicians, including certified technicians, from contacting prescribers concerning therapy modification. A later pharmacist final check does not grant authority for the prohibited communication.

options.option_text: With the on-duty pharmacist's approval, the noncertified licensed technician may request and receive the unchanged refill authorization; the proposed dose modification must be referred to the pharmacist rather than handled independently by either technician.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 8.02(6)(c), an ordinary licensed technician can request and accept a refill authorization if nothing has changed and the pharmacist approves. Section 8.02(6)(d) and 8.04(4)(e) reserve therapy clarification or modification to the pharmacist, regardless of whether a technician holds national certification.

options.option_text: The certified technician may independently clarify or authorize the dose modification because 247 CMR 8.04 permits receipt of new or omitted prescription information, while the noncertified technician must transfer both calls to a pharmacist.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Although a certified technician has additional limited authority to receive new or omitted prescription details with pharmacist approval, 247 CMR 8.04(4)(e) expressly prohibits therapy clarification or modification. The ordinary licensed technician may handle the unchanged refill under 8.02(6)(c).

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy stocks prescription naloxone rescue kits and participates in the statewide naloxone standing order. An adult asks to obtain a kit to help a sibling who is at risk of opioid overdose, but has no patient-specific prescription. That afternoon, the pharmacy dispenses a lawful Schedule II oxycodone prescription to an unrelated patient. For its naloxone dispensings, the pharmacy chooses NOT to submit naloxone data through its daily Massachusetts PMP transmissions. It follows all other applicable counseling, labeling and dispensing requirements. Under M.G.L. c.94C §§19B–19C and Massachusetts Board Policy 2024-01 (revised February 6, 2025), which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §§19B–19C; MA Board Policy 2024-01 §§I(B)–(E), II(A)–(B), revised Feb. 6, 2025; 2026 Statewide Standing Order for Pharmacy Naloxone

options.option_text: A licensed pharmacist may dispense a naloxone rescue kit to the person seeking to assist the sibling under the statewide standing order without requiring a separate patient-specific prescription for the sibling.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §19B and the July 2026 statewide standing order permit a licensed pharmacist to supply a naloxone rescue kit to a family member, friend, or other person positioned to help someone at risk of overdose; Board Policy 2024-01, §I(B), allows dispensing under that order rather than requiring an individual prescriber-issued prescription.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may omit any offer of naloxone to the unrelated oxycodone patient because federal approval of some OTC naloxone products superseded the Massachusetts Schedule II opioid offer requirement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Board Policy 2024-01, §I(C), specifically states that a pharmacy MUST offer to dispense naloxone whenever a Schedule II opioid is dispensed. The separate existence of FDA-approved OTC naloxone does not remove the state standing-order policy's offer requirement.

options.option_text: For insurance and cost-sharing under the statewide standing order, the pharmacy must always label the kit and create its prescription profile using the purchasing person's legal name and address; the words 'Naloxone Rescue Kit' cannot replace those fields.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Policy 2024-01, §I(E), expressly instructs use of 'Naloxone Rescue Kit' in place of the name and address when creating the profile and prescription label for the standing-order insurance transaction. The option reverses the Board's specific labeling direction.

options.option_text: Because the pharmacy does not report naloxone through its daily PMP submissions, it must send the required report for the preceding calendar year by January 15, including the total number of naloxone DOSES dispensed and the number of those doses paid for with insurance.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Board Policy 2024-01, §II(B), specifies an alternative annual report due January 15 when a pharmacy chooses not to report naloxone through the PMP. It includes pharmacy name/ZIP, total doses (not the number of kits or prescriptions), and the number of doses paid for by insurance.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy receives an adult patient's valid request to correct a dispensing date in the pharmacy's designated record set. The record was created by the pharmacy, the pharmacy confirms it is inaccurate, and no regulatory ground for denying amendment applies. On day 55 after receipt, the pharmacy knows its records team cannot finish processing by day 60. The patient has received no extension notice. Which proposed plan BEST satisfies the federal HIPAA amendment rule?
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.526(a)(1)–(2), (b)(2), (c)(1)–(3); distinction from HIPAA access deadline at 45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)

options.option_text: Treat the request like a right-of-access request, which requires action within 30 days; because that date has passed, automatically deny the amendment and ask the patient to submit a new request.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. HIPAA differentiates access under 45 CFR 164.524, generally 30 days, from AMENDMENT under 45 CFR 164.526(b)(2), generally 60 days. Expiration of an unrelated access deadline does not justify denying a valid request to correct inaccurate PHI.

options.option_text: Treat the pharmacy software vendor as the sole creator of the record, deny responsibility for correction, and refer the patient to the vendor even though the pharmacy created the inaccurate dispensing entry.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 164.526(a)(2)(i) permits denial in some circumstances when the covered entity did not create the record. Here the covered pharmacy itself created the inaccurate record; using a software vendor does not make that denial ground applicable.

options.option_text: Notify the patient orally on day 60 that two successive 30-day extensions will be taken, and silently overwrite the original date without attaching a record of the accepted amendment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 164.526(b)(2)(ii) permits only ONE extension of no more than 30 days and requires a written explanation and completion date within the original 60-day window. Section 164.526(c)(1) requires identifying affected records and appending or linking the amendment rather than an undocumented silent change.

options.option_text: Before the original 60-day deadline, provide written reasons and a completion date for ONE extension of no more than 30 days; upon accepting the correction, identify the affected record, append or link the amendment, notify the patient, and address notification to appropriate recipients.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 164.526(b)(2) allows one written-notice extension of up to 30 days beyond the 60-day amendment response window. Section 164.526(c)(1)–(3) requires linking or appending the amendment, notifying the individual, obtaining the individual's identification/agreement where relevant, and making reasonable efforts to inform appropriate prior recipients and business associates.

questions.question_stem: On November 16, 2026, a patient requests that Massachusetts Pharmacy A transfer TWO previously filled Schedule VI maintenance-drug prescriptions to licensed Massachusetts Pharmacy B. Prescription X was issued February 3, 2026 and has TWO authorized refills remaining. Prescription Y was issued October 20, 2025 and also has TWO authorized refills remaining; its most recent dispensing occurred October 10, 2026. Both were legitimate when issued. The patient has requested the transfers, the pharmacies can follow the applicable transfer procedure, and no new prescriber authorization has been issued. Pharmacy A proposes a $12 processing charge. Under 247 CMR 9.14, which response is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.14(1)–(4): timely transfer, no fee, Schedule VI remaining refills and one-year issuance limitation

options.option_text: Transfer both prescriptions because the one-year Schedule VI transfer period is measured from the most recent dispensing date, not the date each original prescription was issued.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) expressly prohibits transferring a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year after the prescription's ISSUE DATE. Prescription Y was issued October 20, 2025; the October 2026 dispensing does not restart that window.

options.option_text: Transfer Prescription X in a timely manner without charging a transfer fee, but do not transfer Prescription Y for refills under the original prescription because more than one year has elapsed since issuance.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.14(1) requires timely transfers on patient request, §9.14(3) forbids a transfer fee, §9.14(4)(b) permits transfer of Schedule VI prescriptions with authorized refills remaining, and §9.14(4)(c) establishes the one-year issue-date limit. X qualifies; Y is outside its original time window.

options.option_text: Refuse Prescription X because any Schedule VI prescription that has previously been dispensed can no longer be transferred; transfer Prescription Y because its last refill was recent.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The regulation explicitly permits transferring a Schedule VI prescription with remaining authorized refills. It is not categorically limited to never-filled prescriptions. Prescription Y is too old based on its issuance date, regardless of recent dispensing.

options.option_text: Transfer Prescription X but charge the $12 fee if necessary to cover staff time; keep Prescription Y at Pharmacy A until the patient uses the remaining refills there.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.14(3) does not permit a processing or labor fee for the transfer. Moreover, the expired one-year issue-date limit cannot be bypassed merely by keeping Prescription Y at the original pharmacy for dispensing under the old authorization.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered Massachusetts community pharmacy is preparing for a joint federal and state recordkeeping inspection. It has paper Schedule II, paper Schedule III–V, and paper Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions, together with electronic controlled-substance prescription records. It also retains purchasing, return, disposal, and destruction records. There is no exception for an institutional sterile-compounding pharmacy. Which proposed practices comply with BOTH applicable Massachusetts and federal requirements? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.16(1)–(6); 21 CFR 1304.04(a), (h)(1)–(5) (paper, electronic, readily retrievable and separately maintained records)

options.option_text: Keep paper Schedule II prescriptions in a separate Schedule II prescription file at the DEA-registered pharmacy location, rather than mixing them with ordinary Schedule VI paper prescriptions.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Federal 21 CFR 1304.04(h)(1)–(2) requires Schedule II pharmacy inventories/records separately and paper Schedule II prescriptions in a separate file at the registered location. Massachusetts 247 CMR 9.16(2) also requires paper Schedule II prescription segregation.

options.option_text: Segregate the paper Schedule III–V prescriptions and separately segregate Massachusetts Schedule VI paper prescriptions, even though federal law provides a red-'C' filing method for some readily retrievable Schedule III–V prescriptions.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Massachusetts 247 CMR 9.16(3)–(4) expressly requires segregation of paper prescriptions for Schedules III–V and for Massachusetts Schedule VI. Federal 21 CFR 1304.04(h)(4) contains a red-'C' readily-retrievable method, but that federal allowance does not eliminate a more restrictive Massachusetts filing requirement.

options.option_text: Store electronic Schedule II–V prescriptions only on a remote vendor system that cannot promptly retrieve or print records at the pharmacy, because off-site electronic storage always removes the DEA registered-location retrieval requirement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 21 CFR 1304.04(h)(5), electronic controlled prescriptions may reside on computers elsewhere only if they are readily retrievable at the registered location and printable or transferable in a readily understandable format. Massachusetts 247 CMR 9.16(2)–(6) also demands electronic separability and printable records.

options.option_text: Keep prescription records plus purchasing, returns, disposal, and destruction records readily retrievable for at least TWO YEARS, and maintain the capacity to print readable electronic prescriptions and stored prescription images.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Massachusetts 247 CMR 9.16(1) requires at least two years of readily retrievable prescription, purchasing, return, disposal, and destruction records, while (5)–(6) requires readable printouts of electronic prescriptions and electronically stored images. Federal 21 CFR 1304.04(a) sets a general two-year DEA minimum for records covered by Part 1304.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist has seven years of licensed practice and participates in a current hypertension collaborative drug therapy management (CDTM) agreement with TWO supervising physicians. The agreement authorizes patient-specific prescribing. The pharmacist's liability policy has a $1 million annual aggregate limit but covers only $250,000 per occurrence, and the Board has just imposed a practice restriction through an agreed disciplinary disposition. The pharmacist is reviewing what must be corrected or reported before continuing CDTM activities. Under 247 CMR 16.02, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b),(e)–(f), (3); Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy, Collaborative Drug Therapy Management regulation

options.option_text: The pharmacist must maintain professional liability insurance specifically covering CDTM with at least $1 million PER OCCURRENCE throughout the agreement; the stated aggregate limit does not cure the inadequate per-occurrence limit.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b) expressly requires liability insurance of at least $1,000,000 per occurrence, specifically covering drug therapy management, throughout the collaborative practice agreement. The described $250,000 per-occurrence coverage is insufficient even with a $1 million aggregate.

options.option_text: Completion of five CDTM-related CE hours during the FIRST year satisfies the additional CDTM education requirement for the full two-year agreement because the ordinary pharmacist license requires continuing education separately.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 16.02(1)(e) requires at least five ADDITIONAL Board-approved contact hours in EACH year of the CDTM agreement, addressing practice areas generally related to that agreement. Completing five hours in only one year does not cover another year.

options.option_text: Because prescribing is included, the pharmacist must maintain the applicable Massachusetts controlled-substance registration and meet the prescribing-related training and MassHealth participation/application attestation requirements.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 16.02(1)(f) adds a current Department-issued MCSR, the applicable initial and biennial training, and a signed MassHealth participation-or-application attestation when prescriptive practices form part of the CDTM agreement. Ordinary licensure or a physician's signature does not replace these obligations.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must give WRITTEN notice of the Board-imposed practice restriction to EACH supervising physician, even though the restriction resulted from an agreement rather than a formal Board order.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 16.02(3) expressly applies to Board discipline by agreement or order and to other practice restrictions, requiring written notification to every supervising physician. Having two physicians does not allow notification of only one.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives a valid new electronic apixaban prescription from an authorized practitioner. The patient's profile still lists rivaroxaban as active, and the computer flags potentially dangerous therapeutic duplication. The patient says the physician intended a switch but cannot recall exactly when the previous anticoagulant was to be stopped. A certified technician suggests clearing the alert because the new prescription is electronically authenticated. No dispensing has yet occurred. Which action is MOST consistent with 247 CMR 9.17 and the pharmacist's professional responsibility?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.17(1)(b),(i), (2); M.G.L. c.94C §21A (prospective drug review)

options.option_text: Allow the technician to close the alert and dispense immediately, because electronic prescriber authentication satisfies the pharmacist's prospective review obligation for a clinically significant therapy change.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An electronically authenticated prescription may still present a clinically significant drug-therapy problem. Section 9.17(1) places the prospective DUR responsibility on the pharmacist and specifically includes therapeutic duplication and significant changes in therapy. Technician or software clearance cannot substitute for the pharmacist's clinical review.

options.option_text: Have the pharmacist assess the duplication BEFORE dispensing, obtain sufficient clarification from the patient and/or prescriber as clinically necessary, document the measures taken in response to DUR, and dispense only after the therapy plan is determined appropriate.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 9.17(1)–(2), the pharmacist must conduct prospective DUR before dispensing, make a reasonable effort to identify therapeutic duplication and significant therapy changes, take appropriate patient-protective measures, and document the measures taken. Contact with the prescriber is a possible means of clarification, not a universal fixed requirement for every alert.

options.option_text: Permanently refuse every prescription whenever the computer detects two drugs in the same therapeutic class, even if further investigation confirms that the old drug was discontinued before the new one starts.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.17 requires professional assessment and appropriate measures, not categorical refusal whenever an automated duplicate-therapy warning appears. A clinically appropriate transition may be lawful once properly evaluated.

options.option_text: Dispense now and perform the pharmacist's prospective DUR at the patient's next refill, because the patient verbally confirmed that a switch was intended.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The statute and 247 CMR 9.17(1) require prospective DUR BEFORE a new prescription is dispensed or delivered. The patient's uncertain timing does not justify postponing assessment of a potentially significant overlap.

questions.question_stem: In November 2026, a properly trained Massachusetts pharmacist who is otherwise qualified under the applicable statewide oral HIV PEP prescribing guidance evaluates a clinically eligible 25-year-old adult. Thirty-six hours earlier, the patient shared injection equipment with someone whose HIV status is unknown; the pharmacist has assessed the exposure and documented a sufficiently substantial risk to warrant PEP after individualized clinical evaluation. The patient gives consent and has no known HIV infection, symptoms suggesting acute HIV, interacting medicines, or other protocol exclusion. A baseline blood-based HIV test has been ordered urgently, but the result is not yet available; no appropriate rapid test is immediately accessible. What is the BEST next action?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19F; Massachusetts DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 (Aug. 25, 2026); CDC MMWR 2025 nPEP recommendations (72 hours, baseline testing and 28-day treatment); Massachusetts statewide oral PEP protocol exists (Sept. 2026 DOCX), details not independently authenticated

options.option_text: Defer all PEP until the laboratory HIV-negative result arrives even if the delay causes initiation to occur more than 72 hours after exposure.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. CDC 2025 nPEP recommendations emphasize starting indicated PEP as soon as possible, no later than 72 hours, without delaying the first dose for pending laboratory results. Baseline HIV testing should still be obtained promptly and interpreted.

options.option_text: Decline because Massachusetts pharmacist HIV PEP prescribing always requires a patient-specific physician-signed CDTM agreement, even when all applicable statewide prescribing criteria are satisfied.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §19F and Massachusetts DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 independently authorize appropriately qualified pharmacists to prescribe specified HIV prevention medications under statewide guidance. A separate patient-specific CDTM agreement is not inherently required for that distinct authority.

options.option_text: Issue a 90-day PrEP prescription with two refills as a substitute for urgent PEP and postpone follow-up HIV testing until a refill is requested.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An exposure that occurred 36 hours ago calls for the PEP pathway when clinically indicated. PEP is a 28-day course with baseline and follow-up testing; it is not interchangeable with routine PrEP, which is intended for prospective prevention.

options.option_text: Arrange timely baseline HIV testing and follow-up, initiate an appropriate 28-day oral PEP regimen promptly without awaiting a pending laboratory result, and coordinate the medical evaluation and monitoring required by the statewide protocol.
options.original_rationale: Correct. CDC 2025 nPEP recommendations support starting eligible patients' 28-day PEP as soon as possible within 72 hours without waiting for pending laboratory test results, while still performing baseline and follow-up HIV evaluation. M.G.L. c.94C §19F and DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 authorize appropriately qualified Massachusetts pharmacists to prescribe covered HIV-prevention medications under statewide guidance. The stem explicitly assumes other state-protocol eligibility requirements are met.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy filled a patient-specific, nonhazardous Schedule VI tablet prescription, but the patient NEVER picked it up and the prescription was NEVER delivered. Staff want to return the tablets to available pharmacy stock for possible later lawful dispensing. The pharmacy also learns that one manufacturer's lot of this medication is being recalled; it is not yet known whether the prepared tablets came from the recalled lot. The pharmacy has a compliant general return-to-stock policy. Which approach BEST complies with 247 CMR 9.13?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.13(1)(a)–(b), (2)–(3); compare 247 CMR 9.01(5)–(7) for medication returned AFTER dispensing
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.13(1)-(3): never-dispensed return to stock and recalled lot status

options.option_text: Pour the uncollected tablets into the manufacturer's bulk stock bottle after comparing the NDC; a pharmacist's visual check overcomes the regulation's restriction on refilling bulk bottles.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.13(1)(a) expressly states that a pharmacy may NOT return a medication to the manufacturer's stock bottle. NDC matching or pharmacist inspection does not create an exception.
options.independent_option_analysis: Original manufacturer bulk bottle cannot receive prepared, uncollected tablets.

options.option_text: Destroy the tablets in all circumstances, because creation of a patient label makes the preparation legally equivalent to a medication already dispensed to a patient.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.13(1) expressly allows return to stock when a prescription was PREPARED but the medication was NOT dispensed. This is different from a patient returning medication after it was dispensed under 247 CMR 9.01(5)–(7).
options.independent_option_analysis: Uncollected preparation is not the same as previously dispensed medication.

options.option_text: Retain the tablets in the original patient container or an appropriate alternate container labeled with product, strength, manufacturer/supplier or NDC, and the expiration assigned at filling; do not dispense this potentially recalled return-to-stock medication unless its actual lot is confirmed outside the recall.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.13(1)(b) requires the four return-to-stock labeling elements and permits the original patient container or an appropriate alternative. Section 9.13(3) prohibits dispensing returned-to-stock medication potentially subject to a recall until the pharmacy can confirm the specific lot is NOT included. The product cannot simply be poured back into the manufacturer bottle.
options.independent_option_analysis: Traceable original/alternate container requires label elements; recall lot must be resolved before redispense.

options.option_text: Place the tablets in an unlabeled internal bag and use them for another patient as soon as a barcode scan matches the product, because recall restrictions apply only to medication remaining in the original manufacturer's packaging.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Return-to-stock containers require specific identifying information under §9.13(1)(b), and §9.13(3) applies to potentially recalled medication that has been returned to stock, not just to manufacturer's original containers. A matching product barcode is not confirmation that a lot is outside the recall.
options.independent_option_analysis: Unknown recalled lot cannot be ignored based on scan or unlabeled storage.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts licensed community pharmacy plans TWO separate technologies: a wall-secured Automated Pharmacy System (APS) for patients to collect already filled prescriptions and a Pharmacy Processing Automation (PPA) machine to count and fill prescription containers. The pharmacy maintains the applicable policies and all requirements not explicitly addressed below. Which proposed arrangements are permitted under 247 CMR 9.10–9.11? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.10(1)(a)–(h), 9.11(1)(a)–(b); Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy, Professional Practice Standards

options.option_text: Use a continuously video-monitored, technology-verified APS located in the SAME BUILDING as the pharmacy to release an otherwise valid Schedule IV prescription after hours, with patient choice, an identifying electronic audit trail and a pharmacist consultation opportunity whenever it dispenses.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.10(1)(a)–(h) permits an APS to release Schedule IV–VI medications during or after pharmacy operating hours when, among other conditions, it remains in the same building, is secured and video-monitored, verifies the drug and patient, keeps a traceable audit trail, offers pharmacist consultation whenever dispensing, and permits the patient to decline APS use.

options.option_text: Use that same APS to release a Schedule II oxycodone prescription after hours because DEA registration, camera surveillance, and barcode verification make the device eligible for EVERY controlled-substance schedule.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.10(1) limits retail APS dispensing to Schedules IV–VI. Added identification technology and DEA registration do not expand the APS's legal scope to Schedule II.

options.option_text: If the PPA machine commingles different manufacturing lot numbers in one dispensing cell, maintain a procedure to quarantine ALL commingled lot numbers whenever one lot is recalled.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.11(1)(b) specifically requires a pharmacy whose PPA commingles lot numbers in a single cell to maintain a policy and procedure to quarantine all the commingled lot numbers if one lot number is recalled. Verification technology remains required under §9.11(1)(a).

options.option_text: Stock insulin that REQUIRES refrigeration in the APS for patient pickup if the appliance incorporates a reliable temperature logger and a pharmacist verifies stability before loading.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.10(1)(d) categorically prohibits stocking any medication requiring refrigeration or reconstitution in an APS. Temperature logging cannot override this rule.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy is NOT providing vaccination services. One pharmacist supervises a prescription-filling team of FOUR licensed support personnel: TWO licensed certified pharmacy technicians, ONE licensed noncertified technician, and ONE licensed pharmacy technician trainee (PTT). The PTT is directly supervised by an ADDITIONAL licensed certified technician assigned exclusively as the PTT's dedicated trainer. The trainer and trainee have appropriate name badges and were designated on the pharmacy's published staffing schedule BEFORE that training day; written training policies are in place. The trainer does not independently fill, process, or otherwise support prescriptions. No separate Board waiver applies. Under Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-02, which staffing conclusion is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-02, §§I(A)(1)(b), I(B), III(A)–(B) (adopted Sept. 3, 2026); 247 CMR 8.00

options.option_text: The pharmacist may count only the two certified technicians and the noncertified technician, because a dedicated trainer and the associated PTT are BOTH excluded from the supervisory ratio.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Board Policy 2026-02, Section III(A)(2)(c), specifically counts a supervised 'Trainee' in the pharmacist ratio as a pharmacy technician. Excluding the dedicated trainer does not also exempt the trainee while the trainee performs prescription-support duties.

options.option_text: The four-person filling team meets the ordinary 1:4 ratio with two certified technicians; the separately designated trainer may be excluded while working solely in the trainer–trainee role, but the PTT remains counted among the four.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2026-02, Section I(A)(1)(b), permits 1:4 with at least two licensed certified technicians. Sections III and III(A)–(B) exclude a properly designated trainer who performs NO independent pharmacy-support duties, while requiring the actively participating trainee to count as a pharmacy technician. The advance schedule, badges, and supervision meet the stated training conditions.

options.option_text: The dedicated trainer can remain excluded if the trainer starts independently preparing an additional patient's prescription, as long as another technician checks the work.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under Policy 2026-02, Sections III and III(A)(1)(c), a trainer who performs professional support work outside the trainer–trainee relationship must be counted. That would make five counted filling-support personnel here, exceeding the ordinary 1:4 ratio at a pharmacy not providing vaccinations.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may use the 1:6 immunization-service ratio regardless of whether it vaccinates anyone, so the number and certification status of the support staff are irrelevant.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Policy 2026-02, Section I(B), makes the 1:6 provision conditional on a pharmacy providing vaccination services and on the minimum qualifying certified/intern support mix. Neither condition can be presumed at this nonvaccinating pharmacy.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts community pharmacy routinely calls a household landline and mails refill notices to the patient's home. An adult patient asks that FUTURE prescription-related communications instead be sent only to the patient's personal mobile number because several other people share the household. The pharmacy can reasonably accommodate the request using its existing workflow. The patient supplies the alternate number but refuses to describe the personal reason for confidentiality. No separate disclosure law or unusual operational burden applies. Which response BEST follows the federal HIPAA confidential-communications rule?
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.522(b)(1)(i)–(ii), (b)(2)(i)–(iv); HHS OCR guidance, alternative confidential communications

options.option_text: The pharmacy must reject the request until the patient proves that a communication to the household could endanger the patient's safety; this is required for every covered provider.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 45 CFR 164.522(b)(1)(i), a covered HEALTH CARE PROVIDER must accommodate a reasonable alternative-contact request without a required endangerment statement. The express endangerment-statement condition in 164.522(b)(1)(ii) applies to HEALTH PLANS, not automatically to this pharmacy.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may require a signed explanation identifying the sensitive diagnosis that motivated the request; without it, the pharmacy has no duty to use the supplied alternate contact method.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 45 CFR 164.522(b)(2)(iii) explicitly prohibits a covered health care provider from conditioning confidential communications on an explanation of the patient's reason. Requiring a diagnosis disclosure would contradict the rule.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must withhold all future prescription counseling, refill reminders and treatment communications until the patient signs a separate HIPAA authorization covering each communication.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 164.522(b) concerns reasonable changes to the means or location of communications. It does not turn routine permitted provider–patient treatment or prescription communications into disclosures requiring individual HIPAA authorizations.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must accommodate this reasonable alternate-contact request; it may require the request in writing and an alternate address or contact method, but cannot demand an explanation of the patient's reason as a condition of accommodating it.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 45 CFR 164.522(b)(1)(i) obligates covered providers to accommodate reasonable confidential communications requests. Section 164.522(b)(2) permits a written request and information concerning alternate contact or payment when appropriate, but expressly prohibits a provider from demanding a reason.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist correctly administers a federally covered inactivated influenza vaccination to an adult under a valid standing order. The pharmacy provided the current Vaccine Information Statement (VIS) before the injection, and all Massachusetts MIIS reporting and clinical requirements have been met. An internal audit finds that the patient's permanent immunization record lacks some federal documentation elements, although the electronic system contains the patient's name and the administered dose. Under the federal National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act (NCVIA) and CDC VIS instructions, which additions or practices are required or permitted as described? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 42 U.S.C. §300aa-25(a)(1)–(4); 42 U.S.C. §300aa-26; CDC Instructions for Using VISs, 'Record information for each VIS provided'

options.option_text: Record the vaccine's administration date, manufacturer, and lot number in the patient's permanent medical record or an authorized permanent office log.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 42 U.S.C. 300aa-25(a)(1)–(2) requires the vaccine administration date plus manufacturer and lot number in the patient's permanent record or a qualifying permanent office log, even where the dose is already recorded in the state registry.

options.option_text: Omit the name, address and professional title of the vaccinator because the patient is an adult and the pharmacy's name is visible on the retail receipt.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 300aa-25(a)(3) applies to covered vaccinations given to any person, not just children, and requires the vaccinating provider's name, address and, if appropriate, title in the permanent record or qualifying log. A retail receipt without those elements is not a substitute.

options.option_text: Document BOTH the edition date of the VIS furnished and the date it was given; recording only the vaccination date does not meet the separate VIS documentation requirement.
options.original_rationale: Correct. CDC's Instructions for Using VISs, implementing 42 U.S.C. 300aa-26, require documentation of the specific VIS edition date AND the date the VIS was provided. Those are distinct from the administration date required by §300aa-25.

options.option_text: Document the name, address and appropriate title of the vaccinating healthcare provider in the recipient's permanent medical record OR in a permanent office log accessible to the patient's legal representative on request.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 300aa-25(a) explicitly permits an appropriate permanent office log or file accessible to the legal representative rather than requiring that every field appear exclusively in the main electronic patient chart. The vaccinator identity and address must still be recorded.

questions.question_stem: Four INDEPENDENT prospective purchasers are at different federally compliant, self-certified sellers in Massachusetts, seeking additional over-the-counter pseudoephedrine. All quantities are PSE BASE equivalents, all earlier purchases below are within the relevant 30-day window, all required photo IDs and sales records are available, and no state-specific or other restrictions apply. Each proposed sale would occur in a single transaction. Under the federal Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act (CMEA), which proposed sale is permissible?
questions.author_citation: 21 U.S.C. 830(d)(1), (e)(1)(A)(ix), 844(a); 21 CFR 1314.20(a)–(b); DEA CMEA General Information
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 21 CFR 1314.20(a)-(b) 3.6g/day, mobile vendor 7.5g per customer/30d; 21 USC 844(a) 9g total purchases

options.option_text: A MOBILE retail vendor sells an additional 0.60 gram to a purchaser who has already obtained 7.20 grams from that mobile vendor within the preceding 30 days, with no purchases earlier today.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(A)(ix)(II) and 21 CFR 1314.20(b) limit mobile retail vendor sales to 7.5 grams of pseudoephedrine base per purchaser in any 30-day period. The resulting 7.80 grams exceeds that mobile-vendor limit, despite being below the general 9-gram individual-purchase ceiling.
options.independent_option_analysis: Mobile 7.2+0.6=7.8g exceeds 7.5g vendor-specific limit.

options.option_text: A conventional walk-in retail pharmacy sells another 0.50 gram to a purchaser who already purchased 8.60 grams of pseudoephedrine base at retail in the same 30-day period, with no earlier purchases today.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Although the calendar-day quantity would be below 3.6 grams, the federal individual retail-purchase limit is 9 grams per 30 days under 21 U.S.C. 844(a). The proposed 9.10 grams exceeds it.
options.independent_option_analysis: Normal retail 8.6+0.5=9.1g exceeds purchaser 9g/30d limit.

options.option_text: A MOBILE retail vendor sells an additional 0.60 gram to a purchaser who previously bought 6.90 grams from that vendor in the current 30-day period and made no other purchases today.
options.original_rationale: Correct. A mobile retail vendor's 30-day ceiling is 7.5 grams of pseudoephedrine base, and 6.90 + 0.60 = exactly 7.50 grams. The same calendar day's sale is below the federal 3.6-gram daily limit. The scenario assumes compliance with all other seller and buyer requirements.
options.independent_option_analysis: Mobile 6.9+0.6=7.5g and daily 0.6g within both limits.

options.option_text: A conventional walk-in retail pharmacy sells another 0.60 gram to a purchaser who already purchased 3.10 grams from that pharmacy earlier on the SAME calendar day, despite having bought only 3.10 grams in the entire 30-day period.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal 21 U.S.C. 830(d)(1) and 21 CFR 1314.20(a) limit sales to 3.6 grams per purchaser in a single calendar day regardless of how many transactions occur. The combined 3.70 grams exceeds that daily limit despite remaining below the general 30-day ceiling.
options.independent_option_analysis: Normal retail 3.1+0.6=3.7g violates 3.6g one-day limit.

questions.question_stem: Two Massachusetts-based entities are reviewing federal human-drug compounding exemptions. Pharmacy A is a state-licensed community pharmacy whose pharmacists compound under section 503A, NOT an FDA-registered outsourcing facility. Facility B is an FDA-registered 503B outsourcing facility compounding sterile products. Assume all other respective federal and Massachusetts compounding, product-quality, licensure and distribution conditions are met unless a choice expressly violates the cited patient-prescription requirement. Which statements correctly describe these different pathways? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: FD&C Act §§503A(a)(1)–(2), 503B(d)(4)(C) (21 U.S.C. §§353a, 353b); FDA Human Drug Compounding Laws and Prescription-Requirement-Under-503A Final Guidance

options.option_text: Pharmacy A may compound LIMITED quantities before receiving an identified patient's valid prescription if a documented history of valid orders for that drug arose from established relationships with the patients or the prescribers expected to write those orders; distribution still requires the valid patient-specific prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FD&C Act §503A(a)(2) (21 U.S.C. 353a(a)(2)) allows LIMITED anticipatory compounding based on historical valid prescriptions within established pharmacist/patient or pharmacist/prescriber relationships. FDA's final §503A prescription-requirement guidance states that anticipated doses may not be distributed before a valid individual-patient prescription is received.

options.option_text: Pharmacy A qualifies for the 503A exemptions by sending a compounded batch to a physician's office for use on unnamed future patients based only on a general 'office stock' purchase order.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A general office-use purchase order without any patient-specific prescription does not satisfy the federal §503A patient-prescription requirement. FDA distinguishes 503A from the qualified §503B outsourcing pathway, which can supply office stock. State authorization alone cannot replace the federal requirement for the 503A exemptions.

options.option_text: Facility B, if compliant with all §503B conditions, may compound and distribute eligible sterile products for office stock without prescriptions identifying individual patients, while remaining subject to applicable current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FD&C Act §503B(d)(4)(C) expressly permits an outsourcing facility to obtain or not obtain prescriptions for identified individual patients. FDA explains that qualifying 503B facilities may supply office stock but remain subject to CGMP and other §503B requirements.

options.option_text: Facility B is exempt from CGMP merely because its batches are compounded rather than conventionally manufactured, exactly as a qualifying 503A pharmacy is.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The FD&C Act §503A exemption includes CGMP requirements only when every 503A condition is satisfied, whereas §503B does NOT exempt qualifying outsourcing-facility compounding from CGMP. The two pathways are not interchangeable.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist also holds a New Hampshire license. The New Hampshire board places that license on probation by a signed consent agreement after finding falsified controlled-substance inventory records; the same conduct would violate Massachusetts pharmacy law. In an unrelated Massachusetts matter, the Massachusetts Board issues only an ADVISORY LETTER, not a reprimand or probation order. Which description BEST reflects the Massachusetts Board's authority and the status of that letter?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 10.06(2)–(4),(6)–(7); 247 CMR 10.03(1)(t); M.G.L. c.112 §32 (protected-services limitation where applicable)

options.option_text: The Massachusetts Board cannot initiate reciprocal discipline because the New Hampshire case was resolved by consent instead of a contested hearing; its advisory letter is non-disciplinary.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 247 CMR 10.06(6)–(7), a consent agreement can impose discipline, and out-of-state discipline may support a Massachusetts proceeding when the conduct violates Massachusetts law. A contested hearing in New Hampshire is not an absolute prerequisite to initiating Massachusetts action.

options.option_text: The New Hampshire probation automatically suspends the Massachusetts pharmacist license, and the Massachusetts advisory letter is itself a formal reprimand.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 10.06(7) makes out-of-state action a possible basis for INITIATING Massachusetts discipline, not an automatic Massachusetts suspension. Section 10.06(2) explicitly says an advisory letter is not formal disciplinary action.

options.option_text: The Massachusetts Board must immediately impose identical probation whenever any state disciplines a pharmacist, regardless of whether the underlying conduct would violate Massachusetts law.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 10.06(7) uses MAY and conditions reciprocal action on conduct that constitutes a Massachusetts-law violation. Disciplinary action is not automatically identical or mandatory, and statutory protections can also restrict particular reciprocal discipline.

options.option_text: The Massachusetts Board MAY initiate its own proceeding based on the New Hampshire discipline because the underlying conduct would violate Massachusetts law; the Massachusetts advisory letter itself is not formal discipline.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 10.06(7) permits, rather than automatically imposes, disciplinary proceedings based on another state's action when the underlying conduct would violate Massachusetts law.
