Section 10.06(2) states that an advisory letter identifies concerns but does NOT constitute formal disciplinary action; probation and reprimand are different formal sanctions under 10.06(3)–(4).

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives prescriptions prepared by physician assistants (PAs). For the fully licensed PA, current Massachusetts controlled-substance registration (MCSR), individual DEA registration for the appropriate schedules, mutually approved written prescribing guidelines, supervising-physician arrangements and other prescription formalities are in place. A second PA holds only a TEMPORARY Massachusetts PA license. No emergency or other exception changes the stated licensing rules. Which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 263 CMR 5.06(1)–(4),(7); M.G.L. c.94C §§7,9,20; Massachusetts PA Board FAQs on DEA numbers and supervisor name

options.option_text: The fully licensed PA may issue a Schedule II prescription using ONLY the supervising physician's DEA number when the physician has approved the written prescribing guidelines.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The Massachusetts PA practice FAQ and M.G.L. c.94C require a PA who prescribes federally controlled Schedules II–V to have the PA's OWN appropriate DEA registration, in addition to the required MCSR; a physician's DEA number is not interchangeable with the PA's registration.

options.option_text: The fully licensed PA may issue a Schedule III prescription within the PA's authorized scope using the PA's own registrations; Massachusetts does not universally require the supervising physician's name to appear on the PA's prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 263 CMR 5.06(1),(4),(7) permits an appropriately registered, fully licensed PA to prescribe within the agreed guidelines and applicable law. Massachusetts PA Board FAQs state that the supervising physician's name is NOT required on a PA prescription, while the PA must possess the PA's own MCSR and DEA authorization for Schedules II–V.

options.option_text: A PA holding only a temporary license may issue an otherwise permitted WRITTEN prescription in the temporary PA's own name and signature, provided the supervising physician cosigns it after the patient receives the prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 263 CMR 5.06(2)(a),(c), a temporarily licensed PA may PREPARE a written prescription, but the supervising or designated physician must sign it BEFORE issuance and it must be issued in that physician's name. After-the-fact cosignature is not sufficient.

options.option_text: A Schedule II prescription issued by a fully licensed PA is subject to the supervising or designated physician's review within 96 hours after issuance, even when the PA was authorized to issue it.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 263 CMR 5.06(3) specifically requires the supervising physician (or designated temporary supervisor) to review the PA's Schedule II prescription or medication order WITHIN 96 HOURS after issuance. This is a distinct follow-up duty from an improperly delayed countersignature for a temporary PA.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed nurse practitioner (NP) has obtained independent prescriptive-practice authority after completing the required supervised experience. The NP transmits an otherwise valid, properly signed electronic Schedule IV prescription using the NP's own current appropriate MCSR and DEA registrations. The prescription does NOT identify a supervising physician, and the pharmacist has no clinical or authenticity concerns. Under Massachusetts law and DPH Circular DCP 21-10-111, which conclusion is BEST?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.112 §80E; 105 CMR 721.020(E); DPH Circular DCP 21-10-111 (supervised versus independent prescribers); MA Board of Nursing APRN prescriptive-authority guidance

options.option_text: The pharmacist may dispense without independently obtaining proof of the NP's independent-practice status solely because the supervisor's name is absent, while continuing ordinary validity and patient-safety checks.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.112 §80E permits independent prescriptive practice after the relevant experience and authorization. 105 CMR 721.020(E) requires a supervisor name for certain nurse prescribers UNLESS they have independent authority; Circular DCP 21-10-111 says a pharmacist is NOT required to verify that status solely because the name is missing on an otherwise valid prescription.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must always reject any NP-controlled prescription that lacks a supervising physician's name, even when the NP has valid independent prescriptive authority.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts explicitly exempts independently authorized NPs from the supervising-professional-name requirement. A blanket rejection would ignore 105 CMR 721.020(E), M.G.L. c.112 §80E and DPH's pharmacist-specific clarification.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must contact the NP's former supervising physician to authorize this prescription, because two years of supervised experience never permits independent Schedule IV prescriptive practice.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.112 §80E provides an independent-practice pathway after the required supervised experience and authorization. Under the facts stated, there is no current supervising physician from whom patient-specific permission is required.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may fill this Schedule IV order only if the NP substitutes a supervising physician's DEA number, because nurse practitioners may hold MCSRs but not their own DEA registrations.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Properly authorized nurse practitioners may hold their own appropriate MCSR and DEA registrations for federally controlled drugs. Using another practitioner's DEA number would not cure a problem and contradicts the NP's individual registration.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is classifying four products in November 2026. Each named codeine product is a lawfully marketed prescription product in the stated strength; combination products contain their nonnarcotic ingredients in recognized therapeutic quantities. The gabapentin product is conventional prescription-only oral gabapentin. Under current federal DEA schedules and Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.002 and PMP rules, which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1)(i), 1308.13(e), 1308.15(c)(1); 105 CMR 700.002(B),(C),(E),(F); MA DPH MassPAT pharmacy reporting and data submission

options.option_text: A single-ingredient codeine sulfate 30-mg oral tablet is a Schedule II controlled substance, rather than a Schedule III product solely because its unit dose is below 90 mg.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Codeine alone is generally Schedule II under 21 CFR 1308.12. The Schedule III allowance for codeine doses up to 90 mg per unit requires a qualifying COMBINATION with recognized nonnarcotic active ingredient(s), which the single-ingredient tablet lacks. 105 CMR 700.002 incorporates the federal schedule.

options.option_text: An acetaminophen 300 mg/codeine 30 mg oral tablet is Schedule II merely because codeine appears in its ingredient list, so the qualifying combination-drug rules do not apply.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 21 CFR 1308.13 and DEA's classification guidance, a qualifying codeine 30 mg/acetaminophen 300 mg combination meets Schedule III requirements (no more than 90 mg codeine per dosage unit with a recognized therapeutic nonnarcotic ingredient). Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.002 generally tracks this federal Schedule III designation.

options.option_text: A promethazine/codeine syrup containing 10 mg of codeine per 5 mL (200 mg per 100 mL) with qualifying nonnarcotic promethazine is Schedule V, not Schedule III solely because it contains codeine.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The codeine concentration is exactly 200 mg per 100 mL, within the Schedule V ceiling for qualifying codeine combination cough preparations under 21 CFR 1308.15. Under 105 CMR 700.002(E), Massachusetts includes federally Schedule V products in its Schedule V.

options.option_text: Prescription gabapentin is NOT a federally scheduled controlled substance, but remains Massachusetts Schedule VI and must be reported to MassPAT under the state's additional-drug reporting rule.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Gabapentin is not listed as federally controlled in DEA Schedules II–V. Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.002(F) defines unscheduled prescription medicines as Schedule VI, and the DPH PMP reporting guidance specifically includes gabapentin as an additional reportable drug without changing its schedule.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy prepares a NONHAZARDOUS Category 1 compounded sterile preparation (CSP) from sterile ingredients in an ISO Class 5 primary engineering control inside an otherwise suitable UNCLASSIFIED segregated compounding area (SCA). Personnel meet applicable USP <797> aseptic training, garbing and environmental requirements; manufacturer stability supports at least 48 hours refrigerated, with no additional shorter limiting factor. Which BUD/facility decision is permitted under the currently applicable USP <797>?
questions.author_citation: USP <797> §§3–4, 14 (Category 1 CSP environment and BUD limits); USP <797> Official FAQs (Dec. 11, 2023), Questions 31, 74 and 93; 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Assign a 24-hour controlled-room-temperature BUD because ISO Class 5 air quality allows a Category 1 CSP to exceed the usual 12-hour controlled-room-temperature maximum.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. ISO Class 5 PECs are required for Category 1 sterile compounding but do not independently extend the Category 1 beyond-use limit. Under USP <797>, Category 1 CSPs are limited to no more than 12 hours at controlled room temperature or 24 hours refrigerated, assuming no shorter restriction.

options.option_text: Assign a BUD no longer than 24 hours when refrigerated (or 12 hours at controlled room temperature), using the ISO Class 5 PEC in the SCA and the same minimum compounding-garb requirements applicable to Category 2.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <797> §§3–4, 14 permits Category 1 compounding in an ISO Class 5 PEC within a qualifying unclassified SCA. The current Category 1 BUD ceilings are 12 hours at controlled room temperature and 24 hours refrigerated. USP's December 2023 official FAQ explains that minimum garbing, including sterile gloves, is not relaxed merely because the PEC is in an SCA.

options.option_text: Assign the Category 2 four-day controlled-room-temperature BUD in the same SCA merely by performing extra sterility testing, without relocating the ISO Class 5 PEC to a compliant cleanroom suite.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Category 2 CSPs require the applicable cleanroom suite and other Category 2 controls under USP <797>; a Category 1 SCA is not automatically upgraded into a Category 2 compounding environment through supplemental testing.

options.option_text: Assign a 48-hour refrigerated BUD because the ingredients are sterile and the manufacturer supports at least 48 hours of chemical stability, regardless of Category 1's microbiological limits.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Chemical stability data do not override USP <797>'s Category 1 microbiological BUD ceilings. When using Category 1 conditions, the shorter Category 1 limit remains controlling even if physical or chemical stability extends beyond it.

questions.question_stem: The Massachusetts Board obtains sworn affidavits and dispensing records indicating that a licensed pharmacist presents an immediate or serious threat to public safety. The allegations have not yet been adjudicated at a final merits hearing. Under 247 CMR 10.07, which action is authorized?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 10.07 (Suspension Prior to Hearing, effective Jan. 9, 2025); contrast 247 CMR 10.06(2),(8)–(9)

options.option_text: The Board may issue an advisory letter but cannot suspend the pharmacist's license until a final merits hearing or a criminal conviction.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An advisory letter is a different, non-disciplinary response under 247 CMR 10.06(2). Section 10.07 specifically permits a prehearing suspension or refusal to renew when affidavits or other documentary evidence establish an immediate or serious public threat; a criminal conviction is not a universal prerequisite.

options.option_text: The Board may suspend or refuse to renew the license pending the final merits hearing, but must afford a hearing on the necessity of that summary action within seven days of its action.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 10.07 allows temporary summary action based on affidavits or other documentary evidence of an immediate or serious threat to public health, safety, or welfare. A separate hearing focused on whether the summary action is needed must be afforded within seven days, even though the full merits hearing may occur later.

options.option_text: The Board may suspend the license before a merits hearing, but the pharmacist is entitled to no hearing about that suspension until the final allegations are resolved.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Although summary action may precede a final merits adjudication, 247 CMR 10.07 expressly guarantees a prompt, limited hearing about its necessity within seven days of the Board's action. A later full hearing does not substitute for the limited summary-action hearing.

options.option_text: A Board cease-and-desist notice is the only possible immediate remedy; license suspension or refusal to renew is reserved for matters already finally adjudicated.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Summary cease-and-desist and quarantine notices are distinct enforcement tools under 247 CMR 10.06(8)–(9), but 10.07 separately permits a license suspension or refusal to renew before the final merits hearing when the stated threat and evidence standards are met.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts dentist holds a valid license, MCSR and applicable DEA registration. Assume each proposed prescription meets all other state and federal requirements, including ePrescribing and opioid limits. Which prescription is within the dentist's authority under 234 CMR 5.06?
questions.author_citation: 234 CMR 5.06(1)–(3); M.G.L. c.94C §§7, 9 and 18 (otherwise valid practitioner prescribing)

options.option_text: Schedule II oxycodone for the dentist's spouse after an elective dental procedure, when no emergency exists.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Although treating genuine dental pain can be within the practice of dentistry, 234 CMR 5.06(3) separately prohibits a dentist from prescribing Schedule II substances to immediate family, including a spouse, except in an emergency. The scenario expressly states that no emergency exists.

options.option_text: Schedule IV zolpidem to an unrelated patient for chronic insomnia that has no connection to dental treatment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The patient is unrelated, but 234 CMR 5.06(2) limits controlled-substance prescribing by dentists to legitimate DENTAL purposes in the ordinary course of professional practice. An unrelated chronic sleep disorder does not become a dental indication simply because the prescriber has a DEA registration.

options.option_text: A properly limited Schedule II oxycodone prescription for an unrelated patient with acute postoperative pain following an extraction performed by the dentist.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 234 CMR 5.06(1)–(2), a properly registered dentist may prescribe controlled substances for legitimate dental purposes in the usual course of practice. Appropriate acute post-extraction pain in an unrelated patient meets the scope condition on the stipulated facts, unlike self-use, a nonemergency immediate-family Schedule II prescription, or unrelated disease management.

options.option_text: Schedule III acetaminophen/codeine for the dentist's own recurring tension headaches because the dentist can independently confirm the diagnosis.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 5.06(2) explicitly prohibits a dentist from prescribing Schedule II–IV controlled substances for PERSONAL use, regardless of professional expertise or a self-diagnosis. Chronic tension headaches unrelated to dental care also fall outside the stated dental-purpose limitation.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses two separate FDA-approved outpatient prescriptions for which a Medication Guide is required under 21 CFR Part 208. One is an ordinary refill collected by a patient's agent. For the other, the practitioner has directed that the Medication Guide not be provided because of significant concerns about its effect, but the patient explicitly requests the Guide at dispensing. No other FDA exemption applies. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 208.24(b)–(e) and 208.26(b) (FDA Medication Guide requirements in force November 2026); proposed Patient Medication Information rule not yet effective

options.option_text: Because the manufacturer is responsible for supplying Medication Guides to distributors, the dispensing pharmacy has no independent obligation to provide one to a patient or agent.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Manufacturer and wholesaler supply duties under 21 CFR 208.24(b)–(c) exist alongside the DISPENSER'S separate duty under 208.24(e) to provide a Medication Guide when a covered prescription drug is dispensed to a patient or agent. Availability from the manufacturer does not remove the pharmacy's delivery obligation.

options.option_text: For the refill collected by the patient's agent, the dispenser must provide the Medication Guide directly to that agent, unless a valid exemption applies.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 21 CFR 208.24(e), the Medication Guide is furnished when a covered product is dispensed to a patient OR the patient's agent. The rule does not provide a routine refill exception merely because an earlier supply was accompanied by a Guide; the scenario excludes other exemptions.

options.option_text: A Medication Guide furnished at the first fill automatically satisfies all later outpatient refills of the same product, so no Guide is needed at subsequent dispensings.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 208.24(e) links the dispensing duty to the current dispensing event, not only to the first fill. Without a regulatory exemption or qualifying patient-specific direction, a previous handout does not eliminate the duty at the next refill.

options.option_text: Despite the practitioner's direction not to provide the Guide, the dispenser must provide it when the patient affirmatively requests the information at dispensing.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 21 CFR 208.26(b), the prescriber may direct withholding for a particular patient when significant concerns warrant it, BUT the authorized dispenser SHALL furnish the Medication Guide to any patient who requests the information when the drug is dispensed, notwithstanding that direction.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives otherwise valid prescriptions for (X) FDA-approved synthetic dronabinol in sesame oil encapsulated as a soft-gel capsule and (Y) FDA-approved dronabinol oral solution. Neither is a different cannabinoid formulation or an unapproved cannabis product. Which federal AND Massachusetts schedule classification and refill consequence is correct?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.12(f)(2), 1308.13(g)(1), 1306.12(a); 105 CMR 700.002(B)–(C); DEA Controlled Substances—Alphabetical Order (updated Nov. 12, 2026)

options.option_text: X is Schedule II and cannot be refilled; Y is Schedule III and may have otherwise valid authorized refills.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The schedules are reversed: the FDA-approved synthetic dronabinol sesame-oil soft-gel formulation is specifically in federal Schedule III under 21 CFR 1308.13(g)(1), while the FDA-approved dronabinol oral solution is federal Schedule II under 1308.12(f)(2). Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.002 incorporates those listings.

options.option_text: Both are Schedule III, because one active ingredient necessarily carries one DEA schedule across all FDA-approved formulations.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal law schedules these precise FDA-approved preparations in DIFFERENT subsections. The capsules are Schedule III, but the oral solution is Schedule II. Classifying only by active ingredient and ignoring dosage form would produce an invalid dispensing/refill decision.

options.option_text: Both are Schedule II, because the active ingredient is related to tetrahydrocannabinol and no FDA-approved preparation is eligible for Schedule III.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1308.13(g)(1) explicitly names the FDA-approved synthetic dronabinol in sesame oil and a soft-gel capsule as Schedule III, even though the approved oral solution is Schedule II under 1308.12(f)(2).

options.option_text: X is Schedule III and can have otherwise lawful authorized refills; Y is Schedule II and cannot be refilled under the original prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. DEA regulations separately list the FDA-approved sesame-oil soft-gel capsule as Schedule III and the approved dronabinol oral solution as Schedule II. Massachusetts follows the corresponding federal Schedules II and III under 105 CMR 700.002(B)–(C). Under 21 CFR 1306.12(a), Schedule II prescriptions cannot be refilled; Schedule III may be refilled if properly authorized within applicable limits.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts institutional pharmacy receives intact external shipping cartons containing NIOSH Table 1 antineoplastic hazardous drugs. It has a designated neutral-pressure receiving zone within an existing room and a positive-pressure ISO 7 sterile compounding room. Appropriate receiving procedures and a trained staff are available. Under USP <800> receiving requirements and USP's January 2026 FAQs, which actions or conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: USP <800> §§5.1,10 (receiving and PPE); USP <800> Official FAQs updated Jan. 21, 2026, Questions 68–71 (technical support, not formal interpretation); 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Unpack the external shipping cartons in the designated neutral-pressure receiving zone within the existing room; a separate dedicated room is not required solely for this function.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <800> §5.1 and the January 2026 USP FAQ #71 require unpacking NIOSH Table 1 antineoplastics in neutral/normal- or negative-pressure areas relative to surroundings. USP states that a designated area WITHIN an existing room is acceptable and a separate room is not mandatory.

options.option_text: Unpack the cartons in the positive-pressure ISO 7 sterile compounding room because the classified environment provides superior protection from external contamination.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <800> §5.1 expressly prohibits unpacking antineoplastic HDs from external shipping containers in sterile compounding areas or positive-pressure areas. ISO classification and product protection do not override the occupational contamination-control requirement.

options.option_text: Personnel unpacking the Table 1 antineoplastic HD cartons must wear at least one pair of chemotherapy gloves tested to ASTM D6978.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <800> §10 and official USP FAQ #68 require at least one pair of ASTM D6978-tested chemotherapy gloves when unpacking NIOSH Table 1 antineoplastic HDs. Additional PPE should be determined by facility policy and the risk associated with intact or damaged packages.

options.option_text: Reject every shipment lacking an impervious plastic outer bag because USP <800> mandates that all suppliers ship HDs inside impervious plastic.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP's January 2026 FAQ #69 describes impervious-plastic shipping as RECOMMENDED for suppliers, not an absolute mandatory packaging requirement. A pharmacy must still use safe receiving procedures and evaluate the condition and containment of the shipment.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is unable to perform final prescription checks safely due to sedation from a legally prescribed medication. No patient has been harmed. An impairment-related Board complaint is pending, and the pharmacist applies to the Unified Recovery and Monitoring Program (URAMP). Which statement accurately describes Massachusetts law?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 10.03(1)(g) (eff. Jan. 9, 2025); M.G.L. c.112 §65G(f)–(g); Massachusetts DPH URAMP Frequently Asked Questions

options.option_text: The pharmacist cannot be disciplined without proof of a patient injury because the sedating drug was lawfully prescribed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(g) lists practicing while impaired by medication, illness, or another condition as a ground for discipline. A lawful prescription and lack of a known error do not eliminate unsafe impairment. The pharmacist should stop unsafe professional tasks.

options.option_text: Impaired practice may warrant discipline; after URAMP admission, the Board may dismiss a related complaint or impose non-disciplinary license conditions.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(g), actual impaired professional practice is a possible disciplinary ground even if the medication was legally obtained. M.G.L. c.112 §65G(g) authorizes, but does not require, the Board to dismiss related pending matters after URAMP admission; non-disciplinary license conditions may remain.

options.option_text: The pharmacist can be admitted to URAMP only after a final formal disciplinary hearing has resolved the pending complaint.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 65G(f)–(g) expressly provides for applicants or Board referrals and addresses pending complaints upon admission. A final adjudicatory finding is not required before a pharmacist seeks appropriate recovery monitoring.

options.option_text: Submitting a URAMP application automatically dismisses the pending complaint and guarantees unrestricted pharmacist practice.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The statutory discretion arises on admission, not submission of an application, and the Board MAY, rather than MUST, dismiss a related complaint. Section 65G(g) also permits public non-disciplinary restrictions or conditions during monitoring.

questions.question_stem: An actively licensed Massachusetts podiatrist has a personal DEA registration and Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration. The podiatrist writes two otherwise valid Schedule II prescriptions: one for brief postoperative pain after performing foot surgery, and another to treat an unrelated migraine with no connection to any foot or ankle condition. Assume legitimate patient relationships and compliance with all other opioid and electronic-prescribing requirements. Which assessment is correct?

options.option_text: Both prescriptions are within scope because DEA and Massachusetts registrations allow the podiatrist to prescribe for any medical diagnosis.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Prescribing registrations are necessary for covered controlled drugs but do not enlarge the podiatrist's authorized clinical scope. Under 249 CMR 4.01–4.02 and 21 CFR 1306.04(a), prescriptions must arise from legitimate medical purpose within lawful professional practice.

options.option_text: Neither is within scope because Massachusetts excludes podiatrists from prescribing any Schedule II medications.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 249 CMR 4.02 expressly permits reasonable prescription and controlled substances in podiatric practice; it does not impose a blanket Schedule II prohibition. Appropriate postoperative foot pain is a podiatric indication.

options.option_text: Only the migraine prescription is valid because podiatrists may make systemic diagnoses but cannot prescribe for postoperative foot pain.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Podiatrists may assess systemic problems affecting the foot but do not thereby acquire unlimited authority to treat unrelated migraine. Foot-surgery pain is connected to the practitioner's authorized podiatric treatment.

options.option_text: The postoperative foot-pain prescription can be within the podiatrist's authority, but the unrelated migraine prescription exceeds that professional scope.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 249 CMR 4.01–4.02, a properly registered podiatrist may prescribe reasonable controlled medication, including Schedule II, within podiatric practice. The unrelated migraine is outside that scope. The pharmacist should verify authority and not dispense a prescription solely because DEA/MCSR numbers are valid.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy evaluates a supplier's quality alert. Lot X was held in insanitary conditions where contamination could occur, though cultures are negative. Compendial lot Y tests materially below its represented strength without an accurately labeled exception. Lot Z has materially false strength information on the label. No patient injury or FDA recall has been reported. Which conclusions are supported by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Lot X may be adulterated even though no finished unit has cultured positive for contamination.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §351(a)(2)(A) covers drugs held under insanitary conditions WHEREBY they MAY have been contaminated or rendered injurious. A positive test or actual patient injury is not required. The pharmacy should not return a questionable lot to dispensable inventory without resolving the hazard.

options.option_text: Lot Y cannot be adulterated as long as its container is sealed and the manufacturer intended to meet the labeled strength.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 21 U.S.C. §351(b), a compendial drug with strength different from the compendial standard is adulterated absent an applicable plainly labeled difference. The stem excludes such disclosure; an intact seal and a claim of intended potency do not cure a subpotent lot.

options.option_text: Lot Z may be misbranded because a materially false label claim is misleading even without proof that a patient was harmed.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §352(a)(1) defines a drug as misbranded when labeling is false or misleading in any particular. Patient harm, a broken seal, or a formal FDA recall is not a necessary element of the violation.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may dispense the lots normally until FDA formally orders a recall, because adulteration and misbranding have no effect before then.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 U.S.C. §§351–352 define adulteration/misbranding independently of a recall, and federal prohibitions under §331 apply to unlawful distribution and acts affecting products held for sale. Pharmacies must evaluate and segregate unsafe stock rather than assume it may be dispensed until a recall notice.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives an otherwise complete and authentic electronic prescription for oxycodone (Schedule II). It lacks the mandatory statement that the patient may request a partial fill. The patient presently wants the full quantity, and the pharmacist can reach the prescriber or the prescriber's authorized agent. What should the pharmacist do under Massachusetts law and DPH guidance?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §22(c) (partial-fill opioid notice); 105 CMR 721.020(D)(7) and 721.055 (effective Sept. 27, 2024); Massachusetts DPH Circular DCP 18-10-104 (Nov. 1, 2018) expressly superseding outdated DCP 16-12-665, pp.1–2

options.option_text: Confirm the missing statement with the prescriber or authorized agent and document the notation on the prescription in writing or electronically.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §22(c) and 105 CMR 721.020(D)(7) require that notation on Schedule II opioid prescriptions regardless of whether a partial fill is sought. Massachusetts DPH specifically directs pharmacist contact with the prescriber or authorized agent and written/electronic documentation of the confirmed notation.

options.option_text: Dispense without a notation because the statutory statement is required only when a patient actually requests a partial fill.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §22(c) applies to any Schedule II opioid prescription. The patient's request for the full quantity does not make the missing notation optional. Obtain confirmation and document it.

options.option_text: Add the standard partial-fill language through a pharmacy technician without any prescriber or authorized-agent confirmation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DPH's clarification does not authorize the pharmacy to fabricate the omitted prescriber statement unilaterally. The pharmacist must contact the prescriber or authorized agent for confirmation before recording the missing notation.

options.option_text: Reject the electronic prescription and require a new one because confirmation and documentation of that omission are always forbidden.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DPH expressly provides the confirmation-and-documentation procedure for this particular omission on an otherwise lawful prescription. Another genuinely invalid aspect might require a new prescription, but this specific omission does not automatically do so.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy sends prescriptions to patients using a common carrier. A refrigerated noncontrolled biologic comes back unopened after a failed delivery; its temperature logger shows an excursion outside the labeled range, and no product-specific stability assessment has been obtained. The pharmacy also sends Schedule III prescriptions through the carrier. Which conclusions comply with 247 CMR 9.02 and medication-integrity duties? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.02(1)–(3) (Prescriptions by Mail; eff. Dec. 6, 2024); 247 CMR 9.01; relevant manufacturer-labeled storage and product-specific stability data

options.option_text: The returned biologic may be immediately resent, because an intact package seal establishes stability despite the logged temperature excursion.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A sealed container does not establish product stability after exposure outside the labeled storage range. Under 247 CMR 9.02(2), the pharmacy must ensure transport does not adversely affect integrity or stability. The unresolved excursion requires evaluation before redelivery.

options.option_text: Common-carrier dispensing is permitted, but the pharmacy must ensure that packing, shipping and transportation do not undermine medication stability.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.02(1) allows mail/common-carrier dispensing consistent with applicable law. Section 9.02(2) makes preservation of drug integrity and stability a pharmacy responsibility, not exclusively the carrier's.

options.option_text: Every logged temperature excursion mandates immediate destruction under 247 CMR 9.02, even if reliable product-specific stability data support use.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.02 does not set a universal automatic-discard threshold. A specific medicine's labeled conditions, temperature history, and scientifically supported stability assessment determine whether it remains suitable; absent such support, keep it from dispensing.

options.option_text: The biologic should be held pending a supported stability determination, and the pharmacy must maintain its own policies for transporting and delivering controlled substances.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Redelivery before resolving the excursion would not satisfy the pharmacy's §9.02(2) integrity responsibility. Section 9.02(3) separately requires pharmacy policies and procedures for packing, shipping, transportation and delivery of controlled substances, even when a commercial carrier is used.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy technician trainee started employment at age 16, has worked 1,620 cumulative trainee hours in 15 months, and is still 17. The Board has not granted an extension. The trainee turns 18 next week. Under 247 CMR 8.03(5), which statement is accurate?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.03(5)(a)–(c), final sentence; 247 CMR 8.02(3)(a) (Board corrected text Apr. 25, 2025; effective 2018)

options.option_text: Because the trainee is not yet 18, the hours/one-year employment cap has an exception; a technician-license application must be submitted within 30 days of turning 18.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 8.03(5)(b) expressly excepts a person who has not yet reached age 18 from the earlier of one year or 1,500 hours. A person who exceeded either threshold before turning 18 must submit an application for a pharmacy technician license within 30 days of the eighteenth birthday. The pharmacy should plan the timely application and verify continuing lawful licensure.

options.option_text: The trainee's license automatically ends at the 1,500th hour, even while age 17; a Board extension is the only possible exception.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The regulation lists alternative exceptions, including the person not yet having reached age 18. A Board extension is not the sole exception; the pharmacy must still follow the post-eighteenth-birthday application requirement.

options.option_text: The trainee can continue indefinitely under the trainee license after turning 18 because the excess hours were accrued before the birthday.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The under-18 exception does not permanently remove the ordinary employment limitation. Section 8.03(5) specifically requires the person who previously exceeded the limit to apply for a technician license within 30 days of turning 18.

options.option_text: The trainee must immediately obtain a pharmacist-intern license on the eighteenth birthday, because technician applicants are not eligible until age 21.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 8.02(3)(a) generally sets 18 as the age for pharmacy technician licensure; pharmacy intern licensure is a different educational pathway under §8.01. The required application here is for a pharmacy technician license, not a pharmacist-intern license.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts licensed clinic maintains a clinic pharmacy that is not registered as a retail drug business. It has no pharmacy-services authorization on the facility license and no separate M.G.L. c.94C §9(e) authorization to dispense take-home controlled substances. A clinic practitioner legally authorized to prescribe issues several orders. Which proposed dispensing fits 105 CMR 722.091?
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 722.020 (Clinic Pharmacy, Clinic Employee, Clinic Patient); 105 CMR 722.091(A)–(B) (effective Sept. 27, 2024)

options.option_text: Fill a take-home Schedule III prescription for a clinic employee because an employee health benefit overrides the facility-license requirement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Although §722.091(A) permits lawful prescriptions for clinic employees under employee health policies, §722.091(B) separately prohibits dispensing controlled substances other than for immediate administration unless the facility has the specified pharmacy-services licensing or §9(e) authorization.

options.option_text: Fill an otherwise lawful noncontrolled prescription for a current clinic employee pursuant to the clinic's employee health policy.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 722.091(A) expressly allows prescriptions for current clinic patients and employees under employee health policies when issued by a legally authorized clinic practitioner. The case assumes no additional obstacle, and no take-home controlled substance is involved.

options.option_text: Fill a noncontrolled prescription for any unrelated walk-in customer who chooses the clinic pharmacy for convenience.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Clinic pharmacies under §722.091(A) are not unrestricted retail pharmacies; dispensing is tied to current clinic patients, employees within the described policies, or medication orders for immediate administration by clinic practitioners.

options.option_text: Fill a take-home Schedule IV prescription for anyone on the clinic's payroll because it is less restricted than Schedule II.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 722.091(B)'s facility-authorization condition covers controlled substances dispensed for take-home use, not only Schedule II medications. A payroll relationship does not itself supply the missing authorization.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy handles FDA-regulated patient labeling. It dispenses outpatient oral contraceptives and prescription estrogen products, plus a third medication whose FDA-approved Patient Information leaflet is voluntary under federal regulations. No acute-care or long-term-care institutional schedule applies. Which statements about Patient Package Inserts (PPIs) are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 310.501(a),(b)(2); 21 CFR 310.515(a),(b),(e); FDA Patient Labeling Resources (mandatory versus voluntary PPIs)

options.option_text: A required oral-contraceptive PPI must accompany each outpatient package dispensed to the patient or appropriate agent.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 310.501(a) requires a patient package insert in or accompanying each package of an oral contraceptive drug product supplied to patients or their agents. Providing an insert at only the first fill does not satisfy the ordinary outpatient requirement.

options.option_text: An FDA-approved PPI for every prescription medicine is federally required to accompany every refill merely because the manufacturer authored patient information.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA states that PPIs for non-estrogen, non-oral-contraceptive drugs may be voluntarily submitted and FDA-approved without the special mandatory distribution rule. The pharmacist must distinguish specific federally required PPIs from voluntary patient labeling and from 21 CFR Part 208 Medication Guides.

options.option_text: Prescription estrogen products covered by 21 CFR 310.515 generally require a PPI to accompany dispensing; oral contraceptives with estrogen and progestogen are instead addressed under §310.501.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 310.515(a),(e) requires estrogen product patient inserts and expressly excepts estrogen-progestogen oral contraceptives because §310.501 governs those contraceptives. The practitioner and pharmacist must apply the correct drug-class rule.

options.option_text: An outpatient pharmacy may replace each mandatory PPI with a generic verbal counseling offer because written instructions are not required once a pharmacist offers counseling.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Counseling requirements and the federal package-insert mandate serve different purposes. Sections 310.501(a) and 310.515(a) impose patient-facing written labeling obligations not displaced by offering verbal counseling.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives valid prescriptions for Lyrica (pregabalin) capsules and Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) capsules. Both prescriptions were written by an authorized prescriber for a legitimate purpose. Which statement correctly identifies both federal and Massachusetts schedules and their basic refill implications?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.15(e)(7) (pregabalin), 1308.12(d)(5) (lisdexamfetamine), 1306.12(a); 105 CMR 700.002(B),(E); 21 CFR 1306.22 (Schedule III–V refills)

options.option_text: Lyrica is Schedule IV in both systems and may be refilled within applicable limits; Vyvanse is Schedule II with no refills.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Lisdexamfetamine is Schedule II, but pregabalin is expressly listed in federal Schedule V, not IV, at 21 CFR 1308.15(e)(7). Massachusetts Schedule V follows the applicable Schedule V classification. The pharmacist must use the schedule of the actual molecule, not the broad therapeutic class.

options.option_text: Lyrica is Schedule V in both systems and may have properly authorized refills; Vyvanse is Schedule III and may have five refills.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Pregabalin is Schedule V, but lisdexamfetamine is specifically listed in 21 CFR 1308.12(d)(5) as Schedule II. Schedule II prescriptions cannot be refilled under 21 CFR 1306.12(a), regardless of an otherwise routine ADHD treatment.

options.option_text: Lyrica is Schedule V in both systems and may have lawfully authorized refills; Vyvanse is Schedule II in both systems and cannot be refilled.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Pregabalin is in 21 CFR 1308.15(e)(7) and the corresponding Massachusetts Schedule V; lisdexamfetamine is in 21 CFR 1308.12(d)(5) and Massachusetts Schedule II. Valid Schedule V refills are possible within federal/state limits; an original Schedule II prescription may not be refilled.

options.option_text: Lyrica is unscheduled federally and only Schedule VI in Massachusetts; Vyvanse is Schedule II in both systems.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. This wrongly treats pregabalin like gabapentin. Pregabalin is federally controlled in Schedule V and is classified as Schedule V in Massachusetts, while lisdexamfetamine is Schedule II.

questions.question_stem: Three out-of-state pharmacies want to mail prescriptions to Massachusetts residents. Each holds a valid license in its own state and is otherwise compliant. Pharmacy A ships conventional prescription products; B ships compounded sterile preparations; C ships complex nonsterile compounded preparations. Which Massachusetts licensure statements are correct under 247 CMR 6.02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 6.02(4)–(6); 247 CMR 6.09 (nonresident pharmacy applications); M.G.L. c.94C §1 Schedule VI definition (247 CMR 6.00 effective Apr. 25, 2025)
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 6.02(4)-(6) MA nonresident baseline and specialty pharmacy licensing

options.option_text: A nonresident pharmacy shipping prescription controlled substances into Massachusetts must hold the Massachusetts nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license; its home-state license alone does not replace this requirement.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 6.02(4) expressly requires a nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license to dispense or ship controlled substances into Massachusetts. This includes Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drugs as defined by M.G.L. c.94C; other state licensure alone is not an exemption.
options.independent_option_analysis: Nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license required for Rx controlled substances into MA.

options.option_text: Shipping sterile compounded prescriptions into Massachusetts requires both a Massachusetts nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license and a Massachusetts nonresident sterile compounding pharmacy license.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 6.02(5) expressly requires the combination of those two nonresident licenses before an out-of-state pharmacy dispenses or ships a sterile compounded preparation into Massachusetts.
options.independent_option_analysis: Sterile compounded shipment requires nonresident drug store and sterile specialty licenses.

options.option_text: Shipping complex nonsterile compounded prescriptions requires only a nonresident complex nonsterile compounding license; a nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license is optional.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 6.02(6) expressly requires BOTH the nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license and the nonresident complex nonsterile compounding pharmacy license for that shipment category.
options.independent_option_analysis: Complex nonsterile shipment requires both baseline and complex specialty licenses.

options.option_text: A nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license automatically authorizes shipment of compounded sterile doses without any additional specialty license.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Sections 6.02(4) and (5) separate the baseline nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license from the distinct nonresident sterile compounding pharmacy authorization. The specialty license is not supplied automatically.
options.independent_option_analysis: Baseline nonresident drug store license alone does not grant sterile specialty privilege.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist is arrested in another state for a misdemeanor, before any criminal charge or conviction. In an independent later event, another state's licensing board formally disciplines the pharmacist's professional license. The pharmacist reviews BOTH 247 CMR 20.03 and the grounds for discipline in 247 CMR 10.03. Which reporting approach is BEST supported by the two published regulations?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 20.03(3)-(4); 247 CMR 10.03(1)(y)-(aa); Massachusetts Board Mandatory Disclosure Form, revised Dec. 6, 2024; concurrent triggers, not claimed supersession
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 20.03(3)-(4) fourteen calendar days; 247 CMR 10.03(1)(y)-(aa) distinct shorter seven business day discipline triggers
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: The case intentionally states concurrent duties; applicability of 247 CMR 10.03 provisions depends on actual action type. Do not simplify to a single universal personal deadline.

options.option_text: Neither event requires a report until the pharmacist has a final criminal conviction in Massachusetts.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 20.03(3) separately requires reporting any arrest, pending charge, or conviction. Out-of-state professional discipline is also reportable under §20.03(4) and can trigger the additional reporting provisions in §10.03.
options.independent_option_analysis: Arrest and out-of-state discipline are separately reportable; conviction not prerequisite.

options.option_text: Report the arrest within 14 calendar days under §20.03(3); report the out-of-state disciplinary action within the 14-calendar-day §20.03(4) period AND meet any independently applicable, shorter seven-business-day §10.03(1)(y)-(z) reporting obligation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 20.03(3)-(4) expressly provides 14 calendar days for arrests and reportable discipline. Separately, §10.03(1)(y)-(z) lists failure to report qualifying discipline or governmental final actions within seven business days as a possible disciplinary ground. A pharmacist must not assume that the 14-day provision universally overrides this potentially earlier duty; the exact action and deadlines should be assessed together.
options.independent_option_analysis: Answer explicitly accounts for both clocks when independently applicable.

options.option_text: Defer both reports until the next biennial pharmacist renewal, as §10.03 governs only discipline imposed by the Massachusetts Board itself.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Neither §20.03 nor §10.03 authorizes waiting for renewal, and the §10.03 reporting duties may extend to acts of other licensing authorities.
options.independent_option_analysis: Renewal is not a permissible substitute for timely reports.

options.option_text: Only the employer reports these individual matters, and seven business days is automatically the sole deadline for both the arrest and the disciplinary action.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. §§20.03(3)-(4) address individual licensee duties directly. The separate §10.03 seven-business-day requirement concerns qualifying disciplinary and governmental actions, not a generic seven-day arrest rule. §10.03(1)(aa) also addresses pending charges or convictions on a different clock.
options.independent_option_analysis: Employer-only and one blanket seven-day clock are unsupported.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital has a current DEA hospital registration. A physician resident is legally authorized under Massachusetts law to prescribe the relevant Schedule II drug, but lacks an individual DEA registration. The hospital has verified the resident's authority and may grant use of its registration. Assume any necessary state controlled-substance registration and ePrescribing rules are separately met. Which federal DEA conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1301.22(c)(1)–(6); DEA Pharmacist's Manual and DEA Medical Resident Guidance; 21 CFR 1306.04(a); applicable 105 CMR 700 and 721 must also be satisfied

options.option_text: The resident may use the hospital DEA registration while prescribing in the usual course of practice within the resident's hospital employment, if the institution authorizes it and assigns a unique internal suffix.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1301.22(c)(1)–(5) allows an individual practitioner who is an agent or employee of a registered hospital to prescribe under the hospital registration if practicing lawfully within employment and the hospital verifies authority, authorizes the use, and assigns a practitioner-specific suffix.

options.option_text: The resident may use the hospital's number for unrelated private-office prescriptions because holding hospital privileges is enough, even when acting outside hospital employment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 1301.22(c)(4) confines the exemption to the scope of the individual's employment at the registered hospital/institution. Privileges alone do not authorize using the institutional registration for a private practice.

options.option_text: The institution may use one shared suffix for all residents and has no duty to keep a current list connecting suffixes to individual prescribers.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 1301.22(c)(5) requires an individual code number for EACH authorized practitioner, and §1301.22(c)(6) requires a CURRENT list identifying each authorized practitioner by code available for verification.

options.option_text: The hospital must maintain a current roster connecting unique internal codes to prescribers and make the information available to other registrants or law-enforcement agencies on request.
options.original_rationale: Correct. This is expressly required by 21 CFR 1301.22(c)(6). The pharmacist receiving such a prescription should verify the specific prescriber's authorization and suffix as appropriate rather than rejecting all institutional identifiers.

questions.question_stem: A practitioner plans to prescribe two different prescription drug products on one record. In one case the prescriptions are issued for community outpatient dispensing; in a separate case they are issued in the hospital setting with clear use and interchange directions for each product. All other requirements are met. Which decision correctly applies 105 CMR 721.050?
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 721.050 (Prescribing More than One Drug Product); 105 CMR 721.020(A),(D) (effective Sept. 27, 2024)

options.option_text: Both records are valid solely because the practitioner clearly separates the drug names and dosing directions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.050 ordinarily directs practitioners prescribing more than one drug product to place EACH prescription on a separate form or record. Clarity alone does not authorize combining community prescriptions under the hospital exception.

options.option_text: Neither record is permitted because Massachusetts never allows more than one drug product on a prescription form or record.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.050 explicitly allows more than one drug product in the hospital setting on a single form or record if clear directions for each drug's use and interchange are provided.

options.option_text: Separate records are required for the ordinary outpatient case; the hospital record may include multiple drug products if each has clear directions for use and interchange.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 105 CMR 721.050 generally requires separate forms or records per drug product, but provides a narrow hospital-setting exception with clear instructions for EACH product. The pharmacist should verify the applicable setting and readable product-specific directions.

options.option_text: The separate-record requirement applies only to Schedule II drugs; ordinary Schedule VI prescriptions may always be combined at community pharmacies.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.050 uses the broader phrase 'more than one Drug Product' and does not confine its separate-record rule to Schedule II drugs or exempt ordinary Schedule VI community prescriptions.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist reviews the schedule of FDA-approved Lomotil tablets containing 2.5 mg diphenoxylate hydrochloride and 25 micrograms atropine sulfate per unit. For comparison, the pharmacist also checks the federal schedule of diphenoxylate itself outside this qualifying combination. Assume no separate exception or rescheduling order. Which classification is correct?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.15(c)(4) (combination threshold); 21 CFR 1308.12(c)(8) (diphenoxylate); 105 CMR 700.002(B),(E) (Massachusetts corresponding schedules)

options.option_text: The qualifying diphenoxylate/atropine combination is Schedule II, as is diphenoxylate by itself.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The Schedule V exemption for certain combination products is product-specific: 21 CFR 1308.15(c)(4) covers no more than 2.5 mg diphenoxylate AND at least 25 micrograms atropine sulfate per dosage unit. The qualifying combination is not Schedule II.

options.option_text: The qualifying diphenoxylate/atropine combination is Schedule V in federal and Massachusetts law, while diphenoxylate itself is federally Schedule II.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.15(c)(4) explicitly defines the qualifying Schedule V combination by dosage-unit content; 21 CFR 1308.12(c)(8) separately lists diphenoxylate as Schedule II. Massachusetts adopts the corresponding schedules in 105 CMR 700.002. The pharmacist must classify the actual formulation.

options.option_text: Both the qualifying combination and the individual active diphenoxylate ingredient are Schedule V because a low-dose antidiarrheal indication controls scheduling.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Indication and dose do not automatically reschedule the isolated active substance. The Schedule V provision is limited to qualifying combinations with the specified atropine content; uncombined diphenoxylate is listed under federal Schedule II.

options.option_text: The qualifying combination is Schedule III, and diphenoxylate alone is Schedule II, because any mixture with atropine is automatically Schedule III.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The pertinent federal combination schedule is V, not III. The governing provision uses exact diphenoxylate and atropine quantities, not a class-wide rule for all mixtures.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy trains a new employee for Category 2 compounded sterile preparations (CSPs). The trainee has no previous sterile-compounding qualification. The facility follows the currently official USP <797> requirements and the USP FAQ explanations of §§2.2–2.3. Which procedures are correct BEFORE the employee begins compounding CSPs? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Current USP <797> §§2.2–2.3 (official Nov. 1, 2023); USP <797> Official FAQ updated Dec. 11, 2023, Q49–50, 57; 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Complete an initial garbing competency with visual observation and gloved fingertip/thumb sampling successfully on at least three separate occasions in succession.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <797> §2.2 and official USP FAQ 50 and 57 call for THREE successful initial garbing evaluations (each distinct complete hygiene and garbing with glove fingertip/thumb sampling), consecutively. One garbing session with three plates does not count as three evaluations.

options.option_text: Require three separate successful media-fill tests as the initial aseptic manipulation competency because the three-test rule applies identically to garbing and media fill.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP FAQ 50 distinguishes the initial three complete GARBlNG competency evaluations from ASEPTIC manipulation competency, which includes one successfully completed initial media-fill test and gloved fingertip/thumb sampling following that media fill.

options.option_text: Complete an initial aseptic manipulation competency including a media-fill test and gloved fingertip/thumb sampling after that test.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <797> §2.3 and USP FAQ 50 identify the media fill plus post-media-fill gloved fingertip/thumb sampling as the initial aseptic manipulation competency; it is separate from initial garbing evaluation.

options.option_text: Permit the trainee to compound for patients immediately under observation without initial garbing qualification, because only independent compounding requires successful garbing tests.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP FAQ 49 clarifies that personnel must successfully complete initial garbing competency BEFORE any compounding, whether independently or under supervision. Observing the worker is not an exemption.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy has an employee with a current Massachusetts pharmacy technician license whose certification from a Board-approved national certifying body expired yesterday. The pharmacist is reviewing the employee's duties, name badge, and supervisory-ratio roster. Under 247 CMR 8.04(3), which changes or conclusions are required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: The worker remains eligible to perform ordinary licensed pharmacy technician functions under 247 CMR 8.02, assuming the Massachusetts license remains valid.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 8.04(3)(a) expressly limits a formerly certified person with lapsed certification to the duties of an ordinary pharmacy technician; it does not automatically revoke the person's separately valid Massachusetts pharmacy technician license. The pharmacist still performs required clinical checks and final validation.

options.option_text: The worker may continue to use the 'Certified Pharmacy Technician' title and expanded certified duties indefinitely because state technician licensure is active.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 8.04(3)(a)–(b) explicitly requires a downgrade to ordinary technician duties and title after national certification lapses. The manager should revise the worker's badge and assignments instead of using the expired credential.

options.option_text: For the supervisory-ratio calculation the employee must be counted as an ordinary pharmacy technician, not a certified pharmacy technician.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 8.04(3)(c) expressly directs that a person whose national certification lapses be counted as a pharmacy technician under §8.06(3). Scheduling decisions must reflect that reclassification.

options.option_text: The worker must cease all pharmacy technician duties and apply for an entirely new Massachusetts technician license, even though the existing Massachusetts license is current.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The specific §8.04(3) rule permits ordinary technician duties and requires proper title and ratio treatment while state licensure remains valid. A lapsed national certification alone does not imply that a new state license is necessary.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy receives an otherwise valid prescription for an emergency department patient who has completed treatment and is leaving the hospital. The prescribed medication is routinely stocked by community retail pharmacies and is available in quantities that permit dispensing exactly a 14-day supply. The prescriber orders 30 days plus two refills. No waiver applies. What may the hospital pharmacy dispense under 105 CMR 722.090?
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 722.090(A)–(C), especially (B)(1)–(2) (regulation published Sept. 27, 2024; substantive §722.090(B) text dates May 5, 2017)

options.option_text: The full prescribed 30-day supply and two refills, because the emergency department is part of the hospital.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 722.090(B) allows a hospital pharmacy to fill an emergency room or discharge patient's prescription for no more than a 14-day supply, and §722.090(B)(1) specifically forbids that hospital pharmacy from refilling those prescriptions. The ordinary retail-available drug has none of the stated exceptions.

options.option_text: At most an initial 14-day supply without refills at the hospital pharmacy; the remaining continuing therapy needs an appropriate lawful outpatient dispensing arrangement.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 105 CMR 722.090(B) limits ED and discharge patient prescriptions to a 14-day supply, and (B)(1) bars hospital-pharmacy refills of those prescriptions. The manufacturer's smallest-package and unavailable-in-retail exceptions are inapplicable under the stated facts.

options.option_text: A 72-hour emergency supply only, regardless of the prescriber's authorization, because no outpatient hospital pharmacy may dispense more than three days.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 722.090(B) normally establishes a 14-day limit, not a general 72-hour emergency supply limit. The pharmacist must not import an unrelated controlled-substance emergency rule into institutional pharmacy dispensing.

options.option_text: No take-home supply at all, because hospital pharmacies may dispense only to admitted inpatients and never to emergency department patients.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 722.090(B) expressly authorizes eligible prescriptions for emergency room and discharge patients, subject to the 14-day cap, no-refills rule, and stated exceptions. The pharmacist should follow the specific patient category rather than reject all discharge prescriptions.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacist receives several otherwise authentic prescriptions in November 2026. A prescriber may rely on an enumerated exception from electronic prescribing, but the pharmacist did not personally witness the underlying reason. In another case, a purported electronic prescription arrived only as a fax (not a verified technical failover). Which legal conclusions follow 105 CMR 721.040 and 721.070? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: The pharmacist is not required to independently verify that an otherwise valid written or oral prescription falls within a prescriber's ePrescribing exception, though other validity and safety checks remain required.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 721.070(C) expressly says a pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid Written or Oral Prescription is not required to verify that the issuance properly falls under an enumerated exception, including waiver status. This does not excuse verification of the prescription's authenticity, prescriber authority, or clinical appropriateness.

options.option_text: Any purported electronic prescription that arrives by ordinary facsimile is valid because the sending prescriber signed it electronically, even when no qualifying failover occurred.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.040(C) declares an Electronic Prescription transmitted by a means other than compliant Electronic Transmission invalid, except for a verified Failover under §721.020(G). A routine fax is not automatically a valid electronic prescription.

options.option_text: A properly issued Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription falls under an express state ePrescribing exception, so it need not be transmitted electronically solely because it is a prescription drug.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 721.070(A)(9) expressly lists prescriptions for controlled substances in Massachusetts Schedule VI as an exception to mandatory ePrescribing. Oral/written prescriptions must still meet all other applicable legal conditions.

options.option_text: Massachusetts permits a prescriber to choose paper or telephone for any Schedule II–V prescription merely for convenience, and the pharmacist must accept it as valid without further checks.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.070(A) limits exceptions and prohibits use of them to circumvent ePrescribing. Section 721.070(C)'s no-duty-to-verify-the-exception rule does not legalize a nonauthentic or otherwise invalid controlled prescription or remove federal requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives practitioner-signed PAPER Schedule II prescriptions transmitted by fax for three patients: (1) a current long-term care facility resident, (2) a patient in an eligible hospice program whose narcotic prescription bears the required hospice notation, and (3) an ordinary community outpatient with no listed federal fax exception. Assume each paper prescription is otherwise lawful under a Massachusetts ePrescribing exception and meets federal requirements. Which federal dispensing determination is correct?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1306.11(a),(e)–(g); 21 CFR 1306.05; 105 CMR 721.020(F),721.070(A),(C) (assumed valid MA ePrescribing exception)

options.option_text: The fax is the original signed prescription for all three, because an authenticated fax has the same federal legal status as an electronic controlled-substance prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 21 CFR 1306.11(a), a fax of an ordinary paper Schedule II prescription generally does NOT replace the manually signed original; it may be transmitted for advance review, but the original must be presented before dispensing unless a specific exception applies. Fax is not DEA-compliant EPCS.

options.option_text: The ordinary outpatient qualifies for a fax-as-original exception, but the LTCF and hospice prescriptions require paper originals at the pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. This reverses the federal exceptions. Section 1306.11(f) allows fax to serve as original for a resident of a Long Term Care Facility; §1306.11(g) permits it for qualifying narcotic hospice prescriptions with the required notation. An ordinary outpatient without an exception requires the original.

options.option_text: The fax may serve as the original for the LTCF resident and for the appropriately noted hospice narcotic prescription, but not for the ordinary outpatient's nonexceptional Schedule II prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Federal 21 CFR 1306.11(f) and (g) create two fax-as-original exceptions. Under §1306.11(a), the ordinary outpatient fax is not sufficient by itself; the pharmacist must obtain and review the original signed paper prescription before filling unless another legitimate exception applies. This assumes the separate Massachusetts issuance/format rules are already satisfied.

options.option_text: Only the hospice case qualifies if the pharmacist gets a verbal confirmation; all LTCF Schedule II medications are excluded from fax-as-original status.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 1306.11(f) expressly covers any Schedule II prescription for a qualifying LTCF resident without a narcotic-only limitation, whereas §1306.11(g) is specific to hospice narcotics. Oral confirmation alone does not replace a missing original in an ordinary nonexceptional case.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy wants to assign a beyond-use date longer than the Category 2 BUD limit to one nonhazardous compounded sterile preparation. It has a compliant cleanroom suite and trained staff but has not implemented Category 3 additional qualifications or sterility testing. Manufacturer component expiration does not limit the proposed date. Which approach is consistent with the currently official USP <797> standard?
questions.author_citation: Official USP <797> §§14.3–14.4 (revision official Nov. 1, 2023); USP <797> FAQs Dec. 11, 2023, Q12, 174, 182; 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Assign the longer Category 3 BUD because working in an ISO 5 primary engineering control is the only extra condition for Category 3 classification.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <797> §14.4 and USP FAQ Q12 require additional Category 3 quality assurance, including sterility testing, applicable endotoxin testing, more stringent personnel and environmental controls, and stability evidence. ISO 5 airflow alone is not sufficient.

options.option_text: Assign the Category 3 BUD as long as a compounder signs a policy waiver, even if sterility and applicable endotoxin tests are omitted.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A facility's internal policy cannot waive the compendial Category 3 requirements. USP FAQ Q12 describes the additional testing and other requirements; an authorized shorter BUD may be used rather than labeling a noncompliant CSP Category 3.

options.option_text: Treat every CSP manufactured in a facility that meets Category 3 requirements as a Category 3 product and never use a shorter Category 2 BUD.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP FAQ Q174 explicitly permits a facility otherwise capable of Category 3 compounding to assign a shorter Category 2 BUD to a particular CSP. The qualification level of the facility does not force every product to take the extended date.

options.option_text: Do not assign the extended Category 3 BUD until all additional Category 3 requirements and required testing for that CSP are met; a suitable shorter BUD may be chosen.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <797> §§14.3–14.4 and USP FAQ Q12, Q174 and Q182 condition longer-than-Category-2 BUDs on additional Category 3 safeguards including sterility testing and, where indicated, endotoxin testing and supportable stability. The pharmacy must apply those requirements rather than extrapolate from cleanroom classification alone.

questions.question_stem: The Massachusetts pharmacist Manager of Record (MOR) of Retail Pharmacy A plans to be away for six weeks. Before leaving, the MOR proposes that Pharmacy A wait five days to name an interim manager, and that the pharmacist simultaneously become MOR of a separate Retail Pharmacy B. Both retail stores have sufficient staffing. Which approach meets 247 CMR 9.23?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.23(3)–(5)(a),(c) (effective Dec. 6, 2024); compare 247 CMR 9.23(5)(b),(d) for unplanned absences and 100-day changes

options.option_text: Appoint the interim MOR five days after departure; that deadline applies to all absences over 30 days, even those planned in advance.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.23(5)(a) requires appointment of an Interim Manager registered by the Board BEFORE a planned absence expected to last 30 days or longer. The five-day period in §9.23(5)(b) is for UNPLANNED absences.

options.option_text: Appoint a Board-registered interim manager before the planned absence and do not concurrently serve as MOR for the second retail pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.23(5)(a) requires the interim appointment before a planned 30-day-or-longer absence. Section 9.23(3) prohibits a retail pharmacy MOR from being MOR of more than one pharmacy at a time. A controlled-substance inventory and required signatures under §9.23(5)(c) also need appropriate handling before departure.

options.option_text: Maintain both MOR titles if the pharmacist averages 30 combined hours per week across the two locations.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.23(3) forbids simultaneous retail MOR positions, and §9.23(4) independently requires an MOR to work an average of at least 30 hours PER WEEK at the pharmacy managed; combining hours between pharmacies cannot cure either problem.

options.option_text: No interim manager is required as long as the pharmacist intends to return and another pharmacist handles final dispensing.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. When a planned absence is expected to last at least 30 days, §9.23(5)(a) expressly requires a Board-registered Interim Manager before it begins. Staffing a working pharmacist at the counter is not automatically the designated interim appointment.

questions.question_stem: Three people contact the SAME Massachusetts pharmacy about medications it previously dispensed. Patient X received the wrong drug. Patient Y's product is suspected to be contaminated. Patient Z received the correct, nondefective drug but no longer wants it. Assume no other specific legal return exception. Which practices follow 247 CMR 9.01? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(5),(7)(a)–(b) (effective Dec. 6, 2024); distinct from 247 CMR 9.13 undelivered return-to-stock
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.01(5),(7): wrong-drug and suspected-contamination return distinction

options.option_text: Accept X's wrongly dispensed medication and Y's suspected defective or contaminated medication, then quarantine and properly dispose of the returned items.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 9.01(7)(a)–(b), a pharmacy SHALL accept its previously dispensed drug if it was dispensed in error or is suspected to be defective/contaminated. The accepted item cannot go back to inventory and must be quarantined and properly disposed of.
options.independent_option_analysis: Both error and suspected defect independently trigger acceptance and quarantine/disposal.

options.option_text: Put Y's returned medication back on the shelf if its bottle is unopened and a pharmacist sees no visible damage.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.01(7) specifically prohibits putting medications accepted under its error/defect provision back into inventory, regardless of whether a retail seal appears intact. Visual appearance does not eliminate a possible contamination defect.
options.independent_option_analysis: An unopened defective/contaminated return cannot reenter saleable stock.

options.option_text: Accept Z's properly dispensed, nondefective medication as a mandatory return and routinely redispense it to another patient after cleaning the label.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.01(7) says a pharmacy is not required to accept a medication that was properly dispensed and not defective, and §9.01(5) generally bars redispensing a previously dispensed medication absent a specific exception.
options.independent_option_analysis: Properly dispensed nondefective unwanted drug is not mandatory-return or ordinary restock.

options.option_text: The pharmacy is not required by this regulation to take back Z's properly dispensed, nondefective medication, while X's and Y's returns cannot be restocked.
