options.original_rationale: Correct. The last sentence of §9.01(7) excludes mandatory acceptance of a properly dispensed nondefective medicine. It mandates quarantine/disposal rather than restoration of returned error/defect stock.
options.independent_option_analysis: Express regulation distinguishes nonmandatory proper return from no-redispense rule.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist receives an authentic Schedule IV prescription from a registered, ordinarily authorized physician. The prescriber confirms that the intended patient has never been examined, contacted, or otherwise assessed by the physician or any collaborating practitioner and that no patient–practitioner relationship was established. No standing-order, emergency, or statutory exception applies. Which response follows Massachusetts pharmacy law?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.15(2)(a)–(d); 21 CFR 1306.04(a) (legitimate medical purpose and corresponding responsibility)

options.option_text: Dispense after confirming the physician's DEA number because registration and signature establish all required conditions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.15(2)(a)–(c) requires the pharmacist to determine legitimacy, a VALID patient–practitioner relationship, and authenticity. A valid registration and authentic signature alone do not resolve the missing relationship.

options.option_text: Dispense if the patient pays cash because payer type is not relevant to the Board's validation criteria.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Whether payment is cash or insured does not waive 247 CMR 9.15(2)(b). The issue is the absence of a valid patient–practitioner relationship, not financial coverage.

options.option_text: Do not dispense this prescription as described; clarify or obtain appropriate lawful prescribing care rather than rely solely on registration and authentication.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.15(2) prohibits filling unless the pharmacist's professional judgment establishes legitimate purpose, valid patient–practitioner relationship, authenticity and legal compliance. Federal 21 CFR 1306.04(a) also imposes a corresponding dispensing responsibility for legitimate controlled prescriptions.

options.option_text: Treat the prescriber confirmation as permission to create a new relationship retroactively in the pharmacy computer and proceed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A pharmacist cannot manufacture a clinical relationship from identity verification or a documentation shortcut. The relationship must be real and legally adequate; this case expressly excludes exceptions and any clinician-patient interaction.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist verifies three separately issued, legitimate prescriptions: hydrocodone/acetaminophen (Vicodin), buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone), and tramadol (Ultram). Which federal and corresponding Massachusetts schedule assignments are correct in November 2026?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1)(vi) hydrocodone; 21 CFR 1308.13(e)(2) buprenorphine; 21 CFR 1308.14(b)(3) tramadol; 105 CMR 700.002(B)–(D); DEA 2014 hydrocodone combination rescheduling

options.option_text: Vicodin III, Suboxone III, and tramadol IV; hydrocodone combinations remained Schedule III after 2014.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DEA moved ALL hydrocodone combination products to Schedule II effective October 6, 2014. Codeine combination exceptions do not apply to hydrocodone/acetaminophen.

options.option_text: Vicodin II, Suboxone II, and tramadol IV; all opioid agonists are Schedule II if prescribed for human pain or OUD.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Buprenorphine, including the named buprenorphine/naloxone combination, is listed in Schedule III under 21 CFR 1308.13(e)(2), regardless of the therapeutic indication. Hydrocodone combinations are Schedule II.

options.option_text: Vicodin II, Suboxone III, and tramadol V; the weaker opioid's lower potency makes tramadol Schedule V.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Tramadol is specifically listed in Schedule IV under 21 CFR 1308.14(b)(3). Subjective opioid potency does not determine a drug's legal schedule.

options.option_text: Vicodin II, Suboxone III, and tramadol IV; Massachusetts uses the same II–IV classifications through 105 CMR 700.002.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Hydrocodone combination products are Schedule II, buprenorphine is Schedule III and tramadol is Schedule IV. 105 CMR 700.002(B)–(D) adopts the federal corresponding controlled schedules. The pharmacist must use those product-specific categories when applying refills and dispensing limits.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy compounds four different NONHAZARDOUS nonsterile preparations. There is no USP–NF compounded preparation monograph, formulation-specific stability study, or shorter component limitation, and all have otherwise compliant packaging. Under currently official USP <795> Section 10, which default beyond-use-date (BUD) statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Current USP <795> Section 10.3/Table 4 (official Nov. 1, 2023); USP General Chapter <795> 2022 Open Forum BUD slide; 247 CMR 9.01(3)
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: MA Board Retail Inspection Template item 90: 14d nonpreserved aqueous, 35d preserved aqueous, 90d oral nonaqueous, 180d other nonaqueous
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Board's inspection table directly states time categories; licensed USP <795> normative chapter not accessed.

options.option_text: A nonpreserved aqueous suspension (water activity at least 0.60) generally has a maximum 14-day BUD and requires refrigerated storage.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Official revised USP <795> Table 4 classifies nonpreserved aqueous CNSPs with water activity at least 0.60 as 14 days refrigerated unless shorter stability or an applicable authoritative formula imposes otherwise.
options.independent_option_analysis: Nonpreserved aqueous CNSP maximum 14d when refrigerated.

options.option_text: A preserved aqueous solution with no substantiated specific stability has a default maximum BUD of 90 days at room temperature.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under USP <795> Table 4, preserved aqueous CNSPs generally have a 35-day maximum BUD at controlled room temperature or refrigerated, not 90 days. Ninety days is the category for nonaqueous ORAL liquids.
options.independent_option_analysis: Preserved aqueous default 35d, not 90d.

options.option_text: A properly preserved aqueous CNSP generally has a 35-day maximum BUD under the stated assumptions and may be stored at controlled room temperature or refrigerated.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Revised USP <795> Table 4 specifies preserved aqueous forms with water activity at least 0.60: 35 days, controlled room temperature or refrigerated. Preservative effectiveness and drug-specific stability must still be adequate.
options.independent_option_analysis: Preserved aqueous default 35d at controlled room/refrigerated when formulation otherwise compliant.

options.option_text: A nonaqueous oral liquid can automatically use the 180-day maximum reserved for other nonaqueous preparations such as capsules.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <795> distinguishes nonaqueous ORAL LIQUIDS (90 days) from OTHER nonaqueous preparations (180 days). Category selection depends on dosage form and water activity, not merely the absence of free water.
options.independent_option_analysis: Other nonaqueous 180d does not apply to nonaqueous oral liquids.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist updates a personal mailing address and telephone number, and legally changes their surname following a court order. The pharmacist's professional license is otherwise in good standing. Under 247 CMR 20.03(1)–(2), which action is required?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 20.03(1)–(2) (effective Dec. 6, 2024); Massachusetts Board Reporting Requirements Overview

options.option_text: Notify the Board only at the next biennial renewal; neither a contact change nor name change is reportable earlier.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 20.03(1) requires the online licensing profile to be updated within 14 calendar days of mailing-address, telephone or email changes; subsection (2) independently addresses changes of name within the same 14-day period.

options.option_text: Update personal contact information within 30 business days; a name change requires no evidence as long as the online profile was edited.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts uses 14 CALENDAR days rather than 30 business days, and §20.03(2) requires a sworn name-change statement plus a copy of valid picture identification and any other Board-required records.

options.option_text: Update the contact details in the DPH online licensing profile within 14 calendar days and submit the required sworn name-change statement and identification within 14 calendar days.
options.original_rationale: Correct. These are separate duties imposed by §20.03(1)–(2). Editing the profile addresses changes to mailing address, telephone and email; a legal name change additionally requires the sworn statement, ID and any Board-requested supporting documentation.

options.option_text: Submit a sworn statement only for the telephone number, and treat the legal surname change as automatically transferred from court records.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The sworn-statement procedure attaches to the NAME change under §20.03(2), not merely the phone number. A court order does not by itself update a pharmacist's DPH license profile.

questions.question_stem: A community pharmacy is offered manufacturer-labeled prescription samples bearing 'drug sample—not for resale.' The pharmacist proposes to use the samples to make compounded prescriptions, relabel part of the stock into ordinary pharmacy vials, and bill patients for the resulting medications. No specific exception applies. What does Massachusetts pharmacy law require?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(6) (effective Dec. 6, 2024); Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act §503(c)–(d), 21 U.S.C. §353(c)–(d) (PDMA sample distribution and sale)

options.option_text: Allow repackaging but not compounding, because the package label bans sale only in the original sample container.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.01(6) expressly prohibits accepting or purchasing medications designated 'drug samples not for resale' for purposes of compounding, REPACKING or any kind of resale. Removing the sample label does not erase the restriction.

options.option_text: Decline the proposal: a pharmacy may not accept or buy these samples for compounding, repacking, or resale, regardless of whether it could charge only for labor.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The exact §9.01(6) prohibition attaches to accepting/purchasing samples for compounding, repacking or reselling. The federal PDMA framework in the FD&C Act also restricts drug-sample distribution and sale; a payment characterization does not convert sample stock into saleable prescription inventory.

options.option_text: Use the samples as ingredients if the FDA-approved commercial medicine is not being chemically changed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The specific ban in §9.01(6) is activity- and product-marking-based; it does not depend on whether the active substance is chemically altered. Samples cannot be accepted for compounding under the proposed activity.

options.option_text: Release the sample stock to patients as ordinary saleable prescriptions if the pharmacy adds a manufacturer lot number and expiration date.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Ordinary stock-labeling completeness does not lift the sample-resale restriction. This differs from a valid commercial product or an uncollected prescription eligible for return to stock under an entirely different rule.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist reviews otherwise authentic outpatient prescriptions issued by authorized practitioners. None is a standing order, expedited partner therapy, or another special exception except the one expressly identified. Which statements about the required prescription contents under 105 CMR 721.020 are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 721.020(C),(D)(1)–(6) (effective Sept. 27, 2024); DPH Elements of a Written Prescription; M.G.L. c.94C §22(a)

options.option_text: For an ordinary Schedule VI human prescription, the issuance date, practitioner registration number, drug identification/strength/quantity, directions, and authorized refill information remain required.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 721.020(C)–(D)(1)–(6) specifies the prescriber identification, issuance date, drug details, patient information, directions, and refill statement across Massachusetts prescription drugs, including Schedule VI. Schedule VI is not generally exempt from these basic elements.

options.option_text: A community prescription for an ordinary adult human patient may omit the patient's address whenever the pharmacist can verify the patient's phone number.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.020(D)(4) generally requires patient NAME and ADDRESS. The rule lists limited exemptions such as veterinary orders, specified naloxone/opioid-antagonist prescriptions, and certain specified 721.070 exceptions; a verified phone number alone is not one.

options.option_text: A veterinary prescription may omit the patient's name and address under the expressly listed 721.020(D)(4) exception; the other applicable veterinary and controlled-prescription requirements still apply.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) expressly lists veterinary prescriptions as an exception to the patient name/address field, without exempting the practitioner, medication, directions, or other requirements. The pharmacist still needs an authentic, lawful veterinary order.

options.option_text: The practitioner registration number is a required field only for federal Schedule II products; Schedule III–VI prescriptions have no registration-number requirement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.020(D)(1) requires a practitioner registration number without limiting the field to Schedule II. For Massachusetts Schedule VI the MCSR may satisfy the state identification requirement, while federal Schedules II–V have applicable DEA registration requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist compares (X) FDA-approved Xyrem (sodium oxybate), issued under all otherwise required special dispensing restrictions, with (Y) a separate unapproved gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB) preparation. Which federal AND Massachusetts controlled schedules apply to these two distinct products?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.11(e)(6) (GHB); 21 CFR 1308.13(c)(6) (FDA-approved GHB-containing drug products); 105 CMR 700.002(A),(C); DEA Nov. 2026 GHB fact sheet

options.option_text: Both are Schedule I because they contain chemically related gamma-hydroxybutyric acid.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal 21 CFR 1308.13(c)(6) specifically places FDA-approved drug products containing GHB or its salts in Schedule III; unapproved GHB is separately controlled in Schedule I under 1308.11(e)(1). Massachusetts follows the corresponding federal categories.

options.option_text: Xyrem is Schedule III while unapproved GHB is Schedule I; the FDA-approved-drug-product exception does not extend to illicit or unapproved preparations.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.13(c)(6) specifically covers FDA-approved products containing gamma-hydroxybutyric acid/sodium oxybate, while §1308.11(e)(1) covers ordinary GHB as Schedule I. Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.002(A),(C) incorporates those respective federal classifications. Applicable REMS and product restrictions also still apply to Xyrem.

options.option_text: Xyrem is Schedule IV and unapproved GHB is Schedule II because a medically indicated dose reduces both by one controlled schedule.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Controlled-substance schedules are set by federal law, not by a pharmacist's dose-dependent inference. The listed categories are Schedule III for approved GHB-containing drug products and Schedule I for unapproved GHB.

options.option_text: Xyrem is Massachusetts Schedule VI because it is FDA approved, whereas unapproved GHB is Massachusetts Schedule III.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts Schedule VI does not capture drugs already in federally incorporated Schedules I–V. FDA approval alone does not make a controlled drug Schedule VI; the special §1308.13(c)(6) listing makes the approved product Schedule III.

questions.question_stem: Massachusetts Board pharmacy inspectors visit a licensed community pharmacy without notice and cite deficiencies. The Board's written notice does not specify a shorter or longer plan-of-correction deadline. The first submitted plan is later returned as unacceptable. Under 247 CMR 9.24–9.25, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Board inspectors may make an unannounced visit and inspect staff, activities and relevant pharmacy records; the pharmacy must supply requested inspection documents.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.24(1),(3) gives the Board or its designees authority to inspect licensed pharmacies at any time without notice and requires provision of requested documents during an inspection or investigation.

options.option_text: Inspectors must provide 72 hours' notice unless they first obtain a court order, because prescription records are categorically exempt from Board inspection.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.24(1) permits unannounced regulatory inspections, and §9.24(3) requires requested documents; pharmacy confidentiality obligations do not establish the proposed universal advance-notice rule.

options.option_text: The pharmacy need submit only one general corrective promise without dates, responsible persons, or MOR signature.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.25(2) requires corrective steps for EACH cited violation, projected completion/implementation dates and responsible individuals; §9.25(3) requires the MOR and, where applicable, supervising licensee signatures.

options.option_text: The first written plan is due within 21 days unless the Board directs a different period, and an unacceptable plan must be revised within seven days.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.25(1) sets 21 days OR the timeframe directed by the Board; §9.25(5) requires resubmission of a corrected plan within seven days after the Board returns the prior plan as unacceptable.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy technician has already practiced in a retail pharmacy for 12 hours in the preceding 24-hour period. A last-minute staffing emergency threatens access to urgent patient prescriptions. The technician can work only 45 more minutes, and management is able to document the extenuating circumstances and minimize the extra work. Which statement most accurately applies 247 CMR 9.01(17)?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(17) (effective Dec. 6, 2024); distinguish pharmacy meal-break arrangements from consecutive rest

options.option_text: An extenuating circumstance may permit the additional minimized, documented work in the patient's best interest; ordinarily eight consecutive hours of rest are required before resuming practice.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.01(17) limits pharmacist, intern and technician practice to 12 hours in a 24-hour period without completing eight consecutive hours' rest prior to resumption. An extenuating circumstance permits extra time to serve a patient's best interests only when minimized and documented. The exception is not routine scheduling permission.

options.option_text: The exception is available to licensed pharmacists only; technicians can never work beyond 12 hours, regardless of a documented patient need.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.01(17) expressly includes pharmacy technicians as well as pharmacists and interns in both the work/rest provision and the extenuating-circumstance clause.

options.option_text: The pharmacy can routinely schedule a 15-hour shift whenever the technician agrees, because a signed employee consent substitutes for a rest period.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Employee agreement alone is not an enumerated exception. The regulation requires a genuine extenuating circumstance serving patient interests, minimal extra time and documentation.

options.option_text: A 30-minute meal break automatically resets the 12-hour limit, so neither a consecutive eight-hour rest period nor any written explanation is needed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.01(17) specifies EIGHT CONSECUTIVE HOURS of rest, not a meal break, before resuming ordinary practice following the limit. A separate meal-break rule does not replace this requirement.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has a trained technician, a pharmacy intern and an on-duty pharmacist. The technician offers counseling to a patient with a newly prescribed drug. The patient accepts and asks how to take the drug with food and what to do after a missed dose. Under 247 CMR 9.18, who may fulfill the requested counseling?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.18(1)–(5) (effective Dec. 6, 2024); compare 9.18(10) for inpatient practice exclusion

options.option_text: The trained technician alone may answer the clinical counseling questions because the technician appropriately offered counseling.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.18(2) allows a properly trained designee to make the OFFER, but §9.18(3) expressly limits the actual counseling to a pharmacist or pharmacy intern. Asking about food interactions and missed doses requires counseling, not mere administrative intake.

options.option_text: Only the pharmacist may counsel, because Massachusetts prohibits even a properly supervised pharmacy intern from advising patients.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.18(3) explicitly authorizes counseling by a pharmacist OR pharmacy intern; supervised intern counseling is not categorically forbidden.

options.option_text: The pharmacist or the pharmacy intern may provide the counseling; the trained technician's role may be to offer it, but not to provide clinical counseling.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under §9.18(1)–(4), an appropriately trained designee can make the offer, but only a pharmacist or pharmacy intern counsels each new drug therapy. Relevant content in §9.18(5) includes food interactions and missed-dose instructions.

options.option_text: No counseling is required once the patient receives a printed drug-information leaflet; the technician may simply mark the offer completed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A leaflet does not erase the pharmacist/intern counseling duty for a new drug therapy when counseling is sought. Sections 9.18(3)–(5) require qualified counseling on information needed for safe use.

questions.question_stem: A community pharmacy offers a bedside delivery service at a Massachusetts inpatient healthcare facility for patients being discharged. A hospital discharge planner wants all patients automatically enrolled in the hospital's preferred community pharmacy, with medications dropped at the nurses' station whether or not the patient agrees. Under 247 CMR 9.04(4), which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.04(4) (bed-side discharge prescription delivery, effective Dec. 6, 2024); 247 CMR 9.02 not a substitute for bedside-delivery consent

options.option_text: The pharmacy may waive individual patient consent because the patient is already hospitalized and an authorized discharge planner selected the pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.04(4) expressly requires consent from the patient to provide bedside discharge prescription delivery. A hospital's preferred-pharmacy workflow does not create an automatic exemption.

options.option_text: The bedside-delivery pharmacy must obtain patient consent to use the service and cannot restrict the patient's freedom to choose a pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Both duties are expressly stated in 247 CMR 9.04(4). A bedside-delivery program should be opt-in and protect patient choice, not function as an exclusive mandatory hospital arrangement.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may leave a patient's discharge medication at the nurses' station for later pickup by anyone available because it has fulfilled the delivery requirement by reaching the building.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.04(4) requires bedside-service prescriptions to be delivered DIRECTLY to the patient or patient's agent. Unattended placement at a station is not the prescribed delivery to the intended recipient.

options.option_text: For a consenting patient who selects the pharmacy, the bedside service must deliver medications directly to that patient or the patient's authorized agent.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.04(4) couples the consent and freedom-of-choice conditions with direct handoff to the patient or patient's agent. All other controlled, labeling, and counseling rules still apply.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist reviews otherwise lawful prescriptions for oral lacosamide (Vimpat), ketamine (Ketalar), and zolpidem (Ambien). All products are conventional, non-exempt FDA-approved medicines. Which classification accurately states their federal and Massachusetts controlled schedules?

options.option_text: Vimpat Schedule V, Ketalar Schedule III, Ambien Schedule IV.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Lacosamide is specifically listed in 21 CFR 1308.15(e)(5), ketamine in §1308.13(c)(7), and zolpidem in §1308.14(c)(59). Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.002(C)–(E) adopts these categories. The pharmacist should apply refill and dispensing limits to each product's actual schedule.

options.option_text: Vimpat Schedule IV, Ketalar Schedule II, Ambien Schedule IV.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Lacosamide is Schedule V, not IV, and ketamine is Schedule III, not II. Zolpidem is Schedule IV; the other two classifications make this option invalid.

options.option_text: Vimpat Schedule V, Ketalar Schedule IV, Ambien Schedule III.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Lacosamide is V, but ketamine is III rather than IV and zolpidem is IV rather than III under the federal controlled-substance schedules.

options.option_text: All three are Schedule VI in Massachusetts because they are not conventional opioid or stimulant prescriptions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts Schedule VI covers prescription drugs not in the other incorporated schedules. Lacosamide, ketamine and zolpidem are explicitly federally scheduled and therefore retain the corresponding MA Schedules V, III and IV.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy handles NIOSH-listed hazardous drugs (HDs) and considers documented assessments of risk (AOR) to use alternative containment. It receives commercially manufactured, intact Table 1 antineoplastic tablets for counting only; it also crushes a different Table 1 antineoplastic into an oral suspension, and compounds from a hazardous API. Under USP <800> and USP's January 2026 technical FAQs, which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: USP <800> §§2–5 (hazardous drug list, assessment of risk and engineering controls); USP <800> FAQs updated Jan. 21, 2026, Q11–14 and Q18 (technical support, not a formal interpretation); 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: A documented product- and dosage-form-specific AOR may permit alternative containment when only counting intact commercially manufactured Table 1 antineoplastic tablets, absent manufacturer instructions requiring more.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <800> and FAQ 14 allow an AOR for final manufactured antineoplastic dosage forms not further manipulated beyond counting or repackaging, unless a manufacturer requires otherwise. The pharmacy must implement and document appropriate alternative controls and assess the individual drug and dosage form.

options.option_text: The AOR can replace all required containment when a Table 1 antineoplastic is crushed into a compounded suspension, as long as one technician wears a disposable face mask.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Crushing Table 1 antineoplastic products is manipulation that triggers the full USP <800> containment strategies and work practices, not a general AOR exception. A face mask alone does not replace required engineering controls and PPE.

options.option_text: One single AOR covering all Table 1 products is automatically sufficient, even where dosage forms and handling activities are entirely different.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP FAQ 12 explicitly explains that each HD and dosage form must be identified individually in the risk assessment; tablet counting, capsule opening, and crushing involve different exposure risks. Group-wide generic assessment without the drug/dosage-form specifics is inadequate.

options.option_text: A hazardous active pharmaceutical ingredient used in compounding remains subject to full USP <800> containment requirements; a pharmacy cannot substitute a reduced-containment AOR for that API.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <800> and USP FAQ 14, 18 require full containment for hazardous APIs and for manipulated Table 1 antineoplastics. AOR alternatives are available only to eligible dosage forms or other listed hazardous drugs as the standard specifies.

questions.question_stem: A resident Massachusetts pharmacy learns that an improper dispensing caused serious injury to a patient. Separately, a patient experiences a serious adverse drug event linked to a preparation compounded by that pharmacy. Under 247 CMR 20.02, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: The Manager of Record must report the serious-injury improper dispensing to the Board within seven business days of discovering the injury.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 20.02(1) imposes this specific seven-BUSINESS-day duty on the MOR for improper dispensing resulting in serious injury or death. The pharmacy's separate CQI responsibilities remain in force.

options.option_text: The pharmacy can postpone reports of both incidents until renewal if it promptly documents them in the CQI log.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. CQI documentation does not replace the separately required §20.02(1)–(2) reports. The statute uses an event-specific reporting clock, not a license-renewal deadline.

options.option_text: The MOR must report the compounded-product serious adverse drug event to the Board, FDA MedWatch and Betsy Lehman Center.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 20.02(2) lists all three recipients, with reporting due within seven business days of any employee's awareness. This is distinct from ordinary medication errors that do not qualify as the specified compounded/manufactured event.

options.option_text: Once the pharmacy completes CQI documentation, it may destroy the serious-event reports after two years.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 20.02(4) requires the records for reportable events to remain readily retrievable for at least FIVE years from the date the report is filed. The general QRE minimum under 247 CMR 15.04 cannot shorten it.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts optometrist holds the special glaucoma/ocular certification required by M.G.L. c.112 §66C and the proper state prescriptive registration. Assume every candidate prescription is authentic and all other legal conditions are met. Which proposed prescription is within this optometrist's professional scope?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.112 §66C(a)(i)–(ii),(a)(A)–(D), effective Jan. 1, 2021; M.G.L. c.94C §7(h)

options.option_text: Oxycodone for severe ocular postoperative pain, because the pain arises from eye treatment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.112 §66C(a)(D) expressly excludes opioid substances and drug products from the qualified optometrist's authority, even in an ocular setting.

options.option_text: An appropriate oral anti-infective for an ocular infection being managed by the optometrist.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 66C(a)(ii) authorizes necessary eye-related medicines INCLUDING oral anti-infective drugs for properly certified optometrists. The patient and condition must remain within lawful optometric practice.

options.option_text: Lisinopril for unrelated systemic hypertension that the optometrist discovered during an eye visit.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 66C(a)(A) forbids therapeutic agents for treatment of systemic diseases. Discovering hypertension during an eye examination does not confer general medical prescriptive authority.

options.option_text: An agent administered by routine subcutaneous injection to treat an ocular disorder.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 66C(a)(C) excludes specified injection routes including subcutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous and intraocular routes. Certification does not eliminate those restrictions.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist offers counseling for a new outpatient prescription. The patient clearly declines, and the pharmacist completes the necessary prospective drug review. A staff member asks whether the patient's refusal needs a record. Which interpretation follows M.G.L. c.94C §21A?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §21A (counseling refusal and record presumption); 247 CMR 9.18

options.option_text: The pharmacist must force a counseling session despite the patient's refusal because new prescriptions never permit refusal.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 21A explicitly permits the person presenting the prescription to decline the offer; the pharmacist need not provide counseling after refusal, although the offer and DUR duties remain.

options.option_text: No attempt to document refusal is appropriate, because the statute presumes refusal whenever the record is silent.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 21A requires reasonable efforts to maintain relevant patient data, including failure to accept counseling. Missing a refusal record leads to a presumption of counseling provided, not declined.

options.option_text: The pharmacy should reasonably record the refusal; without a recorded refusal, §21A presumes that counseling was provided.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 21A directs reasonable efforts to document any failure to accept the offer and provides the specified presumption. A truthful refusal record matters even though the patient may lawfully decline.

options.option_text: The staff member may record that counseling took place because offering counseling is legally the same as delivering a counseling session.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An offer and the actual service are not identical. The pharmacist should not record counseling as performed when the patient declined; documenting the refusal is the proper course.

questions.question_stem: Which federal and corresponding Massachusetts schedules correctly classify ordinary prescription testosterone cypionate injection, phentermine capsules and phenobarbital tablets in November 2026?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.13(f)(84) (testosterone), 1308.14(c)(49) (phenobarbital), 1308.14(f)(10) (phentermine; shifted on Nov. 12, 2026); 105 CMR 700.002(C)–(D)

options.option_text: Testosterone III, phentermine IV, phenobarbital IV.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Testosterone is a listed Schedule III anabolic steroid at 21 CFR 1308.13(g). Phentermine and phenobarbital are expressly Schedule IV under §1308.14(f)(9) and (c)(49). Massachusetts uses corresponding Schedules III–IV.

options.option_text: Testosterone VI, phentermine II, phenobarbital III.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Being FDA-approved hormone therapy does not exempt testosterone from Schedule III, and neither phentermine nor phenobarbital has the stated II/III classification.

options.option_text: Testosterone III, phentermine III, phenobarbital II.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Only the testosterone classification is correct; phentermine is Schedule IV and phenobarbital is Schedule IV regardless of their indications.

options.option_text: All three are Schedule IV because each is a prescription-only medicine.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Prescription-only status does not make every drug Schedule IV. Testosterone remains Schedule III as an anabolic steroid.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is considering a dorm-style refrigerator with an interior freezer compartment for medicines. Management proposes storing lunches in the same refrigerator and keeping temperature excursion logs only six months. Which statements comply with 247 CMR 9.22? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.22(1)–(5), effective Dec. 6, 2024

options.option_text: The proposed dorm-style refrigerator is prohibited because its freezer compartment is within the refrigerator space.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.22(2) explicitly bans this design. The pharmacy must use appropriate combination or standalone equipment with compliant freezer design.

options.option_text: Food is permitted if it stays on a shelf separate from the medication stock.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.22(5) prohibits food or beverages in a refrigerator/freezer used to store medications, without a shelf-based exception.

options.option_text: Temperature logs must identify excursions and the pharmacy response, and must be retained for at least one year.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.22(4) requires out-of-range readings and response actions to be documented with a one-year minimum. The pharmacy's policy must include integrity assessment under §9.22(1).

options.option_text: An intact commercial package eliminates the need to assess drug integrity after an out-of-range temperature.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.22(1) requires an excursion response protocol including integrity assessment. An intact seal is not proof of stability under the actual temperature conditions.

questions.question_stem: During 2026, a Massachusetts pharmacist verifies several compounded sterile preparations and several complex nonsterile preparations during brief coverage shifts. Other approved annual CE totals 20 hours, including required law and live hours, but none concerns compounding. No Board waiver applies. What additional specialty CE compliance is necessary?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 4.03(4)(c)–(d); Massachusetts Board Policy 2021-04 §§V–VII, revised Sept. 4, 2025

options.option_text: None, because temporary compounding coverage does not require subject-specific CE.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 247 CMR 4.03(4)(c)–(d) and Board Policy 2021-04, even limited involvement in verifying sterile or complex nonsterile preparations triggers the corresponding annual specialty education.

options.option_text: Five hours in sterile compounding only; complex nonsterile education is unnecessary when a pharmacist also does sterile work.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The applicable five sterile and three complex nonsterile annual requirements are independent; sterile responsibility does not extinguish complex nonsterile responsibility.

options.option_text: Exactly eight specialty hours in addition to the annual 20, because compounding education is legally excluded from general CE credit.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Board Policy 2021-04 §VII allows appropriate specialty compounding education to count toward the annual 20-hour general requirement. The issue is required content, not necessarily eight hours above 20.

options.option_text: Five sterile-compounding and three complex-nonsterile-compounding CE hours in the calendar year; qualifying specialty credit may count within the general annual 20.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 4.03(4)(c)–(d) specifies five annual sterile and three annual complex nonsterile hours for relevant work. The Board's revised CE policy applies to temporary verification and allows qualified specialty hours toward general CE.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist discovers a Quality-Related Event: a patient received the wrong prescription drug, but there is no known serious injury. The pharmacy has a CQI program. Which measures are required under 247 CMR 15? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 15.02(1)(f), 15.03(1)–(3), 15.04(1)–(4); 247 CMR 20.02 (separate serious-event reporting)

options.option_text: The pharmacist must promptly address patient notification, corrective directions and measures to minimize potential harm.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 15.03(1), staff alert the pharmacist/MOR immediately; the pharmacist addresses the patient and any professionally indicated prescriber/healthcare-team contact and corrective steps without waiting for injury.

options.option_text: Initial event documentation may be delayed until the next monthly CQI meeting because no serious injury has occurred.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 15.03(2)(a) requires the informed or discovering pharmacist to complete initial documentation within 24 hours. The separate serious-injury reporting threshold under 20.02 is not a CQI exemption.

options.option_text: Maintain QRE records for at least two years and provide pharmacy personnel with CQI education at least annually.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 15.04(2) mandates two-year QRE records; §15.02(1)(f) requires at least annual CQI education. More serious events may carry additional and longer reporting requirements.

options.option_text: A wrong-drug dispensing is excluded from CQI unless the patient is hospitalized or dies.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A qualifying dispensing QRE triggers §15 event handling and documentation independent of whether it produced serious harm.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy wants to provide medication orders for residents of a skilled nursing facility on its premises and solely owned by the hospital. The hospital DOES NOT meet the federal criteria for a 'sole community hospital' in 42 CFR 412.92. Under 105 CMR 722.090(A), which conclusion is correct?
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 722.090(A) (hospital-based SNF/LTCF exception); 42 CFR 412.92 sole community hospital

options.option_text: Ownership and location alone do not establish the specific hospital-patient exception; the owning hospital must also satisfy the referenced federal sole-community-hospital criteria.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 722.090(A) requires the nursing facility to be solely owned by a qualifying sole community hospital and located on its premises. Without the separate federal-status condition, that special pathway is not established. The pharmacy should evaluate any other independently lawful arrangement.

options.option_text: All nursing-facility residents automatically count as hospital inpatients if their facility shares an address with a hospital.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 722.090(A) has more conditions than location, and it expressly ties its nursing-facility exception to a sole community hospital.

options.option_text: Hospital ownership alone is enough even if the facility is off-site and the hospital lacks the federal designation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Both on-premises status and the referenced owning-hospital qualification are conditions. Ownership does not waive either of them.

options.option_text: The law never permits a hospital pharmacy to serve any nursing-facility resident under any circumstances.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Qualifying solely hospital-owned on-premises facilities at a sole community hospital CAN fall within §722.090(A); the scenario fails a particular condition, not a universal prohibition.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts practitioner issues three separate authentic electronic prescriptions for methylphenidate on November 1, 2026, each for 30 days. The second and third give earliest-fill dates December 15 and January 15, and diversion risk and legitimate-purpose conditions are satisfied. No new prescription is issued afterward. What follows from 21 CFR 1306.12(b) and M.G.L. c.94C §23(a)?

options.option_text: The delayed prescriptions remain valid because DEA permits separate prescriptions totaling up to 90 days, overriding all state issue-date expiration rules.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DEA §1306.12(b) conditions multiple issuance on applicable STATE law. Massachusetts Schedule II paper/electronic prescriptions expire 30 days after issue; a later earliest-fill date cannot extend that period.

options.option_text: Issuing multiple Schedule II prescriptions is always an illegal refill; therefore none of the prescriptions, including the first, can be dispensed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal law can permit separately issued Schedule II prescriptions; they are not all automatically refills. But each must independently remain valid under Massachusetts law at dispensing.

options.option_text: The federal multiple-prescription option is conditional on state law, and both delayed originals would already be invalid under the Massachusetts 30-day validity limit.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Federal 21 CFR 1306.12(b)(1)(iv) requires state-law permission. M.G.L. c.94C §23(a) invalidates Schedule II prescriptions 30 days after issuance, counting under 247 CMR 9.04(10). The proposed dates occur well beyond that window.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may merge all three authorizations into one 90-day dispensing from the first prescription to avoid the delayed-date problem.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A permission for selected nonopioid Schedules II–III 90-day SINGLE fills does not let the pharmacist rewrite the prescriber's three separately issued, future-dated prescriptions into one 90-day order.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy supplies emergency medication kits and proposes delivering them to any facility on request, without formal kit procedures or reconciliation against medication orders. Which statements accurately describe 247 CMR 9.09? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.09(1)–(3), effective Dec. 6, 2024

options.option_text: The pharmacy must have procedures for kit security, maintenance and use.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.09(1) expressly requires pharmacy policies and procedures for proper dispensing through emergency kits, including security, maintenance and use.

options.option_text: Any assisted living or commercial facility is eligible if its administrator agrees to accept the kit.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under §9.09(3), pharmacies may provide kits ONLY to types of facilities approved by the Massachusetts Board, not to any willing recipient.

options.option_text: Once medications are removed, the pharmacy has no responsibility to reconcile dispensing with valid prescriptions or orders.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.09(2) expressly obliges the pharmacy to reconcile medication dispensed through the kits with prescriptions or medication orders.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must reconcile kit use with orders and may provide kits only to Board-approved facility types.
options.original_rationale: Correct. These two independent requirements appear in 247 CMR 9.09(2) and (3). The pharmacist should verify both records and destination authorization.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist keeps a current Board-issued license readily available at the pharmacy but not wall-posted. The pharmacist's badge states only 'Staff Member' without a first name, and the pharmacist has no NABP e-profile number. What does 247 CMR 9.01(18)–(20) require?

options.option_text: Post the license on the wall; the generic badge and lack of e-profile are permissible.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The license may be carried, wall-posted OR readily available. However, the pharmacist must have the required identifying badge and maintain an NABP e-profile number.

options.option_text: Keeping the license readily available is acceptable, but the badge must show at least the pharmacist's first name and recognized pharmacist title, and an NABP e-profile is required.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.01(18) permits three license-availability options; (19) requires first name plus 'Pharmacist,' 'Registered Pharmacist' or 'R.Ph.' on the badge; (20) requires the pharmacist to maintain an NABP e-profile number.

options.option_text: The pharmacy manager's NABP e-profile satisfies the requirement for every pharmacist and staff can use generic role badges.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The requirement in §9.01(20) applies to each pharmacist personally. Section 9.01(19) does not allow pharmacists to conceal their title behind a nonspecific badge.

options.option_text: All license, badge and e-profile requirements apply only at biennial renewal and can be deferred in daily practice.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Sections 9.01(18)–(20) are ongoing professional practice obligations, not renewal-only administrative tasks.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist evaluates medication orders issued by a licensed certified PROFESSIONAL midwife (not an APRN certified nurse-midwife). The professional midwife holds the required Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and is practicing within the officially recognized midwifery scope. Which interpretation of M.G.L. c.112 §295 is correct?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.112 §295(a)–(b), effective Nov. 21, 2024; 274 CMR 3.07, effective Sept. 11, 2026; M.G.L. c.94C §7(j)

options.option_text: The midwife may order and administer covered Schedule VI medicines such as oxytocin and vitamin K in authorized practice, but cannot use Schedule II–V drugs under this license.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 295(a) lists authorized medicines such as oxytocin and vitamin K; §295(b)(i) prohibits controlled drugs other than Massachusetts Schedule VI for licensed certified professional midwives. The LCPM license must not be confused with an APRN certified nurse-midwife credential.

options.option_text: The license gives exactly the same Schedule II–V prescribing privileges as an APRN certified nurse-midwife, because both titles contain 'midwife'.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Licensed certified professional midwives and APRN nurse-midwives have separate legal scopes. Section 295(b) prohibits the former from Schedule II–V use under this authority.

options.option_text: Even approved Schedule VI medicines are prohibited to LCPMs because Massachusetts calls them 'controlled substances'.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 295(a) specifically permits named agents within approved practice and §295(b) explicitly excepts Schedule VI medicines from its exclusion.

options.option_text: A clinic may authorize a Schedule IV analgesic simply by including it in its midwifery policy, bypassing §295's schedule restriction.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Internal policies cannot expand statutory authority. Section 295(b) excludes Schedule II–V drugs for this practitioner class regardless of a clinic's preference.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives an authentic brand prescription marked 'no substitution.' The brand is unavailable during an actual medical emergency, but a less expensive drug on the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs is available. No additional restriction applies. Under 247 CMR 9.05(1), which actions are permissible or required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.05(1)(a)–(b), effective Dec. 6, 2024

options.option_text: The pharmacist may dispense the eligible less expensive interchangeable medicine in the qualifying emergency even though the brand order says 'no substitution'.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.05(1)(a) permits this limited emergency exception if the prescribed brand is unavailable and the alternative is on the state interchange list. It is not routine discretionary substitution.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may replace the drug with any other medicine treating the same disease, whether or not it is legally interchangeable.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The exception is for a qualifying, listed interchangeable drug, not simply a medication with a related therapeutic indication.

options.option_text: Document the date, hour and nature of the medical emergency and obtain the purchaser's written acceptance of the deviation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.05(1)(b) demands BOTH a documented emergency and purchaser written acceptance. The pharmacy must retain an identifiable prescription for Board review.

options.option_text: Documenting the emergency is sufficient; the patient or purchaser may not be asked to accept the change in writing.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Purchaser written acceptance is expressly required by §9.05(1)(b) in addition to documenting the medical emergency.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy classifies (X) FDA-approved Epidiolex cannabidiol oral solution with no more than 0.1% THC and (Y) FDA-approved Cesamet nabilone capsules. Which statement accurately describes the CURRENT federal and corresponding Massachusetts schedules in November 2026?
questions.author_citation: 85 FR 51639 (Aug. 21, 2020), removal of FDA-approved CBD Schedule V listing; 21 CFR 1308.12(f)(1) nabilone; 105 CMR 700.002(B),(F); DEA Drugs of Abuse Guide 2024

options.option_text: Epidiolex is still federal Schedule V and Cesamet is not federally controlled because its ingredient is synthetic.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA-approved qualifying CBD products such as Epidiolex were removed from federal Schedule V in 2020, while nabilone remains expressly Schedule II in 21 CFR 1308.12(f)(1).

options.option_text: Both are Schedule I because any cannabis-related medicine must be federally prohibited even after FDA approval.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The two specific approved products have different current statuses; neither is properly characterized as Schedule I in this case.

options.option_text: Epidiolex is federally unscheduled but Massachusetts Schedule VI as a prescription medicine; Cesamet/nabilone is Schedule II in both federal and Massachusetts systems.
options.original_rationale: Correct. DEA's 2020 federal rule eliminated Schedule V control of qualifying FDA-approved CBD formulations, while Massachusetts includes other nonscheduled prescription drugs in Schedule VI. Nabilone remains Schedule II under §1308.12(f)(1), adopted correspondingly by Massachusetts.

options.option_text: Epidiolex is Massachusetts Schedule III because it treats epilepsy, while Cesamet is Schedule IV because it treats chemotherapy nausea.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Therapeutic indications do not replace formal scheduling. The correct distinction is qualifying CBD product federal decontrol/state VI versus nabilone federal and state II.

questions.question_stem: A licensed Massachusetts pharmacy proposes controlled-substance use of an automated dispensing device (ADD) inside a licensed hospital, with hospital nursing staff obtaining medicines near the point of care. A community pharmacy also has a separate patient-pickup automated pharmacy system (APS). Which statements follow 247 CMR 9.12 and Board ADD requirements? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.12(1)–(4) and 9.10 (distinguish ADD versus APS), effective Dec. 6, 2024; Board Policy 2019-02, revised Jan. 9, 2025

options.option_text: The ADD must be in a licensed healthcare facility and dispensing must be pursuant to a valid patient-specific prescription or medication order.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.12(1)–(2) imposes both conditions. A healthcare-facility ADD is not an unrestricted medication supply solely because it uses secure cabinets.

options.option_text: An institutional ADD is identical to an outpatient APS, so the APS rule allowing Schedule IV–VI patient pickup substitutes for ADD authorization.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Sections 9.10 and 9.12 govern different systems and purposes. The community APS rule does not replace healthcare facility ADD requirements.

options.option_text: The pharmacy's ADD procedures must address location, maintenance, security, controlled-substance accountability, quality assurance, stocking/returns and confidentiality.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.12(4)(a)–(g) expressly enumerates these requirements, irrespective of whether the manufacturer also provides device instructions.

options.option_text: A complete electronic access log allows ADD dispensing without a valid patient-specific order.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.12(2) still requires a valid prescription or order; electronic audit trails cannot independently create prescribing authority.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist's personal registration expired on December 31 of an even-numbered year. The pharmacist did not renew, has not been suspended or revoked, and now applies 65 days after expiration. A pharmacy proposes that the pharmacist immediately resume final prescription validation while the late-renewal application is reviewed. Which statement BEST reflects 247 CMR 4.02?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 4.02(1)–(5), Personal Registration Expiration and Renewal (MA Register 1330, Jan. 13, 2017)

options.option_text: The pharmacist may work during the first 90 days after expiration because late fees automatically preserve practice authority.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 4.02(3) treats ANY pharmacy practice after the personal registration expires as unlicensed practice. The regulation creates no general 90-day right to practice while a late renewal is pending; fees do not restore an expired license automatically.

options.option_text: The pharmacist cannot resume practice until the registration is renewed; for a lapse exceeding 60 days, the Board may impose renewal conditions, including additional CE.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 4.02(1),(3) registration expires December 31 of even-numbered years, and practice after expiration is unlicensed. Subsection (4) permits an applicant lapsed more than 60 days, without suspension or revocation, to seek renewal subject to conditions the Board may impose, including additional CE. The pharmacist must verify active renewal before validating prescriptions.

options.option_text: The Board must require a new NAPLEX and MPJE after every 60-day lapse, even when the registration has not been revoked.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 4.02(4) gives the Board discretion to impose conditions such as further continuing education after a lapse exceeding 60 days; it does not automatically require both exams at that threshold. A separate more-than-two-year lapse provision in §4.02(5) requires MPJE, not the proposed universal rule.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may resume upon paying the regular renewal fee because the Board's authority to add conditions applies only to pharmacy facility licenses.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 4.02 specifically governs PERSONAL pharmacist registrations; payment alone is not permission to practice with an expired registration, and subsection (4) expressly covers delayed individual renewal conditions.

questions.question_stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy is considering disclosure of ordinary outpatient medication information to family or caregivers. No 42 CFR Part 2 record, controlled-drug pickup identification requirement, or stricter special confidentiality rule applies. In case X, a capable patient is present and expressly objects to sharing with a friend. In case Y, an absent patient's friend asks to collect a specific filled prescription on the patient's behalf. In case Z, an incapacitated patient cannot be asked and a caregiver needs medication instructions relevant to ongoing care. Which interpretations of 45 CFR 164.510(b) are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 164.510(b)(1)–(3) (disclosures relevant to care, opportunity to object, best-interest professional judgment); HHS OCR FAQ, family and pharmacy prescription pickups

options.option_text: In case X, the pharmacy may reveal the medication information to the friend over the capable patient's express objection merely because the friend says they help with care.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 164.510(b)(2) allows sharing with someone involved in care when the present, capable patient agrees, has an opportunity to object without objecting, or the professional reasonably infers no objection. An actual express objection to this disclosure defeats the claimed permission absent a different legal basis.

options.option_text: In case Y, the pharmacy may use professional judgment and common practice to allow the friend to pick up the specified prescription without a prefiled written authorization naming the friend.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under §164.510(b)(3), when the patient is absent the pharmacist may make a reasonable best-interest inference permitting a person to collect filled prescriptions. HHS expressly identifies friends picking up a named patient's prescription as an allowed common-practice example. Any separate state or controlled-product requirements still apply, and HIPAA does not require automatic release.

options.option_text: In case Z, the pharmacy may use professional judgment to share only information directly relevant to the caregiver's involvement when disclosure is in the incapacitated patient's best interest.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 164.510(b)(3) permits a best-interest disclosure when incapacity makes it impracticable to obtain agreement or objection, but limits the protected information to what is directly relevant to that person's involvement in care or payment. The pharmacist should tailor the instructions and avoid unrelated profile history.

options.option_text: Because HIPAA recognizes family involvement, a spouse automatically has access to the patient's entire prescription history even when the patient objected and much of the history is unrelated.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 164.510(b)(1) limits discretionary family disclosure to information directly relevant to the person's involvement; a spouse is not automatically entitled to the entire profile, and an expressed objection matters. Formal patient access under another HIPAA provision is a different issue.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a credible manufacturer's voluntary recall notice for a particular lot of injectable medicine. The notice describes a defect creating a REASONABLE PROBABILITY of serious adverse health consequences or death, although no injury has yet been confirmed. FDA has not assigned or published a recall class. Which response and interpretation is best supported by 21 CFR 7.3(m) and FDA recall guidance?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 7.3(m)(1)–(3), 7.40–7.42; FDA Enforcement Report Information and Definitions (FDA classification may follow company-initiated voluntary recall); 247 CMR 9.01 product integrity duties

options.option_text: It must be Class III because no actual patient injury has been confirmed, and the pharmacy should await FDA's final classification before addressing affected stock.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Class III is for exposure NOT likely to cause adverse health consequences. Class determination is based on expected risk, not whether actual injury has already occurred; FDA explains that companies can initiate recalls before FDA classifies them. The pharmacy should promptly identify and segregate the affected product rather than keep distributing it.

options.option_text: It cannot be a valid recall because only FDA may initiate one; a manufacturer warning before FDA classification has no practical relevance.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Recalls commonly begin on a firm's own initiative. FDA may classify them after receiving necessary information, so an unclassified manufacturer's recall notice still calls for a timely pharmacy response.

options.option_text: The described hazard meets the Class I risk DEFINITION; a manufacturer may start a recall before FDA classifies it, so the pharmacy should segregate the affected lot and follow appropriate recall procedures.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 7.3(m)(1) defines Class I by a reasonable probability of serious health consequences or death. FDA's Enforcement Report guidance explains that voluntary recalls are often initiated BEFORE formal classification. The pharmacist should treat the credible notice as a patient/product integrity concern and prevent dispensing affected stock while handling the recall; this does not claim that FDA has already assigned Class I.

options.option_text: Any voluntary medicine recall is Class II regardless of its severity, and the pharmacy must continue filling until FDA posts the event.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Voluntary describes how the recall is initiated, not its hazard classification. Class II is defined by temporary/reversible harm or a remote chance of serious harm; it does not fit the described reasonable probability of severe harm. There is no general requirement to keep dispensing pending FDA's database posting.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist reviews three otherwise lawful outpatient prescriptions: Fycompa (perampanel), Onfi (clobazam), and Briviact (brivaracetam). Which combination correctly identifies their current FEDERAL and corresponding MASSACHUSETTS schedules as of November 2026?

options.option_text: Fycompa Schedule IV, Onfi Schedule III, Briviact Schedule V.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Perampanel is specifically Schedule III under 21 CFR 1308.13(c)(11), not IV; clobazam is Schedule IV under §1308.14(c)(12), not III. Brivaracetam is V.

options.option_text: Fycompa Schedule III, Onfi Schedule IV, Briviact Schedule IV.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Perampanel and clobazam are correctly III and IV, but brivaracetam is explicitly listed as Schedule V at 21 CFR 1308.15(e)(1). All antiseizure agents do not share a controlled schedule.

options.option_text: Fycompa Schedule II, Onfi Schedule IV, Briviact Schedule V.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Clobazam and brivaracetam are IV and V, but perampanel's specific federal listing in §1308.13(c)(11) makes it Schedule III, not II. The name or indication cannot override the schedule.

options.option_text: Fycompa Schedule III, Onfi Schedule IV, Briviact Schedule V.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.13(c)(11) lists perampanel as Schedule III, §1308.14(c)(12) lists clobazam as IV, and §1308.15(e)(1) lists brivaracetam as V. Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.002(C)–(E) adopts the corresponding federal schedules; the pharmacist applies each drug's specific refill/record rules.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy receives a microbiology report showing 11 CFU per cubic meter from VIABLE AIR sampling in its ISO Class 7 BUFFER room. There is no ISO 5 or non-viable particle action-level finding, and the Board has not directed a more restrictive plan. The pharmacy begins immediate assessment, develops and implements a remediation plan, completes a documented risk and product-risk assessment, and schedules repeat monitoring. Under Board Policy 2026-03 (adopted September 3, 2026), which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-03, §§I–II, III(A),(D)–(F), IV(B), V (adopted Sept. 3, 2026; supersedes Policy 2023-09); USP <797> official Nov. 1, 2023; 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: The result exceeds the ISO 7 viable-air action level, and the MOR, designated PIC or pharmacist designee must report the result to the Board within one business day of receiving the microbiology report.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2026-03 establishes an ISO 7 viable-air action level of MORE THAN 10 CFU/m³; 11 exceeds it. Section II requires notification using the Board reporting form within ONE BUSINESS DAY of receipt of the microbiology report by the MOR, designated PIC or pharmacist designee. This is a Board policy requirement, not a federal DEA reporting deadline.

options.option_text: Because the remediation plan has begun, the pharmacy can immediately assign the usual unrestricted Category 2 BUDs to all CSPs prepared in the affected ISO 7 buffer room.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. During remediation of a VIABLE ISO 7 buffer-room action level, Policy 2026-03 §V caps applicable CSP BUDs at 24 hours room temperature or four days refrigerated, unless the Board directs otherwise. Restoration of usual BUDs depends on proper remediation confirmed by repeat sampling below action levels.

options.option_text: The same limited-BUD permission applies to a NON-VIABLE particle action level, so a pharmacy never needs to stop compounding for particle-count findings.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section III(D) differentiates non-viable particle action levels: absent other Board direction, compounding must be suspended until full remediation and recertification of all classified areas. The reduced-BUD pathway in §V applies to VIABLE action levels under specified safeguards.

options.option_text: After the required initial assessment and remedial steps, the pharmacy may consider compounding during remediation in the affected ISO 7 buffer room only with the capped 24-hour room-temperature or four-day refrigerated BUD, subject to the policy's risk controls.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section V requires initiated remediation, repeat EM scheduling, documented risk assessment and mitigation before considering continuation in ISO 7 buffer rooms with those reduced BUDs. This is conditional permission, not an automatic duty to compound; the pharmacy should preserve patient continuity with a safe plan.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed supervising pharmacist knows that an employee has no pharmacist or intern license. To reduce the queue, the pharmacist knowingly lets that employee perform independent final clinical and dispensing validation of prescriptions. The pharmacy has no applicable waiver. No patient has yet been harmed. Which statement BEST describes the pharmacist's Board exposure?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m), (k) (grounds for individual discipline; effective Jan. 9, 2025); 247 CMR 9.04(1) (pharmacist final validation; effective Dec. 6, 2024)

options.option_text: The pharmacist's license cannot be disciplined unless the Board documents a specific patient's physical injury.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) makes KNOWINGLY permitting, aiding or abetting unlicensed pharmacy activities a disciplinary ground; the provision does not require patient injury. The pharmacist must stop unlicensed validation immediately.

options.option_text: The pharmacy owner alone is accountable because an individual pharmacist cannot be disciplined for an employee's unlawful work.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 10.03(1)(m) addresses the licensee who knowingly enables unlicensed work. The individual supervisor's responsibility is not removed by the owner's hiring or staffing decisions.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may face discipline for knowingly permitting unlicensed activity, even before a patient is harmed; independent final validation must return to a licensed pharmacist.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) and 247 CMR 9.04(1), the pharmacist must not knowingly allow an unlicensed person to perform tasks requiring professional pharmacy licensure. Actual harm is not a prerequisite to this ground, and any incident must be addressed under applicable patient-safety policies.

options.option_text: The employee may validate dispensing independently if a pharmacist later signs a weekly supervisory log.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A retrospective log does not authorize a nonpharmacist to perform independent final dispensing validation. 247 CMR 9.04(1) requires pharmacist final validation; deliberate circumvention can separately support Board discipline.

questions.question_stem: A properly qualified Massachusetts community pharmacist holds an active CDTM agreement for asthma, including individual physician referral, physician-approved protocol, the required MCSR and detailed patient consent documentation. An otherwise eligible patient is 17 years old and a parent signs the written consent. The pharmacist plans to initiate a Schedule VI inhaler under that CDTM agreement. What is the best legal assessment?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(a),(c)–(e); 247 CMR 16.04(1)–(2) (community CDTM patient eligibility and limited prescribing, effective Dec. 15, 2017)

options.option_text: The prescribing is permitted because a parent's written consent removes any CDTM minimum age.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(a) specifically limits the community-pharmacy CDTM setting to patients age 18 or OLDER. Parent consent does not convert a 17-year-old into an eligible adult under the rule.

options.option_text: The community pharmacist cannot use the CDTM prescribing authority for this 17-year-old; an authorized practitioner must arrange another lawful path to treatment.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Even with properly documented referral and consent, §16.03(5)(a)'s adult-patient requirement remains. The pharmacist should refer the minor to an authorized treating practitioner and must not treat the collaboration as overriding that patient-eligibility limit.

options.option_text: The prescription may be issued because CDTM prohibits only Schedule II–V medicines and therefore any Schedule VI patient is eligible.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 16.03(5)(e) restricts controlled-drug scheduling, but §16.03(5)(a) imposes a SEPARATE adult-only community CDTM rule. Compliance with one requirement does not waive the other.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may instead prescribe Schedule IV for the minor if the physician modifies the written referral.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Community-pharmacy CDTM authority cannot include Schedules II–V under §16.03(5)(e)3 and cannot be used for a 17-year-old under subsection (5)(a). Physician referral wording cannot override either restriction.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy purchases covered finished human prescription medicines from wholesalers and contracts with an outside records vendor. The pharmacy is NOT subject to a relevant DSCSA waiver, exemption, or enforcement-discretion relief. Under FD&C Act §582(d), which actions or conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: FD&C Act §582(d)(1)(A)(iii), (d)(1)(B), (d)(3) (21 U.S.C. §360eee-1); FDA Drug Supply Chain Security Act product tracing and authorized trading partner guidance

options.option_text: The pharmacy may purchase covered product from any low-price distributor if it records the distributor's address, even if the distributor is not an authorized trading partner.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 21 U.S.C. §360eee-1(d)(3), a dispenser's trading partners must be AUTHORIZED. Keeping an address or favorable invoice does not replace verification of authorized trading-partner status.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must conduct covered transactions with authorized trading partners and maintain applicable tracing records for at least six years after the transaction.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 582(d)(1)(A)(iii) requires retention of transaction information and statements (and applicable history) for not less than SIX years, and §582(d)(3) restricts dispenser trading partners to authorized entities. These duties are separate from investigating suspect products.

options.option_text: A written agreement may allow a third party to maintain the tracing records, but the pharmacy remains responsible for its statutory recordkeeping obligations.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 582(d)(1)(B) expressly allows a written third-party records arrangement, while requiring the dispenser to keep the agreement and remaining liable for compliance. The pharmacist should ensure records are accessible when required.

options.option_text: Once the third-party vendor accepts the records, all DSCSA duties transfer legally from the pharmacy to that vendor, so a pharmacy may discard its own agreement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 582(d)(1)(B) expressly provides that a third-party retention agreement does NOT relieve the dispenser of the statutory duty and requires maintaining a copy of that agreement.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist reviews three otherwise valid prescriptions: Quviviq (daridorexant), Belsomra (suvorexant), and Rozerem (ramelteon). Which federal and corresponding Massachusetts scheduling description is correct as of November 2026?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(17),(54); 105 CMR 700.002(D),(F); current FDA DailyMed Rozerem labeling (DEA Schedule: None, Apr. 15, 2026)

options.option_text: Quviviq is Schedule III, Belsomra is Schedule IV, and Rozerem is Schedule VI.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Daridorexant is specifically listed in federal Schedule IV under 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(17), not III. Belsomra is IV and ramelteon is not federally scheduled, making the first classification wrong.

options.option_text: All three are Schedule IV because each treats insomnia and requires a prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Clinical indication and prescription status do not control DEA scheduling. Ramelteon is not federally scheduled (its current FDA label states DEA Schedule: None) and is Massachusetts Schedule VI as a prescription-only drug.

options.option_text: Quviviq and Rozerem are Schedule VI and Belsomra is Schedule IV.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Rozerem is a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription medicine, but daridorexant/Quviviq is federally controlled Schedule IV, and Massachusetts adopts the corresponding Schedule IV.

options.option_text: Quviviq and Belsomra are Schedule IV federally and in Massachusetts; Rozerem is federally unscheduled and Massachusetts Schedule VI.
