options.original_rationale: Correct. Daridorexant (21 CFR 1308.14(c)(17)) and suvorexant (§1308.14(c)(54)) are Schedule IV; ramelteon is not federally controlled according to its FDA/DailyMed product labeling and is a Massachusetts prescription-only Schedule VI drug under 105 CMR 700.002(F).

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy handles final dosage forms of NIOSH Table 1 antineoplastic hazardous drugs (HDs), a separate non-antineoplastic hazardous tablet, and liquid HD solutions. It is evaluating automated pill counters and pneumatic-tube carriers using the January 2026 USP <800> technical FAQs. Which decisions are consistent with those standards? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Current USP <800> §12 (final dosage form dispensing and transport); USP <800> FAQs updated Jan. 21, 2026, Q80, 85–86 (technical support, not official interpretation); 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Keep the NIOSH Table 1 antineoplastic tablets out of automated counting or packaging machinery because breakage and powder contamination can expose workers.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <800> Section 12 and FAQ #85 prohibit placing Table 1 antineoplastic tablets and capsules into automated counting or packaging machines. Manual or otherwise compliant handling avoids machinery contamination.

options.option_text: A liquid hazardous drug may be sent by pneumatic tube as long as the bottle has a child-resistant closure.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <800> and FAQ #80 specifically prohibit liquid hazardous drugs in pneumatic tubes due to breakage and contamination risks. A child-resistant cap is not an exception.

options.option_text: For a hazardous tablet that is NOT a Table 1 antineoplastic, facility-specific assessment of risk and SOPs may support an automated counting process when safe and otherwise permitted.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FAQ #85 expressly distinguishes non-Table 1 antineoplastic HD tablets, which MAY be eligible for an assessed alternative using automated systems. The facility must evaluate product, exposure and contamination risks and establish controls.

options.option_text: Every hazardous-drug dosage form is categorically prohibited from any mechanical transport, including conveyors or carts, regardless of product-specific risk assessment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FAQ #80 restricts pneumatic tubes for liquid HDs and Table 1 antineoplastic HDs, while #86 permits risk-based handling of eligible final dosage forms on conveyors. The absolute ban on ALL mechanical transport is unsupported.

questions.question_stem: A graduate of a foreign pharmacy school not approved by the Massachusetts Board is seeking to start an internship in a Massachusetts community pharmacy. NABP authorized the graduate to sit for the FPGEE 14 months ago. The graduate holds no newer authorization and otherwise has all paperwork ready. Which action is required under 247 CMR 8.01(7) before the internship begins?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.01(7) (Graduates of Non-approved Colleges/Schools of Pharmacy; effective Jan. 9, 2025), plus other applicable pharmacy intern licensing prerequisites

options.option_text: Obtain NABP authorization to sit for the FPGEE issued within the preceding year and furnish a copy to the Board with its other required documentation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. For a graduate of a non-approved pharmacy college or school, §8.01(7) expressly requires FPGEE test authorization issued WITHIN THE PRECEDING YEAR before starting a Massachusetts pharmacy internship, with a copy submitted to the Board. The 14-month-old authorization is insufficient.

options.option_text: Begin the internship immediately because any FPGEE authorization, regardless of issue date, remains acceptable if the candidate has not yet taken the examination.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 8.01(7) contains a specific one-year recency condition on the authorization. No general indefinite-validity substitute is provided.

options.option_text: Complete 500 hours before submitting an FPGEE authorization, because the document is necessary only when the graduate applies for the pharmacist MPJE.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The regulation requires the authorization BEFORE COMMENCEMENT of the Massachusetts internship, rather than only after hours accrue or at MPJE scheduling.

options.option_text: Use a licensed pharmacy technician credential in place of the FPGEE authorization to receive pharmacy intern credit.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Pharmacy technician licensure and an applicant's foreign-graduate pharmacist-intern eligibility are separate pathways. A technician credential cannot waive §8.01(7)'s NABP authorization requirement.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist receives two authentic methadone Schedule II prescriptions from a DEA-registered non-OTP physician. Prescription X is for severe persistent pain treated in the physician's usual professional practice; prescription Y explicitly orders a daily outpatient supply for OUD maintenance instead of referral to an opioid treatment program. Assume X otherwise satisfies state and federal prescribing limits and is clinically appropriate. Which statement BEST addresses the prescriber's federal authority?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1306.04(a), 1306.07(a)–(c), 1306.12(a); DEA Methadone Drug Fact Sheet updated Aug. 2026; applicable M.G.L. c.94C

options.option_text: Neither prescription may be filled because all methadone prescribing requires certification as a federal opioid treatment program.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Methadone is Schedule II and may be legitimately prescribed for pain by an appropriately registered practitioner in the usual course of practice. The special OTP restriction concerns its use for ongoing OUD maintenance or detoxification, not every analgesic prescription.

options.option_text: Both may be filled because the individual DEA registration permits a non-OTP physician to use methadone for any outpatient purpose.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A conventional DEA practitioner registration does not authorize a routine non-OTP take-home methadone prescription for OUD maintenance. The limited three-day emergency rule concerns direct dispensing, not ordinary outpatient maintenance prescriptions.

options.option_text: X can fall within ordinary legitimate pain prescribing, whereas Y is not a lawful routine non-OTP outpatient prescription for methadone OUD maintenance.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Methadone is available for severe persistent pain by otherwise qualified DEA-registered prescribers under 21 CFR 1306.04(a). Under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) and the DEA's Aug. 2026 methadone guidance, ongoing methadone OUD maintenance is provided through a certified opioid treatment program; §1306.07(b)'s limited emergency dispensing exception does not convert Y into a routine prescription.

options.option_text: Y is valid as a refillable Schedule II prescription if the patient has previously received methadone at a hospital, but X must be rejected.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Previous inpatient administration does not authorize outpatient methadone maintenance by a non-OTP prescriber, and Schedule II prescriptions generally cannot be refilled. Legitimate pain treatment is not automatically prohibited.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives several prescriptions for SIMPLE or MODERATE nonsterile compounded preparations customary to community needs. The pharmacists have appropriate training and facilities. Management does not want to compound because a nearby chain offers cheaper commercially manufactured products. There is no extenuating circumstance or Board waiver. Which interpretations of 247 CMR 9.01(15) are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(4),(15) (professional practice standard, effective Dec. 6, 2024); USP <795> current compendial nonsterile standards

options.option_text: The pharmacy may decline any simple or moderate customary nonsterile compounded prescription solely to improve its margin, without documenting an exception.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.01(15) prohibits refusing simple or moderate customary nonsterile preparations except for extenuating circumstances or a waiver of Board regulation. A routine business preference alone is not the stated legal exception.

options.option_text: The professional-practice rule generally forbids refusing those customary simple or moderate nonsterile preparations when neither an extenuating circumstance nor Board waiver exists.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.01(15) creates a specific duty for licensees, in contrast to a general assumption that compounding is always discretionary. Staff should assess patient safety and comply with the applicable USP <795> standards.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must accept any hazardous sterile Category 3 compound under the same provision even when personnel and facilities are not competent to prepare it.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.01(15) is specifically about SIMPLE or MODERATE NONSTERILE compounded preparations customary to the community; it does not mandate complex sterile or hazardous compounding without competent facilities and current USP compliance.

options.option_text: A genuine extenuating circumstance or Board regulatory waiver can provide an exception to that particular nonsterile compounding non-refusal rule.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.01(15) expressly permits refusal under extenuating circumstances or Board waiver. The licensee should document the applicable basis and still protect patient continuity and safety.

questions.question_stem: Three otherwise valid outpatient prescriptions reach a Massachusetts pharmacy: Soma (carisoprodol), Flexeril (cyclobenzaprine), and Lioresal (baclofen). All are conventional prescription products. Which federal and corresponding Massachusetts schedule classification is correct?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(7) (carisoprodol); DEA final rule 76 FR 77330, effective Jan. 11, 2012; 105 CMR 700.002(D),(F); FDA prescription-only status for cyclobenzaprine and baclofen

options.option_text: Soma is Schedule II, Flexeril Schedule IV, and Lioresal Schedule VI because a muscle relaxant's abuse potential tracks its sedative strength.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Carisoprodol was placed in Schedule IV effective Jan. 11, 2012, not Schedule II. Cyclobenzaprine is not federally scheduled and is not Schedule IV. Clinical sedation is not the controlling schedule list.

options.option_text: Soma is federally and Massachusetts Schedule IV; Flexeril and Lioresal are federally unscheduled but Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drugs.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(7) expressly controls carisoprodol in Schedule IV; FDA-approved prescription cyclobenzaprine and baclofen are not in federal Schedules I–V and are treated as Massachusetts Schedule VI under 105 CMR 700.002(F). Specific ingredient status controls, not drug-class labels.

options.option_text: Soma and Flexeril are Schedule IV, while Lioresal is Schedule III because it can be used for neurologic disease.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Cyclobenzaprine is not a federal controlled substance and baclofen is not Schedule III; the indications do not set a drug schedule.

options.option_text: All three are Schedule VI because none is a DEA-controlled opioid, stimulant, or benzodiazepine.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Schedule IV includes non-benzodiazepine depressants such as carisoprodol. A muscle relaxant can be controlled despite not belonging to the named example classes.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy offers multi-drug-single-dose solid oral compliance packaging for patients receiving stable daily medicines. It has appropriate staff training, compatible medication packaging, labeling and controlled-substance accounting policies. Which actions comply with 247 CMR 9.08? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.08(1), (3)(a)–(c), (4)(a)–(c), (5)(d) (Compliance Packaging, effective Dec. 6, 2024)

options.option_text: Package a 30-day supply of daily Schedule IV and Schedule VI tablets together in compliant multi-drug-single-dose cells when the medications are compatible and all other rules are met.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.08(3) prohibits Schedule II and III medicines and PRN orders in multi-drug-single-dose packs, but does not categorically bar appropriate Schedule IV and VI daily medication together; the pharmacy must meet all packaging, compatibility and labeling requirements.

options.option_text: Include a Schedule II stimulant in the same multi-drug-single-dose cells if the patient has authorized monthly refills and the packet is tamper-evident.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.08(3)(b) categorically prohibits Schedule II and III drugs in multi-drug-single-dose packs; Schedule II also is generally not refillable. Tamper-evidence does not create an exception.

options.option_text: Supply a 90-day supply in multi-drug-single-dose packages if the medicines' commercial expiration dates are at least one year away.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.08(3)(a) caps these packages at 60 days, and the packaging BUD is independently limited by §9.08(5)(d) to the earliest manufacturer's expiration or 60 days. A manufacturer's long expiry does not remove these caps.

options.option_text: When a pharmacy previously dispensed a multi-drug pack to a patient and one drug is discontinued, it may accept that pack, remove the discontinued medicine and relabel/re-dispense the remaining medicines to that SAME patient while recording the pharmacist's changes.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.08(4)(a) permits limited return and repackaging for the original patient after a therapy change, with updated labeling and documented pharmacy accountability. Removed medicines must not return to stock or be dispensed to a different patient.

questions.question_stem: During a Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy investigation, a pharmacist is lawfully requested to produce specified pharmacy records and appear in response to a valid Board subpoena. The pharmacist refuses without cause because no final disciplinary order has yet been entered. Which assessment is correct?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) (grounds for discipline, effective Jan. 9, 2025); 247 CMR 9.24(1)–(3) (Board pharmacy inspections and records)

options.option_text: The pharmacist need cooperate only if the Board has first imposed formal discipline after a full merits hearing.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) expressly addresses failure without cause to cooperate with the Board's request or subpoena; the duty can arise DURING investigation and is not conditional on a prior final sanction.

options.option_text: No disciplinary exposure exists if the pharmacy owner, rather than the pharmacist, controls the physical record storage.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The legal duty attaches to a licensee's cooperation and legally available records/information. Employment ownership alone is not a categorical basis to refuse lawful Board investigatory requests without cause.

options.option_text: Refusing to appear or furnish legally entitled records is permissible until the pharmacist has received a criminal court subpoena.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The pharmacy Board has its own regulatory investigation and subpoena authority. Section 10.03(1)(q) does not require a separate criminal case or court-issued criminal subpoena.

options.option_text: Without cause, failure to cooperate with Board requests or a valid subpoena may itself support discipline, even before the Board adjudicates the underlying allegation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 10.03(1)(q) identifies failure to cooperate, appear, respond to subpoena, or furnish information to which the Board is legally entitled as independent grounds for action. The pharmacist should arrange lawful and confidential production rather than ignore the investigative demand.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital uses a medication whose FDA-approved labeling requires a Medication Guide. One adult patient receives doses administered by nurses during inpatient admission; a different patient is discharged home with a prescription that the patient will self-administer. No special Medication Guide REMS/ETASU term applies, neither patient has requested a guide during inpatient care, and no practitioner withholding instruction exists. Which is the best description of FDA's CURRENT guidance?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 208.24(e), 208.26(b); FDA Guidance 'Medication Guides—Distribution Requirements and Inclusion in REMS' (nonbinding enforcement discretion), and FDA Medication Guides Distribution for Health Care Professionals (Mar. 2020)

options.option_text: Every nurse-administered inpatient dose must legally be accompanied by a new physical Medication Guide, without exception or FDA enforcement discretion.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA's published Medication Guide distribution guidance provides enforcement discretion for medication dispensed to a healthcare professional for inpatient administration absent a more specific requirement; automatic guide distribution at every such dose is not the agency's stated policy.

options.option_text: FDA generally exercises enforcement discretion for routine healthcare-professional administration in an inpatient setting, but a Medication Guide is ordinarily provided when dispensed directly for outpatient self-administration at home.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FDA Medication Guides distribution guidance and 21 CFR 208.24(e) distinguish inpatient professional administration from direct patient/agent outpatient dispensing. The inpatient practice reflects a nonbinding FDA enforcement-discretion policy, not an amendment of all Part 208 legal language. REMS-specific distribution terms and patient requests must still be honored.

options.option_text: Once the patient has been hospitalized, no Medication Guide is required for any subsequently dispensed take-home supply because the first dose occurred in a hospital.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The status of the particular dispensing matters. A take-home outpatient prescription intended for self-administration generally requires a Medication Guide even if earlier doses were administered by hospital staff.

options.option_text: Hospital inpatient distribution discretion automatically eliminates all drug-specific REMS requirements to review or provide Medication Guides.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA's guidance expressly preserves Medication Guide distribution required by a product-specific REMS with elements to assure safe use. A general enforcement-discretion policy does not void those conditions.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist is negotiating with a nursing-home admissions coordinator who offers to steer residents' prescriptions to the pharmacy for a monthly referral payment. The pharmacist also considers supplying medical offices with blank prescription forms printed with the pharmacy's contact details. Under 247 CMR 9.01, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(11),(14) (referral remuneration and blank pharmacy-identified prescription forms; effective Dec. 6, 2024)
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.01(11),(14): referral remuneration and blank pharmacy-named forms

options.option_text: The pharmacist may not pay the facility employee for referral or generation of pharmacy business, even if residents retain freedom to choose another pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.01(11) forbids remuneration or things of value to or from specified healthcare facility owners or employees IN RETURN FOR referral or pharmacy-related business. A theoretical choice to opt out does not legalize the referral payment.
options.independent_option_analysis: Referral payment to nursing-home employee is specifically prohibited even if patients retain choice.

options.option_text: The payment is permitted if it is described in the contract as a consulting fee for generating new prescriptions, regardless of the actual referral purpose.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The regulation covers direct or indirect payment in exchange for referral/business; relabeling the same quid pro quo as a consulting fee does not change its purpose. Legitimate independent services would require their own analysis rather than this stated referral bargain.
options.independent_option_analysis: Calling a referral payment a consulting fee does not change its quid pro quo character.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may freely distribute blank prescription forms bearing that pharmacy's name because the forms are not signed prescriptions yet.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.01(14) expressly forbids a pharmacy licensee from giving practitioners blank prescription forms that refer to a pharmacist or pharmacy. Unsigned status is not an exception.
options.independent_option_analysis: Supplying practitioner blank forms referring to a pharmacy violates 9.01(14).

options.option_text: The pharmacist should not give practitioners blank prescription forms that refer to the pharmacy, regardless of whether a particular patient has yet been selected.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The independent prohibition in §9.01(14) applies to the act of supplying such preprinted blank forms; it is separate from the ban on referral remuneration.
options.independent_option_analysis: Independent prohibition applies to blank pharmacy-identified prescription forms.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives otherwise valid prescriptions for Sunosi (solriamfetol), Provigil (modafinil) and Wakix (pitolisant). Which description correctly matches federal DEA and corresponding Massachusetts schedules in November 2026?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.14(f)(7),(14) (modafinil, solriamfetol; renumbered Nov. 12, 2026); 105 CMR 700.002(D),(F); FDA Wakix/pitolisant labeling updated Feb. 2026 (DEA Schedule: None)

options.option_text: All three drugs are Schedule IV because all treat excessive daytime sleepiness associated with narcolepsy.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Solriamfetol and modafinil are Schedule IV, but pitolisant is not a federally controlled substance and is a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drug. Indication does not make scheduling uniform.

options.option_text: Sunosi Schedule II, Provigil Schedule IV and Wakix Schedule VI.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Solriamfetol is federally Schedule IV under 21 CFR 1308.14(f), not Schedule II. The other two classifications do not salvage this option.

options.option_text: Sunosi and Provigil are Schedule IV federally and in Massachusetts; Wakix is federally unscheduled and Massachusetts Schedule VI.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.14(f)(13) controls solriamfetol and §1308.14(f)(7) modafinil in Schedule IV. FDA's 2026 Wakix labeling lists pitolisant as an unscheduled prescription product; Massachusetts Schedule VI covers prescription drugs outside federal/MA Schedules I–V.

options.option_text: Wakix is Schedule III and both Sunosi and Provigil are federal Schedule V because treatment of narcolepsy is less restrictive than treating ADHD.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The applicable federal Schedule IV listings expressly include solriamfetol and modafinil, and pitolisant is unscheduled. Comparing indications cannot override the DEA list.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy has an appropriately designed negative-pressure containment segregated compounding area (C-SCA) with a suitable ISO Class 5 containment primary engineering control and qualified personnel. It plans to compound non-antineoplastic and antineoplastic hazardous sterile preparations under the current USP <797> Category system. Which statements are supported by USP <800> and its January 2026 technical FAQ? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Current USP <797> Category 1–3 framework (official Nov. 1, 2023); USP <800> §5 and Jan. 21, 2026 FAQs Q5 (compendial applicability and Category 1 HD CSPs in C-SCA, informational technical support); 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Any Category 2 or 3 hazardous CSP may be compounded routinely in the C-SCA whenever the ISO 5 containment hood is certified.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <800> FAQ #5 explains that the earlier low/medium risk wording now maps to Category 1 only in a C-SCA; ISO 5 performance alone does not make the segregated area eligible for Categories 2 or 3.

options.option_text: Category 1 hazardous CSPs, including sterile-to-sterile and nonsterile-to-sterile preparations, may be compounded in a compliant C-SCA when all applicable containment and USP <797> requirements are met.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <800> FAQ #5 explicitly recognizes Category 1 HD CSPs of both described component types in a C-SCA. The pharmacy must satisfy the negative-pressure containment, ISO 5 C-PEC and applicable Category 1 BUD/quality limits.

options.option_text: For Category 2 hazardous CSPs, the pharmacy must use an appropriately classified compliant cleanroom suite rather than treating the C-SCA as universally sufficient.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under the current USP <797> Category classification and USP <800> FAQ #5, Category 2 HD CSPs do not qualify for the C-SCA-only pathway. A compliant sterile hazardous cleanroom suite is necessary for those Category 2 operations.

options.option_text: The old 'low-risk/medium-risk' terminology remains the current USP <797> primary classification, so the Category 1/2/3 distinction must be ignored.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <797> replaced older risk-level labels with Categories 1, 2 and 3. USP's 2026 FAQ #5 explicitly explains how to apply the current categories to the legacy wording in <800>.

questions.question_stem: At a Massachusetts community pharmacy, a prescriber's authorized agent calls in a NEW, otherwise valid Schedule VI amlodipine prescription. A certified pharmacy technician with a current Massachusetts technician license, a noncertified licensed technician and a licensed trainee are present. The on-duty pharmacist approves appropriate delegation and will personally perform DUR and final dispensing validation. Who MAY receive and record this new oral information as described?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.02(6), 8.03(4)(c), 8.04(4)(c),(e); 247 CMR 9.04(1); 105 CMR 721.030 (Massachusetts oral prescription format)

options.option_text: The certified technician may receive the new or omitted prescription information with the on-duty pharmacist's approval, but may not independently resolve therapy changes or validate final dispensing.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) authorizes a licensed certified technician, identifying themself as such and with pharmacist approval, to receive NEW or omitted prescription information unless other law prohibits it. The delegated intake does not permit therapy clarification, counseling, DUR or final validation under §8.04(4)(e) and 247 CMR 9.04(1).

options.option_text: The trainee may take the new prescription by telephone if the supervising pharmacist signs it after the call.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.03(4)(c) expressly prohibits a technician trainee from taking prescriptions over the telephone. Later pharmacist validation does not transform prohibited telephone reception into a lawful trainee task.

options.option_text: The noncertified licensed technician may independently accept any NEW oral Schedule VI order because ordinary refill-authorizations and new-prescription intake have identical scope.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.02 allows ordinary licensed technicians to request and receive refill authorization for an unchanged Schedule VI prescription subject to restrictions; §8.04(4)(c) grants the additional specified NEW-information reception to certified technicians. New orders and unchanged refills are not the same activity.

options.option_text: No technician may record new Schedule VI oral information, because federal DEA Schedule II oral-emergency restrictions apply to every Massachusetts Schedule VI medicine.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Conventional amlodipine is Massachusetts Schedule VI and is not federal Schedule II. The certified-technician delegation provision applies to new information for otherwise lawful orders; federal emergency Schedule II prescription limitations are not a universal ban on Schedule VI technician intake.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts-licensed certified nurse practitioner has only nine months of qualifying prescriptive-practice experience. The NP has an active individual Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and DEA registration for Schedule III. An otherwise authentic Schedule III prescription is sent for a patient within the NP's usual specialty. When the pharmacist calls about an unrelated discrepancy, the NP volunteers that no mutually agreed written prescriptive-practice guidelines or qualified healthcare professional supervision have ever been established. No special exception applies. What is the best dispensing decision?
questions.author_citation: 244 CMR 4.07(2)(c) (NP supervised prescriptive-practice guidelines/transition); M.G.L. c.112 §80E; 105 CMR 700.004; 21 CFR 1306.04(a); MA DPH Circular DCP 21-10-111

options.option_text: Dispense because possession of both individual registration numbers automatically establishes independent prescriptive practice.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. MCSR and DEA registrations are necessary for the applicable controlled schedules, but 244 CMR 4.06 also requires supervised prescriptive practice with mutually agreed guidelines during the initial qualifying period for a CNP. The prescriber has explicitly disclosed the missing legal practice condition.

options.option_text: Treat the supervising physician's DEA number as a substitute for the NP's registered prescriber identity, without resolving the missing guidelines.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Borrowing another practitioner's DEA identifier is not a remedy for a missing required supervised-prescribing arrangement. The pharmacist should not alter the prescriber identity or overlook a known scope deficiency.

options.option_text: Dispense because a pharmacist is never required to inquire about NP supervision, even after receiving an explicit statement that required prescribing guidelines do not exist.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Pharmacists generally are not required to independently investigate a qualifying NP's independent-practice status merely because a supervisor name is absent, but this pharmacist has affirmative information that the still-supervised NP lacks the required practice arrangement. Ordinary lawful-authority and corresponding-responsibility checks still apply.

options.option_text: Do not dispense under the disclosed circumstances until authorized prescriptive practice is established or an appropriately authorized practitioner issues a valid prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 244 CMR 4.06, a CNP below the supervised experience threshold must practice with the required mutually agreed prescriptive guidelines and qualified healthcare professional supervision. Knowing those conditions are absent is materially different from merely not seeing a supervisor's name on a valid independent NP prescription; valid DEA/MCSR numbers alone cannot supply professional scope.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist reviews four separate Schedule II–IV controlled prescriptions issued by credentialed prescribers for existing patients. Each signature and DEA number is authentic. The pharmacist has information about whether the order is clinically and legally legitimate, and will document relevant investigation. Under 247 CMR 9.15 and DEA's corresponding responsibility, which actions or conclusions are defensible? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.15(2)(a)–(d), 9.17 (prospective DUR); 21 CFR 1306.04(a); Massachusetts Board advisory 'Controlled Substance Prescriptions' (revised 2025), discussion of red flags and independent pharmacy judgment

options.option_text: Fill a Schedule II prescription without further review whenever its DEA number is active, because registration conclusively proves legitimate medical purpose.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.15(2) and 21 CFR 1306.04(a) impose the pharmacist's own corresponding responsibility. Registration and signature authenticity do not automatically establish legitimate purpose or safe dispensing when clinical red flags exist.

options.option_text: Investigate an unexpectedly early opioid refill with conflicting medical history, consult the prescriber as needed and withhold dispensing if the legitimate purpose cannot be established.
options.original_rationale: Correct. A genuine early refill plus inconsistent history warrants professional judgment, clarification and documentation. The pharmacist must determine legitimacy and lawfulness before filling, but no automatic refusal rule is inferred solely from the early timing.

options.option_text: Automatically reject every cash-paid opioid prescription, even when the prescriber verifies the legitimate purpose, the patient relationship is established and no unresolved concern remains.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Cash payment may be a red flag when viewed in context but neither 247 CMR 9.15 nor DEA corresponding-responsibility rules make all cash purchases unlawful. Assess actual concerns rather than impose an invented categorical ban.

options.option_text: After resolving a plausible red flag with credible clinical documentation and appropriate verification, dispense an otherwise lawful prescription if professional judgment supports legitimate purpose and safety.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The law requires a genuine decision based on legitimate purpose, valid relationship, authenticity and legal compliance; it does not require permanent denial of a resolved red flag. The pharmacist should document the reasoning and perform clinical DUR.

questions.question_stem: On November 3, 2026, an authorized in-state prescriber issues a valid electronic Schedule II prescription for 60 tablets. On November 4, the patient asks the pharmacy to dispense only 20 tablets even though all 60 are in stock; the pharmacist properly documents the patient-requested partial fill. On November 22, the patient asks for the remaining 40 tablets at the SAME pharmacy, and the prescription remains otherwise valid. No stock shortage, LTCF status or hospice exception applies. What may the pharmacist do under current Massachusetts law?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §18(d¾) (amended by Acts 2018 c.208); 105 CMR 721.055(A)–(C) (effective Sept. 27, 2024); 21 CFR 1306.13; DPH Circular DCP 18-10-104 superseding 2016 Circular DCP 16-12-665

options.option_text: Dispense the remaining 40 tablets if federal conditions and documentation are satisfied, because a patient-requested partial fill may be completed by the original pharmacy within 30 days of the prescription issue date.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §18(d¾) and 105 CMR 721.055(B) permit patient-requested remainders only at the original pharmacy and no later than 30 days from issue, with documentation under subsection (C). November 22 is inside 30 days of November 3. This is NOT a partial fill caused by insufficient stock.

options.option_text: Treat the balance as void immediately after the first smaller dispense because the 2016 DPH circular still controls despite the later amendment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The older 2016 DPH circular's remainder-void wording was superseded; 2018 statutory amendments and current 105 CMR 721.055(B) expressly permit the remaining balance to be dispensed upon patient request at the original pharmacy within the issue-date limit.

options.option_text: Refuse the balance because the 72-hour completion limit for a Schedule II stock shortage governs every type of partial fill.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The 72-hour federal shortage pathway addresses dispensing LESS than the full quantity because the pharmacy cannot supply it. Here full stock was available and the patient affirmatively requested less; 105 CMR 721.055's separate remainder rule governs.

options.option_text: Direct the patient to any other licensed pharmacy to obtain the remaining 40 tablets under the first pharmacy's partial-fill record.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 721.055(B)(1) and c.94C §18(d¾) specify that ONLY the pharmacy which originally dispensed the smaller quantity may dispense the remaining portion under this patient-requested pathway.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts DEA-registered retail pharmacy identifies expired Schedule II and Schedule III stock that remains in its own inventory; there is NO theft, loss or damage. It plans to transfer the expired stock to an appropriately registered reverse distributor for lawful destruction and to replenish usable Schedule II stock from a wholesaler. Which federal controlled-substance procedures are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(2), 1317.10, 1304.21(d)–(e), 1305.03–1305.13, 1301.76(b); DEA Disposal Q&A (Forms 41/106/222 and reverse distributor responsibilities)

options.option_text: Document the lawful transfer of expired controlled stock to the registered reverse distributor; the reverse distributor performing destruction completes its required DEA Form 41 record.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 21 CFR 1317.05 and 1304.21, a practitioner registrant may transfer lawfully held expired controlled inventory to a reverse distributor at its registered location, with shipment and transfer records. The reverse distributor documents destruction on DEA Form 41, rather than treating a pharmacy's transfer invoice as the reverse distributor's destruction record.

options.option_text: The retail pharmacy must report the ordinary expired stock on DEA Form 106 within one business day, even though no theft or significant loss occurred.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DEA Form 106 is for theft or significant loss under 21 CFR 1301.76(b), not an ordinary accountable inventory of expired medication awaiting lawful reverse distribution. The pharmacy still keeps complete inventory/transfer records.

options.option_text: Use a compliant paper DEA Form 222 or an authorized electronic CSOS order to acquire replacement Schedule II stock, independently of any destruction documentation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. DEA Form 222 or the corresponding CSOS process is an ordering/transfer authorization for Schedule I or II acquisitions under 21 CFR Part 1305; it is separate from records for sending expired stock to a reverse distributor.

options.option_text: DEA Form 41 replaces all Schedule II ordering forms and automatically authorizes the pharmacy to acquire the exact quantity it discarded.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Form 41 documents destruction, not permission to order new Schedule II products. Schedule II ordering still uses the authorized Part 1305 mechanism, and inventory disposal does not generate an automatic replacement allotment.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist-licensure candidate earned 600 supervised intern hours at a licensed pharmacy in another state, before moving to Massachusetts. The candidate presents a signed employer time sheet, but NO affidavit or certificate from the state where the experience was acquired confirming that those hours were approved in that jurisdiction. All other intern-licensure and school requirements are satisfied. What does 247 CMR 8.01(11) allow the Massachusetts Board to do?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.01(1),(9),(11), corrected Apr. 25, 2025 (out-of-state internship credit and jurisdiction-issued approval proof)

options.option_text: Automatically accept the 600 hours because a signed time sheet is the exact proof required for all out-of-state internship credit.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 8.01(11) expressly contemplates an AFFIDAVIT or certificate of approval from the JURISDICTION where the experience was acquired, indicating that the experience was duly approved there. A supervisor's time sheet alone is not the specified jurisdictional approval.

options.option_text: Reject the hours permanently because Massachusetts can never approve internship experience acquired outside the Commonwealth.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 8.01(11) expressly provides a route for the Board to GRANT credit for otherwise qualified out-of-state experience when appropriate approval proof from the jurisdiction is supplied. It is not categorically disallowed.

options.option_text: Consider granting credit once the candidate produces an affidavit or certificate of approval issued by the jurisdiction where the hours were earned; credit is not automatic on an employer log alone.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 8.01(11), the Board MAY grant credit for out-of-state pharmacy internship experience when documentation issued by the other jurisdiction indicates those hours were duly approved there. The intern should obtain that official proof and request Board acceptance.

options.option_text: Accept the hours only if the candidate first completes another 600 hours in Massachusetts, because the Board must match each out-of-state hour one-to-one.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 8.01(11) imposes no universal 1:1 Massachusetts match. The issue is the Board's discretionary credit and the other state's official internship approval; overall licensure hour requirements are evaluated separately.

questions.question_stem: An adult in Massachusetts wants naloxone to help a neighbor at risk of opioid overdose. A grocery store has FDA-labeled OTC naloxone nasal spray on its shelf. A nearby pharmacy has both the same OTC-labeled product and a DIFFERENT naloxone presentation labeled 'Rx only.' The pharmacy participates in the current Massachusetts statewide naloxone standing order. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §§19B–19C; MA DPH Advisory 'DCP Regulations and Over-The-Counter Naloxone' (Oct. 10, 2024); Board Policy 2024-01 revised Feb. 6, 2025; 2026 statewide naloxone standing order

options.option_text: The adult may purchase the OTC-labeled naloxone directly without an individual prescription; Massachusetts Drug Control Program prescribing/controlled-substance rules do not apply to activities involving that OTC product.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The Massachusetts DPH Drug Control Program's October 10, 2024 advisory distinguishes OTC naloxone products from prescription naloxone. An FDA-approved OTC-labeled product may be bought at ordinary retail without an individual or standing-order prescription; no MCSR is required for OTC-product activities.

options.option_text: Because naloxone is a single active ingredient, all its formulations require identical pharmacy-only controlled-prescription processing even when FDA approves one presentation for OTC sale.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA labeling makes OTC and Rx-only products legally distinct under Massachusetts' 2024 DPH advisory. A product labeled OTC does not automatically inherit prescription-only obligations of a separate Rx-labeled presentation.

options.option_text: A Massachusetts pharmacy may dispense Rx-labeled naloxone for use by another person under the statewide standing order, without a separate patient-specific prescription for the neighbor, while applying the prescription-pathway rules.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §19B and Board Policy 2024-01 allow an individual to obtain prescription naloxone for a person at risk, and the statewide standing order serves as the required authorizing prescription. Product-specific counseling, labeling and related prescription reporting rules still apply.

options.option_text: The existence of a retail OTC naloxone alternative automatically cancels Massachusetts' statewide standing order for Rx-labeled naloxone and makes prescription insurance billing unlawful.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The DPH and Board expressly maintain the standing-order pathway for Rx-labeled naloxone despite some OTC products. Eligible pharmacy prescriptions under the standing order can be processed through insurance subject to plan terms.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy is certified under the current SPRAVATO REMS. It receives an otherwise legitimate esketamine (SPRAVATO) prescription for an adult patient whose outpatient psychiatric clinic is ALSO REMS-certified. The patient requests that the pharmacy mail the sealed product to the patient's home for unsupervised self-administration, avoiding travel. The prescribing clinic instead offers to supervise administration on site. What is the legally appropriate REMS decision?
questions.author_citation: FDA SPRAVATO (esketamine) current prescribing information §5.5 (REMS), certified pharmacy/healthcare setting and two-hour monitoring; 21 CFR 208 and current FDA REMS database

options.option_text: Mail the product directly to the patient's home if the pharmacist provides a Medication Guide and a telephone number for questions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The current SPRAVATO REMS requires certified pharmacies to dispense it ONLY to certified healthcare settings. Direct patient home dispensing cannot be substituted by counseling or an enclosed Medication Guide.

options.option_text: Dispense or ship to the REMS-certified healthcare setting for observed self-administration and required professional monitoring; do not dispense for unsupervised home use.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Current SPRAVATO labeling and REMS require the product to be dispensed and administered only in certified healthcare settings, with patients self-administering under direct observation and monitoring by providers for at least two hours. The pharmacy must verify the destination's certification.

options.option_text: Dispense to any licensed clinic, even if it is not REMS-certified, because the prescriber's own DEA registration satisfies the REMS certification.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DEA registration for Schedule III esketamine and healthcare-setting SPRAVATO REMS certification are separate conditions. A pharmacy participating in the REMS may dispense only to a certified healthcare setting.

options.option_text: Give the patient one nasal device for unsupervised use and reserve two devices for the clinic because only the first dose needs onsite observation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The REMS does not create a routine first-dose-only supervised requirement. Treatment sessions must occur in certified settings with observation/monitoring, so distributing a patient take-home device violates the stated program safeguards.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital prescriber orders lorazepam (a Schedule IV benzodiazepine) to be administered by nurses to an admitted inpatient during hospitalization. On discharge, the prescriber issues a separate outpatient lorazepam prescription that may be filled at a community pharmacy. The hospital's pharmacy later dispenses the outpatient prescription to the departing patient. Assume no special emergency exception and all other requirements are met. Which interpretation of MassPAT obligations is correct?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §24A (prescriber query of PMP for benzodiazepines/narcotics); 105 CMR 700.012(A),(G) (dispenser reporting); MA DPH 'Prescription Monitoring Program frequently asked questions' question 'Opioid Rx’s to an inpatient at discharge'

options.option_text: MassPAT lookup is exempt for BOTH orders because the patient was admitted when the drug was first considered, and hospital outpatient prescriptions are not reportable.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts DPH PMP FAQ expressly states the inpatient-medication-order exception applies only to doses administered in the healthcare setting, NOT discharge outpatient prescriptions. A covered outpatient pharmacy dispensing can also trigger dispensing-report requirements.

options.option_text: The physician must query MassPAT before every inpatient-administered lorazepam dose, but no query is needed before writing the outpatient discharge prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. This reverses the relevant distinction in the DPH FAQ: inpatient medication orders administered in the facility qualify for the exemption, whereas an outpatient prescription at discharge requires query before issuance.

options.option_text: The pharmacist alone must query MassPAT before issuing the physician's discharge prescription; the physician has no MassPAT query duty when ordering benzodiazepines.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §24A imposes the specified QUERY responsibility on the PRESCRIBER before writing certain controlled prescriptions, including benzodiazepines, subject to exceptions. Separately, the dispensing pharmacy has its OWN reporting duties under 105 CMR 700.012.

options.option_text: The inpatient-administered medication order qualifies for the inpatient MassPAT query exception; the discharge outpatient benzodiazepine prescription requires the prescriber to query MassPAT, and the pharmacy reports the covered outpatient dispensing.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The DPH MassPAT FAQ states discharge prescriptions that may be filled by a retail or hospital outpatient pharmacy are NOT covered by the inpatient administration exemption. Under c.94C §24A and 105 CMR 700.012, prescriber query and pharmacy submission are separate obligations.

questions.question_stem: During transport in a Massachusetts hospital oncology unit, a small container of a hazardous antineoplastic drug breaks, causing a visible spill. No one is injured yet, but trained hazardous-drug spill responders and an appropriately supplied spill kit are available. The hospital follows applicable USP <800> and hazardous-waste rules. Which steps are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Current USP <800> §16 (Spill Control) and §15 (Deactivating, Decontaminating, Cleaning and Disinfecting); USP <800> FAQs Jan. 21, 2026; 247 CMR 9.01(3), applicable federal/state hazardous waste requirements

options.option_text: Keep visitors and unprotected personnel away while trained designated workers promptly contain and clean the spill with appropriate hazardous-drug protective equipment and supplies.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <800> §16 requires hazardous drug spills to be contained and cleaned immediately by trained personnel using suitable protective equipment and spill-management supplies. An unprotected bystander should not be assigned the exposure.

options.option_text: Allow nearby nurses to continue preparing and administering drugs directly through the contaminated area until routine housekeeping is available at the end of the shift.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <800> calls for prompt spill control; continuing routine work in the exposed area risks spreading contamination. Restrict traffic and initiate trained response rather than waiting until a normal end-of-shift cleaning cycle.

options.option_text: Place contaminated absorbents and protective equipment into the appropriate hazardous-drug waste stream, and document and evaluate any personnel exposure as required by facility procedures.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Spill cleanup is not ordinary trash disposal: contaminated materials must be disposed of in accordance with applicable hazardous-drug/waste policies. The pharmacy and facility must maintain spill documentation and evaluate possible employee exposure.

options.option_text: Flush contaminated materials into the nearest sink because a drug dissolved in water is no longer a hazardous substance and requires no spill records.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Dilution does not erase a drug's hazardous status. USP <800> and hazardous-waste requirements do not authorize routine sink disposal of hazardous-drug spill waste; the response and any exposure require appropriate procedures.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy qualified a licensed technician for Category 2 CSPs eight months ago. The technician initially passed the required garbing and aseptic manipulation assessments, but has completed neither the scheduled repeat garbing nor media-fill-based aseptic manipulation competency during the intervening eight months. The technician wants to resume preparation tomorrow under a pharmacist's direct observation, and the pharmacist offers to perform final validation afterward. What should the designated supervisor require first?
questions.author_citation: Current USP <797> §§2.2–2.3/Table 1 and associated aseptic manipulation competency requirements (official Nov. 1, 2023); USP official FAQs updated Dec. 11, 2023; 247 CMR 9.01(3), 9.04(1)

options.option_text: Allow the technician to compound because initial media-fill qualification is permanent as long as a pharmacist signs every final CSP label.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Current USP <797> §§2.2–2.3 require ongoing garbing and aseptic-manipulation competency at least EVERY SIX MONTHS for Category 1 and 2 personnel who compound. Pharmacist final validation does not replace those personnel qualification prerequisites.

options.option_text: Require successful overdue ongoing garbing and aseptic-manipulation competency evaluations before returning the technician to Category 2 compounding; retain the pharmacist's independent final validation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The technician's last successful ongoing assessments were eight months ago, exceeding the Category 2 six-month interval. USP <797> requires those activities at the specified intervals, including media-fill assessment followed by glove sampling and associated testing. Massachusetts pharmacists remain responsible for final validation under 247 CMR 9.04(1).

options.option_text: Ask only for a renewed national technician certification because certification alone resets USP <797> competency intervals.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Professional certification is not the same as facility-specific cleanroom garbing and aseptic compounding qualification. USP <797> personnel competency recurs regardless of national technician certification status.

options.option_text: Permit Category 2 compounding under observation until one year has elapsed because Category 2 personnel follow the annual oversight-only competency interval.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The every-12-month interval applies to some personnel who have DIRECT OVERSIGHT but do not compound; Category 1/2 active compounding personnel must satisfy the SIX-month competency intervals. Being observed does not make the compounding technician an oversight-only person.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts state-licensed 503A compounding pharmacy has a patient-specific prescription requesting a nonsterile medicine compounded from bulk Substance X. FDA confirms that X has NO applicable USP/NF monograph, is NOT a component of an FDA-approved drug, and is NOT on FDA's established 503A bulks list. A supplier notes only that someone NOMINATED X for future FDA review; the supplier provides a valid certificate of analysis and is FDA-registered. Assume no temporary enforcement-discretion statement applicable to X is being invoked. Which conclusion is correct about qualifying for the FD&C Act §503A bulk-ingredient exemptions?
questions.author_citation: FD&C Act §503A(b)(1)(A) (21 U.S.C. §353a(b)(1)(A)); FDA 'Bulk Drug Substances Used in Compounding Under Section 503A' (updated 2026); FDA 503A bulks list regulations and category-status distinctions

options.option_text: A nomination automatically places X on the 503A bulks list until FDA expressly rejects the nomination.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA distinguishes substances nominated for evaluation from substances actually included on the established 503A bulks list. A nomination alone does not satisfy 21 U.S.C. §353a(b)(1)(A)'s statutory ingredient eligibility requirement.

options.option_text: The supplier's certificate of analysis and FDA establishment registration independently make X eligible even though none of the three listed substantive ingredient pathways applies.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Valid COA and supplier registration are additional necessary conditions for qualifying 503A bulk substances, not substitutes for an applicable USP/NF monograph, FDA-approved product component status, or inclusion on the established 503A list.

options.option_text: The individual patient prescription makes all bulk ingredients eligible, regardless of their legal monograph, FDA approval or bulks-list status.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A patient-specific prescription is a separate prerequisite for the 503A exemption pathway and does not override §503A's limits on which BULK DRUG SUBSTANCES may be used.

options.option_text: Do not treat the proposed compound as satisfying the statutory 503A bulk-substance exemption on the stated evidence; select a lawfully eligible ingredient or pursue another authorized route.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FDA's 503A bulks explanation and FD&C Act §503A(b)(1)(A) require one of three substantive eligibility bases: a compliant applicable compendial monograph, FDA-approved-drug component, or actual inclusion on the established 503A bulks list, with COA and manufacturer registration additionally required. No route is satisfied for X. A separate FDA enforcement-discretion policy, if any, requires its own current specific analysis.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives an otherwise valid prescription for a brand-name extended-release oral tablet (Drug A, 100 mg). The patient has not requested the brand, and the prescriber has not indicated 'no substitution.' Products available include (X) a cheaper FDA Orange Book A-rated generic extended-release TABLET 100 mg of Drug A, (Y) the same drug as an FDA-approved immediate-release tablet 100 mg, and (Z) the same extended-release drug as a 50-mg tablet. Assume all other prescription and safety requirements are satisfied. Under 105 CMR 720 and Massachusetts pharmacy interchange rules, which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 720.020 (pharmaceutical/interchangeable equivalence), 720.050 and 720.200 Appendix A (Massachusetts List and Orange Book A-rated equivalent comparison); M.G.L. c.112 §12D; 247 CMR 9.05

options.option_text: Product X can qualify for ordinary interchange because the same drug, strength and dosage form has a therapeutically equivalent A-rated generic and the prescriber did not prohibit substitution.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 105 CMR 720.050 and 720.200 base interchange on products therapeutically equivalent to the prescribed drug in the same active ingredient, dosage form and strength (or separately specifically listed). The stated Orange Book A rating supports the appropriate same-strength ER tablet substitution.

options.option_text: Product Y is automatically interchangeable because its milligram strength is the same, even though its release mechanism and dosage form differ.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Identical strength alone is insufficient: immediate-release and extended-release forms are not treated as automatically equivalent. Under 105 CMR 720.020, pharmaceutical equivalence includes dosage form/route and in practice an appropriate Orange Book equivalence designation; a prescriber-authorized change may be needed.

options.option_text: Product Z is automatically equivalent if the pharmacy gives two 50-mg tablets instead of one 100-mg tablet, because arithmetic equality replaces the legal same-strength requirement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Different tablet strength and tablet count are not the identical 100-mg dosage-unit product contemplated by an ordinary legally interchangeable equivalent. The pharmacist may clarify a distinct therapeutic substitution with the practitioner, but cannot infer automatic equivalence from arithmetic.

options.option_text: If the pharmacist needs a product with a different dosage form or strength, the pharmacist should obtain an appropriate lawful prescriber clarification or authorization rather than silently treat it as mandatory generic interchange.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drug Products operates on equivalent active ingredients, forms and strengths. A clinically plausible change in formulation or dosage may require prescriber consultation and documentation rather than substitution under the ordinary interchange mandate.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist checks two actual butalbital combination capsules in November 2026. Product A: Fioricet 50 mg butalbital/300 mg acetaminophen/40 mg caffeine, package NDC 52544-080-01 (product NDC 52544-080), appears on DEA's April 1, 2026 exempt prescription-product list; its FDA DailyMed label says DEA Schedule 'None'. Product B: butalbital/acetaminophen/caffeine 50/325/40 capsules, NDC 72162-2665-1, which FDA DailyMed labels DEA Schedule CIII. DEA's November 9, 2026 determination removed specified INACTIVE NDC exemptions, not active ones. Both require prescriptions. Which classification applies?
questions.author_citation: DEA Table of Exempted Prescription Products Apr. 1, 2026 (NDC 52544-080); 91 FR 64618 Oct. 9, 2026 effective Nov. 9; FDA DailyMed Fioricet NDC 52544-080-01 (DEA None) and butalbital/APAP/caffeine NDC 72162-2665-1 (CIII); 105 CMR 700.002(C),(F)

options.option_text: Both become federal CIII after November 9 because DEA revoked every butalbital-containing combination exemption.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The October 9 final DEA determination targeted specified inactive NDCs and expressly did not revoke active exemption listings, including Fioricet product 52544-080.

options.option_text: Both are federally exempt because acetaminophen and caffeine always cancel out butalbital control regardless of the actual marketed product and NDC.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Exemption under 21 CFR 1308.31–.32 is PRODUCT-specific, not an entire-ingredient-class exemption. Product B has its own FDA DailyMed federal CIII listing.

options.option_text: Product A remains federally exempt and Massachusetts Schedule VI as an otherwise noncontrolled prescription drug; Product B is federally and Massachusetts Schedule III.
options.original_rationale: Correct. DEA's April 2026 exempt table lists Fioricet 52544-080; FDA DailyMed labels its 52544-080-01 package 'DEA None'. FDA DailyMed July 2026 labels Product B NDC 72162-2665-1 CIII. MA 105 CMR 700.002(C),(F) applies the respective III and VI classifications.

options.option_text: The pharmacy can assign both products the exemption tied to NDC 52544-080 because their therapeutic purpose and butalbital amount are similar.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Each product's current DEA exemption and marketed NDC must be verified independently. Product B's different 50/325/40 preparation does not inherit exemption from Fioricet 50/300/40.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy aseptically compounds a NONHAZARDOUS Category 2 IV preparation from only sterile manufactured components. It has a qualified ISO Class 5 laminar airflow PEC in a properly maintained ISO Class 7 positive-pressure buffer room with an ISO Class 8 anteroom, and suitable personnel/monitoring. No sterility test is performed, stability data support at least 10 days under refrigeration, and no component imposes a shorter BUD. Under the currently official USP <797>, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Official USP <797> §§4.1 and 14.3/Table 13 (revision official Nov. 1, 2023); USP <797> official FAQs updated Dec. 11, 2023, Q181 and room-classification guidance; 247 CMR 9.01(3)
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: MA Board Sterile Compounding Inspection Tool item 73.4 lists Category 2 BUD under USP <797> Table 13, 4d room/10d fridge
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: 2026-11-22: Corrected prior explanation-only cross-reference from USP <797> Category 2 Table 12 to Table 13 in original bank. Answer keys, stem and choices unchanged. Massachusetts Board sterile inspection item 73.4 substantiates numeric BUD; full subscription USP normative chapter still unverified.

options.option_text: The stated ISO 5 PEC in an appropriate classified buffer/anteroom cleanroom suite can support Category 2 compounding when other <797> requirements are satisfied.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The normal Category 2 nonhazardous aseptic-compounding configuration is an ISO 5 PEC in a properly classified cleanroom suite (e.g., ISO 7 buffer and ISO 8 anteroom). Facility and personnel/EM requirements still apply.
options.independent_option_analysis: Classified suite can qualify for Category 2 subject to controls.

options.option_text: Moving the ISO 5 hood to a nonclassified segregated compounding area automatically retains all Category 2 BUDs because ISO 5 primary airflow alone determines category eligibility.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Category 2 preparation requires the appropriate classified cleanroom environment; an unclassified SCA generally supports only Category 1 and its shorter BUD limits under USP <797>. ISO 5 primary control by itself does not make an SCA an ISO-classified Category 2 suite.
options.independent_option_analysis: Moving PEC to unclassified SCA does not preserve Category 2 BUD.

options.option_text: For an aseptically prepared Category 2 CSP containing only sterile starting components and no sterility test, a BUD of up to four days at controlled room temperature or ten days refrigerated may be assigned when supported by stability and all other conditions.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <797> §14.3/Table 13 gives these maximum BUDs for this particular sterile-starting-component, aseptic, untested Category 2 formulation. Shorter stability limits would supersede them; not all Category 2 formulations share these values.
options.independent_option_analysis: As-authored choice C numbers 4d/10d match inspection Table 13, but the WHY incorrectly calls it Table 12. Explanation-only Table 12 typo corrected to Table 13 in original question bank.

options.option_text: Because the product is Category 2, it always requires completed sterility testing before any BUD can be assigned, even for a short BUD.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP <797> includes explicit Category 2 maximum BUDs WITHOUT sterility testing for specified sterile-component cases. Longer assigned BUDs or other category formulations may have separate testing requirements, but sterility testing is not universally mandatory for every Category 2 CSP.
options.independent_option_analysis: Category 2 sterile-source CSP without sterility test has published BUD limits; testing not universally mandatory.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy offers routine influenza vaccine to an eligible FIVE-YEAR-OLD under a valid standing order. A qualified pharmacist selects the formulation, completes screening/counseling, consent, VIS, MIIS and emergency procedures, and supervises vaccinators. Each proposed worker has CPR; further credentials and vaccine training are specified below. Which workers can administer under Board Policy 2023-02 revised Sept. 4, 2025? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board Vaccine Administration Policy 2023-02, revised Sept. 4, 2025, §§II–IV; 247 CMR 8.00

options.option_text: A Massachusetts-registered pharmacy intern with all required intern vaccination training and direct pharmacist supervision.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Board Policy 2023-02 permits suitably trained registered pharmacy interns to administer designated vaccines to patients age five and older with required pharmacist supervision.

options.option_text: A licensed noncertified pharmacy technician who completed all vaccine training but has only 420 documented post-license hours, no accepted national certification, and pharmacist supervision.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The policy's technician pathway requires national certification OR at least 500 documented hours worked AFTER technician licensure in addition to vaccine training.

options.option_text: A licensed noncertified pharmacy technician with 520 documented post-license work hours, all required vaccine-specific training and the supervising pharmacist's approval.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2023-02 §III(D) permits a qualified licensed technician with 500+ post-license hours as an alternative to national certification, subject to the training and supervision described.

options.option_text: A nationally certified and vaccine-trained technician administering after the pharmacy's algorithm selected the vaccine, without the pharmacist completing the patient-specific clinical assessment and formulation selection.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The supervising pharmacist, not a technician or automated algorithm alone, remains responsible for patient assessment, vaccine selection and counseling under the policy.

questions.question_stem: A properly trained Massachusetts pharmacist independently supplied a guideline-concordant 28-day oral HIV postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen after a qualifying recent exposure. At follow-up, the patient reports finishing the course but continuing HIV exposure risk. The patient asks the pharmacist to provide another 28-day PEP course each month instead of discussing other prevention. The pharmacist's practice meets the applicable MCSR and prescribing requirements. What is the MOST appropriate next step under Massachusetts' 2026 HIV prevention prescribing framework?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19F; DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125, Pharmacist Prescribing of Certain Medications; Massachusetts Pharmacist Oral PrEP Guidelines 8-2026 and PEP Guidelines 9-2026

options.option_text: Automatically dispense monthly PEP courses without reassessment because an initial PEP prescription establishes permanent ongoing eligibility.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. PEP is a time-limited response to an exposure, not a standing indefinitely renewable substitute for ongoing prevention. Continuing risk calls for current clinical assessment.

options.option_text: Refuse to discuss oral PrEP because pharmacist prescribing authority applies only before any PEP exposure has occurred.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts authorizes appropriately trained pharmacists to prescribe oral PrEP under the separate statewide guidance when the patient meets its requirements. Prior PEP use does not, by itself, bar a PrEP assessment.

options.option_text: Evaluate the patient for an appropriate transition to oral PrEP using the current PrEP guidance, required HIV screening and clinical assessment, and arrange follow-up or referral as indicated; do not automatically renew PEP.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Massachusetts c.94C §19F and DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 authorize pharmacist prescribing for both HIV PEP and oral PrEP, each under its own statewide guideline. Ongoing exposure risk after completing a PEP course requires PrEP eligibility/testing and follow-up evaluation, not automatic repeated PEP.

options.option_text: Start oral PrEP without any HIV-status evaluation because a recent course of PEP is proof that the patient is HIV-negative.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Taking PEP does not substitute for the required HIV evaluation before PrEP initiation; potential acute HIV infection and the guideline's testing/follow-up remain important.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist has a valid license/MCSR, has completed accredited STI-TREATMENT prescribing training, and is prepared to apply the 2026 statewide STI treatment guideline. A 24-year-old patient has documentation of a positive gonorrhea test and asks for appropriate pharmacist-prescribed treatment. The patient ALSO asks for a separate prescription for an unexamined partner labeled only 'EPT' based on the Board's expedited partner therapy policy. Assume no other diagnosis, contraindication or independent prescriber order. Which is the BEST legal distinction?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19F; DPH Pharmacist Guidance for STI Treatment 8-2026, including gonorrhea; Massachusetts Board/DCP Policy 2020-08 Expedited Partner Therapy Prescriptions (May 25, 2023), chlamydia only

options.option_text: Neither request is within any pharmacist pathway because Massachusetts pharmacists may independently prescribe for chlamydia but never for gonorrhea.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The 2026 Massachusetts independent pharmacist STI-treatment guidance expressly includes gonorrhea as well as chlamydia; the existence of a condition-specific pathway does not mean the pharmacist must refuse all gonorrhea evaluation.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may evaluate and prescribe treatment for the diagnosed patient IF every requirement of the 2026 guideline is met, but cannot extend the CHLAMYDIA-only EPT prescription mechanism to an unexamined gonorrhea partner.
options.original_rationale: Correct. These are two different authorities: 2026 pharmacist independent STI-treatment guidelines cover eligible gonorrhea patients, whereas Board Policy 2020-08's special EPT protocol is limited to partners of people diagnosed with chlamydia. The partner requires an appropriate authorized clinical/prescribing route.

options.option_text: The 2026 pharmacist authority automatically amends all EPT policies to include gonorrhea, so both prescriptions may be issued without further partner assessment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A new authority to treat a patient does not expand the separate EPT policy. Massachusetts Policy 2020-08 explicitly states that its EPT procedure applies only to chlamydia.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may supply the partner's gonorrhea treatment as EPT only if the first patient promises to deliver it personally.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Promised delivery by the index patient does not change the disease-specific scope of the Board's EPT policy; gonorrhea is not covered by that chlamydia-only mechanism.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy fills a valid non-compounded Schedule VI tablet prescription in the correct child-resistant container. The computer-generated label shows the date filled, pharmacy name/address, prescription serial, patient's name, prescriber's name, medicine, directions, applicable cautions and tablet count. HOWEVER, it shows only the pharmacy's internal employee login number in a back-office record; the label itself omits the filling pharmacist's initials. The pharmacist has completed the final clinical/dispensing review. What must occur before lawful handoff?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §21 (current as amended effective January 1, 2026), first paragraph; 247 CMR 9.04 dispensing and labeling responsibility

options.option_text: Nothing further; the prescription serial number legally substitutes for the pharmacist's initials when records are computerized.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §21 specifies both the pharmacy's serial number and the filling pharmacist's initials as distinct label elements; an internal login does not erase the separate label obligation.

options.option_text: Dispense as labeled because Schedule VI drugs are outside the Massachusetts controlled-substance labeling law.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts Schedule VI is part of the state controlled-substance scheme, and §21 labeling applies. Federal noncontrol does not remove the state label elements.

options.option_text: Obtain a new prescription signed by the prescriber because any omission on a dispensing label invalidates the original order.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The stated prescription itself is valid; the defect is on the pharmacy-generated DISPENSING LABEL. It is corrected by the pharmacy, without obtaining a new prescriber order.

options.option_text: Correct the container label to include the filling pharmacist's initials, while retaining all other mandatory information, before dispensing.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §21 requires the filling pharmacist's initials on the affixed label in addition to date, pharmacy identifiers, Rx serial, patient/prescriber/drug, directions, cautions, and quantity for tablets or capsules. Final electronic validation alone does not replace the specified label.

questions.question_stem: Two Massachusetts-licensed retail pharmacies begin a central-fill/shared-processing arrangement in 2026. The originating pharmacy receives the prescription; its partner performs remote processing and physical filling. Both have authorized personnel, an appropriate written agreement and a secure common information system. The corporate compliance officer proposes the following operating procedures under revised Board Policy 2021-02. Which procedures are required or correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2021-02, Shared Pharmacy Service Models, revised February 6, 2025, §§III(h)–(p), IV

options.option_text: The retail pharmacy informs patients that another pharmacy may process or fill their prescriptions and provides a workable patient opt-out mechanism.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Massachusetts Board Policy 2021-02, General Requirements III(k)–(l), expressly requires retail patient notification and a mechanism to opt out of the shared-service model.

options.option_text: Only the originating pharmacy is responsible for errors, because the central pharmacy's professional responsibility ends when it ships the product.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section III(i) makes ALL participating pharmacies jointly responsible for properly processed and filled prescriptions; division of tasks does not erase either participant's accountability.

options.option_text: The pharmacies maintain a transaction audit trail that can identify the date/time and personnel involved at EACH step, and review documented joint procedures at least annually.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy III(h) mandates a traceable step-by-step date/time/personnel audit trail, while III(n)–(o) requires jointly maintained policies and documented review at least annually.
