options.option_text: After signing the original agreement, the two pharmacies may skip documented personnel training and a continuity plan because the central site has a pharmacist-in-charge.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Policy III(m) and III(p) require documented participant training and a continuity-of-care plan if a shared-services participant cannot operate; a PIC does not eliminate these requirements.

questions.question_stem: A 25-year-old applicant for an initial Massachusetts pharmacy technician license has completed a Board-approved training path, passed the applicable assessment and has no problem with age or education. The disclosed court record establishes that the applicant previously ADMITTED TO SUFFICIENT FACTS WARRANTING A FINDING OF GUILTY to a DRUG-RELATED FELONY; the criminal case was continued without a formal guilty verdict. The applicant argues that the absence of a conviction makes this record irrelevant. What is the MOST accurate assessment of the stated eligibility condition?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 8.02(3)(a)–(e), Pharmacy Technicians: application eligibility including drug-related felony conviction OR admission to sufficient facts; 247 CMR 10.03(1)(p) false information

options.option_text: The applicant satisfies 247 CMR 8.02(3)(d) because a drug-related offense matters only after a formally entered guilty verdict.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The text expressly covers both conviction of a drug-related felony AND an admission to sufficient facts warranting such a finding. Absence of a formal judgment does not automatically satisfy that condition.

options.option_text: The applicant is barred from every type of Massachusetts professional license forever, without any need to read the relevant profession's rule.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The question concerns the specific pharmacy technician eligibility condition in 247 CMR 8.02, not an automatic permanent prohibition from every health profession.

options.option_text: The applicant does not meet the express pharmacy technician application condition under 247 CMR 8.02(3)(d); the Board must evaluate the disclosed record under the applicable legal standards rather than treating it as irrelevant.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The technician application rule expressly requires that an applicant not have been convicted of a drug-related felony OR admitted to sufficient facts to warrant such findings. The problem asks about satisfying that stated condition, not about speculative later relief or a blanket rule for unrelated arrests.

options.option_text: The applicant may conceal the admission and file a clean application because Board suitability review covers only paid work history.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An applicant must not provide false information on licensure materials. Concealment does not cure an express eligibility issue and can introduce independent professional-conduct concerns.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital maintains a properly registered hospital pharmacy but no separately licensed open-to-public retail drug-store pharmacy. Its pharmacist receives four otherwise valid medication requests. Each is for a routine drug in a quantity allowed for the patient class; there is no emergency-department, discharge, sole-community-hospital nursing-facility or other special exception. Under 105 CMR 722.020 and 722.090(A), which requests fall within the ordinary hospital-pharmacy patient categories? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 105 CMR 722.020 definitions Hospital Inpatient and Hospital Outpatient; 105 CMR 722.090(A), Hospital Pharmacies; separate emergency/discharge 722.090(B) not invoked

options.option_text: A medication order for a patient formally admitted for overnight care in the hospital.
options.original_rationale: Correct. A formally admitted hospital inpatient is expressly within 105 CMR 722.090(A), and 722.020 defines the inpatient class.

options.option_text: An ordinary prescription for a person who visits a physician's PRIVATE office located inside the hospital building but is not registered as a hospital clinic outpatient.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under the definition in 105 CMR 722.020, an individual seen in a private physician office is NOT deemed a hospital outpatient merely because that office is physically inside the hospital.

options.option_text: A prescription for a patient formally registered in the hospital's outpatient department and currently receiving treatment at the hospital's specialty clinic.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Hospital outpatient status in 105 CMR 722.020 requires formal registration and current services at a hospital clinic. Section 722.090(A) permits hospital pharmacy prescriptions for hospital outpatients.

options.option_text: A walk-in community resident with a prescription from an independent outside practice who has no hospital patient or employee relationship.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A general community walk-in who fits none of 722.090(A)'s groups does not become a hospital patient because the facility has an in-house pharmacy; ordinary retail dispensing requires a distinct lawful route.

questions.question_stem: A licensed Massachusetts hospital pharmacist and an authorized supervising physician draft a written collaborative drug therapy management (CDTM) agreement to adjust inpatient anticoagulant therapy under approved protocols. The pharmacist has satisfied all professional CDTM eligibility requirements and the proposed agreement includes required protocol/supervision safeguards. The physician and pharmacist have both signed, but the HOSPITAL MEDICAL STAFF EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE (or its designee) has not approved the hospital program. Which assessment is BEST?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 16.03(1), hospital CDTM setting requiring medical staff executive committee or designee approval; 243 CMR 2.12(4)(a), parallel physician CDTM requirements

options.option_text: The physician's signature alone is sufficient for hospital CDTM because medical staff executive committee approval is a rule only for community pharmacies.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Hospital CDTM is a specifically listed practice setting requiring approval by the medical staff executive committee or designee in addition to otherwise compliant supervising-physician arrangements.

options.option_text: The hospital may proceed if a community pharmacy somewhere in the health system has a Board-recognized CDTM agreement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A separate community site's protocol does not substitute for the hospital-specific setting approval required by Massachusetts CDTM rules.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must instead apply the community CDTM rule requiring an adult community-patient referral to cure the missing hospital committee approval.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Community-specific patient eligibility/referral mechanics are not a replacement for the institutional practice-setting approval mechanism. The institutional agreement must meet its own rules.

options.option_text: Obtain approval by the hospital medical staff executive committee or authorized designee before operating under the hospital CDTM agreement, along with all other applicable requirements.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 16.03(1) (and parallel physician regulation) makes licensed hospital CDTM subject to approval by the medical staff executive committee or designee. The signatures and professional qualifications do not replace institutional approval.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives four SEPARATE new Schedule II prescriptions, each otherwise valid and clinically appropriate. In each case the pharmacist has verified the underlying information, has documented the proposed change with the date and pharmacist identity, and no federal law imposes a stricter special rule. The prescriber is not available for consultation. Under Massachusetts Board/DCP Joint Policy 2018-01, which actions may be taken AS STATED without contacting the prescriber? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Joint Board/Drug Control Program Policy 2018-01, Permitted Prescription Changes and Additions, §§II(A),(D), III(A)(i)(c)–(d), IV, revised through August 1, 2019; 21 CFR 1306.05

options.option_text: ADD a patient's previously omitted street address to a correctly identified patient's new Schedule II prescription, after confirming the address.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Joint Policy 2018-01 §III(A)(i)(c)(i) expressly permits adding a missing patient address without consultation; CHANGING an existing patient address is different.

options.option_text: CHANGE the named patient to a different individual after the family explains that the prescriber selected the wrong chart.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section II(A) says the patient's name cannot be changed to a DIFFERENT patient on prescriptions in Schedules II–VI; a new prescription is required, even if the explanation is credible.

options.option_text: ADD the correctly verified omitted prescriber's DEA registration number without calling the prescriber, with the change properly documented.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section III(A)(i)(d) expressly allows addition of the prescriber's DEA number without consultation; the professional must still verify the number and legality of the prescription.

options.option_text: ADD a missing prescriber signature based only on an office printout or a telephone assurance by a technician.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under Joint Policy 2018-01 §II(D), a prescriber's signature may NEVER be changed or added through the permitted-correction policy; a new valid prescription is required.

questions.question_stem: A licensed Rhode Island community pharmacy, with no Massachusetts physical premises, intends to ship only ordinary noncompounded lisinopril and amlodipine prescriptions to Massachusetts residential addresses. Its home-state pharmacy license is active, it holds any necessary Rhode Island registrations, and it does NOT compound sterile or complex nonsterile medicines. Management claims no Massachusetts registration is needed because these are not DEA-scheduled products. What is the required Massachusetts licensing approach BEFORE dispensing/shipping to those Massachusetts patients?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 6.02(4)–(6), License Requirements; 105 CMR 700.002 definition and Massachusetts Schedule VI; 2025 Massachusetts nonresident pharmacy registration requirements

options.option_text: No Massachusetts pharmacy license, because federal nonscheduled prescriptions can never be Massachusetts controlled substances.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts defines ordinary prescription drugs such as these as state Schedule VI controlled substances; MA nonresident pharmacy licensing applies regardless of their absence from federal DEA Schedules II–V.

options.option_text: Obtain the Massachusetts nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license required by 247 CMR 6.02(4); specialized sterile/complex nonsterile compounding endorsements are not needed for the stated conventional drugs.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 6.02(4) prohibits an out-of-state pharmacy from dispensing or shipping ANY Massachusetts controlled substance into the Commonwealth without a nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license. State Schedule VI is included. Specialty compounding licenses are conditional on actual compounding type.

options.option_text: Obtain a Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy license but not a nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license, because a shipping service counts as sterile preparation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The pharmacy is shipping conventional manufactured oral tablets; transporting the product does not itself constitute sterile compounding or replace the required nonresident Drug Store Pharmacy license.

options.option_text: Only register the Rhode Island pharmacy technician staff with the Massachusetts Board, then ship without licensing the pharmacy premises.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Individual technician credentials do not license the out-of-state pharmacy facility to dispense/ship Massachusetts controlled substances.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a legitimate Board request to provide continuing-education records supporting the pharmacist's recent license renewal. The pharmacist discovers a documented CE deficiency and deliberately edits a completion certificate to show credits never earned, then submits the altered certificate to the Board. No patient has yet been harmed and the pharmacist later completes additional authentic education. Under 247 CMR 10.03, which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 10.03(1)(l),(o),(p), Grounds for Discipline; 247 CMR 4.00 continuing education documentation; M.G.L. c.112 §61

options.option_text: The deliberate fabrication is an independent potential disciplinary ground for deceit/fraud and false licensure-related information; later education and lack of proven patient injury do not make it permissible.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(l) covers conduct capable of deceiving or defrauding, and §10.03(1)(p)/(o) covers false renewal information/fraudulent procurement; the Board need not first establish patient harm from a particular dispensing error.

options.option_text: The Board may act only if a patient can demonstrate financial damages caused by the forged certificate.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Board disciplinary grounds cover deceit and fraudulent license-renewal representations independent of a civil damages claim or actual patient injury.

options.option_text: A certificate is automatically accurate if the pharmacist later earns an equal number of unrelated CE credits.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Subsequent education does not retroactively make a prior false attestation or fabricated dated certificate truthful.

options.option_text: The Board must accept the certificate because it has no authority to request or review renewal/CE documentation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts CE rules require supporting records, and the Board has statutory/regulatory authority to inspect documentation and take action on dishonest license-renewal submissions.

questions.question_stem: On NOVEMBER 17, 2026, a Massachusetts pharmacy owned by a company with only 14 full-time licensed pharmacists/qualified pharmacy technicians receives a prescription-drug carton with signs of tampering and an unexpectedly altered product identifier. The pharmacist has a credible reason to believe the carton is a SUSPECT PRODUCT. Management cites FDA's August 6, 2026 small-dispenser exemption notice, extending certain electronic tracing requirements through November 27, 2027, and asks that the product be dispensed immediately. What is the best response?
questions.author_citation: FD&C Act §582(d)(4)(A)(i) (21 U.S.C. §360eee-1(d)(4)); FDA August 6, 2026 'DSCSA Exemptions from Certain Requirements ... Until November 27, 2027' (pp.1–3); FDA 2024 small-dispenser exemption remains applicable to Nov. 27, 2026

options.option_text: Dispense the carton, since FDA's DSCSA notice waives every requirement in section 582 for any pharmacy with 25 or fewer full-time pharmacy professionals.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA's August 2026 notice identifies limited specific exemptions from §582(g)(1) and certain §582(d)(4) identifier checks; it explicitly does NOT waive other section 582 duties, including the initial quarantine/investigation obligation for a suspect product.

options.option_text: Hold the carton only after FDA individually denies the pharmacy's exemption application; all smaller pharmacies must file a waiver request first.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA's published class exemption does not require individual submission; suspected-product response is a separate statutory duty and is not delayed until FDA answers a waiver application.

options.option_text: Quarantine the suspect product, investigate as required, follow applicable notification and disposition duties if it proves illegitimate, and do not treat the electronic-tracing exemption as permission to dispense it.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FD&C Act §582(d)(4)(A)(i) requires quarantining and investigating suspect product. FDA's Aug. 6, 2026 notice expressly states that its relief is limited to named requirements and does not apply to other §582 obligations. The 2024 relief still applies through Nov. 27, 2026, with the announced successor interval thereafter.

options.option_text: Ship the carton back to the wholesaler without recording the suspect-product investigation because returns are exempt from all DSCSA verification duties.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Merely returning a suspicious package without following the statutory suspect-product verification and disposition process is not justified by the exemption. A return may occur only through the lawful response process.

questions.question_stem: A federally assisted Massachusetts SUD treatment program subject to 42 CFR Part 2 begins ordinary outpatient services for a new adult patient in November 2026. The program posts its privacy notice online but has not provided it to the patient. The program wants to use its Part 2 records to send fundraising letters for the benefit of the program. The patient specifically asks NOT to receive fundraising communications. Which statements comply with current Part 2? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 42 CFR 2.22(a), (b)(1)(iii)(B), (b)(1)(iv)(G), (c)(1), (c)(3); HHS Part 2 Final Rule (compliance February 16, 2026)

options.option_text: The program must furnish its Part 2 Notice of Privacy Practices to this patient no later than the initial service delivery; merely posting it online does not satisfy the patient-specific notice obligation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 42 CFR 2.22(a),(b),(c)(1) requires a plain-language Part 2 notice by first nonemergency service delivery. Website availability is a separate duty, not a substitute for furnishing the notice.

options.option_text: The program needs a separate signed opt-IN from every patient before engaging in any fundraising under Part 2, even if patients have a clear and conspicuous chance to decline.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under 42 CFR 2.22(b)(1)(iii)(B), fundraising for the benefit of the program uses a clear, conspicuous OPT-OUT approach. This circumstance does not require universal separate opt-in consent for fundraising.

options.option_text: The program must give a clear opportunity to elect not to receive fundraising communications before using records for that purpose and must honor the patient's expressed opt-out.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Sections 2.22(b)(1)(iii)(B) and (b)(1)(iv)(G) make opt-out notice and the patient's election central to the Part 2 fundraising pathway; treatment enrollment does not revoke this right.

options.option_text: Because the patient is already receiving services, the clinic may continue fundraising letters after the opt-out so long as the mailing does not list the patient's SUD diagnosis.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The patient's express election to refuse fundraising communications remains applicable. Omitting a diagnosis does not nullify 42 CFR 2.22's right to elect not to receive them.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-self-certified Massachusetts pharmacy with trained personnel proposes an ordinary in-person OTC sale of a MULTI-DOSE pseudoephedrine package containing much more than 60 mg of pseudoephedrine base. The buyer is over 18, presents acceptable government-issued photo identification, and is under both federal quantity limits. The seller properly enters product and quantity data in an electronic CMEA logbook, but the buyer refuses to SIGN or electronically attest to the required purchaser entry. No state-specific exception applies. What should the pharmacist direct?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1314.30(a)–(d), Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act (CMEA): purchaser identification, signed logbook and 60-mg single-package exception; 21 CFR 1314.40 retailer certification

options.option_text: Complete the transaction because satisfying the gram limits replaces the buyer's signature requirement.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal weight limits and identity/logbook requirements are separate. The absence of an over-limit purchase does not eliminate the purchaser-signature obligation.

options.option_text: Have the technician sign as the purchaser, since the store has already authenticated the buyer's photo ID.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A seller may enter factual log data subject to verification, but cannot substitute the employee's signature for the purchaser's required signature or attestation.

options.option_text: Apply the single-package 60-mg logbook exception to any product sold in one box, regardless of pseudoephedrine content.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1314.30(a)'s narrow exception applies to a single SALES PACKAGE containing no more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine, not every single box. The question explicitly excludes that threshold.

options.option_text: Do not complete the sale until the purchaser supplies the required signature/attestation and the other 21 CFR 1314.30 conditions are met.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 21 CFR 1314.30(b), the purchaser generally must present acceptable photo ID and sign the written/electronic logbook. The 60-mg single-package exception does not apply to the stated multi-dose package.

questions.question_stem: A corporation operates a facility that compounds and distributes sterile drugs without having prescriptions for each identified patient. It elects FDA outsourcing-facility status under FD&C Act §503B and wants to ship these compounded preparations into Massachusetts. It is not a Massachusetts-licensed retail pharmacy and does not claim any temporary exception. The chief executive proposes the following compliance interpretations. Which are legally supported? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: FD&C Act §503B (21 U.S.C. §353b); 247 CMR 21.04 and 21.05 (Massachusetts nonresident outsourcing facility registration); FDA Information for Outsourcing Facilities, CGMP/adverse events

options.option_text: FDA §503B registration alone automatically authorizes shipment into Massachusetts without any Massachusetts outsourcing facility registration.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA §503B registration is a federal pathway; 247 CMR 21.04 separately requires a Massachusetts NONRESIDENT outsourcing facility registration when the facility is outside the Commonwealth.

options.option_text: Properly registered §503B outsourcing facilities remain subject to FDA CGMP standards and applicable FDA adverse-event/product reporting requirements.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 503B does NOT exempt compounded drugs from CGMP; FDA expressly states outsourcing facilities must report adverse events and required product information, alongside federal registration and inspections.

options.option_text: A corporation can treat any FDA-registered facility as FDA-approved, so the compounded products require no independent quality review.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FDA makes clear §503B registration is not FDA product approval or a determination of CGMP compliance. Each facility's quality/compliance requires appropriate review.

options.option_text: An out-of-state §503B facility supplying Massachusetts must satisfy the state's separate nonresident outsourcing registration pathway, including proof of valid current FDA outsourcing registration.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 21.04 and 21.05 require specific state registration and continuing current FDA status for nonresident outsourcing facilities; federal enrollment does not displace state oversight.

questions.question_stem: A Connecticut pharmacist, originally licensed there by examination and in good standing in every state where licensed, is applying to Massachusetts by reciprocity. NABP approved the preliminary transfer eight months ago; the applicant has submitted internship documentation and has passed the Massachusetts MPJE. The Massachusetts Board has not yet approved/issued the actual pharmacist license. Which statements are true? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 3.02 (2025 revision), introductory paragraphs, (1)(b)–(c), (2)(a); Massachusetts Board pharmacist license application guidance

options.option_text: The applicant may practice in a Massachusetts pharmacy as a licensed pharmacist immediately because NABP has approved the transfer.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. NABP conducts preliminary evaluation; Board-issued Massachusetts licensure, not preliminary NABP approval, is required to practice as a Massachusetts pharmacist.

options.option_text: The Massachusetts Board retains final authority to determine eligibility for pharmacist licensure by reciprocity.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 3.02(1)(b) expressly assigns final eligibility determination to the Board notwithstanding NABP's initial screening.

options.option_text: An applicant licensed by examination elsewhere must always pass NAPLEX again to use the Massachusetts reciprocity pathway.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 3.02(2)(a) for ACPE graduates requires NABP approval, appropriate internship documentation and an MPJE passing result; it does not universally require repeat NAPLEX.

options.option_text: A NABP-approved reciprocity application is valid for one year after NABP approval, and good standing in all licensing jurisdictions is required.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 3.02 opening paragraphs and (1)(c) state both the across-jurisdictions good-standing condition and one-year validity of NABP approval.

questions.question_stem: Eight months after a Massachusetts pharmacist prescribed a combined estrogen/progestin pill, a 26-year-old requests a NEW prescription for that product. A current self-screen documents newly diagnosed migraine WITH visual aura. No other contraceptive method has yet been screened and no separate emergency-supply exception is present. Under the 2026 DPH pharmacist prescribing guidelines and CDC U.S. MEC, which decision is BEST?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c94C §19F; DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125 Aug. 25, 2026; CDC U.S. MEC 2024, CHC with migraine with aura Category 4

options.option_text: Supply another 30 days of the combined pill while contacting the original clinician because previous well-tolerated use justifies a short bridge after a newly identified risk.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Migraine with aura is CDC U.S. MEC Category 4 for combined hormonal contraception. A short repeat does not remove that established contraindication.

options.option_text: Switch immediately to any progestin-only product without completing a new patient-specific screening because the aura contraindication automatically establishes another method's eligibility.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Progestin-only options do not share the same categorical aura risk, but each new method still requires its own eligibility assessment and relevant screening.

options.option_text: Decline to issue the requested combined pill, record/counsel about the new contraindication, and evaluate a guideline-appropriate alternative or arrange clinical referral.
options.original_rationale: Correct. CDC U.S. MEC Category 4 applies to combined hormonal contraceptives for migraine with aura; MA DCP 26-08-125 requires risk-based screening and appropriate response.

options.option_text: Issue the same combined pill with instructions to stop if another episode occurs because a single report of visual aura does not satisfy the CDC contraindication.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Migraine WITH aura is Category 4; there is no requirement for another subsequent aura episode before acting on the current diagnosis.

questions.question_stem: A duly licensed Massachusetts veterinarian holding an MCSR examines a dog and sends an otherwise valid Schedule VI prescription for oral amoxicillin to a Massachusetts community pharmacy. The clinic has an established veterinarian-client-patient relationship. The software blocks dispensing because the veterinarian has neither a human-health NPI nor a federal DEA registration number. No federally controlled Schedule II–V medication is involved. Which action is legally appropriate?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §22(a) veterinary exception; 105 CMR 700.002(F); Board Best Practice Recommendations, 'Veterinary Prescriptions,' January 9, 2025, p.6

options.option_text: Confirm the veterinarian's license/MCSR and animal-patient order, then use the veterinary processing workflow; neither NPI nor DEA registration is required for this Schedule VI prescription.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The Board's January 2025 Veterinary Prescriptions recommendations specifically note that veterinarians do not have NPIs, DEA numbers are not required for Schedule VI, and MCSR is the pertinent identifier. A software field cannot add a legal prerequisite.

options.option_text: Demand an NPI because every electronically processed Massachusetts prescription must list one, including all veterinary animal orders.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. NPIs identify human health providers, not veterinarians as animal-only prescribers; the Board specifically cautions pharmacies about software configurations.

options.option_text: Demand a DEA number because Massachusetts Schedule VI is identical to the federal DEA-controlled Schedule V.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. MA Schedule VI covers ordinary prescription-only drugs not in federal Schedules I–V; this amoxicillin order requires an MCSR rather than a DEA number.

options.option_text: Rewrite the order in the dog's owner's name for treatment of the owner's own infection because a veterinarian can prescribe for an animal's immediate household.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Veterinary prescribing privileges relate to animal patients; an animal prescription cannot become a lawful human prescription for the owner.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts customer requests 60 mL of FDA-marketed promethazine hydrochloride/codeine phosphate oral solution (6.25 mg/10 mg per 5 mL), product NDC 70752-139. Its actual FDA DailyMed label says 'Rx Only' and federal 'CV'. The customer presents photo ID and offers to sign the federal nonprescription Schedule V purchase log, but NO authorized prescription has been issued. No emergency or other exception applies. What is the pharmacist's lawful response?
questions.author_citation: FDA DailyMed promethazine HCl/codeine phosphate NDC 70752-139 (Rx Only, Schedule CV); M.G.L. c94C §17(c); 21 CFR 1306.26(f); 105 CMR 700.002(E)

options.option_text: Sell the 60 mL under federal 21 CFR 1306.26 because small Schedule V quantities are automatically nonprescription after identification and logbook entry.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The exact marketed NDC is FDA Rx Only, and federal §1306.26(f) cannot override another law requiring a prescription. Massachusetts c94C §17(c) requires a valid Rx for this Schedule V product.

options.option_text: Do not dispense without a valid prescriber prescription; the FDA Rx-only labeling and Massachusetts Schedule V prescription requirement are not replaced by the customer's ID, requested quantity or log signature.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FDA DailyMed NDC 70752-139 lists Rx Only and Schedule CV. M.G.L. c94C §17(c) requires a prescription outside specific exceptions; 21 CFR 1306.26(f) does not supersede stricter state law.

options.option_text: Dispense as long as the prescriber's office confirms the customer has a cough without actually issuing a prescription, because the clinical indication is the only required authorization.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Confirming a diagnosis is not issuing a prescription. The patient must have an appropriately authorized order under Massachusetts c94C §17.

options.option_text: Reclassify the syrup as Massachusetts Schedule VI because it also contains promethazine, and apply the Schedule VI pharmacist emergency continuity supply pathway.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The codeine combination is federally Schedule V per its FDA label and Massachusetts follows the federal V classification. An additional nonnarcotic ingredient does not turn this specifically labeled C-V product into Schedule VI.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy uses DEA-approved CSOS to buy Schedule II stock from a DEA-registered wholesaler. An authorized purchaser has a current personal DEA CSOS certificate, and both parties can archive electronic orders. Which statements about lawful order execution and receipt are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1305.21(a) and 1305.22(c),(g); DEA CSOS Ordering and FAQ, current 2026

options.option_text: The authorized person's valid DEA-certificate digital signature may serve for a compliant electronic Schedule II order without an additional paper DEA Form 222.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1305.21(a) authorizes a personally signed electronic order; DEA confirms CSOS is the compliant electronic alternative to paper Form 222.

options.option_text: The PIC may lend an individual CSOS private-signing certificate to any technician whenever the pharmacist is absent.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DEA CSOS certificates are issued to specific authorized individuals and cannot be shared as a generic pharmacy credential.

options.option_text: On receipt, the purchaser records actual quantity for each item and the date received, electronically links those details to the initial order, and archives the record.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1305.22(g) requires precisely this purchaser receipt record. A signed order by itself does not establish quantities received.

options.option_text: The supplier is exempt from checking the certificate's expiration and revocation because only the purchaser is responsible for authentication.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1305.22(c) directs supplier validation of signature integrity, certificate expiry/revocation, and eligibility before fulfilling.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy received a specific 247 CMR Board waiver on November 15, 2021. The manager submitted a new waiver petition November 1, 2026, but as of November 17, 2026 the Board has NOT granted a subsequent waiver. The original fifth anniversary passed two days ago; no independent extension was granted. Which procedure is permitted today?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 14.01(5)(b)–(d), Petition for Waiver, effective Sept. 22, 2017

options.option_text: Continue under the 2021 waiver because the timely and complete renewal petition automatically preserves the earlier authorization.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 14.01(5)(b)–(d) gives no automatic renewal stay when a successive petition is filed.

options.option_text: Continue for a default 30-day administrative grace period starting on the fifth anniversary, subject only to later Board review.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The waiver expires on its fifth anniversary and §14.01(5)(d) provides no automatic 30-day grace.

options.option_text: Continue if the MOR documents that patient-safety controls are unchanged from 2021, without waiting for Board waiver approval.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A manager's safety analysis does not replace the Board's grant of a subsequent waiver.

options.option_text: Comply with the underlying 247 CMR requirement after the old waiver expired unless and until the Board grants another waiver.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 14.01(5)(d) requires following applicable regulations once a waiver expires unless the Board granted a subsequent waiver.

questions.question_stem: A Connecticut doctor with active Connecticut license and DEA registration examined the patient IN CONNECTICUT and, with legitimate medical purpose and no red flags, issued two otherwise valid electronic prescriptions four days ago for Massachusetts dispensing: alprazolam (Schedule IV federal/MA) and gabapentin (MA Schedule VI and separately MassPAT-reportable). The MA pharmacist can verify the doctor's basic licensing data but has NOT completed telephone-or-other-means verification of the out-of-state Schedule IV order. Neither prescription involves a Massachusetts telehealth encounter. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §18(c); 105 CMR 700.002(F), 700.012; Massachusetts DPH Pharmacy Reporting and Data Submission (gabapentin)

options.option_text: Gabapentin may be dispensed after ordinary legal/clinical authenticity review without the special §18(c) Schedule III–V verification step, but its MA PMP reporting duty still applies.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §18(c) requires special telephone/other verification for out-of-state Schedules III–V, not VI. Gabapentin still is a separately reportable state Schedule VI drug of concern.

options.option_text: A Connecticut practitioner must hold a Massachusetts MCSR for every otherwise eligible prescription issued in Connecticut to be dispensed in Massachusetts.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. §18(c) supplies an out-of-state prescriber pathway if authorized in the prescriber's state and appropriately DEA-registered; it is not a blanket MA-MCSR requirement.

options.option_text: The pharmacist must not dispense the out-of-state Schedule IV alprazolam until required additional verification by telephone or other means succeeds, despite the secure electronic transmission.
options.original_rationale: Correct. §18(c) expressly requires separate out-of-state verification for Schedules III–V and directs that an Rx whose verification cannot be obtained may not be filled.

options.option_text: Gabapentin is exempt from all MassPAT submissions solely because its Massachusetts designation is Schedule VI.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DPH states the opposite: pharmacies report Schedule II–V dispenses AND gabapentin, which is a special additional Schedule VI drug of concern.

questions.question_stem: A 28-year-old brings a valid prescriber-issued order for FDA-approved cabotegravir long-acting IM injection to prevent HIV. A Massachusetts pharmacist has appropriate training and CPR certification and can meet all screening, consent, documentation and product handling rules. The patient also asks the pharmacist to prescribe future injectable cabotegravir doses independently, citing pharmacists' separate authority to initiate ORAL PrEP. What is the best response under current 2026 DPH circulars?
questions.author_citation: DPH Circular DCP 26-03-124 March 11, 2026, pp.1–3 (administration/eligible cabotegravir/valid Rx); DCP 26-08-125 Aug. 25, 2026 (prescribing); Statewide Pharmacist Oral PrEP Guidelines 8-2026

options.option_text: Refuse to administer cabotegravir because pharmacists can give vaccines but never injectable HIV-prevention drugs.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DCP 26-03-124 specifically includes cabotegravir as a pharmacy-administered HIV-prevention drug for eligible adults under a valid prescription.

options.option_text: Administer the already-prescribed eligible dose if all DCP 26-03-124 safeguards are met, but do not assume the ORAL-PrEP independent prescribing guidance authorizes new pharmacist-originated injectable orders.
options.original_rationale: Correct. DCP 26-03-124 independently permits properly trained pharmacist or intern IM administration under a lawful prescription. DCP 26-08-125 and the statewide ORAL PrEP guideline are different prescribing authority; administration does not confer carte-blanche injectable prescribing.

options.option_text: Authorize all future injections because any patient's valid first prescription delegates all future prescribing authority to the administering pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A valid prescription permits the stated administration subject to the order and safeguards; it does not transfer general independent prescribing authority.

options.option_text: Replace the IM injection with an IV infusion at the patient's request, since injection route does not matter under the 2026 DPH policy.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Circular DCP 26-03-124 restricts authorized administration to prescribed subcutaneous or intramuscular routes consistent with product labeling; intravenous administration is excluded.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives requests for refills under two otherwise lawful outpatient prescriptions, each issued EIGHT MONTHS AGO with unused refills. Product X is regular XCOPRI (cenobamate) oral tablets and Product Y is regular KEPPRA (levetiracetam) oral tablets. No updated Rx, emergency authority or other exception applies. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.15 (cenobamate); 105 CMR 700.002(E),(F); 247 CMR 9.04(12)–(13); DPH Pharmacy Reporting and Data Submission; FDA Keppra Rx labeling

options.option_text: Xcopri is Massachusetts Schedule VI because all antiseizure medicines follow the same state classification; its eight-month-old Rx is usable for a year.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Cenobamate is expressly DEA Schedule V under 21 CFR 1308.15; Massachusetts adopts that Schedule V designation, which has a six-month refill expiration.

options.option_text: Xcopri is federal and MA Schedule V; its original eight-month-old Rx cannot be used for refills, and a new lawful outpatient dispensing is MassPAT-reportable.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.15 lists cenobamate; MA 105 CMR 700.002(E) adopts federal V, 247 CMR 9.04(13) limits the Rx to six months, and PMP reporting covers Schedules II–V.

options.option_text: Keppra must also be federal Schedule V because levetiracetam and cenobamate both treat seizures.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Drug indication or class does not determine DEA schedule. Levetiracetam is not DEA-scheduled; as a prescription drug it is Massachusetts Schedule VI.

options.option_text: Keppra is federal nonscheduled and MA Schedule VI; its unchanged eight-month-old Rx can be refilled under the one-year rule when other conditions are met, and it is not routinely reported to MassPAT.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 105 CMR 700.002(F) places unscheduled Rx levetiracetam in MA VI, and 247 CMR 9.04(12) allows one year. DPH additionally reports gabapentin, not ordinary levetiracetam, among Schedule VI drugs.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy receives a FINAL viable-air report showing 18 CFU recovered at its ISO Class 5 primary engineering control. Some CSPs prepared there have already been dispensed and are WITHIN their assigned BUDs; another separate ISO 5 PEC has acceptable results. No remediation has been completed. What is the best response under Board Policy 2026-03?
questions.author_citation: Board Policy 2026-03 adopted Sept. 3, 2026, §§II,III(C),V; USP <797>; 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Stop affected routine compounding, promptly investigate, notify the Board within one business day of report receipt, consult a microbiologist, recall the within-BUD CSPs, contact prescribers and monitor for adverse events; make risk-based decisions about the unaffected PEC.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2026-03 §§II,III(C),V mandates reporting in one business day; ISO5 >15 CFU is significant loss of control with microbiologist, recall, prescriber contact and surveillance requirements.

options.option_text: Report the result, but continue Category 1 CSPs in the contaminated PEC with their shorter BUDs while a single repeat sample is pending.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A significant loss of ISO5 control invokes stricter policy response; simply shortening BUD does not permit unrestricted routine compounding in an affected PEC.

options.option_text: Quarantine undistributed CSPs but delay recall of already-dispensed within-BUD CSPs until a second sample establishes persistence of the 18-CFU excursion.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The finalized report exceeds the >15 CFU significant loss criterion; the policy requires a within-BUD CSP recall rather than awaiting another positive sample.

options.option_text: Notify the Board within one business day measured from SAMPLE COLLECTION and recall only expired CSPs that were prepared before that sample.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The Board notification clock starts when the microbiology report is RECEIVED; required recall concerns CSPs still WITHIN their BUDs.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy repeatedly receives a valid antiseizure prescription, but the patient's insurer requires prior authorization (PA). Staff know that the patient risks an interruption of essential treatment. They tell the patient only that there is an 'insurance problem' and do not inform the prescriber that a PA is required. Based on the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court's pharmacy-negligence decisions, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Correa v. Schoeck, 479 Mass. 686, 694–702 (2018); Cottam v. CVS Pharmacy, 436 Mass. 316, 319–326 (2002); distinguish 247 CMR 10.03 Board discipline

options.option_text: The pharmacy must guarantee approval of the insurance authorization and keep contacting the prescriber until the prescriber confirms receiving every message.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Correa expressly rejected an open-ended duty to ensure that the physician received and acted on a PA request; the duty is to take reasonable notification steps, not to guarantee insurer coverage or prescriber response.

options.option_text: A pharmacy may owe a limited duty to take reasonable steps to notify BOTH the patient and prescriber that prior authorization is needed.
options.original_rationale: Correct. In Correa v. Schoeck, 479 Mass. 686 (2018), the SJC recognized a limited duty to take reasonable steps to notify the patient and prescribing clinician of a PA barrier at each attempted fill; no universal duty to obtain the insurer's approval was imposed.

options.option_text: Once an insurer rejects a claim, Massachusetts law categorically eliminates any pharmacy duty to communicate the reason to a patient or prescriber.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The specific PA communication duty recognized in Correa is a counterexample. A payment rejection is not an automatic blanket exemption from reasonable patient/prescriber notice, particularly where a serious treatment gap is known.

options.option_text: A civil negligence duty does not require a prior formal Board disciplinary order; proving civil liability still requires the applicable elements, including breach, causation, and injury.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Civil negligence and professional license discipline are separate processes. The SJC's limited duty analysis does not depend on a Board conviction, but proving duty alone does not establish compensable negligence without breach and injury caused by it.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is covered by Section 1557 because it receives qualifying HHS financial assistance. A patient who has limited English proficiency accepts counseling for a new medicine but cannot understand the pharmacist's English explanation. The pharmacy has immediate access to a qualified remote interpreter. What should it do?
questions.author_citation: 45 CFR 92.201(a)–(c) (meaningful access; qualified language assistance); 45 CFR 164.506(c) (HIPAA TPO); HHS OCR Section 1557 language-access guidance

options.option_text: Provide qualified interpretation at no charge, counsel in a language the patient understands, and protect confidentiality throughout.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 45 CFR 92.201 requires meaningful, timely, accurate, no-cost language assistance in covered health programs. An appropriate qualified interpreter can facilitate counseling while protecting confidentiality; HIPAA generally permits provider use of interpreters for treatment or health care operations.

options.option_text: Ask the patient's 12-year-old child to interpret as the default because a family member is always the preferred source of medical interpretation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 1557's language-access protections generally prohibit reliance on accompanying minors for interpreting except narrowly defined exigent circumstances; convenience and assumed fluency do not establish qualified medical interpretation.

options.option_text: Require the patient to pay for the remote interpreter before any counseling because the drug itself is covered by insurance.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 1557's required language assistance must be free of charge to the individual with limited English proficiency. Drug insurance coverage does not transfer this accessibility cost to the patient.

options.option_text: Have any bilingual cashier translate clinical directions without checking competence or confidentiality, because fluent conversation automatically qualifies that employee as a medical interpreter.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Qualified interpretation requires accuracy, impartiality, relevant terminology and privacy safeguards. Being conversationally bilingual is not a categorical substitute for qualified healthcare interpretation.

questions.question_stem: A DEA-registered physician sends a Schedule II oxycodone 'prescription' to a retail pharmacy listing the clinic as the patient and requesting 80 tablets for a shared cabinet. The physician intends to dispense doses later to whichever patients need them. No individual patient is named. What is the pharmacist's best response?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1306.04(a)–(b) (legitimate medical purpose; prohibition on Rx for office stock); 21 CFR 1306.05(a) (patient information); 21 CFR Part 1305 for qualifying Schedule II registrant orders

options.option_text: Fill the order as a normal outpatient prescription because the physician has a DEA registration and will document each future patient later.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A practitioner's valid DEA registration does not turn general office inventory into a patient-specific prescription. 21 CFR 1306.04(b) explicitly prohibits using an individual-practitioner prescription to obtain stock for future general dispensing.

options.option_text: Enter the doctor's own name as the patient and dispense, provided the doctor initials the pharmacy's stock log.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Relabeling the clinic's planned office stock as a personal prescription would not create a legitimate patient-specific order. Documented intent still remains supply for general office dispensing.

options.option_text: Dispense it if the practice promises to provide patient names at month's end, because retrospective patient assignment satisfies 21 CFR 1306.05.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A prescription must be legitimate at issuance and bear required patient information; a month-end accounting cannot retroactively convert a general stock replenishment into lawful patient-specific prescribing.

options.option_text: Do not fill it as a patient prescription. The clinic must acquire general stock through a lawful registrant ordering process.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1306.04(b) prohibits an individual practitioner issuing a controlled prescription to supply general dispensing stock. If the practitioner may lawfully acquire stock, that requires appropriate registrant purchasing or transfer processes rather than a disguised retail prescription.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacy dispenses (X) sublingual nitroglycerin tablets, (Y) a cyclic oral contraceptive in the manufacturer's mnemonic dispenser, and (Z) ordinary oral antibiotic tablets. The patient and prescribers have requested no conventional-container waiver. Which description follows the federal PPPA prescription-drug packaging provisions?
questions.author_citation: 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10)(i),(iv) (special-packaging exemptions); 16 CFR 1701.1 and PPPA consumer/prescriber conventional-packaging requests; CPSC Healthcare Professional Guide (2023)

options.option_text: All three products universally require child-resistant packaging because every drug taken by mouth is included with no exceptions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10) expressly excepts specified products, including sublingual nitroglycerin and qualifying cyclic hormonal contraceptives in manufacturer mnemonic dispensers.

options.option_text: X and the qualifying Y are listed exemptions; Z ordinarily needs compliant special packaging unless a separate valid exception or consumer/prescriber request applies.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 1700.14(a)(10)(i) exempts sublingual nitroglycerin; (iv) exempts certain cyclically administered contraceptives in manufacturers' mnemonic packages. An otherwise covered ordinary oral antibiotic remains subject to special-packaging requirements absent a valid exception.

options.option_text: Every package of any hormonal contraceptive is exempt, including loose tablets moved into an ordinary pharmacy vial regardless of the container.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The cited cyclic contraceptive exception is tied to a qualifying manufacturer's mnemonic dispenser and specified hormone activity; it does not convert all repackaged contraceptive tablets into a blanket exemption.

options.option_text: A pharmacist may choose non-child-resistant packaging for Z based solely on convenience without an applicable statutory exemption or any patient/prescriber request.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The pharmacist cannot unilaterally replace PPPA-compliant packaging simply for convenience. A qualifying request or specific product-based exception is needed under the PPPA.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts DEA-registered pharmacy is being acquired by a different legal owner, which will operate under its own appropriate DEA authority. The outgoing registrant will discontinue its controlled-substance business by transferring remaining stock, including Schedule II medications, to the buyer. No DEA Special Agent in Charge waiver of advance notice applies. Which steps meet 21 CFR 1301.52? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1301.52(a)–(b),(d)(1)–(2); 21 CFR 1304.11 (inventory); 21 CFR Part 1305 (Schedule II orders); 247 CMR 6.11 (separate MA pharmacy ownership process)

options.option_text: Send the required transfer information to the DEA Special Agent in Charge at least 14 days before the proposed controlled-stock business transfer, absent an individual waiver.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 21 CFR 1301.52(d), a registrant discontinuing controlled business by transferring stock to another person generally submits prescribed information to the local Special Agent in Charge at least 14 days in advance unless this period is waived.

options.option_text: Skip the transfer-date inventory because the seller's annual accounting statement already lists the acquisition price of all narcotics.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A financial asset valuation does not replace the mandatory complete controlled-substance inventory required at the transfer, nor does it satisfy the required registrant records.

options.option_text: Take a complete inventory on the transfer date serving as the seller's final and buyer's initial inventory, preserve copies for both parties, and use DEA Form 222 or authorized electronic ordering for Schedule II transfers.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 1301.52(d)(1)-(2) uses the on-transfer inventory for both registrants and directs Schedule I–II transfers to Part 1305 order forms, in addition to transferring the required controlled-substance records.

options.option_text: Continue indefinitely using the seller's DEA registration at the new entity solely because the pharmacy name and Manager of Record did not change.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under §1301.52(a)-(b), DEA registration does not automatically transfer to a different legal registrant. DEA authority must independently support the acquiring registrant's operations; name or MOR continuity is not a substitute.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts licensed, nationally certified pharmacy technician completed the full initial vaccine-administration training and on-the-job skills assessment in 2023. The technician has current CPR certification and remains otherwise qualified, but completed NO immunization-related CE or updated training in the last three years. The pharmacy plans to assign vaccines tomorrow. What requirement must be addressed first under revised Board Policy 2023-02?
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts Board Policy 2023-02, revised September 4, 2025, §III(D)(1)–(5): initial qualifications and two-hour immunization CE/updated training every two years

options.option_text: Repeat an entire new 1,500-hour pharmacy technician trainee experience because immunization authorization always expires after two years.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Policy 2023-02 establishes a biennial immunization education/update requirement, not an automatic reset of the technician licensure/training-employment pathway after two years.

options.option_text: No additional training is necessary while national certification and CPR remain active, because vaccine training is permanently valid once completed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. National technician certification and CPR are separate prerequisites. The policy expressly adds periodic immunization-specific education or updated training regardless of those other credentials.

options.option_text: Complete at least two hours of immunization-related continuing education or updated training during the required two-year cycle as a vaccinator.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Revised Policy 2023-02, §III(D)(5), requires at least two hours of immunization-related continuing education or updated training every two years. The prior initial six-hour program and two on-the-job hours do not substitute for maintaining this ongoing requirement.

options.option_text: A supervising pharmacist may waive the biennial education entirely by reviewing the technician's last five administered vaccines.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Supervising-pharmacist clinical oversight does not create an exception to the Board's specified two-hours-every-two-years requirement. Reviewing past injections alone is not the stated education or updated training.

questions.question_stem: A community pharmacist's current CDTM agreement includes protocols for hypertension and diabetes. One adult patient has signed informed consent, but the supervising physician's written patient-specific referral identifies HYPERTENSION only and no diabetes comorbidity. The patient asks the pharmacist to start diabetes drug therapy under the existing agreement. Which statements follow 247 CMR 16.03–16.04? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)(1)–(4),(d),(e)(1)(b)(ix),(e)(3)–(4); 247 CMR 16.04(1) (patient-specific referral/consent and community CDTM prescriptive limits)

options.option_text: The supervising physician should include the patient's diabetes diagnosis in a valid written referral or subsequent referral before CDTM management of that added condition.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)(2), the supervising physician must specify each primary and secondary diagnosis in the written patient referral or a subsequent referral. Community-CDTM prescribing for comorbidities additionally must be authorized in the patient referral.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may start any diabetes drug listed in the general CDTM protocol solely because that disease appears in the agreement, even though it is absent from this patient's referral.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The community pathway requires the physician's individual referral to specify the patient's primary and secondary diagnoses; a broad agreement listing diabetes does not automatically make the patient referred for that condition.

options.option_text: A new individual referral automatically permits the community pharmacist to initiate a Schedule III controlled medication whenever the physician agrees orally.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The patient-specific referral cannot extend community CDTM prescribing beyond the authorized Schedule VI scope under 247 CMR 16.03(5), even when a physician is aware of the new condition.

options.option_text: The physician must obtain and record written informed consent for this collaboration, provide the patient a copy, and maintain the original consent while supplying the pharmacist a copy as required.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Sections 16.03(5)(c)-(d) and 16.04(1) require patient-specific written informed consent and defined distribution/record custody. The physician retains the original and transmits a copy to the pharmacist within 24 hours.

questions.question_stem: A manufacturer proposes sending sealed 'Drug Sample — Not for Resale' packages by courier to a hospital pharmacy at the signed WRITTEN request of a physician licensed to prescribe the drug. The manufacturer verifies the physician's authority before shipment; a hospital recipient signs the required receipt, and the samples will be provided only under lawful practitioner sample procedures. Which assessment is most accurate?
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 203.30(a)(1)–(4),(b)–(c), 203.31(a) (PDMA drug sample requests and receipts); 247 CMR 9.01(6) (sample resale/compounding/repackaging restriction)

options.option_text: This hospital-practitioner sample route can be lawful, but the samples may not then become ordinary retail saleable stock or be used for pharmacy repackaging/compounding resale.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Federal PDMA rules recognize the licensed-practitioner request and hospital-pharmacy recipient with documented receipt. Massachusetts 247 CMR 9.01(6) separately prohibits pharmacies accepting/purchasing samples for compounding, repacking, or reselling them.

options.option_text: The manufacturer must refuse because all shipment of drug samples to any pharmacy is forbidden, even when a physician has submitted the specific request allowed by federal law.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 CFR 203.30–203.31 expressly permit qualifying manufacturer or authorized-distributor shipments to a hospital or other healthcare-entity pharmacy at a licensed practitioner's written request when verification, delivery receipt and other rules are met.

options.option_text: A hospital recipient can sell the samples to outpatients at full retail price as soon as the receipt is signed because the receipt converts the inventory to commercial product.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The signed receipt provides required traceability and confirmation of sample delivery; it does not authorize selling products marked as drug samples not for resale.

options.option_text: Only a verbal promise by the physician is needed, and the supplier need not verify prescribing licensure or obtain a documented delivery receipt.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 CFR 203.30(a) imposes an advance signed written request, verification of the requester's prescriptive authority, and a written recipient receipt returned to the manufacturer or distributor, among other requirements.

questions.question_stem: A patient requests transfer of an UNFILLED electronic Schedule II prescription from Massachusetts retail Pharmacy A to another registered Massachusetts retail Pharmacy B. Both systems can transfer the original EPCS without altering any content. Pharmacy A instead proposes to print a PDF, email it to B's technician, and delete the old electronic record. Which procedure complies with Massachusetts Policy 2023-10 and 21 CFR 1306.08?
questions.author_citation: MA Board Policy 2023-10 I–II (Unfilled Prescriptions); 21 CFR 1306.08(e)–(h) (initial-fill EPCS transfer, documentation, retention); 247 CMR 9.14

options.option_text: A may send the printed PDF to a technician at B because the transfer remains electronically documented in an email attachment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal 21 CFR 1306.08(f)(1) requires an EPCS initial-fill transfer to stay in electronic prescription form; a PDF, email document or fax intermediary is not lawful conversion of that electronic prescription.

options.option_text: The certified technician at A can conduct the entire Schedule II transfer without pharmacist involvement when the pharmacies share a cloud platform.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 1306.08(f)(3) requires communication directly between TWO licensed pharmacists for the controlled initial-fill transfer. Massachusetts technician authority for Schedule VI transfers does not extend to Schedule II EPCS.

options.option_text: A may delete the transmitting pharmacy's EPCS record after sending it once because DEA requires the receiving pharmacy alone to retain proof of the transfer.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1306.08(f)(4)-(h) requires specified annotations at both transferring and receiving pharmacies and retention of electronic transfer records by both for two years.

options.option_text: Transfer the intact electronic prescription directly between pharmacists and preserve the required transfer records at both sites.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Massachusetts Policy 2023-10 adopts 21 CFR 1306.08(e)-(h) for unfilled Schedule II–V EPCS. The electronic prescription stays intact, both pharmacists communicate directly, required dates/DEA IDs/names are annotated and retained at both pharmacies.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy had an above-action-level VIABLE AIR result in its ISO 7 buffer room. It notified the Board and performed an RCA, appropriate remediation, CAPA and risk assessment; no nonviable particle excursion or additional Board restriction exists. The pharmacy now wants to return to ordinary beyond-use dates. Under Board Policy 2026-03, which actions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: MA Board Policy 2026-03 §IV(A)–(C), especially IV(B)(1)–(3), Environmental Monitoring action level response (adopted September 3, 2026); USP <797> applicable EM standards

options.option_text: Immediately restore ordinary Category 2 BUDs after completing a deep clean, without microbiology results, because the original excursion was viable rather than nonviable.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Under §IV(B)(2), restoration of standard BUDs depends on repeat EM falling below action levels; deep cleaning alone, particularly a sample collected immediately after cleaning, is not accepted proof of sustained control.

options.option_text: Perform repeat environmental monitoring based on the affected ISO-classified area and action-level type; re-sample ALL sampling locations in the affected ISO area at the same time.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2026-03 §IV(B)(1) permits repeat EM focused on the affected classified area/type as supported by the monitoring plan, but requires all sampling locations within that affected area to be re-sampled simultaneously.

options.option_text: If proper remediation has occurred and repeat EM is below the policy's action levels, the pharmacy may resume its standard BUDs or compounding, as otherwise permitted.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy §IV(B)(2) expressly allows restoration of standard BUDs or resumption of compounding when repeat EM is below action levels, subject to compliance with otherwise applicable sterile standards.

options.option_text: If repeat EM still exceeds the action level, it is sufficient to record a numerical improvement and ignore the Board's response and remediation requirements.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section IV(B)(3) sends repeated action-level results back to §III response duties. A smaller but still above-threshold CFU reading is not clearance and cannot automatically support normal BUDs.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist earned three hours of qualifying non-ACPE professional education 18 months ago. Those credits do NOT appear in NABP CPE Monitor, and the Board requests proof during a random CE audit. The pharmacist has only a calendar entry showing the seminar title. Which action best addresses 247 CMR 4.06 and Board Policy 2021-04?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 4.06(1)–(2) (CE completion records retained at least two years and provided on audit); Board Policy 2021-04 §I (most recent two full calendar years; non-ACPE certificate details)

options.option_text: Tell the Board that CPE Monitor is the only acceptable record and therefore the missing non-ACPE credit cannot be checked.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Board Policy 2021-04 recognizes certain non-ACPE credits but requires the pharmacist to retain sufficient completion documentation when the education does not appear in CPE Monitor; the Board may request those records.

options.option_text: Provide the Board the required provider, participant, program, completion-date and credit-hour evidence retained from the CE activity.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 4.06(1)-(2) requires documentation or statements of credit containing the specified identifying details, maintained at least two years from completion and submitted on Board request/random audit. Policy 2021-04 further describes evidence expected for non-ACPE activity.

options.option_text: Submit the personal calendar entry alone because a pharmacist's own note is automatically equivalent to a statement of completed contact hours.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An unauthenticated calendar entry showing only a seminar title does not demonstrate successful completion or identify all required provider, participant, activity, date and credit details.

options.option_text: Refuse the audit request until the next license renewal because the Board may verify CE only at the end of a biennial renewal period.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 4.06(2) expressly permits random audits and Board requests for documentation independent of the moment of renewal.

questions.question_stem: A federally assisted Part 2 treatment program received a patient's valid written consent using a GENERAL designation for disclosures through a named intermediary. The patient now sends that intermediary a WRITTEN request for a list of recipients of identifying records disclosed under that designation in the preceding three years. Which statements accurately describe 42 CFR 2.24? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 42 CFR 2.24(a)–(b) (specific intermediary's 30-day response and 3-year request); contrast 42 CFR 2.25 and HHS 2024 Part 2 final-rule fact sheet (accounting compliance-date caveat)

options.option_text: The intermediary may refuse to identify recipient organizations because the patient previously consented to disclosures through a general designation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The list requirement specifically protects patients who used general-designation consents; prior consent does not waive their ability to learn who received information under that designation.

options.option_text: The intermediary must respond to the patient's qualifying written request within 30 days of receipt.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under 42 CFR 2.24(b)(1), an intermediary named on the general-designation consent must respond in 30 or fewer days after receiving the qualifying written request.

options.option_text: This intermediary list automatically establishes an unrestricted, immediately effective right to a full accounting of every HIPAA treatment disclosure through any technology, regardless of applicable HHS compliance-date limits.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The narrow §2.24 intermediary list is not the broader §2.25 electronic-health-record accounting right. HHS has stated that the §2.25 accounting compliance date depends on the separate HIPAA accounting rule update; the two rights should not be conflated.

options.option_text: For disclosures within the permitted three-year lookback, the list must identify the entities receiving information, disclosure date, and a brief description of the patient-identifying information disclosed.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 2.24(a) limits the written request to the previous three years and §2.24(b)(2) specifies recipient entity name(s), date and a brief description of identifying information.

questions.question_stem: A Lenalidomide REMS-certified pharmacy has a valid new lenalidomide prescription from a certified prescriber for an appropriately enrolled patient. All risk-category and pregnancy-test obligations have been met. The pharmacy obtained the required REMS CONFIRMATION number 26 hours ago but has not yet handed over or shipped the drug. The confirmation was not renewed. What must it do?
questions.author_citation: FDA-approved Lenalidomide REMS Pharmacy Guide, steps 3–4: valid 24-hour pharmacy confirmation, cancellation/reissue when expired, Medication Guide; 247 CMR 9.01(21) (comply with product REMS)

options.option_text: Do not dispense; cancel the expired confirmation number and obtain a new valid REMS confirmation before dispensing, with required counseling.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The active Lenalidomide REMS pharmacy procedures state that a confirmation number is valid for only 24 hours. When it has expired, the pharmacy must cancel the old number and obtain a new one before dispensing while complying with the remaining REMS safeguards.

options.option_text: Dispense immediately because once a confirmation number is issued it remains valid until the prescriber writes the next prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The Lenalidomide REMS Pharmacy Guide limits a pharmacy confirmation number's validity to 24 hours. A confirmation obtained 26 hours earlier is no longer sufficient for dispensing.

options.option_text: Convert the order into an ordinary Schedule VI prescription with automatic refills because enrollment in the REMS makes subsequent confirmation optional.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A REMS is a distribution/safe-use restriction, not a controlled-schedule exception. Lenalidomide REMS independently requires confirmation before each dispensing and does not allow ordinary automatic refills.

options.option_text: Send the medication without the Medication Guide if the prescriber countersigns the expired number, because pharmacist certification alone satisfies the REMS.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A prescriber countersignature cannot extend the 24-hour program confirmation; pharmacist certification also does not cancel the Medication Guide and patient-counseling requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts Drug Store Pharmacy receives a brand-name tablet prescription without 'no substitution' and lawfully dispenses a LOWER-COST interchangeable generic manufactured by Company Z. The pharmacist accurately applies all routine label elements. Which additional interchange labeling follows 247 CMR 9.05(3)?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a)–(e), generic/brand interchange container label and abbreviations; M.G.L. c.112 §12D (interchange authority)

options.option_text: The label needs only the originally prescribed brand name; the identity of the actual lower-cost generic manufacturer is confidential commercial information.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.05(3)(a) specifically requires the label to identify the actual generic product and its manufacturer in an interchange statement; showing only the prescribed brand would not communicate what was dispensed.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may label the generic as if it were the brand when both are therapeutically equivalent, with no interchange statement if the price is lower.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Therapeutic interchangeability authorizes selection under applicable circumstances but does not waive the separate container labeling obligation in §9.05(3).

options.option_text: Label the product 'Interchange' or 'IC' with the actual generic name and Company Z on the container label; the originally prescribed brand may also be shown.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.05(3)(a),(c)-(d) requires the 'Interchange' generic name/manufacturer presentation for a less expensive dispensed generic and permits recognized abbreviations, e.g. 'IC', plus an optional 'for [prescribed brand]' notation.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must print the manufacturer's complete legal corporate name in full and is never permitted to abbreviate 'interchange' or the manufacturer's name.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.05(3)(d) expressly allows commonly understood abbreviations, including 'IC' and recognized abbreviations for manufacturer names.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts hospital moves bulk Schedule II–V controlled drugs from its pharmacy to an authorized nursing-unit medication cart. Its procedures are being evaluated against the Massachusetts DPH 'General accountability guidelines for controlled substances in hospitals and clinics with pharmacies.' Which measures comply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Massachusetts DPH General Accountability Guidelines for Controlled Substances in Hospitals and Clinics with Pharmacies, Nursing Units—General and Schedule II–V; 105 CMR 700.005 (security and accountability); 247 CMR 9.12 (separate institutional ADD)

options.option_text: Use a double-locked, permanently affixed cabinet or medication cart for nursing-unit Schedule II–V stock, with hard-copy or electronic perpetual inventory.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Massachusetts DPH's nursing-unit accountability guidance states that Schedule II–V controlled drugs must be in a double-locked, permanently affixed unit/cart with perpetual inventory records.

options.option_text: Permit any unlicensed visitor to access the cart if the nurse on duty says the visitor is trustworthy and the medication orders are patient-specific.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The DPH guidance restricts controlled-substance access to licensed, authorized staff; familiarity or visitor trust does not replace controlled inventory security.

options.option_text: Have unused Schedule II–V portions wasted under the facility's controlled procedures by two licensed staff with co-signed documentation, unless more restrictive hospital policy applies.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The state DPH accountability guidance specifies two licensed staff and co-signature for disposal of unused Schedule II–V portions, subject to stricter facility policy.
