options.option_text: Skip documented nursing/pharmacy management accountability reviews once the cart has a software audit log, because electronic data eliminates ongoing diversion monitoring.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DPH calls for a documented quality-assurance review of controlled substances administered on nursing units not less than once weekly; an access log does not replace the management review.

questions.question_stem: A pharmacist graduates from an approved PharmD program in May 2026 and obtains an active Massachusetts pharmacist license that August. They are not participating in vaccination, compounding, or CDTM activities requiring additional specialty CE. For the 2026 and 2027 calendar years, which statement correctly applies 247 CMR 4.03?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 4.03(4),(5),(8) (annual CE, no carryover and graduation-year exception); Massachusetts Board Policy 2021-04 general compliance (revised Sep. 4, 2025)

options.option_text: They must complete 20 CE contact hours by December 31, 2026 because the exemption applies only to students who have not received a license.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 4.03(8) expressly exempts a registrant from continuing education in the calendar year the registrant graduated from an approved pharmacy school; obtaining licensure that same year does not remove the exemption.

options.option_text: Their first required CE calendar year is 2028, because every new pharmacist receives a two-year grace period after the first Massachusetts license.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The regulatory exception is tied to the specific calendar year of graduation. It is not a two-year rolling extension of the annual CE requirement into 2027.

options.option_text: The pharmacist is CE-exempt for graduation year 2026; normal yearly requirements resume in 2027 without carryover.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 4.03(8) exempts the pharmacist from CE in the 2026 graduation calendar year. Section 4.03(4)-(5) imposes yearly CE requirements afterward and disallows carrying prior-year contact hours into the next calendar year. Other practice-specific CE would be analyzed separately if relevant.

options.option_text: The pharmacist may complete 40 contact hours in 2026 and carry them forward to satisfy both 2026 and 2027 continuing education obligations.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 4.03(5) expressly disallows carrying contact hours between calendar years. Extra activity during an exempt graduation year does not prepay a later calendar year's requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy offers routine adult influenza, recombinant zoster, and COVID-19 immunizations under otherwise valid standing orders. The pharmacist has current access to the Massachusetts Immunization Information System (MIIS), and the patients have no separate exemption. Under Board Policy 2023-02 revised 2025, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: Board Policy 2023-02 §§IV(E)–(G), revised September 4, 2025; 105 CMR 222.100(A) (MIIS immunization reporting)

options.option_text: The same policy mandates MIIS review before each COVID-19 dose and gives no other way to verify prior vaccine formulation or dates.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section IV(F) RECOMMENDS checking earlier COVID-19 vaccine formulation and dates and recognizes MIIS, pharmacy/EHR records or the vaccination card; that is not the identical mandatory pre-lookup rule used for zoster.

options.option_text: Because influenza is excepted from pre-administration MIIS review, any influenza vaccine given at this pharmacy may be omitted entirely from MIIS reporting.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section IV(G) requires pharmacy personnel to report administered vaccination information to MIIS, and 105 CMR 222.100 generally imposes a 72-hour reporting duty. A lookup exception is not a reporting waiver.

options.option_text: The policy excludes INFLUENZA vaccination from its general mandatory pre-administration MIIS lookup requirement.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy 2023-02 §IV(E) requires reviewing MIIS before vaccines OTHER THAN influenza or COVID-19. The exemption is to that particular pre-administration lookup, not to the separate vaccine-record reporting requirements.

options.option_text: For a routine recombinant ZOSTER vaccine, the pharmacy must check MIIS before administration to make sure the requested vaccination was not already administered by another provider.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The zoster vaccine is not one of the influenza/COVID-19 exceptions listed in §IV(E); the pharmacy must review MIIS in advance under the Board's vaccination policy.

questions.question_stem: A federally assisted substance-use-disorder treatment program subject to 42 CFR Part 2 discovers and confirms a BREACH of unsecured Part 2 patient records affecting 120 individuals. No low-probability-of-compromise finding or other exception applies. Under the Part 2 breach rule in force during November 2026, which notification plan is most accurate?
questions.author_citation: 42 CFR 2.16(b) (Part 2 unsecured-record breach adopts HIPAA Breach Rule); 45 CFR 164.404(b) (individual notices), 164.408(c) (under-500 Secretary annual report); HHS OCR Part 2 breach guidance (compliance February 16, 2026)

options.option_text: Because fewer than 500 individuals are affected, Part 2 requires neither patient notices nor reporting to HHS.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The HIPAA-equivalent breach rules apply to Part 2 records. The 500-person threshold changes some Secretary/media notification timing, but does not eliminate the obligation to notify affected patients of an actual breach.

options.option_text: Give the notice only to the facility's qualified service organization because any Part 2 breach notice to patients would itself violate Part 2 confidentiality rules.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Part 2's confidentiality protections do not prohibit the specific notifications required by §2.16(b). An appropriately handled qualified service organization does not replace individual breach notices.

options.option_text: Report to the Massachusetts Board of Pharmacy within seven business days and omit HHS notification, because Part 2 programs are not HIPAA covered entities.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Part 2 independently establishes breach notification obligations even for programs not otherwise HIPAA covered; a Board pharmacy-reporting clock does not replace Part 2's HHS/individual notifications.

options.option_text: Notify patients without unreasonable delay, within 60 days, and report the under-500 breach to HHS within 60 days after year-end.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 42 CFR 2.16(b) applies HIPAA Breach Notification Rule requirements. 45 CFR 164.404 requires individual notification without unreasonable delay and within 60 calendar days, while §164.408(c) permits the annual HHS report for breaches affecting fewer than 500 people within 60 days after the end of the calendar year.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy wants to activate automatic monthly refills for a patient's valid Schedule VI maintenance prescription. The patient has authorized refills on file but has NEVER agreed to enroll in auto-refill. The patient later says they do not want automated fills. Which workflow follows 247 CMR 9.19(13)?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.19(13) (patient/agent recorded consent before auto-refill enrollment; discontinuation method); 247 CMR 9.04(12) (separate Schedule VI prescription validity)

options.option_text: Obtain and record the patient's or agent's consent BEFORE enrollment and give the patient a way to discontinue participation; authorized refills alone do not waive either requirement.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.19(13) requires prior recorded patient/agent consent and a mechanism to end participation in an automatic refill program. Refill validity and amount remain independently governed by prescription laws.

options.option_text: Enroll the patient automatically because having refills remaining on the original prescription is legally the same as consenting to a pharmacy's automatic refill program.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Prescription refill authorization from the prescriber and patient agreement to participate in pharmacy AUTOMATION are separate matters. §9.19(13) expressly requires obtaining and recording patient/agent consent before enrollment.

options.option_text: A pharmacy may refuse to process any future ordinary refill unless the patient agrees to join its automatic refill system permanently.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.19(13) recognizes a patient's ability to stop the program. Participating in auto-refill is not an additional legal prerequisite to otherwise authorized ordinary refills.

options.option_text: Once enrolled, the pharmacy may continue automatically dispensing after the prescription expires because the original enrollment consent replaces future prescriptions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Auto-refill consent cannot extend the legal issuance/refill validity of the underlying Schedule VI prescription under 247 CMR 9.04(12).

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy offers to collect prescriptions at a nearby factory for employees and eligible family members, then deliver completed prescriptions to the factory. It uses its own identified, authorized agents and satisfies other dispensing and counseling requirements. Under 247 CMR 9.04(9), which steps are lawful or required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.04(9)(a)–(e) (collection at industrial plants/workplaces, eligible recipients, direct handoff and undistributed return)

options.option_text: Limit the service to employees or others regularly affiliated with the location and eligible immediate family members who live at the same address as those employees or affiliates.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.04(9)(a) allows this particular workplace/group-affiliation collection pathway only for persons regularly employed/affiliated or their immediate family members residing at the same address.

options.option_text: Have a pharmacist, pharmacy employee or authorized pharmacy agent personally collect prescriptions and dispense the medications DIRECTLY to each patient or the patient's agent.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Sections 9.04(9)(b)-(c) require in-person collection by an authorized pharmacy representative and direct handoff of filled medications to the patient or agent. A generic employer mailroom drop does not satisfy this narrow program.

options.option_text: Leave prescriptions not immediately collected in a locked workplace drawer overnight so that the employer can distribute them later, rather than returning them to the pharmacy.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.04(9)(c)-(d) requires direct dispensing to the patient or agent and the return of medication not directly dispensed; medications may not be left or stored at the workplace.

options.option_text: Assume the employer is solely responsible for the pharmacy's delivery agent, so the pharmacy and pharmacist have no legal accountability for that agent's conduct.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.04(9)(e) expressly holds the pharmacy and pharmacist responsible for conduct of the pharmacy employee or authorized agent acting on their behalf.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy hires a pharmacist and a pharmacy technician TRAINEE. HR checked both licenses eight months ago when the applicants were interviewed. On their first scheduled workday, the pharmacist's Massachusetts registration is active but the trainee license has expired. The MOR wants the trainee to prepare prescriptions while a renewal application is pending. What does 247 CMR 9.19(18) require?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.19(18) (current licensure verification at commencement for pharmacist, intern, technician and trainee); 247 CMR 8.03 (pharmacy technician trainee licensure and scope); 247 CMR 9.04(1) (pharmacist final validation)

options.option_text: Permit the trainee to begin preparing prescriptions because an HR check made during the interview is valid for the entire first year of employment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.19(18) makes verification of CURRENT licensure at the commencement of employment a pharmacy obligation. A historic screening months earlier does not excuse checking the worker's status on arrival.

options.option_text: Verify both workers' current Massachusetts licenses when employment commences and do not assign licensed pharmacy-technician trainee tasks to the worker whose personal license has expired.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The pharmacy must verify licensure status upon commencement for pharmacists, interns, technicians and technician trainees under §9.19(18). An expired trainee license cannot be treated as active during application processing; restrict duties until a valid credential is confirmed.

options.option_text: Only the pharmacist's registration needs verification; a technician trainee may work without Board licensure for the first 1,500 hours.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The same current-license verification duty expressly includes technician trainees. A technician's training-hour eligibility limits do not create permission to work before obtaining or renewing the requisite trainee license.

options.option_text: Allow the trainee to count controlled drugs so long as barcode scanning occurs and the pharmacist performs final validation; supervision substitutes for an active trainee credential.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Computer checks and pharmacist supervision do not cure an expired individual credential or create authority to handle prohibited controlled-substance inventory.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts patient taking a stable Schedule VI maintenance medication has an expired prescription with no remaining refills. The pharmacist has tried but cannot obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner and has assessed that continuing therapy is appropriate. Another patient asks for the same emergency authority for Schedule IV alprazolam. No other refill, emergency or waiver provision applies. Under 247 CMR 9.04(12), which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.04(12) (MA Schedule VI one-year validity and narrow 14-day/smallest-unit-of-use emergency continuity supply); compare 247 CMR 9.04(13) and 21 CFR 1306.22 for federal CIII–V

options.option_text: The Schedule VI pharmacist may automatically supply a 90-day quantity on any expired prescription solely because the patient previously used the medicine for years.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The narrowly defined 14-day or smallest-available-unit-of-use limit controls; historical adherence does not confer unlimited extension of a stale prescription.

options.option_text: For the Schedule VI patient, a pharmacist may exercise professional judgment to dispense a continuity quantity not exceeding 14 days OR the smallest available unit-of-use packaging in the stated circumstance.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Current 247 CMR 9.04(12) expressly authorizes pharmacist-judgment dispensing of up to 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use package when a Schedule VI prescription is expired or lacks refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained promptly.

options.option_text: Even though the normal one-year Schedule VI refill period has expired, the narrow continuity pathway may still apply if all its conditions are met; it is not an ordinary authorized refill.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Subsection 9.04(12) explicitly addresses expired/no-refill Schedule VI cases and grants a separate narrow dispensing pathway when timely prescriber authorization cannot be obtained. The pharmacist must still use professional judgment.

options.option_text: The same §9.04(12) authority automatically permits a pharmacist to extend any expired Schedule IV benzodiazepine prescription for 14 days.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.04(12) is written specifically for Massachusetts Schedule VI. A federally controlled Schedule IV refill is subject to its separate federal and state rules and cannot be extended merely by importing this Schedule VI exception.

questions.question_stem: A properly licensed Massachusetts veterinarian examines a dog after surgery and issues an otherwise complete patient-specific prescription for federally Schedule III buprenorphine for appropriate veterinary pain management. The veterinarian holds a Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration (MCSR) covering Schedule VI ONLY and has NO DEA registration. The pharmacy has independently verified these facts. What should it do?
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.94C §§7,18(a); 105 CMR 700.004(C)–(D) (MCSR schedule authorizations); DEA 21 CFR 1306.03–1306.05; Massachusetts DPH Veterinary Prescriptions Best Practice Recommendations (January 9, 2025)

options.option_text: Dispense the Schedule III prescription because veterinarians are exempt from federal DEA registration whenever the medication is for an animal.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Veterinarian status does not grant blanket exemption from federal controlled-substance registration for Schedule II–V prescribing. Massachusetts DPH specifically distinguishes DEA registration for Schedules II–V from Schedule VI-only MCSR authority.

options.option_text: Change the patient to the dog's owner and fill under the owner's human medical history because veterinarians may use a patient's relative to avoid controlled-registration limitations.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The patient is an animal being treated within a legitimate veterinarian-client-patient relationship. Rewriting the patient does not create DEA prescribing authority and can make the prescription fictitious.

options.option_text: Do not dispense; Schedule III veterinary prescribing needs both appropriate DEA and Massachusetts controlled-substance authority for this animal patient.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §§7,18 and 105 CMR 700.004 require appropriate registrations/schedule authorization; DEA registration is needed for federally scheduled III drugs. The same veterinarian could prescribe lawful Schedule VI-only products under the narrower Massachusetts MCSR if other conditions are met.

options.option_text: Apply the federal Schedule III five-refill allowance instead of verifying the prescriber's DEA number; remaining refills cure missing initial prescriptive authority.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Refill rules do not make an order valid when the practitioner lacks required authority for the federal controlled schedule at issuance.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy dispenses prescribed gabapentin, a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug designated for PMP reporting, to an authorized patient representative at the counter. The representative has no government-issued ID. The pharmacist has credible facts showing that refusal today would cause serious hardship for the patient and can document the reason. What does 247 CMR 9.04(14) allow?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.04(14)(a)–(d) (positive identification for Schedules II–V and 'additional drugs', documented serious-hardship alternative); 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) (gabapentin additional-drug reporting)

options.option_text: Ignore the ID requirement solely because gabapentin is federally nonscheduled; Massachusetts Schedule VI products cannot be designated additional drugs.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. DPH designated gabapentin an additional PMP-reportable drug under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1). Section 9.04(14) expressly extends positive identification to such additional drugs even though they are Massachusetts Schedule VI.

options.option_text: Document the serious hardship and get the agent's printed name, address and signature on the reverse of the prescription or pharmacy log before dispensing this additional drug.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.04(14)(b)-(c) generally requires customer positive identification for PMP additional drugs. The specific alternative permits dispensing where denial would cause serious hardship, provided the justification is documented and the ultimate user or agent writes the specified information and signs.

options.option_text: Require an ID without exception; 247 CMR 9.04(14) allows hardship alternatives for Schedule II–V drugs but explicitly excludes PMP additional drugs.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.04(14)(c) expressly covers both federal Schedule II–V products AND additional drugs in its documented serious-hardship alternative.

options.option_text: Automatically treat a photo of a neighbor's driver's license as the representative's positive identification and omit all pharmacy documentation because the drug is not DEA controlled.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Customer identification concerns the actual ultimate user or agent presenting the prescription. Someone else's ID does not satisfy the rule, and a hardship-based dispensing requires the specific signed log and documented reason.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy discovers ransomware and disables its compromised pharmacy computer system to protect patient records. The pharmacist can still obtain reliable lawful prescriptions, consult independent medication-history sources and perform a documented prospective DUR when safe, but new dispensing transactions cannot yet be entered into the normal electronic patient profiles. Under 247 CMR 9.19(22), 9.16 and 9.17, which operational responses are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.19(22)(a)–(d) (mandatory pharmacy computer downtime plan), 9.16(1),(7) (record retention/confidential profile), 9.17(1)–(2) (prospective DUR); HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR 164.308–312 separately governs covered electronic PHI

options.option_text: Follow a readily accessible written computer-downtime procedure that describes how prescriptions can be processed during downtime and how all medications dispensed will be entered into patient profiles when the system returns.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Section 9.19(22)(a)-(b) requires a downtime policy that includes a lawful filling process and later incorporation into the computerized pharmacy patient record. A breach does not eliminate the documentation/reconciliation obligation.

options.option_text: Suspend all prospective DUR for the outage because the computer system normally generates interaction alerts; any technician may then dispense without pharmacist review.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Section 9.19(22)(d) requires an appropriate DUR process during downtime, and §9.17 keeps pharmacist prospective DUR obligations in force. A computerized alert is a tool, not a substitute for pharmacist judgment.

options.option_text: Erase all original electronic prescription records after recovery and generate replacement records with new fictitious dispensing times so the breach will not appear in inspection logs.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Falsifying or deleting records to conceal the incident violates pharmacy recordkeeping duties and undermines lawful traceability. Downtime procedures call for accurate reconciliation, not fabrication or erasure.

options.option_text: Protect confidentiality and use reliable alternative procedures for reviewing relevant patient history and documenting any clinical interventions; reconcile dispensing and DUR records when the system is restored.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Sections 9.16–9.17 require confidential, retrievable patient records and appropriate prospective review. The downtime plan must preserve continuity and ensure eventual patient-profile entry, without pretending records are currently accessible if they are not.
